LLM Evaluation Fundamentals

8 lessons · 34h learner time

Translate an evaluation goal into checks, references and human review.

For New evaluators, QA engineers and developers adding a first evaluation

What you’ll build Build a small deterministic scorer and compare its results with human labels and overlap metrics.

Prerequisites and checkpoint

Required foundations are included in the lesson sequence.

Final checkpoint Score a frozen set, distinguish execution errors from wrong answers and explain a false pass and a false fail.

Open learning plan

LLM-as-a-Judge Specialist

7 lessons · 34h 30m learner time

Design and calibrate pointwise and pairwise judges on the same saved answers.

For Engineers evaluating open-ended responses or introducing a model judge

What you’ll build Produce a judge report that measures coverage, agreement, class errors and order sensitivity.

Prerequisites and checkpoint

Required foundations are included in the lesson sequence.

Final checkpoint Reproduce a swapped pair, reject an unscorable verdict and justify what the judge can reliably decide.

Open learning plan

RAG Evaluation Specialist

5 lessons · 28h learner time

Measure retrieval, source support and answer correctness separately.

For Engineers evaluating systems that retrieve documents before answering

What you’ll build Build a labeled retrieval and claim report with citation checks and a controlled comparison using known-good passages.

Prerequisites and checkpoint

Required foundations are included in the lesson sequence.

Final checkpoint Verify a ranking metric by hand, then show which stage caused a held-out failure and how to detect its return.

Open learning plan

Agent Evaluation Specialist

5 lessons · 27h learner time

Evaluate tool use, task completion, final state and recovery from saved traces.

For Engineers testing tool calls or multi-step workflows

What you’ll build Create a trace replay scorecard that accepts equivalent valid workflows and detects wrong state.

Prerequisites and checkpoint

Required foundations are included in the lesson sequence.

Final checkpoint Pass two valid traces, reject a plausible wrong-state trace and explain the recovery and cost trade-off.

Open learning plan

Production Evaluation Engineer

15 lessons · 78h learner time

Turn reproducible evaluation evidence into ongoing release and monitoring decisions.

For Engineers owning evaluation pipelines, release gates or production monitoring

What you’ll build Build a versioned gate and use synthetic traces to diagnose an incident and add a regression case.

Prerequisites and checkpoint

Required foundations are included in the lesson sequence.

Final checkpoint Replay pass, fail and insufficient-evidence outcomes. Verify the trace diagnosis and justify a rollback trigger.

Open learning plan

Learning Paths and preparation

Topic and module links in this comparison open Complete Course. Choose a path above to study in Quick Learning.

Quick Learning sequences the required topics for a specific goal. Complete Course follows the full core in order and offers elective topics separately. Both use the same topic material and completion checkpoints. A learning plan describes the intended exercises and links to the existing material where it is available.

Preparation / Getting Started

Allow 7 learner hours if all six readiness skills are new. Skip any row once you can demonstrate its checkpoint. Practice locally with synthetic files and saved responses. No model downloads or API credentials are needed. Preparation hours are separate from all path and curriculum totals.

Preparation skills
IDReadiness skillLearning objective and practiceReadiness checkpointLearner total (hrs)
P01Files, folders and the terminalNavigate a sample project with pwd, cd and a directory listing. Recognize absolute and relative paths and save into a new output file.From the project root, locate a fixture and explain where a relative output path will be written.1h
P02Basic Python for evaluationRead strings, numbers, lists and dictionaries. Use a loop, a conditional, a small function and an assertion to count outcomes.Given three saved outcomes, return the number that pass and verify an empty input.1h 30m
P03Run Python scriptsConfirm the Python version, run a local script from the right directory, pass it a file path and read standard output and a traceback.Run a supplied script and fix a deliberately mistyped input path.1h
P04JSON and JSONLRead and write JSON objects and arrays. Read a JSONL file one record at a time with Python and distinguish syntax errors from missing fields.Convert three sample cases to JSONL and identify the invalid line in a second fixture.1h 30m
P05API requests and responsesRead a saved HTTP request and response. Identify method, endpoint, headers, body, status and timeout. Keep sample credentials out of fixtures.Explain the difference between a successful request with a wrong answer and an unsuccessful request.1h
P06Numerical reasoningCalculate rates, percentages, means and percentage-point changes on a small score sheet. Identify the denominator and how an excluded row changes it.Explain why 8 of 10 scored cases and 8 of 12 attempted cases make different claims.1h

Paths A–G

Learning path estimates
PathNameTargetsTopicsLearner total (hrs)
AComplete BeginnerCore44238h
BLLM Evaluation FundamentalsTokens, messages and context windows, Offline, online and the evaluation lifecycle, Exact match, normalization and rules, Structured output and schema validation, Rubrics and a first human evaluation, Token F1, BLEU, ROUGE and reference metrics834h
CLLM-as-a-Judge SpecialistModel judges and comparative evaluation734h 30m
DRAG Evaluation SpecialistRAG system evaluation528h
EAgent Evaluation SpecialistAgent and workflow evaluation527h
FProduction Evaluation EngineerContinuous evaluation and releases, Observability, operations and review loops1578h
GComplete ExpertAll53292h 30m
  • A — Complete Beginner. Use the preparation checkpoints first, then follow the full core in curriculum order. Start at How LLM applications behave. The capstone verifies a reproducible release decision.
  • B — LLM Evaluation Fundamentals. Start with the objective and references, then learn deterministic and structured checks, human review and overlap metrics. Exit by scoring a small frozen set and explaining a false pass.
  • C — LLM-as-a-Judge Specialist. Complete the required reference, schema and rubric topics, then pointwise scoring, calibration and comparisons in Model judges and comparative evaluation. Extend with advanced judge design if needed. Embeddings and RAG can be skipped.
  • D — RAG Evaluation Specialist. Start with objectives and references, then work through RAG system evaluation. The ranked-list and claim exercises use supplied fixtures. Take embeddings or judge setup only for the extensions that require them.
  • E — Agent Evaluation Specialist. Learn JSON schema and evaluation objectives, then study Agent and workflow evaluation. The required labs use mock tools and saved traces. Study retrieval only for the document-tool extension.
  • F — Production Evaluation Engineer. Follow the minimum route to release gates and production monitoring. The route includes versioned cases, sample design and uncertainty. RAG, agent and defensive assessment topics are optional for this path unless they apply to the release under review.
  • G — Complete Expert. Complete core and the electives. Choose the preparation rows you need and add their hours if applicable.

Using the dependency roadmap

Open Learning Roadmap and select a module or topic by name or ID. The required route includes the target and every transitive mandatory topic, each counted once, in suggested study order. Selecting a module uses every topic in that module as a target. Recommended preparation adds context and may be skipped. A conditional link applies only to the exercise named beside it. Implementation readiness describes skills or tool setup you can demonstrate independently, so those notes and preparation hours sit outside the academic dependency graph. A dash means that category has no prerequisite.

Tokens, messages and context windows, Objectives, dimensions and failure taxonomy and Structured output and schema validation have no mandatory course prerequisites. Start with M01-T01 for a first look at model behavior, M02-T01 for evaluation design, or M03-T02 if you already know basic Python and JSON and want to validate structured outputs.

  • I want to learn RAG evaluation. Select RAG system evaluation or Path D. Check the reference-answer prerequisites first. For an interpretation-only refresher, select Context sufficiency, answer correctness and citations. Use the conditional notes before changing a dense encoder or adding a judge.
  • I already know Python and deterministic evaluation. Verify the preparation checkpoints and use Path B's fixture as a diagnostic. Mark familiar topics completed only when you can demonstrate their stated result. For structured data and provenance, enter at Golden schemas, provenance and versioning once its prerequisites are met.
  • I only want to learn LLM-as-a-Judge. Select Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge for pointwise scoring, or Path C to add calibration and pairwise ranking. Use optional extensions as needed.
  • I want to become a complete evaluation engineer. Use Path A through the production capstone, then choose specialization topics or Path G. A short route establishes the advertised skills for its target. Course-wide competency requires the broader assessments and capstone.

Use the module overview to orient yourself and the topic view to inspect exact links. Arrows point to the topic or module that uses the prerequisite. The unlocked list uses your saved completion status and identifies topics that would become available by completing the current target. Use Export graph to share the full module or topic diagram, or choose a target or path and export its required route. Image downloads use the full graph for that scope regardless of pan and zoom. The standalone HTML download opens on the roadmap and supports offline interaction.

In Quick Learning, use Download Learning Plan to share an offline copy that opens on the selected path. Hosted path links use fragments such as #quick-d. For a local copy, share the downloaded HTML file. A local file address only works on the machine where that file is stored. Completion marks belong to the browser and are excluded from the shared plan.

Instructor preparation

Replay the chosen lab offline and grade a good submission and a borderline one. Verify the topic's requirements, exact fixtures, code and expected outcomes before teaching. Prepare a demonstration fallback for any live extension. Pilot the preparation checkpoints and required route timings with your class before planning further sessions.

M01-T01 Tokens, messages and context windows Needs Improvement · 3h 30m
  1. Complete Course
  2. How LLM applications behave
  3. Tokens, messages and context windows

Beginner · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Explain how a language model receives text as tokens and why token counts affect capacity and cost.
  • Label the parts of a saved conversation and put the messages in the right order.
  • Calculate how much room is available for input and output in a model request.
  • Trace which evidence was kept or dropped and judge whether a reply is supported.
  • Run a small program that checks whether the information fits and whether the bank’s policy is still included. It runs without connecting to an AI service.

Why This Lesson Matters

A customer asks Harbor Leaf Bank, “What’s the minimum balance for Standard Savings?” The chat assistant says, “₹5,000.” The customer follows up, “What if I go below that?”

You know what “that” means because you just read the earlier answer. Now imagine seeing only the follow-up on a new screen. You can tell the customer wants help, but you have to guess what they’re referring to. A chat assistant faces that same gap if its app leaves the earlier exchange out.

In this lesson, you’ll follow the question from the chat screen into the information the assistant actually receives. Then you’ll try making the request shorter and see which parts you can safely leave out. By the end, you’ll be able to explain why “the assistant gave a bad answer” and “the app never sent the information it needed” point to different fixes. This is one job an evaluation engineer does. They design checks and use the results to decide where to investigate.

Harbor Leaf is a fictional bank. Its policy in this lesson says Standard Savings has a ₹5,000 minimum and a ₹100 monthly fee below that amount. The model limits, counts, and prices are made up for practice.

Plan your study session

The course sets aside 3.5 hours for the lesson. Start with the conversation and try the short checks as you read. Work through the seven Python examples when you’re ready. Use the final assignment to practice explaining your decision to someone who hasn’t seen the code.

Beginner Explanation

1. Give the assistant enough of the conversation

Look at the customer’s follow-up again. If you replace “What if I go below that?” with “What if my Standard Savings balance goes below ₹5,000?”, the question makes sense by itself. A chat app has another option. It can keep the question natural and send the earlier exchange along with it. The earlier lines are the conversation history.

A large language model, or LLM, is the part of the assistant that writes an answer using the information it receives. When you hit Send, an app like ChatGPT can assemble some earlier parts of the conversation, the new question, and other information. It sends that package to the model as a request. The answer comes back as the reply. In this lesson we call a question and its reply a turn. The chat screen and the package sent for any one turn can contain different amounts of history.

Each entry the app sends is a message. Look at “What’s the minimum balance for Standard Savings?” The words are its content. A separate label tells the model where those words came from. That label is the role. The customer’s two questions have the user role. The earlier “₹5,000” has the assistant role because the assistant wrote it.

Keep the follow-up word for word and try covering up both earlier lines. Here, “that” loses its meaning. In a test, hold the latest question fixed and run it with and without the earlier exchange. Save the messages actually sent. If the follow-up only fails when the app omits the history, check the history selection before trying to change the model.

2. Keep instructions and evidence separate

Suppose the customer adds, “I think the minimum is ₹10,000.” That’s useful information about what they believe. The bank still needs its own approved policy to settle the amount.

The bank sends instructions the customer may never see. In our saved example, the system message says, “You are Harbor Leaf Bank’s assistant.” A separate developer message from the people building the app says, “Use approved policy as evidence. If the policy doesn’t answer the question, say you can’t confirm it.” Read that second instruction as a rule about how to answer. The amount and the fee still have to come from somewhere else.

Try putting the same sentence, “Use approved policy as evidence,” in the customer’s message. The words are unchanged, but now the customer is the speaker. If an app accidentally labels the bank’s instruction as customer text, check that label first when the assistant ignores it. Different model services have different rules for their instruction roles. Check what the chosen service supports and what the app actually sent.

The assistant can ask a policy lookup program for help. A program the assistant can use this way is a tool. An assistant message asking the lookup to search for Standard Savings is a tool call. The excerpt that comes back is a tool result, sent with the tool role in this example. It says the minimum is ₹5,000 and a ₹100 monthly fee applies below it.

Put the follow-up, the lookup call, and its result in order. Try swapping just the call and the result. In our saved example the service rejects that sequence before writing an answer. A real service may also require a matching identifier so the app can tell which result belongs to which call. Keep the ordered messages, the selected policy, and either the reply or the error together. That record is called a trace. A trace helps a reviewer distinguish an answer that was wrong from an attempt that never produced an answer.

3. Count the pieces the model reads

Write “balance ₹5,000” on paper. If you use the space as a dividing line, you get two groups. Try using these five pieces instead. Put a line after “balance”, after “ ₹”, after “5”, after the comma, and at the end of “000”. Join them again and you still have the same text, including the space before ₹.

A language model uses numbers to represent text. Reusing parts of words lets it represent unfamiliar names and numbers without keeping a separate entry for every spelling. A piece can be a whole word, part of a word, a mark such as a comma, or a piece with a space attached. Each piece is a token. A tokenizer splits the text and looks up the number for each piece. When the model writes an answer, its output numbers can be turned back into text. Our split on paper illustrates the idea. The real model’s tokenizer decides the actual boundaries.

Try “balance ₹5000” with the comma removed. You changed one mark without changing the amount. A tokenizer might combine the digits differently. Try adding a second space before ₹ instead. A space can be its own piece or travel with a nearby piece, so that change can also affect the count.

Compare “minimum balance” with “न्यूनतम शेष राशि”, a way to say it in Hindi. A tokenizer’s set of familiar pieces can split those strings differently. You’d need the actual tokenizer to know either count. The language alone doesn’t tell you which string will use more tokens.

Why count these pieces? Imagine two ways of sending the same policy excerpt. One version of the full request uses 42 tokens. With a change in formatting, another uses 46 in this invented example. With room for only 44, the first fits and the second needs a change. At a fictional price of 2 paise per input token, the second also costs eight paise more to send, assuming the billing rule is otherwise the same. A reviewer can hold the policy meaning fixed, vary the formatting or language, then record actual token use, what survived, and whether the answer still works.

Check this before moving on. Would a Python program that counts spaces tell you whether the 46-token version fits? It could count space-separated groups, but you need the chosen model’s tokenizer or measured token usage to make that decision. The Python lab adds the practice counts provided in the examples.

4. Leave room for the answer

The bank wants to send the question, its instructions, some earlier chat, and the policy paragraph the lookup found. It also wants the model to write an answer. The space the model can work with for this request and its generated answer is called its context window. Use the following small limits for practice. They aren’t specifications for a real service.

The window holds 60 tokens. The app sets aside 12 for the reply, leaving 48 for what it sends. What goes in uses input tokens. Some are used to represent message roles and boundaries in this teaching example. We call those extra tokens overhead. The reply uses output tokens. The planned room for the reply is its output reserve. A separate output limit of 16 permits a reserve of 12 here.

The app also has a separate input limit of 54. Since it must satisfy both 54 and 48, the smaller number wins. The resulting input budget is 48. If the input would take 52, the request is four tokens over. We’ll write the difference, 48 − 52 = −4, as input headroom. The negative sign tells you it’s over budget.

Change only the reserve to eight. Now 60 − 8 leaves 52, and the separate limit still allows that much. Exactly 52 input tokens fit. The change also leaves the upcoming reply with less room. If an explanation needs more than eight tokens, look at what you could remove from the input before lowering the reserve. A real service may apply different input and output rules, so use its actual limits when testing.

5. Find what disappeared

Keep the original 12-token reserve. In the practice request, the required instructions, current question, and message overhead take 28 input tokens. The older policy lookup and result take 14, and recent small talk takes 10. That’s 52 tokens of input, four more than the budget allows.

First try a rule that always cuts the oldest optional group. Cross out the 14-token lookup exchange. You have 38 tokens left, and you lost the policy. Cutting part of a request to make it fit is one kind of truncation. Compare that with cutting ten tokens of small talk. The remaining 42 fit, and the policy can still answer the customer. Keep a lookup call and its result together when you cut, and keep retained messages in their original order.

Longer documents can expose the same problem even after small talk is gone. Keep the required 28 tokens, the question, and the output reserve fixed. With the short 14-token policy exchange, the input is 42. Replace it with a 26-token exchange containing a longer document. The input is now 54, six over budget. An app might reject it, send a focused approved excerpt, or leave out something important. Run the short and long cases with the same question. Check whether the fee sentence actually reaches the model before you grade the reply. This can explain why a short test passes while the longer one fails.

Other ways to make room include summarizing earlier chat and keeping the exact policy wording, or deliberately stopping when the required pieces alone won’t fit. A summary can also lose details, so test a question that depends on one of them. For this bank, check that the prepared input keeps both what “that” refers to and the approved fee rule. A request can fit while still losing either one.

6. Give the failure a useful name

Imagine two teammates send you the same note. “The assistant didn’t give the fee.” Open the records before treating these as the same failure.

In the first record, the model had the fee paragraph and said there was no fee. You can mark the answer wrong and point to the paragraph it contradicts. In the second record, the cutoff removed the fee paragraph. The assistant said it couldn’t confirm the fee. The answer followed the bank’s rule for missing information. Declining to make a claim you can’t support is called abstaining. The app still failed to bring the needed policy into that request.

Write two lines for each case. On one line, record what the app actually supplied. On the other, record what the assistant said. For the first case, investigate how the answer was produced given the evidence. For the second, test a change to the app that keeps the policy, then ask the same question again. If you change the question too, you lose the clean comparison.

7. Price the tokens actually used

Go back to the version that keeps the policy and sends 42 input tokens. The app sets aside 12 for the reply. This time the reply uses six.

At the invented prices of 2 paise per input token and 6 paise per output token, input costs 42 × 2 = 84 paise. Output costs 6 × 6 = 36 paise. The bill totals 120 paise, or ₹1.20. The practice bill charges for six generated tokens. The unused space is still part of the planning limit, and actual billing depends on the service.

Try a ten-token reply with everything else held fixed. Four extra output tokens cost another 24 paise. The request still had room for that reply. If the team wants to spend less, compare measured usage after a change and check that the assistant still gets the facts needed to answer.

Worked Demonstration

The customer restates their follow-up so you can test the policy separately from the question’s wording. In all three saved examples, the same bank rule applies. You’re reviewing what happened before deciding what to fix.

Example 1. The bank sends the policy and gets a useful reply

User question. “What if my Standard Savings balance falls below the minimum?”

Approved reference. The lookup finds “Standard Savings requires ₹5,000. A ₹100 monthly fee applies below that amount.” The app drops small talk and keeps the lookup exchange. It sends 42 tokens under a budget of 48.

Actual LLM response. “If your Standard Savings balance falls below ₹5,000, a ₹100 monthly fee applies.”

Before reading the assessment, mark the condition that triggers the fee, the amount, and how often it’s charged. Find each part in the policy. Then check the size separately.

Assessment. The input fits with six tokens left. The reply gives the right condition, amount, and frequency. Each of those details appears in the supplied policy. If a second reply said “₹100 each day,” it would fail even though it repeated the correct number.

Failure classification. This case passes the size and evidence checks. Save the approved excerpt and the accepted behavior so you can repeat the test on a longer request.

Example 2. The lookup result is sent before its call

User question. “What if my Standard Savings balance falls below the minimum?”

Approved reference. The same fee paragraph is present in the saved records. The app has placed the tool result before the lookup call that produced it.

Actual LLM response. None. The service in this saved case rejects the request before generating a reply.

Assessment. The lookup has to come first so the app can match the result to the call that produced it. Step 1 lets you see the ordering mistake using a shorter question about the minimum balance. Run it once to see the correct order, then swap the call and result as directed. The program prints the messages you give it. In a real app, an engineer would send the repaired request with the same question, instructions, and policy, then check whether the service accepts it before grading any reply. The original attempt produced no reply to grade.

Failure classification. The app put the request together in the wrong order. Record answer quality as “not applicable” for this attempt. Rewriting the bank’s fee instructions would leave the ordering problem in place.

Example 3. The request fits but the fee paragraph is gone

User question. “What if my Standard Savings balance falls below the minimum?”

Approved reference. The bank still requires ₹5,000 and charges ₹100 per month below it. This time the app drops the older lookup exchange. It sends 38 tokens, including the question and instructions, but no fee paragraph.

Actual LLM response. “I can’t confirm the fee from the supplied policy.”

Assessment. Compare the information the app had before it cut the request with what it actually sent. The fee paragraph was in the lookup result, but that result is missing from the 38-token request. The request fits. The assistant follows the rule for a missing policy, and the customer still can’t learn what the bank charges.

Failure classification. The app lost the evidence. Keep the same question and try dropping small talk instead. Expect the 42-token request to retain the paragraph. Only after you see the next saved reply can you judge whether that run actually answered the customer.

For a second comparison, remove the small talk in both runs and change only the lookup from the short excerpt to the longer document from Section 5. Record the counts of 42 and 54. The second version cannot fit as proposed. Your evidence check should distinguish a refused request from a shortened one that left out the fee. Those failures call for different changes to the app.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Run your first example

You can run the first example right from this page. Each Python block comes with its own starting data, so a later step works even if you skipped the previous one. The examples use standard Python 3.10 or newer.

  1. Select Open Python Editor. Leave the Academy open in its own tab so you can come back to the instructions.
  2. In the Academy, select Copy Code beside the current Python block. Then paste it into the editor. Replace any starter code you see there. You’ll do the pasting yourself.
  3. Click Run in the editor. Back in the Academy, open Expected output under the block. Check the lines against what the editor printed.
  4. Read the Experiment and predict what will change. Make that one edit in the editor, run again, and compare with the second Expected output. Say why one line changed or why it stayed the same.

Use this routine for each step below. Start each step by replacing the old code with the complete new block. Keep the spaces at the start of lines as you found them. If you get an error after editing, paste the original block, check that it runs, and try the one change again. Use the fictional examples provided.

Step 1 — Store and inspect the messages

You’ll put a saved conversation on the screen in the order it happened. This gives you something you can read from top to bottom before you decide whether each line belongs there.

Each line starts with print(). It shows the text inside its parentheses. The double quotes mark where the text starts and ends. Python calls a piece of text a string. It uses the quotes to read the string and leaves them off when it shows the result.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and run it. Follow the two lines at the end.

Open Python Editor 
print("system - You are Harbor Leaf Bank's assistant.")
print("developer - Use the approved policy as evidence.")
print("user - What is the Standard Savings minimum?")
print("assistant - Look up the Standard Savings policy.")
print("tool - Approved Standard Savings minimum: ₹5,000.")
Expected output
system - You are Harbor Leaf Bank's assistant.
developer - Use the approved policy as evidence.
user - What is the Standard Savings minimum?
assistant - Look up the Standard Savings policy.
tool - Approved Standard Savings minimum: ₹5,000.

The fourth line asks for the policy. The fifth gives the result of that lookup. At this point the assistant hasn’t sent an answer to the customer. Python prints those two lines in that order because that’s how they’re written.

Experiment. Move the last print(...) line above the one beginning print("assistant. Run it again. The result now appears before the request that produced it.

Expected output
system - You are Harbor Leaf Bank's assistant.
developer - Use the approved policy as evidence.
user - What is the Standard Savings minimum?
tool - Approved Standard Savings minimum: ₹5,000.
assistant - Look up the Standard Savings policy.

Checkpoint. Why does the changed program still run? print() can show any text you give it. Python hasn’t checked whether it makes sense as a conversation. If you were sending it to a model service, you’d need a separate check that the lookup comes before its matching result.

Step 2 — Add the token counts in a request

You’ve seen that the app sends more than the customer’s last line. Count the space those extra pieces take before sending anything. The numbers in this example were chosen for practice.

Look at system_tokens = 8. The equals sign gives the number on its right a name. We call a name like system_tokens a variable. Python can add numbers like 8 because they’re written without quotation marks. The plus sign adds the named numbers, and parentheses let you spread the sum over several lines. input_tokens stores the result so you can use it again.

A comma inside print() separates the label from the value you want to display. Python prints them with a space between them. The lines near the end first show the counts, then add the reply reserve in the final line.

In the online editor, replace the previous program with this whole block. Select Run and check both totals in Expected output.

Open Python Editor 
system_tokens = 8
developer_tokens = 8
policy_tokens = 14
recent_chat_tokens = 10
question_tokens = 8
overhead = 4
reserve = 12

input_tokens = (
    system_tokens + developer_tokens + policy_tokens
    + recent_chat_tokens + question_tokens + overhead
)

print("system instructions", system_tokens)
print("developer instructions", developer_tokens)
print("approved policy exchange", policy_tokens)
print("recent chat", recent_chat_tokens)
print("current question", question_tokens)
print("Overhead:", overhead)
print("Input total:", input_tokens)
print("Input plus reserved output:", input_tokens + reserve)
Expected output
system instructions 8
developer instructions 8
approved policy exchange 14
recent chat 10
current question 8
Overhead: 4
Input total: 52
Input plus reserved output: 64

The five groups total 48. With four extra tokens for message overhead, the input takes 52. The last line adds 12 more for the reply, so this plan asks for 64 tokens of shared space.

Experiment. Change recent_chat_tokens = 10 to recent_chat_tokens = 6 and run again. Use the change to explain why both totals go down by four, even though the reply reserve stays the same.

Expected output
system instructions 8
developer instructions 8
approved policy exchange 14
recent chat 6
current question 8
Overhead: 4
Input total: 48
Input plus reserved output: 60

Checkpoint. Did Python work out how the model splits words when it printed 48? It added the numbers you entered. A real count needs the model’s tokenizer or usage reported by its service.

Step 3 — Calculate remaining context capacity

You know the request wants 52 input tokens. Before sending it, work out what the model will allow. In context_window - reserve, - subtracts the room held for the reply. That gives you 48.

min() picks the smaller of the two numbers inside its parentheses. Here it compares the input limit of 54 with the 48 tokens left in the window. Once you have the smaller number, the next line subtracts what the request uses. That leaves the room available, or the amount you’re over if the result is negative.

Copy this block into the editor and select Run. Compare the two lines with your calculation.

Open Python Editor 
context_window = 60
input_limit = 54
reserve = 12
input_tokens = 52

input_budget = min(input_limit, context_window - reserve)
headroom = input_budget - input_tokens

print("Input budget:", input_budget)
print("Input headroom:", headroom)
Expected output
Input budget: 48
Input headroom: -4

With a 12-token reserve, the shared budget allows only 48 input tokens. The saved input needs four more than that.

Experiment. Change only reserve from 12 to 8 and rerun. Both reserves are allowed in this example. Leaving four fewer tokens for the reply makes the input fit exactly.

Expected output
Input budget: 52
Input headroom: 0

Checkpoint. What does zero headroom tell you? The input uses its entire allowance. The eight-token output reserve remains available. Any extra input would need to displace something or increase the budget.

Step 4 — Simulate dropping old history

You’ll make the request smaller and see what the app gives up. First read one history row, {"name": "recent chat", "tokens": 10}. The braces hold named values, so this is a dictionary. A name such as "tokens" is a key. The colon connects it to its value. Commas separate pairs. group["tokens"] asks for the number under that key in the current row.

The two rows sit inside square brackets, which make an ordered list. Here the lookup and its result share one row, so the trim can remove them together. Read for group in history: as “take each row in turn and call the current one group.” This repeating pattern is a loop. The colon and spaces at the start of the next line show what to repeat. Those spaces are called indentation. Add each row’s count to the protected 28 tokens before deciding whether the request needs a trim.

Follow the while line only after reading the first total. It asks whether 52 is greater than 48 using >. It also checks that history still has items. The word and means both checks have to hold. This loop repeats until the input fits or there’s nothing left to remove.

history.pop(0) takes out the first item. Python numbers list positions from zero. The dot gives you an operation that belongs to the list, and pop(0) hands back the row it took out. Save it under removed so you can print its name and subtract its tokens. The next time through, the input fits, so there’s nothing more to remove.

Copy the block into the editor and select Run. Read what was dropped as well as the new count.

Open Python Editor 
protected = 28
input_budget = 48
history = [
    {"name": "approved policy exchange", "tokens": 14},
    {"name": "recent chat", "tokens": 10},
]

input_tokens = protected
for group in history:
    input_tokens = input_tokens + group["tokens"]
print("Before trimming:", input_tokens)

while input_tokens > input_budget and history:
    removed = history.pop(0)
    input_tokens = input_tokens - removed["tokens"]
    print("Dropped:", removed["name"])

print("Input sent:", input_tokens)
for group in history:
    print("History kept:", group["name"])
Expected output
Before trimming: 52
Dropped: approved policy exchange
Input sent: 38
History kept: recent chat

The oldest group is removed as a unit. Removing all 14 tokens leaves more room than the four needed to make the request fit. It also removes the approved amount. “Input sent” describes what the simulated application would send. The program only prints the report.

Experiment. Change only input_budget to 52. Run again. The first check in the while line is now false, so both groups remain.

Expected output
Before trimming: 52
Input sent: 52
History kept: approved policy exchange
History kept: recent chat

Checkpoint. Does a smaller input count prove that the trim preserved the important evidence? Check the kept group names. The 38-token run fits and still loses the policy.

Step 5 — See how missing evidence changes evaluation

Read the two saved replies first. Both say ₹5,000. The difference is what the assistant received. The first row has the policy and marks policy_present as True, which means yes. The second lost it and marks it False, or no.

The program makes two decisions for each row. First, if runs its indented lines when the policy is present. else, which means “otherwise,” chooses the expected reply for a missing policy. That gives the name expected a value. Next == asks whether the saved reply exactly matches that expected text. One equals sign assigns a value. Two equals signs ask whether values are equal.

Copy this block into the editor and select Run. Look for the row whose answer sounds right but fails the check.

Open Python Editor 
cases = [
    {
        "name": "Full request",
        "policy_present": True,
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    },
    {
        "name": "Trimmed request",
        "policy_present": False,
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    },
]

for case in cases:
    if case["policy_present"]:
        expected = "The minimum is ₹5,000."
    else:
        expected = "I can't confirm that from the supplied policy."

    if case["reply"] == expected:
        print(case["name"], "- PASS")
    else:
        print(case["name"], "- FAIL")
Expected output
Full request - PASS
Trimmed request - FAIL

Notice what stayed the same. Both saved replies say ₹5,000. In the first row, the yes value for policy_present stands for a request that contained the approved amount. In the second row, the number still happens to be correct, but the policy is missing. Our rule for grading the reply, also called a rubric, expects the assistant to say it can’t confirm the amount in that case. Python uses the yes-or-no value we supplied to pick the expected sentence, then checks for an exact match.

Experiment. Change only the reply in the Trimmed request to "I can't confirm that from the supplied policy.". Run again. This time the reply matches what we expect when the policy is missing. The app still hasn’t supplied the policy.

Expected output
Full request - PASS
Trimmed request - PASS

Checkpoint. Does the edited result prove the bank answered the customer’s question? The second PASS shows that the saved reply handled missing evidence as expected. The app still owes the customer a way to get the policy. This script checks only these fixed sentences. When you review real answers, check whether different wording means the same thing.

Step 6 — Compare used tokens with reserved space

Write two lines on the pretend bill, one for the request and one for the reply. The version that kept the policy sent 42 input tokens. The reply had space for 12 but used six. In this example, only those six get charged at the output rate.

The * sign multiplies the used count by the price for that kind of token. input_cost holds the input charge and output_cost holds the reply charge. Add them in the last print line. We use whole paise in this example. There are 100 paise in a rupee.

Copy the block into the editor and select Run. Find the reserved amount and the used amount before looking at the total.

Open Python Editor 
input_tokens = 42
reserved_output = 12
generated_tokens = 6
input_rate = 2
output_rate = 6

input_cost = input_tokens * input_rate
output_cost = generated_tokens * output_rate

print("Input tokens:", input_tokens)
print("Output reserved:", reserved_output)
print("Output used:", generated_tokens)
print("Illustrative cost in paise:", input_cost + output_cost)
Expected output
Input tokens: 42
Output reserved: 12
Output used: 6
Illustrative cost in paise: 120

The input costs 84 paise and the reply costs 36. The reserved space could have held more output. The simulated bill counts the six tokens actually generated.

Experiment. Change only generated_tokens to 10 and run again. The reserve stays at 12. Four more tokens at six paise each add 24 paise to the total.

Expected output
Input tokens: 42
Output reserved: 12
Output used: 10
Illustrative cost in paise: 144

Checkpoint. Why did the bill rise while the reserved capacity stayed the same? The reply used four additional tokens. At six paise each they add 24 paise. The application had room for them in the same reserve.

Step 7 — Check what fits and what survives

You can now count the pieces, make room, and check that the policy is still there. This program runs those checks together so you can try a different request without rewriting them. The practice values are at the bottom, just above the line that runs the checks.

A named set of instructions like this is a function. At the top, def gives it the name diagnose. The names between the parentheses are parameters, the names it gives the values you pass in. The colon and indented lines show which instructions belong to it. Those lines run when you call diagnose(...) at the bottom. return ends the run early when there’s no useful trim to try.

Read the function from the top. The less-than sign in reserve < 1 checks for fewer than one reserved token. or means either check can trigger the stop. A reserve above the output limit also stops the run. The next stop protects the required input, such as the current question and the bank’s instructions. If that much won’t fit, trimming optional history can’t fix it.

If both checks pass, history.copy() makes a separate list. Removing entries from it leaves the original list alone. We don’t edit the dictionaries inside either list. Start with [], an empty list for the removed names. As the loop trims, dropped.append(...) adds each removed name to the end of that list.

Start policy_kept at False, meaning no policy has been found in the kept list yet. The last loop checks approved_policy on each remaining row and changes policy_kept to True if it finds the policy. This lets the final lines show both whether the request fits and whether it still has the evidence.

Copy the whole block into the editor and select Run. Read the dropped groups and the final evidence line together.

Open Python Editor 
def diagnose(window, input_limit, output_limit, reserve, protected, history):
    if reserve < 1 or reserve > output_limit:
        print("STOP: output reserve is outside the allowed range.")
        return

    budget = min(input_limit, window - reserve)
    print("Input budget:", budget)
    if protected > budget:
        print("STOP: protected input cannot fit.")
        return

    kept = history.copy()
    input_tokens = protected
    for group in kept:
        input_tokens = input_tokens + group["tokens"]

    dropped = []
    while input_tokens > budget and kept:
        group = kept.pop(0)
        dropped.append(group["name"])
        input_tokens = input_tokens - group["tokens"]

    policy_kept = False
    for group in kept:
        if group["approved_policy"]:
            policy_kept = True

    print("Dropped groups:", dropped)
    print("Input sent:", input_tokens)
    print("Input headroom:", budget - input_tokens)
    if policy_kept:
        print("Evidence: approved policy retained")
    else:
        print("Evidence: missing approved policy; expect abstention")


window = 60
input_limit = 54
output_limit = 16
reserve = 12
protected = 28
history = [
    {"name": "approved policy exchange", "tokens": 14, "approved_policy": True},
    {"name": "recent chat", "tokens": 10, "approved_policy": False},
]

diagnose(window, input_limit, output_limit, reserve, protected, history)
Expected output
Input budget: 48
Dropped groups: ['approved policy exchange']
Input sent: 38
Input headroom: 10
Evidence: missing approved policy; expect abstention

The report prints the names of the removed groups in square brackets. There’s only one in this run. The remaining input fits with ten tokens of room. The last line tells you that the bank’s policy was dropped, so the assistant should say it can’t confirm the amount. The program shows what the app would send and which behavior to look for if you later tested a real model.

Experiment. Change only reserve from 12 to 8. Run again. The input can now use 52 tokens. No group needs to go, so the last line says the policy is still there.

Expected output
Input budget: 52
Dropped groups: []
Input sent: 52
Input headroom: 0
Evidence: approved policy retained

Checkpoint. Could you always shrink the output reserve to save an old policy? A reply still needs enough room for its intended job and must respect the model's output settings. Try retaining relevant evidence and dropping unrelated chat before sacrificing room for the answer.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Tokens and fictional cost

An approved excerpt and question take 42 input tokens in our teaching example. The hypothetical price is 2 paise per input token and 6 paise per generated token. One run generates six tokens. Another run generates ten tokens from the same request. Compute both totals. Explain why counting the words in the replies would not verify the token bill.

Practice 2. Label and order the records

Imagine you’re handed five saved entries from the same chat. They arrive in this order.

  1. The service sets up the assistant with “You are Harbor Leaf support.”
  2. The app’s builders add “Use approved policy only.”
  3. The customer asks “What balance is required?”
  4. The lookup program returns “The policy says ₹5,000.”
  5. The assistant asks the lookup program to “Look up the Standard Savings policy.”

Write the role next to each entry. Reorder the entries so the lookup result follows the call that produced it. Then say what you’d save to show which messages reached the model before it answered.

Practice 3. Decide whether the input fits

You have room for 60 tokens in the teaching model, with a separate input limit of 54 and output limit of 16. You save 12 tokens for the reply. The app plans to send 52 input tokens, including 10 for recent small talk and 14 for the approved policy exchange.

Work out the input budget and how far over it you are. You may drop one group. Which would you drop to leave the assistant able to answer? Write the new input count and how much room remains.

Practice 4. Separate missing evidence from a wrong answer

You’re reviewing two saved attempts for the same ₹5,000 policy. In trace A, the assistant receives the approved policy and replies ₹10,000. In trace B, the app drops the policy to fit the request and the assistant says, “I can’t confirm the minimum from the supplied policy.” In both attempts the developer says to make only claims the supplied evidence supports.

For each trace, write what the reply did and what, if anything, you can verify went wrong in the app. Then write the next check you’d run. Would you ask the same teammate to investigate both?

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The input costs 42 × 2 = 84 paise. The first reply costs 6 × 6 = 36, so its total is 120 paise. The second costs 10 × 6 = 60, so its total is 144 paise. The difference is 24 paise. The tokenizer decides how many pieces the model processes. Ordinary word counts do not establish measured token usage.

Solution 2

The first record is system, the second developer, and the third user. The fourth is tool and the fifth is assistant. The lookup request should follow the user’s question and come before its result. If there are several lookups, match each result to the request that produced it. Save the exact ordered request and the tool evidence, then capture the reply so the next reviewer can check which messages were available before the answer.

Solution 3

The reserve of 12 is within the output limit of 16. The shared window leaves 60 − 12 = 48 tokens for input. The smaller of 54 and 48 is 48. The planned input of 52 is four tokens over that budget. Dropping the ten-token small-talk group leaves 42, or six tokens of headroom. The approved policy is still present. Dropping the policy also frees space but would leave the model without the needed fact.

Solution 4

In trace A, the reply contradicts the policy the app sent. Mark the answer incorrect and check that the policy reached the model in the right order and with the right role before deciding what caused the error. In trace B, the assistant says it can’t confirm the amount, as the instructions require when the policy is missing. Check why the app left the policy out. Run the same question and instructions again with the policy included, then compare the reply from the new run with the approved amount.

Knowledge Check

  1. You keep the amount ₹5,000 but remove the comma before sending the policy. Could the token count change? What would you use to find out?
  2. An app labels “Use only approved policy” as a user message. The wording is right. What should you look at before rewriting the instruction?
  3. A trace contains a policy result before its matching lookup call, and the service refuses the request. Which part of the test failed? Is there an answer to score?
  4. The window is 60, the input limit is 54, and the reserve drops to four. How much can the app send, and what limits it?
  5. A short policy exchange uses 14 tokens. A long one uses 26. The fixed input takes 28, and the input budget is 48. Why could the same test pass with the short exchange and fail with the long one?
  6. The assistant says it can’t confirm the fee. What would make that a sensible reply in one test and a missed answer in another?
  7. The app sets aside 12 tokens for output. The reply uses six. At six paise per generated token, what’s the output cost in this lesson?
  8. You suspect a cutoff is causing the failure. What would you keep the same, what would you change, and what would you record?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. The tokenizer might group the digits differently without the comma. Use the tokenizer for the chosen model or compare measured usage, keeping the rest of the request fixed. A word count might stay the same.
  2. Check how the application set the message’s role. The bank intended an instruction from the people building the app. The recorded role says it came from the customer. Compare the app’s message with the service’s supported roles.
  3. The app failed to put the request together in the order the service required. It tried to provide a result before its call. The service returned no answer, so record the error and leave answer quality unscored.
  4. The reserve leaves 56 tokens of shared space for input. The separate limit still caps input at 54, so 54 is the budget.
  5. The short version uses 42 and fits. The long one uses 54 and is six over. If the app cuts the long version, check whether it kept the actual fee sentence. Passing the short test only shows what happened when that version fit.
  6. With the fee paragraph missing, admitting the gap follows the bank’s rule. With an approved fee paragraph available for this account and question, the same reply leaves an answer on the table. Check the actual request before deciding.
  7. The output charge is 6 × 6 = 36 paise. The unused six tokens were spare capacity in this exercise.
  8. Keep the question, instructions, and model fixed. Try a short approved excerpt and a longer version that contains the same fee sentence. Record input count, what the model actually received, and the reply or error. Use those records to tell where the comparison first went wrong.

Independent Assignment

Go back to Step 7. Open the online editor from the lesson, use Copy Code, and paste the whole block. You’ll test three variations on the same request. Predict each result before selecting Run.

  1. Keep the short policy. Under history, move the whole line that starts with {"name": "recent chat" above the line for the approved policy exchange. Leave window = 60 and the 12-token reserve unchanged. Run the code. Here, moving the lines changes which group gets cut first. In a real app, choose what to cut first, then send the messages that survive in their original conversation order.
  2. Try a longer document. With recent chat first, change only the token count of the approved policy exchange from 14 to 26. Run again. Notice whether removing chat on its own gave the document enough room.
  3. Test a window that’s too small. Restore the policy exchange to 14. Keep recent chat first and change window to 37. Run again. Decide whether the app can solve this one by dropping optional groups.

Write three rows in your notes, one per run. For each, record the input budget, what was dropped, the final input count or stop reason, whether the policy survived, and what the assistant should do if the app can proceed. Finish with two sentences for a teammate. Explain which change helps in the first run and why that same change is insufficient for the longer document.

Check your assignment
  1. The input budget is 48. Dropping recent chat leaves 42 input tokens and six tokens of room. The short policy stays, so the assistant can use the approved amount. You would still need to check the answer it actually gives.
  2. With the longer policy, the initial total is 28 + 10 + 26 = 64. Dropping chat leaves 54, still six over budget. The program then drops the policy and reports 28 input tokens and 20 tokens of room. Expect the assistant to decline to confirm the amount. A shorter approved excerpt could retain the evidence where removing chat alone couldn’t.
  3. The budget is 25 because 37 − 12 = 25. The required input alone uses 28. The program prints STOP: protected input cannot fit. before dropping optional groups. There is no request to grade. The app needs to change what it requires or use a window large enough to fit it.

Common Mistakes

  • Equating tokens with words. Use model-specific counts for real requests. The numbers assigned in this lab are for teaching arithmetic.
  • Assuming the whole chat history reaches the model. Inspect the actual request, including the tool result and any history that was dropped.
  • Keeping all old text at the expense of evidence. Select history and excerpts for the current question and keep any required call and result pairs.
  • Treating a user guess or old assistant reply as policy. Check role, source, and date before treating a value as approved evidence.
  • Using a fit calculation as a quality verdict. Check token headroom and evidence retention separately. The model’s actual reply still requires evaluation.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Start with what the customer meant. The earlier messages can explain what “that” refers to, and the bank’s approved policy can explain what fee applies. The app has to fit both kinds of information into the request while leaving room for the reply.

When you test an answer, read the trace in the same order. Check whether the messages were assembled correctly, whether they fit, and which facts the model actually received. Then grade the reply against those facts. That order helps you decide whether to fix the app’s choice of information or investigate the assistant’s answer.

The next topic in Module 1 is Inference, sampling and repeatability. Here you learned to account for what enters the model. Next you will study why the same request can produce different replies and how to make fair comparisons across runs. If you are in a focused path, use Next Lesson to follow that path's sequence.
