Beginner · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Separate an evidence-backed fact, a reference answer, and an evaluation label for a saved reply.
  • Choose the approved source for a question using its scope, authority, and effective dates.
  • Write several equally acceptable answers and a reference behavior for a question the policy cannot answer.
  • Build an eight-case benchmark with clear evidence, boundary cases, and unresolved cases.
  • Run a small offline benchmark and interpret PASS, FAIL, and NEEDS REVIEW.
  • Repair a faulty benchmark row while keeping earlier results reproducible.

Why This Lesson Matters

You started planning for a Standard Savings account in June, when a Harbor Leaf Bank leaflet said to keep ₹4,000 in it. On July 15 you ask the bank’s chat assistant. It says, “Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.” Should the bank fix the assistant’s reply?

Look at the dates on the two approved policies. The ₹4,000 rule ends on June 30. The ₹5,000 rule starts on July 1. The assistant’s reply fits the July question. If you checked it against the June leaflet, you could send the team off to fix a reply that was already right.

In M02-T01 you decided what to check. Here you’ll find the evidence that lets two people make the same check. Harbor Leaf Bank, its dates, policies, replies, and decisions are fictional. Use them for practice rather than financial guidance.

Plan your study session

Allow about four hours for the full lesson. Spend about an hour on the concepts and worked demonstrations, 90 minutes on the Python steps, 40 minutes on the four practice tasks and knowledge check, and 50 minutes on the independent assignment and a review of your results. The programs run in seconds. Give yourself time to justify the labels and compare your reasoning with the worked solutions.

Beginner Explanation

1. Ground truth starts with the question and the evidence

Put the July question at the top of a page. Before reading the reply, write what you can verify from the policy. Standard Savings required ₹5,000 on July 15, 2026. That’s the fact the answer needs to preserve. The best-supported fact or expected behavior for a case is its ground truth.

On the next line, write one answer you’d accept. “The Standard Savings minimum is ₹5,000” is a reference answer. Another reviewer could say “Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings” and mean the same thing.

Now read the actual reply and record the result. Give the five-thousand-rupee reply PASS and a ₹10,000 reply FAIL. That result is an evaluation label. Change the reply and the label can change, while the policy fact and reference stay the same.

Try the same three lines for a customer asking about the daily ATM withdrawal limit. The policy you gave the assistant covers savings balances and fees. The limit is unknown from that evidence. What you can write down is the expected behavior. The assistant should say it can’t confirm the limit from the supplied policy. A reply that does so can pass as a way of handling the question.

What if one reviewer likes “maintain” and another likes “keep”? Ask them to point to the same policy line and say what the reply needs to mean. A word preference doesn’t decide a bank requirement.

Teams sometimes call reviewed evidence gold evidence or a reviewed answer a gold reference. This means someone checked it for that case. If you later find an error, you can correct it and record why.

Some questions have an answer you can’t verify yet. A policy can change with time, omit an ATM limit, or disagree with another approved document. If an excerpt simply omits the limit, you can test whether the assistant admits the gap.

If two equally authoritative policies disagree and neither takes priority, you can’t verify either policy claim. Mark the case NEEDS REVIEW and ask the person responsible for the policy to resolve it.

2. Read the Harbor Leaf policy records

The help-center draft says ₹3,000 and was edited after the July policy came into force. Before you use it, ask who can set the minimum. The bank gives that job to the Savings Policy team. A document the bank authorizes for the subject is an approved source.

Leave a trail another reviewer can follow. Write down the document ID, version, section, approving owner, and dates. This record of where the evidence came from is called provenance. Here the policy register, the bank’s record of approved documents, gives the Savings Policy team authority over Standard Savings balances and fees. In the short citations below, §2 means section 2. Use the supplied excerpts as the evidence for each case.

  • SV-1, Savings Policy version 1, §2, approved. Effective January 1 through June 30, 2026, inclusive. Standard Savings requires a minimum of ₹4,000. A ₹80 monthly fee applies when the balance is below ₹4,000.
  • SV-2, Savings Policy version 2, §2, approved. Effective July 1, 2026. Standard Savings requires a minimum of ₹5,000. A ₹100 monthly fee applies when the balance is below ₹5,000. At the minimum, the below-minimum fee does not apply. This excerpt is silent about ATM limits and special student waivers.
  • HELP-DRAFT, help-center draft, unapproved. Edited July 10, 2026. It suggests that Standard Savings requires ₹3,000. Its editing date establishes when someone saved the draft. Approval and effective dates determine which policy governs.
  • FEE-A and FEE-B, both approved. These are addenda, or documents that add rules to the main policy. Both list the same Savings Policy owner and take effect on August 1, 2026. A says students can have the below-minimum fee waived, meaning the bank won’t charge it if the waiver applies. B says students can’t get that waiver. The register doesn’t say either document overrides the other. Use SV-2 for questions that don’t depend on the waiver.

Which day is the customer asking about? That’s the as-of date. If they ask about “today,” write down the date the case uses. Try June 30 and July 1. One day changes which policy applies, even if you open the very same documents.

  1. Check that the policy covers the account and subject.
  2. Check who approved it and whether that owner can set the rule.
  3. Check that the policy was in force on the date asked about.
  4. Look for another document with the same authority that gives a different rule. If the register says which one replaces the other, record that. If it doesn’t settle the disagreement, mark NEEDS REVIEW.

A file’s edit or download date shows when someone worked with it. Use the approval and effective dates to decide which policy applies.

Notice how the two approved savings versions can both be accurate for their dates. A reply about June 15 can correctly say ₹4,000 even if the evaluator opens the July policy today. By contrast, the two August addenda overlap in date, scope, and authority. Escalate that conflict because neither of those filters breaks the tie.

3. Build a reference answer from the evidence

Imagine handing another reviewer a short example of what you’d accept. Write the fact or action the reply needs to convey, then write one way to say it. Attach the source, section, version, and date to that reference answer so the next reviewer can check it.

You may also want the assistant to point the customer to the source. That pointer is a citation. A source number next to a wrong claim doesn’t make the claim right.

For “What is the Standard Savings minimum on July 15, 2026?”, all three replies meet the same fact requirement under SV-2 §2.

  1. “The Standard Savings minimum is ₹5,000.” This names the right account and requirement directly.
  2. “Keep at least ₹5,000 in Standard Savings.” “At least” correctly includes the threshold and amounts above it.
  3. “Maintain a minimum of five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.” This spells out the amount and preserves its meaning and scope.

Keep those three reviewed wordings together and you have a reference answer set. It gives a reviewer examples of the same meaning. If the assistant phrases it a fourth way, read what it says before deciding.

Try this saved practice card. The source sentence is “Standard Savings requires a minimum of ₹5,000.” The task is “Copy just the amount as printed.” The stored reply is “₹5,000.” You can point to those exact characters in the source. Asking the assistant to pull a piece of text directly from a passage is an extractive task. Checking the literal text makes sense here because the task asks for a copy.

Keep the passage and change the task to “Explain how much I need to keep.” The reply “Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings” now works because it preserves the meaning. When the assistant writes an answer in its own words, that’s a generative task. Check what the customer would understand from the reply before choosing how to score it.

Now try writing an acceptable reply for the ATM limit. “I can’t confirm the daily ATM withdrawal limit from the supplied policy” tells the customer where the answer stops. Holding back a claim you can’t support is abstention. If the task allows it, the assistant can suggest checking an approved ATM policy. A guessed number should fail. Save the exact excerpt so another reviewer can check what it leaves out.

The August waiver case is different. The documents give opposite answers. A cautious reply can acknowledge that conflict, but the policy owner still needs to settle it. If you want to score the assistant’s handling of the conflict, write a separate expected behavior for that.

4. Build a benchmark that can teach you something

Suppose you want to repeat the July question tomorrow. Save the question, what the assistant had to go on, and what a good reply should do. That saved scenario is a test case. Put several cases together and you have a dataset.

To compare answers fairly across runs, agree on the questions you cover, rules for scoring, and which version of the dataset to use. Together these form a benchmark. When you apply that benchmark to a set of replies, you’re doing an evaluation run. One case can show how a rule works. A benchmark lets you check how that rule and the assistant behave across different situations.

Begin with B01 and B02. Both ask the same question, and the replies express the same minimum in different words. That pair lets you check whether your scoring rule accepts both. Then add a known wrong reply, a historical question, and other situations the bank wants to test. Give each row a case ID that stays the same so you can find it again in the results. For each row, SV-1 and SV-2 refer to §2 and the policy register above.

  • B01, supported. Ask “What is the Standard Savings minimum?” as of July 15, 2026, using SV-2. Reply “The minimum is ₹5,000.” PASS. The minimum matches the current approved policy.
  • B02, accepted paraphrase. Ask the same question using the same date and source. Reply “Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.” PASS. The amount and account are unchanged.
  • B03, incorrect reply. Ask the same question using SV-2 on July 15. Reply “The minimum is ₹10,000.” FAIL. The reply conflicts with the approved amount.
  • B04, historical policy. Ask “What minimum applied on June 15, 2026?” using SV-1. Reply “The minimum was ₹4,000.” PASS. The as-of date is inside version 1’s effective interval.
  • B05, boundary. Ask “Is the below-minimum fee due at exactly ₹5,000?” on July 15 using SV-2. Reply “No below-minimum fee applies.” PASS. The fee applies below the threshold.
  • B06, tempting wrong fee. Ask “What fee applies at a balance of ₹4,999?” on July 15 using SV-2. Reply “A ₹100 fee applies every day.” FAIL. The amount happens to match, but the fee is monthly.
  • B07, unsupported question. Ask “What is the daily ATM withdrawal limit?” on July 15. The evidence packet contains only SV-2. Reply “I can’t confirm that from the supplied policy.” PASS. Abstaining is the approved behavior for this packet.
  • B08, unresolved evidence. Ask “Does the student waiver apply on August 3, 2026?” using both approved addenda, FEE-A and FEE-B. Reply “The student fee waiver applies.” NEEDS REVIEW. The register leaves the conflict unresolved.

B01, B02, and B04 are positive cases for a correct response. B03 and B06 are negative cases for an evaluator that detects known wrong replies. B05 is a boundary case, an input at the edge of a rule where “below” and “at or below” produce different results. B07 checks an unsupported question. B08 checks that you can keep uncertainty visible. Production questions also vary in form, context, topic, and difficulty. This sheet is a teaching set. It contains eight saved cases that test selected distinctions, so it cannot establish production readiness.

Give each real benchmark row a stable ID and include the question, date or account context, source authority and excerpt, expected behavior, acceptable variants, and a short reason reviewers can apply. Keep the saved model reply and your actual run label with the run. A test can have a known expectation before any assistant reply exists. Separate a wrong policy answer from a response that never arrived, as in M02-T01.

5. Check the benchmark itself

Imagine checking whether a new employee can handle the savings help desk by asking only “What is the minimum?” A good answer still leaves you wondering what they’ll do with conflicting documents or an unsupported request. Benchmark validity asks whether your cases and rules measure the behavior you set out to check.

Write a short scoring guide, called a rubric. In B06, tell the reviewer to check both the fee amount and how often it applies. Otherwise one reviewer may accept any answer with ₹100 while another notices that “every day” changes the claim.

Watch for errors in the reference data. If a July row mistakenly cites SV-1, a correct ₹5,000 reply might fail. If a fee reference says “₹100 when low,” reviewers may disagree about what low means and when it is charged. Fix the source or make the cutoff and frequency explicit. If two reviewers disagree, give them the same evidence and ask for their reasons. Use a policy owner for disagreements about authority. Retest with the revised rubric and record who approved the change.

The automated pitfalls from M02-T01 still apply. A strict phrase comparison can produce a false failure on a correct paraphrase. A weak keyword check can produce a false pass on “₹100 every day” because it sees the right amount. Read the entire claim against the evidence. For an unfamiliar reply, route it to review rather than assuming that absence from a list is a failure. Review can mean the source is unresolved or the reply is new to a simple checker. Give the two reasons separate labels when you report them.

Imagine giving a student the answer key to the quiz, then using their score to decide how they’ll do on new questions. If reserved questions, answers, or near-copies reach the assistant or its tuning process and make the test unrealistically easy, that’s data leakage.

Giving the assistant an approved policy is part of its job here. Giving it the reserved cases and their answer key changes the test. Use some cases to improve the assistant and save other realistic questions for the release check. Look for copied and lightly reworded questions across the two groups. Try fresh wording before you claim an improvement.

Imagine the bank’s Monday report says B01 failed. On Tuesday you learn the reviewer used the June amount for a July question. Keep Monday’s report with its benchmark version, HLB-SAV-1. Write down the old label and why it changed, ask another reviewer to check the correction, and give the corrected sheet a new version. A teammate can then read both reports and see which rules produced them.

To compare two versions of the assistant, run both on that same corrected sheet. Keep the questions, dates, policy excerpts, scoring guide, and settings other than the one you’re testing unchanged. Report how many replies passed, failed, or need review. If you give a fraction, say what you counted. “Five of eight attempts passed” leaves three other attempts to explain. “Five of seven reviewed replies passed” leaves the unresolved case outside that fraction, so show it separately.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Accept a paraphrase and repair the check

User question. “What minimum balance do I need for Standard Savings on July 15, 2026?”

Approved reference. SV-2 §2 requires ₹5,000 from July 1, 2026.

Actual LLM response. “Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.”

Assessment. Ask three small questions. Does the reply name the right account? Yes. Is “five thousand rupees” ₹5,000? Yes. Does “keep” convey the requirement? Here it does. Mark PASS. A literal comparison with “The minimum is ₹5,000” would wrongly reject the reply. Keep the paraphrase as a reviewed example and leave room in the scoring guide for other wording with the same meaning.

Example 2. Resolve two conflicting amounts by date and authority

User question. “What minimum balance applied on June 15, 2026?”

Approved reference. SV-1 §2 says ₹4,000 through June 30. SV-2 §2 says ₹5,000 starting July 1. HELP-DRAFT is unapproved.

Actual LLM response. “The Standard Savings minimum was ₹4,000.”

Assessment. Put your finger on June 15 in the calendar. SV-1 covers that date and gives ₹4,000. SV-2 starts after it, and the draft was never approved. Mark PASS. Move the question to July 15 and try the same ₹4,000 reply again. It now fails. Save the question date and policy version so another reviewer knows why.

Example 3. Separate a missing answer from a policy conflict

User question. “What is the ATM limit?” The second customer asks, “Did the student waiver apply on August 3?”

Approved reference. The ATM case supplies only SV-2 §2, which does not cover withdrawals. The waiver case supplies FEE-A and FEE-B, with equally authoritative conflicting claims.

Actual LLM response. For the ATM question, “I can’t confirm the limit from the supplied policy.” For the waiver question, “The student fee waiver applies.”

Assessment. Ask what you can check in each case. For the ATM question, you can verify that the excerpt omits the limit and the assistant says so. Mark PASS for that behavior. A guessed amount would fail. For the waiver question, you can verify that the documents disagree, but you can’t verify the claim that the waiver applies. Mark NEEDS REVIEW, keep both addenda, and ask the policy owner to settle the conflict. To check whether the assistant explains the disagreement to the customer, write that expectation as a separate test.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Each block is a complete program for Python 3.10 or later. The replies and reviewed labels are fictional and included in the code. The programs use no model calls, extra packages, or credentials.

  1. Select Open Python Editor to open a separate tab. Each Python block also has this link.
  2. Select Copy Code in the lesson. Paste the code into the editor yourself, replacing any text already there.
  3. Click Run. Open the first Expected output below the code and compare it with what the editor printed.
  4. Read the Experiment and predict what will change. Make the stated edit, click Run again, and compare with the second Expected output. Use the checkpoint to explain what happened.

Replace the entire editor contents with the next block before starting a new step. Keep the spaces at the start of each line. If an edit produces an error, paste the original block, run it again, then try the edit once more.

Step 1 — Store a question and its approved reference

Start with one question and one answer you’d be willing to show another reviewer. You’ll print them side by side so they’re easy to check.

In question = ..., = gives the name on the left the value on the right. A name like question or reference is a variable. Text in quotation marks is a string. On each print() line, a comma separates the label from the value. Python displays a space between them.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
question = "What is the Standard Savings minimum?"
reference = "The minimum is ₹5,000."

print("Question:", question)
print("Approved reference:", reference)
Expected output
Question: What is the Standard Savings minimum?
Approved reference: The minimum is ₹5,000.

The output displays the two strings from their named values. For this question we assume the July 15 case and SV-2.

Experiment. Change only the question to "What balance must I maintain for Standard Savings?" and run again.

Expected output
Question: What balance must I maintain for Standard Savings?
Approved reference: The minimum is ₹5,000.

Checkpoint. Why can the reference stay the same? The question asks about the same account requirement on the same date in different words.

Step 2 — Compare a reply with the reference

Now ask whether the saved reply repeats the reference word for word. Read reply == reference as “do these two pieces of text match exactly?” The two equals signs ask that question. One equals sign still stores a value.

Python answers True or False, a kind of value called a Boolean. The print line shows that answer beside “Exact match.” A different phrase can mean the same thing, as you’ll see in the edit.

Replace the code in the editor with this block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
reference = "The minimum is ₹5,000."
reply = "The minimum is ₹5,000."

print("Exact match:", reply == reference)
Expected output
Exact match: True

The two strings contain identical characters. Compare the meaning separately.

Experiment. Change the reply to "Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings." and run again.

Expected output
Exact match: False

The result turns false because the words and characters differ. Read the edited reply alongside the policy before judging the claim.

Checkpoint. Should the edited reply fail the July 15 factual criterion? It states the right amount for the right account. A reviewer can accept it even though the strings differ.

Step 3 — Allow several reference answers

What if you have two versions you’d accept? Put them in a list named accepted. A list stores items in order inside square brackets, with commas between them.

Read reply in accepted as “does any whole item in this list match the reply?” Python looks for the full text as one entry. It won’t look up the amount or decide whether the words mean the same thing. Adding a reviewed phrase gives the lookup one more answer it can recognize.

Replace the code in the editor with this block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
accepted = [
    "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    "You must maintain at least ₹5,000.",
]
reply = "Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings."

print("Known reference:", reply in accepted)
Expected output
Known reference: False

The reply expresses the approved amount. This version of the answer set has only two entries, neither of which uses that wording.

Experiment. Add "Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.", as the third item before the closing bracket. Run again.

Expected output
Known reference: True

Checkpoint. What changed when you added the third item? The lookup can now recognize that wording. The source fact stayed the same. An unfamiliar paraphrase still deserves review.

Step 4 — Represent a case as a dictionary

Picture an index card with a labeled box for the ID, another for the question, and one for the source. A dictionary has those named fields inside curly braces. A field name is called a key. A colon joins it to its value, and commas separate the pairs.

case["id"] asks Python for the value under the key "id". The “Evidence” line reads two values, the source and the question date. On the last line, Python reads reply and reference from the same card and compares their text. Keep all these values together so the next reviewer can tell which source you used for which reply.

Replace the code in the editor with this block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
case = {
    "id": "B01",
    "question": "What is the Standard Savings minimum?",
    "as_of": "2026-07-15",
    "source": "SV-2",
    "reference": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
}

print("Case:", case["id"])
print("Evidence:", case["source"], case["as_of"])
print("Exact match:", case["reply"] == case["reference"])
Expected output
Case: B01
Evidence: SV-2 2026-07-15
Exact match: True

Python used the ID and evidence fields when displaying the result. The last line compares the two strings retrieved from the dictionary.

Experiment. Change only the "reply" value to "The minimum is ₹10,000." and run again.

Expected output
Case: B01
Evidence: SV-2 2026-07-15
Exact match: False

The ID and evidence stay the same. The last line changes because the new reply differs from the stored reference. Read both amounts to see why the new reply is wrong for this case.

Checkpoint. Why keep the case's source and date beside the label? They tell the next reviewer why the approved amount is ₹5,000 for this case and let them check the version independently.

Step 5 — Run a two-case benchmark

Now put two of those cards into a list. Use for case in cases: to pick up each card in order. The colon opens the loop. The four spaces before the next two lines mark the work to repeat.

For the current card, Python reads the reply and reference, compares them, and stores the result as exact. It prints that result with the ID before moving to the next card. Look up the ID in the case sheet if you need the full question and evidence.

Replace the code in the editor with this block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
cases = [
    {
        "id": "B01",
        "reference": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    },
    {
        "id": "B03",
        "reference": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹10,000.",
    },
]

for case in cases:
    exact = case["reply"] == case["reference"]
    print(case["id"], "exact match:", exact)
Expected output
B01 exact match: True
B03 exact match: False

B01 and B03 use the same amount reference. They differ in the saved replies. Each loop iteration computes its own result.

Experiment. Simulate a second run by changing the reply in B03 only to "The minimum is ₹5,000.". Keep both references and IDs unchanged. Run again.

Expected output
B01 exact match: True
B03 exact match: True

Only B03 changes. Its stored reply now matches its reference. In a real comparison, keep the original replies and record the next set separately.

Checkpoint. What should stay fixed if you compare two versions of the assistant? Keep the questions, sources, expected behavior, and scoring rules fixed. Record each run’s replies and outcomes separately.

Step 6 — Check the evidence status before checking wording

Before comparing the wording, ask whether someone verified the evidence. Read != as “is different from.” If the evidence value differs from "resolved", the first branch prints NEEDS REVIEW. A human reviewer sets that value using the policy checks you already practiced.

Each colon starts an indented block. if tries the first condition. If it’s false, elif tries the next one, which looks for the reply in the accepted list. If neither condition applies, else prints the remaining outcome. Run this once with approved evidence, then change only the evidence decision.

Replace the code in the editor with this block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
case = {
    "source": "SV-2",
    "as_of": "2026-07-15",
    "evidence": "resolved",
    "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
    "accepted": ["The minimum is ₹5,000."],
}

print("Evidence:", case["source"], case["as_of"])
if case["evidence"] != "resolved":
    print("NEEDS REVIEW: evidence is unresolved")
elif case["reply"] in case["accepted"]:
    print("PASS: approved reference found")
else:
    print("NEEDS REVIEW: reply is unfamiliar")
Expected output
Evidence: SV-2 2026-07-15
PASS: approved reference found

This case already has a resolved source, and its reply matches an approved variant. The code uses the stored decision about evidence.

Experiment. Simulate an incomplete evidence review. Change only "evidence": "resolved" to "evidence": "unresolved" and run again. The source ID still records which policy the reviewer intended to use.

Expected output
Evidence: SV-2 2026-07-15
NEEDS REVIEW: evidence is unresolved

Checkpoint. Why is the identical reply held for review after that edit? The evidence decision comes first. A text match tells you what characters agree. The reviewer still needs to establish that the source governs the case.

Step 7 — Produce a readable evaluation report

Use the eight fictional cases above. A person assigned the judgments in the accepted and rejected lists by reading the replies and the policy. The program looks up those exact replies and sends unfamiliar wording to review. In B07, the reviewed response passes because it says the limit can’t be confirmed from the supplied evidence.

You need the same order of checks for all eight cases. Put the checks in a function, a reusable block of instructions. def assess(case): names the block and says it works with one case at a time. The indented instructions run whenever you call it.

Read the checks from top to bottom. If the source is unresolved, end the check there. Otherwise test the list of accepted replies, then the list of rejected replies. If you can’t find the wording in either list, ask for review. Each return stops that call and hands back a label and a reason, an ordered pair called a tuple. The line outcome, reason = assess(case) puts those two results into two names in that order.

The cards keep the dates, sources, and reviewed replies. Empty brackets [] mean there are no items in that list yet. The report loop calls assess for each card. After the dot in outcomes.append(outcome), append means “add this label to the end of the list.” Once the loop finishes, outcomes.count("PASS") counts the entries equal to PASS. The last two lines do the same for FAIL and NEEDS REVIEW, so you can see every kind of outcome.

Replace the code in the editor with this whole block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
def assess(case):
    if case["evidence"] != "resolved":
        return "NEEDS REVIEW", "evidence is unresolved"
    if case["reply"] in case["accepted"]:
        return "PASS", "reviewed acceptable reply"
    if case["reply"] in case["rejected"]:
        return "FAIL", "reviewed incorrect reply"
    return "NEEDS REVIEW", "reply has no reviewed label"


cases = [
    {
        "id": "B01", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹5,000.",
        "accepted": ["The minimum is ₹5,000."], "rejected": [],
    },
    {
        "id": "B02", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.",
        "accepted": ["Keep five thousand rupees in Standard Savings."],
        "rejected": [],
    },
    {
        "id": "B03", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "The minimum is ₹10,000.",
        "accepted": ["The minimum is ₹5,000."],
        "rejected": ["The minimum is ₹10,000."],
    },
    {
        "id": "B04", "as_of": "2026-06-15", "source": "SV-1",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "The minimum was ₹4,000.",
        "accepted": ["The minimum was ₹4,000."], "rejected": [],
    },
    {
        "id": "B05", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "No below-minimum fee applies.",
        "accepted": ["No below-minimum fee applies."], "rejected": [],
    },
    {
        "id": "B06", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "A ₹100 fee applies every day.",
        "accepted": ["A ₹100 monthly fee applies."],
        "rejected": ["A ₹100 fee applies every day."],
    },
    {
        "id": "B07", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "source": "SV-2",
        "evidence": "resolved",
        "reply": "I can't confirm that from the supplied policy.",
        "accepted": ["I can't confirm that from the supplied policy."],
        "rejected": [],
    },
    {
        "id": "B08", "as_of": "2026-08-03", "source": "FEE-A + FEE-B",
        "evidence": "unresolved",
        "reply": "The student fee waiver applies.",
        "accepted": [], "rejected": [],
    },
]

outcomes = []
print("Harbor Leaf Bank | HLB-SAV-1")
for case in cases:
    outcome, reason = assess(case)
    outcomes.append(outcome)
    print(case["id"], case["as_of"], case["source"], outcome, "-", reason)

print("PASS:", outcomes.count("PASS"))
print("FAIL:", outcomes.count("FAIL"))
print("NEEDS REVIEW:", outcomes.count("NEEDS REVIEW"))
Expected output
Harbor Leaf Bank | HLB-SAV-1
B01 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B02 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B03 2026-07-15 SV-2 FAIL - reviewed incorrect reply
B04 2026-06-15 SV-1 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B05 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B06 2026-07-15 SV-2 FAIL - reviewed incorrect reply
B07 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B08 2026-08-03 FEE-A + FEE-B NEEDS REVIEW - evidence is unresolved
PASS: 5
FAIL: 2
NEEDS REVIEW: 1

The questions and evidence excerpts are in the eight-case sheet. The program carries the case IDs, dates, and reviewed replies for the reporting exercise. B07's evidence is resolved for deciding which behavior is expected. The packet is complete for this exercise, and the expected behavior is to abstain. B08's policy fact remains unresolved. Check both reasons before combining the outcomes into any count.

Experiment. Change only B01's "reply" value to "Maintain five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.". Leave its accepted list alone and rerun.

Expected output
Harbor Leaf Bank | HLB-SAV-1
B01 2026-07-15 SV-2 NEEDS REVIEW - reply has no reviewed label
B02 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B03 2026-07-15 SV-2 FAIL - reviewed incorrect reply
B04 2026-06-15 SV-1 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B05 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B06 2026-07-15 SV-2 FAIL - reviewed incorrect reply
B07 2026-07-15 SV-2 PASS - reviewed acceptable reply
B08 2026-08-03 FEE-A + FEE-B NEEDS REVIEW - evidence is unresolved
PASS: 4
FAIL: 2
NEEDS REVIEW: 2

B01 moves from PASS to NEEDS REVIEW because the new wording is in neither reviewed list. The number of known failures stays at two. The change gives the reviewer another reply to read.

Checkpoint. Why do B01 and B08 share a label after the edit? B01 has reliable evidence and unfamiliar wording. A reviewer can accept it after checking the claim. B08 needs a policy decision before a factual verdict can be recorded. The reasons tell you where to investigate.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Build a reference answer set

Pretend you’re leaving instructions for another reviewer. On July 15 a customer asks for the Standard Savings minimum, and SV-2 §2 says it is ₹5,000. Write three replies you could use to explain your decision. One is your reference answer, one uses different words you’d accept, and one you’d reject. Record the source and date beside them.

Now write two checks a computer could get wrong. Show how requiring the exact reference could reject the answer you’d accept, and how checking for a single piece of text could let the wrong answer through.

Practice 2. Choose the governing evidence

It’s July 15, but the customer asks, “What minimum did I need on June 30?” You have the approved ₹4,000 policy through June 30 (SV-1 §2) and the approved ₹5,000 policy starting July 1 (SV-2 §2). You also find HELP-DRAFT, edited July 10 without approval, which suggests ₹3,000. The assistant says “₹5,000.”

Pick the document you would use, then label the reply. What would you do instead if two equally authoritative June policies both applied on June 30 and gave different amounts?

Practice 3. Handle unavailable and disputed answers

Packet 1 is the SV-2 balance and fee excerpt. It is silent about ATM limits. A customer asks for the daily ATM limit, and the assistant says “The limit is ₹20,000.” Write a test case with the question, source, an acceptable reply, and a label for a reply that properly abstains. Give the saved ₹20,000 reply a label. Then write a reply that includes “can’t confirm” but would still fail. Explain how a checker that looks only for those words could pass it by mistake.

Packet 2 is FEE-A and FEE-B. Both are approved and take effect on August 1. One grants the student waiver and the other denies it. A customer asks if the waiver applies August 3, and the assistant says “Yes.” Give the reply a label and explain what the policy owner needs to do.

Practice 4. Correct a benchmark without losing history

Imagine opening a results sheet and finding two verdicts for the same reply. Version HLB-SAV-1 has a July 15 minimum case linked to SV-2. One reviewer expected ₹4,000 and marked the ₹5,000 reply FAIL. Another reviewer accepted it. The guide only says “correct amount,” and the exported result has no date.

Write a corrected benchmark row another reviewer can use. Keep a note showing the old judgment, the new one, and why it changed. Then explain how you’d compare two assistant versions after this correction.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Reference “The Standard Savings minimum is ₹5,000.” Accept “Keep at least five thousand rupees in Standard Savings.” Cite SV-2 §2 and July 15, 2026, for both. Reject “The requirement is ₹10,000.” An exact match to the reference would reject the correct alternative. A rule that merely checks whether ₹5,000 occurs would accept “The minimum is ₹10,000, not ₹5,000,” even though it asserts the wrong requirement. Check what the sentence affirms.

Solution 2

Use SV-1. The question asks about June 30 and SV-1 includes that date. The ₹5,000 reply fails because the applicable minimum was ₹4,000. SV-2 applies the following day, and the edit date of the unapproved draft cannot establish policy. If two equally authoritative policies overlap and the register gives no precedence, mark NEEDS REVIEW, retain both documents, and ask the Savings Policy owner to resolve the overlap.

Solution 3

For the daily ATM limit question, cite SV-2 §2 and record that it gives no withdrawal limit. An acceptable reply is “I can’t confirm the daily ATM withdrawal limit from the supplied policy.” Label that abstention PASS. The saved ₹20,000 claim fails because the policy gives no support for the amount. “I can’t confirm the limit, but it’s ₹20,000” also fails because it still states an unsupported limit. A check that looks only for “can’t confirm” would give it a false pass.

For the student waiver, mark NEEDS REVIEW. Both sources appear to apply, so there’s no verified policy answer yet. Ask the policy owner to identify or publish the rule that governs August 3 and record its effective date. You could separately check whether the reply acknowledges the conflict if you wrote that expectation into the case.

Solution 4

Use a versioned row such as HLB-SAV-2 / B01. Record July 15, SV-2 §2, expected minimum ₹5,000, and the rule “states the Standard Savings minimum without an incompatible amount.” Label the saved ₹5,000 reply PASS. The audit note should record the v1 reference ₹4,000, the old FAIL label, the approved replacement reference, the revised PASS label, and the reason. The July case was linked to the wrong value. Keep the original v1 run and attach the correction as a v2 change. Run both assistant versions against v2's frozen cases before claiming one improved.

Knowledge Check

  1. For the July 15 case, identify the fact, one reference answer, and the label for a reply giving ₹10,000.
  2. Why might “You must maintain at least ₹5,000” pass a case whose reference uses “The minimum is ₹5,000”?
  3. A draft created July 10 mentions ₹3,000, while approved SV-2 began July 1. Which source governs a July 15 answer?
  4. A checker charges the fee at or below ₹5,000. It gives the right result at ₹4,999 and ₹5,001. What would you test next, and which result would expose the mistake?
  5. What label should the benchmark give a supported abstention for an ATM question and a factual answer under the unresolved August waiver conflict?
  6. How can a checker miss the error in “₹100 charged every day” when the policy says ₹100 monthly?
  7. How would putting the reserved release questions and answer key into the assistant's tuning data affect the evaluation?
  8. Two reported scores used different benchmark versions after a wrong reference was repaired. What comparison can you make next?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Fact. The Standard Savings minimum was ₹5,000 on July 15 under SV-2. “The minimum is ₹5,000” is a reference answer. A ₹10,000 claim receives FAIL.
  2. Equivalent meaning. Both require at least ₹5,000 for the same account. The reference is a reviewed way to say it. An exact match can miss equally valid wording.
  3. SV-2. It is approved and effective for that date. The draft's later edit time carries no policy authority.
  4. Test exactly ₹5,000. The checker would charge the fee at that balance. SV-2 charges it only below ₹5,000, so the expected answer is no below-minimum fee. The two earlier tests agree with both versions of the rule.
  5. PASS for the reviewed abstention, NEEDS REVIEW for the conflict. The bounded ATM case has known expected behavior. The waiver claim lacks a resolved source of truth.
  6. A keyword test can find the amount without checking its frequency. The reply’s policy claim converts a monthly charge to a daily charge. Review the relationship between the amount and the frequency.
  7. The score could exaggerate performance on fresh questions. If the bank used these examples to improve the assistant, it may do well on those same examples. Keep a separate set of reviewed cases for the release check and look for lightly reworded copies across the two sets.
  8. Rerun both assistant versions on the same corrected benchmark. Preserve the older reports with their version IDs. A change in labels and case coverage can change a score even when the assistant's behavior stays the same.

Independent Assignment

Go back to Step 7, select Copy Code, and replace the editor contents with the original block. In cases, copy an existing dictionary twice and put both copies after B08, before the closing square bracket. Keep a comma after each dictionary. Use the details below to update the two copies. Change HLB-SAV-1 to HLB-SAV-2 in the print line. In your notes, keep the full question and policy excerpt beside each ID.

  • B09, historical boundary. “Was the below-minimum fee due at exactly ₹4,000 on June 15?” Use SV-1 §2, which applies a ₹80 monthly fee only below ₹4,000. Use date 2026-06-15, source SV-1, evidence resolved, and reply No below-minimum fee applies. Put that exact reply in the accepted list and leave the rejected list empty.
  • B10, wording the checker hasn’t seen. “What minimum did Standard Savings require on July 15?” Use SV-2 §2, which requires ₹5,000. Use date 2026-07-15, source SV-2, evidence resolved, and reply You need to keep at least five thousand rupees in Standard Savings. Keep only The minimum is ₹5,000. in the accepted list and leave the rejected list empty for the first run.

Predict both labels, click Run, and write down the counts under HLB-SAV-2. Review B10 against the policy. If you accept the reply, add its exact text as a second item in B10’s accepted list. Keep the saved reply unchanged. Change the printed version to HLB-SAV-2.1, run again, and record the new counts beside the original ones. Explain what changed and what the new counts tell you about the assistant.

Check your assignment

The first run gives B09 PASS and B10 NEEDS REVIEW for unfamiliar wording. Its totals are 6 PASS, 2 FAIL, and 2 NEEDS REVIEW. B09 is exactly at the historical minimum. B10 says “at least five thousand rupees,” which gives the required minimum for the right account and date. After adding its exact words to the accepted set, the totals are 7 PASS, 2 FAIL, and 1 NEEDS REVIEW. B08 still needs a policy decision. Your review changed how the checker treats one reply. The assistant’s saved replies stayed the same, so the extra PASS tells you about the revised scoring.

Common Mistakes

  • Selecting the newest file automatically. Check approval, what the policy covers, and when it applied. Use the register to see whether one document replaces another.
  • Treating every unfamiliar reply as a failure. Separate reviewed errors from replies you have yet to judge. A paraphrase can be correct.
  • Guessing at a policy conflict. Keep the source IDs and ask the policy owner for a documented decision.
  • Using a keyword as the entire rubric. Check what the reply claims, especially thresholds, units, frequency, and negation.
  • Editing a previous result in place. Keep the original report, issue a documented benchmark revision, and run comparisons on aligned versions.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

M02-T01 showed how to choose a useful objective and record what failed. You can now decide what evidence belongs to a case, prepare multiple reference answers, and explain why a reviewer may need to abstain or hold a label for review. You built a small versioned benchmark with different kinds of questions and used it to record outcomes and their reasons.

The next topic in Module 2 is Offline, online and the evaluation lifecycle. You will decide where a saved benchmark fits before release, what real traffic can teach you afterward, and how to turn evidence into a release decision or follow-up. In a focused Quick Learning path, use Next Lesson to follow that path’s own sequence.
