Beginner · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Turn a broad instruction to score a reply into a rubric with a clear criterion.
  • Apply a binary policy check and a low, middle, or high completeness rating to the same reply.
  • Review full saved replies without seeing the system that produced them, and record each judgment with its response ID and evidence.
  • Distinguish N/A, missing evidence, and a failed answer.
  • Use a disputed reply to revise an anchor, then compare the original and revised judgments.

Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine you’re using Harbor Leaf Bank’s chat assistant to plan next month’s expenses. The reply gives you a fee of ₹100. You still don’t know whether you’ll pay it once or every month. At the bank, one reviewer gives the reply a high score for the right amount. Another gives it a low score for leaving out the timing. Their scores point to different things the bank could do next.

The customer asked what fee applies below the Standard Savings minimum on July 15, 2026. The full reply reads, “A ₹100 fee applies if your balance falls below ₹5,000.” The relevant policy, SV-2 section 2, says a ₹100 monthly fee applies below ₹5,000. No below-minimum fee applies at exactly ₹5,000.

Both reviewers can point to something real in the reply. In this chapter you’ll turn their observations into judgments the bank can reproduce and act on. The bank, policy, saved replies, and sample judgments are fictional. Allow about 4.5 hours for reading, practice, and the assignment.

Beginner Explanation

1. Ask one question at a time

Read the saved reply in the opening. It states the right fee. It never says whether the customer pays once, each week, or each month. Write those two observations on separate lines.

A criterion is one question you ask about the reply. A rubric is a guide that states those questions and tells reviewers how to give each result. Here are the two questions the bank will use.

  • Policy accuracy. Does the reply give the correct monthly fee amount for the situation, with every fee claim it makes consistent with the July policy? The amount is required. An omitted frequency is handled by the completeness check, while an explicit wrong frequency fails the accuracy check. Record PASS or FAIL. A judgment with two possible outcomes is a binary decision when the criterion applies and the evidence is available.
  • Completeness of fee details. Does the reply state the fee frequency and the condition that triggers the fee? Count which details appear. Check their accuracy separately. A reply can include both details and still give the wrong frequency.

Use the accuracy result to decide whether a claim needs correction. Use the completeness result to decide whether a customer still needs an explanation.

2. Describe what each score looks like

Make three places to put the replies based on what the reply explicitly includes. The fee amount is already covered by the first criterion. For this completeness scale, look for the frequency and the balance condition.

  • Low. The reply states neither detail. “The fee is ₹100” is a low example.
  • Middle. It states exactly one. “A monthly fee of ₹100 applies” gives the timing but leaves out the condition.
  • High. It states both. “The fee is ₹100 per month below ₹5,000” gives the timing and condition.

Each description and its example give a reviewer an anchor, something concrete to match a new reply against. The labels form an ordinal scale, which means there’s an order from low to high. Treat them as ordered categories. Two middle ratings don’t add up to a high rating.

Try two replies that both start “A ₹100 monthly fee applies.” End the first with “below the minimum” and the second with “under five thousand rupees.” The bank wants the cutoff stated in the answer. The first earns middle because it gives the timing without naming the cutoff. The second earns high because it gives the timing, the ₹5,000 cutoff, and the direction relative to it. Put both examples in the rubric so a reviewer knows how to handle an amount written in words.

3. Give reviewers the same evidence

Keep the question, applicable policy, and full reply together. Use a neutral response ID, such as R01, to match a judgment back to the exact reply. Hide the system or model labels until the reviewers have scored the answers independently. This is blind review for model identity. Reviewers still need the question and policy. Hiding those would make their job harder in a different way.

For each judgment, write an evidence note. Quote the words that support the rating and name any required detail that’s missing. To count an omission, read the entire reply. If you only saw a preview, ask for the full text before judging.

Compare the two reviewers’ sheets by response ID. If they disagree, read the notes and revisit the policy and the relevant criterion. Record the original scores and any later decision in separate places. If the rubric changes, give the changed version a name and apply it to all comparable replies before comparing those results.

4. Record why a score is unavailable

A customer asks, “What is the daily ATM withdrawal limit?” The full saved reply R04 is “I can’t confirm the daily ATM withdrawal limit from this savings policy.” Neither fee criterion applies to this question, so record N/A, or not applicable, for both. If you want to know whether the assistant handles the ATM question well, define a criterion for that task.

If the question is about fees and the team hasn’t found the applicable policy, mark fee accuracy NEEDS REVIEW. The criterion applies and the reviewer needs more evidence. If there’s no reply because the request timed out, record UNSCORABLE and track the execution failure. Keep each outcome visible and out of the count of decided accuracy judgments.

Worked Demonstration

The next three cards are saved fictional replies, shown in full. Score them in order without seeing a model name. Before reading each assessment, write one evidence note for fee accuracy and one for completeness.

Example 1. Score the amount and the explanation separately

User question. “What fee applies below the Standard Savings minimum on July 15, 2026?” The response ID is R01.

Approved reference. SV-2 section 2 requires a ₹100 monthly fee below ₹5,000.

Actual LLM response. “A ₹100 fee applies if your balance falls below ₹5,000.”

Assessment. Check accuracy first. “₹100” and “falls below ₹5,000” agree with the policy, so mark PASS. Read the full reply again for completeness. The threshold is there and the frequency is missing. One detail earns middle.

Failure classification. Missing fee frequency. Keep the amount and threshold, and ask the team to clarify the timing. This judgment covers one reply to one question.

Example 2. A complete answer can still give bad advice

User question. Use the same July fee question. The response ID is R02.

Approved reference. The same policy requires a monthly fee of ₹100 below ₹5,000.

Actual LLM response. “A ₹100 fee applies every week if your balance is below ₹5,000.”

Assessment. The reply states two details, so mark high for completeness. Compare “every week” with the monthly rule and mark FAIL for accuracy. If you only saw the completeness score, the reply would look good.

Failure classification. Wrong frequency. Flag it for correction. The high score explains which details were present and gives no basis for accepting the advice.

Example 3. Resolve a difference in scoring

User question. Use the same July fee question. The response ID is R03.

Approved reference. The policy is unchanged. The completeness anchor requires the frequency and the cutoff, including the direction relative to the cutoff.

Actual LLM response. “A ₹100 monthly fee applies if your balance goes under ₹5,000.”

Assessment. Both reviewers pass accuracy. Reviewer A writes “monthly” and gives middle. Reviewer B gives high and quotes two phrases. Check those phrases against R03. Both reviewers found “monthly,” and “goes under ₹5,000” is the other piece of evidence. It gives the direction and the exact cutoff. Count two details under the stated anchor and record high.

Failure classification. Preserve both original scores and add a separate high judgment with both quotes. If the old guide left the wording unclear, put this paraphrase in the next version and test it with the same replies. This resolves the disputed row. It doesn’t tell you how often reviewers will disagree on unseen wording.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Every activity is a standalone Python 3.10+ program with its own fictional data. You’ll make the judging decisions by reading the replies. Python checks the inputs or summarizes the judgments.

  1. Open Open Python Editor. The editor link appears next to every activity.
  2. Select Copy Code and paste the whole block into the editor yourself. Replace anything already in the code box.
  3. Click Run and compare the result with the first Expected output.
  4. Predict the experiment result. Make the one described edit, run again, and compare with the second Expected output.

Keep the spaces at the start of lines. If an edit causes an error, paste the original code and try again.

Step 1 — Retrieve the whole reply by ID

Start by finding the exact reply you’re about to review. Both replies answer the July fee question. The braces hold a dictionary, a set of names and values. Python uses a response ID as the name and the whole reply as its value. The equals sign = stores a value. replies[response_id] looks up the text under the stored ID. print() shows both arguments with a space between them.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
replies = {
    "R01": "A ₹100 fee applies if your balance falls below ₹5,000.",
    "R02": "A ₹100 fee applies every week if your balance is below ₹5,000.",
}
response_id = "R01"

print(response_id, replies[response_id])
Expected output
R01 A ₹100 fee applies if your balance falls below ₹5,000.

The ID points to the reply that omits the fee frequency.

Experiment. Change only response_id from "R01" to "R02". Predict which part of the reply will differ, then run.

Expected output
R02 A ₹100 fee applies every week if your balance is below ₹5,000.

Python looked up a different entry. The new reply states a frequency you can compare against the policy.

Checkpoint. Why store the ID beside a score? It tells another reviewer which exact reply you read. The lookup can’t decide whether the new claim is accurate.

Step 2 — Apply a binary decision to reviewed facts

Use R02’s full reply above. In this activity, a reviewer has entered two yes-or-no answers, one about the amount and one about the other claims. True means yes and False means no. and requires both answers to be yes. The colon and indented line show what Python runs when the if condition holds. else handles the other outcome.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
amount_matches = True
other_claims_match = False

if amount_matches and other_claims_match:
    print("Policy accuracy: PASS")
else:
    print("Policy accuracy: FAIL")
Expected output
Policy accuracy: FAIL

The amount is right, but “every week” contradicts the policy. One failed condition sends the decision to FAIL.

Experiment. Imagine a corrected reply that changes only “every week” to “every month.” Change the corresponding reviewer input, other_claims_match, to True and run again.

Expected output
Policy accuracy: PASS

Both conditions now hold. The program uses your judgment of the corrected reply. In a real review, save the corrected reply separately with its own ID and evidence note.

Checkpoint. Could this program find “every week” in raw text? It works with judgments already entered by a person. The reviewer needs to read and compare the claim.

Step 3 — Apply the three completeness anchors

Start from R01. The reviewer marked the condition present and the timing absent. elif means “otherwise, test this next.” or succeeds if at least one condition is true. The program first checks the pair for high, then checks for middle, then uses low for neither.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
timing_stated = False
cutoff_stated = True

if timing_stated and cutoff_stated:
    print("Completeness: HIGH")
elif timing_stated or cutoff_stated:
    print("Completeness: MIDDLE")
else:
    print("Completeness: LOW")
Expected output
Completeness: MIDDLE

The first test fails and the second succeeds because only the cutoff is present.

Experiment. Imagine adding “monthly” to R01 without changing its balance condition. Change only timing_stated to True and run again.

Expected output
Completeness: HIGH

Both details are now present, so the first branch supplies the rating. Completeness alone asks whether the details are stated. Step 2’s accuracy judgment still has to check that they are right.

Checkpoint. Would adding “weekly” change this completeness result? The frequency would still be present. The accuracy result would become FAIL.

Step 4 — Decide whether a criterion can be scored

Start with R04, the ATM reply. In its row, the three values after the ID mean “a reply arrived,” “this is a fee question,” and “the applicable fee policy is available,” in that order. A reply arrived, so the first value is true. It’s an ATM question, so the second is false and the program will record N/A without needing the third. Square brackets hold the list of rows, and each set of parentheses groups the values for one response. The loop gives each value a name so you can read if not fee_question as “if this isn’t a fee question.”

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
cases = [
    ("R04", True, False, False),
    ("R05", True, True, False),
    ("R06", False, True, True),
]

for response_id, reply_arrived, fee_question, policy_available in cases:
    if not reply_arrived:
        outcome = "UNSCORABLE"
    elif not fee_question:
        outcome = "N/A"
    elif not policy_available:
        outcome = "NEEDS REVIEW"
    else:
        outcome = "READY TO SCORE"
    print(response_id, outcome)
Expected output
R04 N/A
R05 NEEDS REVIEW
R06 UNSCORABLE

A reviewer marked R04 as an ATM reply. R05 answers a fee question but the applicable policy was unavailable. R06 is the attempt where no reply arrived.

Experiment. In the R05 entry, change only the last value, policy_available, from False to True. Run again.

Expected output
R04 N/A
R05 READY TO SCORE
R06 UNSCORABLE

R05 continues past the evidence check because the reviewer has found the policy. The other outcomes stay the same.

Checkpoint. Should you change R05 to PASS now? The evidence is available. A reviewer still has to use it to judge the reply.

Step 5 — Check that a quote belongs to the response

An evidence note can become detached when you sort or copy a review sheet. Use a short quote to check that the note points to the recorded reply. In Python, quote in reply checks whether those exact characters occur in the reply. A match gives you a place to start reading.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
replies = {
    "R01": "A ₹100 fee applies if your balance falls below ₹5,000.",
    "R02": "A ₹100 fee applies every week if your balance is below ₹5,000.",
}
response_id = "R02"
quote = "every week"

print("Response:", response_id)
if quote in replies[response_id]:
    print("Quote found:", quote)
else:
    print("REVIEW: quote not found in this reply")
Expected output
Response: R02
Quote found: every week

The quote occurs in R02. Compare it against “monthly” in the approved policy to justify the failure.

Experiment. Change only response_id to "R01" and keep the same quote. Run again.

Expected output
Response: R01
REVIEW: quote not found in this reply

R01 has a different full reply with no “every week.” Check the ID and the note before using the judgment.

Checkpoint. Would finding a quote prove the score was right? It only verifies that the exact characters are present. Read the surrounding sentence and the policy to see what they mean.

Step 6 — Pair scores by response ID

Two people return their review sheets in different orders. Looking up the ID in each dictionary gives you the scores for the same reply. for response_id in reviewer_a: visits the keys in the first dictionary. == compares the two selected labels.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
reviewer_a = {"R01": "MIDDLE", "R03": "MIDDLE"}
reviewer_b = {"R03": "HIGH", "R01": "MIDDLE"}

for response_id in reviewer_a:
    first = reviewer_a[response_id]
    second = reviewer_b[response_id]
    if first == second:
        outcome = "AGREE"
    else:
        outcome = "DISAGREE"
    print(response_id, first, second, outcome)
Expected output
R01 MIDDLE MIDDLE AGREE
R03 MIDDLE HIGH DISAGREE

The scores for R01 match even though R01 appears in different positions. The disagreement is about R03.

Experiment. In a practice copy, imagine reviewer A rereads R03 with the clarified anchor. Change only reviewer A’s R03 value to "HIGH" and run again.

Expected output
R01 MIDDLE MIDDLE AGREE
R03 HIGH HIGH AGREE

R03 now compares equal. The reply text and reviewer B’s score stayed the same. In an actual review, keep the two original sheets and record the reviewed score separately.

Checkpoint. If the two reviewers agree, has the score been proved correct? Both could misunderstand the same rule. Read their evidence and use the approved policy and rubric to check the decision.

Step 7 — Summarize two independent review sheets

Count agreement separately for each criterion on the same full replies. Each dictionary entry contains a pair of human judgments. accuracy_a, detail_a = reviewer_a[response_id] gives those two labels their own names. A continue line moves straight to the next response. Use it when both reviewers say a reply is outside the fee task. If only one reviewer says N/A, put the reply aside and resolve applicability before comparing its ratings.

The program adds one to a counter, a number that tracks how many times an event happened. Only rows scored by both reviewers enter these agreement counts. This example assumes both sheets have the same IDs and all other rows have decided scores.

Copy the block and click Run.

Open Python Editor 
reviewer_a = {
    "R01": ("PASS", "MIDDLE"),
    "R02": ("FAIL", "HIGH"),
    "R03": ("PASS", "MIDDLE"),
    "R04": ("N/A", "N/A"),
}
reviewer_b = {
    "R04": ("N/A", "N/A"),
    "R03": ("PASS", "HIGH"),
    "R02": ("FAIL", "HIGH"),
    "R01": ("PASS", "MIDDLE"),
}
paired = 0
accuracy_agrees = 0
completeness_agrees = 0
excluded = 0

for response_id in reviewer_a:
    accuracy_a, detail_a = reviewer_a[response_id]
    accuracy_b, detail_b = reviewer_b[response_id]
    if accuracy_a == "N/A" and accuracy_b == "N/A":
        excluded = excluded + 1
        print(response_id, "N/A")
        continue
    if accuracy_a == "N/A" or accuracy_b == "N/A":
        excluded = excluded + 1
        print(response_id, "REVIEW APPLICABILITY")
        continue
    paired = paired + 1
    if accuracy_a == accuracy_b:
        accuracy_agrees = accuracy_agrees + 1
    else:
        print(response_id, "accuracy:", accuracy_a, "vs", accuracy_b)
    if detail_a == detail_b:
        completeness_agrees = completeness_agrees + 1
    else:
        print(response_id, "completeness:", detail_a, "vs", detail_b)

print("Accuracy agreement:", accuracy_agrees, "of", paired)
print("Completeness agreement:", completeness_agrees, "of", paired)
print("Excluded from paired scores:", excluded)
Expected output
R03 completeness: MIDDLE vs HIGH
R04 N/A
Accuracy agreement: 3 of 3
Completeness agreement: 2 of 3
Excluded from paired scores: 1

The reviewers agree on accuracy for all three comparable replies, including the one that failed. They agree on completeness for two. R04 is an ATM question, so it stays visible without entering either total.

Experiment. Simulate reviewer B accidentally applying the fee rubric to R04. In reviewer B’s dictionary, change only R04’s pair from ("N/A", "N/A") to ("FAIL", "LOW"). Run again.

Expected output
R03 completeness: MIDDLE vs HIGH
R04 REVIEW APPLICABILITY
Accuracy agreement: 3 of 3
Completeness agreement: 2 of 3
Excluded from paired scores: 1

R04 now takes the second condition. Keep the same three comparable replies and ask the reviewers to resolve whether the fee criterion applies to R04.

Checkpoint. Did the disagreement on R04 make accuracy agreement drop? It is a disagreement about which question to score. Report it separately so the unchanged count can’t hide it.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Score a reply one criterion at a time

For the July fee question, a saved reply says “A ₹100 monthly fee applies.” Give an accuracy judgment and a completeness rating. For each, write the evidence and recommend one next action.

Practice 2. Keep the reason for a missing score

Review these three records. A asks for an ATM limit and received a full reply. B asks what fee applied in June, but the reviewer only has the July policy. C asks about the July fee, and the request timed out. For each, say what to record for the fee-accuracy criterion and what to investigate next.

Practice 3. Check a disagreement against the whole reply

R08 reads “When your balance falls below ₹5,000, you pay a ₹100 fee. It’s charged each month.” One reviewer wrote “₹100 fee” and rated it middle. Another rated it high. Write an evidence note and justify the rating. What else would you check if the first reviewer saw only the first sentence?

Practice 4. Decide what an agreement count means

Two reviewers agree on accuracy for all three July replies. They pass R01 and R03 and fail R02. They agree on completeness for only two. Another ATM reply is N/A on both sheets. Report the two agreement counts with their totals and the excluded count. Explain why “the assistant was right on three of three replies” would mislead the bank.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Accuracy is PASS. The amount is ₹100 and “monthly” matches the policy. Completeness is middle. Timing is stated, but the full reply never says below ₹5,000. Ask the team to add that condition while retaining the amount and frequency.

Solution 2

A is N/A because the fee criterion doesn’t apply to the ATM task. Define a separate criterion for ATM answers if the bank needs to judge them. B is NEEDS REVIEW because the reviewer needs the policy that applied in June. C is UNSCORABLE because there is no reply. Investigate the timeout and keep it out of the count of replies with a decided accuracy judgment.

Solution 3

Mark high. “Falls below ₹5,000” gives the condition and “It’s charged each month” gives the frequency. Confirm that both reviewers saw the same full text under R08. If one saw a preview, have them score the full reply. Revise the rubric only if a difference in the instructions remains after both reviewers see the same evidence.

Solution 4

Report accuracy agreement of three of three, completeness agreement of two of three, and one excluded ATM reply. Two policy judgments were passes and one was a failure. Agreement counts matching judgments, including matching failures. It cannot establish the assistant’s accuracy beyond these saved examples.

Knowledge Check

  1. A reply states “₹100 every week below ₹5,000.” What scores would it receive, and why?
  2. A reply says “A ₹100 fee is charged per month” and gives no cutoff. Which detail would move it up one level?
  3. Both reviewers see model names before judging replies. What would you change before repeating the review?
  4. The first reviewer’s note quotes “monthly” but the response under that ID says “weekly.” What would you check before accepting the note?
  5. Why is a missing June policy different from N/A on an ATM-limit question?
  6. Two reviewers pass the same reply using a policy that took effect after the date asked about. What does agreement establish here?
  7. An answer says “below the minimum” without a number, and the question never supplies the minimum. What rating is warranted if its frequency is stated?
  8. A team revises a middle anchor and wants to compare two versions of the assistant. What should the team do with the original score sheets and the revised rule?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Accuracy fails because the approved frequency is monthly. Completeness is high because a frequency and condition are both stated.
  2. Add that the fee applies below ₹5,000. The frequency already earns middle, and the condition adds the second required detail.
  3. Keep the same full replies, questions, and applicable policy. Use neutral response IDs and hide model labels until independent judgments have been saved.
  4. Check the ID, the full reply, and the exact evidence quoted. The note may be attached to a different reply or contain a transcription error.
  5. The June fee criterion applies, so a missing policy calls for further review. The ATM reply falls outside this fee criterion.
  6. It shows the reviewers reached the same judgment. They need the policy effective on the question’s date before the team can rely on the result.
  7. Middle. The frequency is present. The rubric requires a direction and the actual cutoff in the answer, so the incomplete condition doesn’t earn the second detail.
  8. Preserve the original scores and document the change. Apply the same revised rubric to both versions’ comparable replies and keep those results as a separate set.

Independent Assignment

Harbor Leaf’s reviewers need to decide whether the completeness guide handles thresholds written in words. Use the same July fee question and policy as R01. The new saved reply, R07, reads “A ₹100 monthly fee applies if your balance drops under five thousand rupees.” Both reviewers pass accuracy. Reviewer A rates it middle because the threshold isn’t written in digits. Reviewer B rates it high.

  1. Write one accuracy note and one completeness note for R07. Draft a revised cue for each of low, middle, and high. Make clear when a threshold written in words counts. Justify the score you would record.
  2. Start with the original Step 7 code. Add a line for R07 before the closing brace in each reviewer’s dictionary. Use the given judgments as pairs like the earlier entries and keep the commas.
  3. Run once and record the disagreements, both agreement totals, and the excluded count. Then simulate how the clarified anchor affects R07 alone. Change reviewer A’s R07 completeness rating to the score you would record and rerun. Leave R03 and the other entries unchanged so you can isolate R07’s effect.
  4. Point to the output line that changed and the one that still shows a disagreement. Explain why the assistant’s replies stayed the same. For a real comparison, save the original independent scores, label the revised rubric, and use it to rescore all comparable replies from both versions.
Check your assignment

Quote “₹100 monthly” for the amount and frequency. Quote “drops under five thousand rupees” for the direction and threshold. Record high. One revised set of anchors is low when neither frequency nor the full threshold condition appears, middle when exactly one appears, and high when both appear. Count an equivalent threshold in digits or words. Keep accuracy separate.

For the first run, add "R07": ("PASS", "MIDDLE"), to reviewer A and "R07": ("PASS", "HIGH"), to reviewer B. The program prints these lines in order.

  1. R03 completeness: MIDDLE vs HIGH
  2. R04 N/A
  3. R07 completeness: MIDDLE vs HIGH
  4. Accuracy agreement: 4 of 4
  5. Completeness agreement: 2 of 4
  6. Excluded from paired scores: 1

For the second run, set reviewer A’s R07 pair to ("PASS", "HIGH"). The program prints these lines in order.

  1. R03 completeness: MIDDLE vs HIGH
  2. R04 N/A
  3. Accuracy agreement: 4 of 4
  4. Completeness agreement: 3 of 4
  5. Excluded from paired scores: 1

The R07 disagreement goes away and the R03 disagreement remains. The same replies were used in both runs. The count changed because the reviewer applied a clearer rule, so it gives no evidence of a change in the assistant.

Common Mistakes

  • Scoring a general impression. Ask which criterion applies and quote the relevant words in the reply.
  • Promoting completeness to an accuracy verdict. A reply can state a wrong frequency clearly and still include all the details.
  • Scoring a preview or an unlabeled reply. Keep the full reply and response ID together.
  • Counting N/A as a failure. Report why it was excluded and keep missing evidence and execution failures separate.
  • Erasing a disagreement after reviewing it. Save the original scores and the reason for the final decision.
  • Calling matching scores proof of correctness. Check that reviewers used the applicable policy and rubric.

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Turn a small worksheet into JSON Lines, with a clear agreement about the fields and types.
  • Keep a case ID attached to the same question and a response ID attached to one captured reply.
  • Check required fields, value ranges, unique IDs, and source references.
  • Preserve old replies and scores when a verified label changes.
  • Create a version manifest that explains why the same replies can receive a different score.

Why This Lesson Matters

A teammate brings two reports to a Harbor Leaf Bank review. Yesterday one of two replies passed. Today both passed. You put the replies side by side and see the exact same wording in both reports. In the worksheet, though, the expected June fee changed from ₹80 to ₹0. Before crediting the chatbot, find out which policy supports that correction.

The question asks whether a customer with exactly ₹4,000 in Standard Savings owed a fee on June 30, 2026. The saved reply says no. The old answer key says ₹80, but the approved June policy charges ₹80 only below ₹4,000. Before the correction, the right reply failed the check.

You’ll preserve the old worksheet and score, make a corrected copy, and show how another reviewer could reproduce both results. The bank, records, and policy here are fictional. Allow about 4.5 hours for the worked examples, Python activities, and assignment. The chapter builds on the evidence and benchmark work in Ground truth, references and benchmarks and the field checks in Structured output and schema validation.

Beginner Explanation

1. Give each question a name that survives sorting

Suppose the June question sits on row 2. You sort the sheet by date, and now row 2 is a July question. A reviewer who wrote “row 2 failed” may now point to the wrong question. Give the June question its own name, FEE-001, and keep that name when you reorder the sheet or correct its answer key. That name is a stable case ID.

The same case can receive a different reply each time the team runs the assistant. Give each captured reply its own response ID. R-001 and R-003 can both refer back to FEE-001. Each response ID identifies only one capture. Store the question and expected behaviour in the dataset. In a separate run record, save the response ID, case ID, exact reply, assistant version, and dataset version used. A captured reply may include prose even if the scorer reads a numeric amount from it. Keep the full reply with the amount the scorer used.

The worksheet you deliberately maintain and check against sources is your golden dataset, or reference set. That name means reviewers intend to use it as the answer key. The mistake in the June case shows why the answer key still needs review.

2. Agree what every row means

A spreadsheet cell may show 80 as text. The scorer needs a whole number of rupees. If two people treat that cell differently, they can end up comparing different things.

Write down the required field names, their types, and the limits you expect. This agreement is a data contract. Its field layout is the schema. In this lesson each case has an ID, task, question, date, balance, source reference, and expected fee. The date and task are metadata, or details about the case that help you interpret the question and label. Balance and expected fee must be whole numbers. The practice limits are 0 through 1,000,000 rupees for balance and 0 through 1,000 rupees for expected fee.

To exchange the worksheet, write each case as one JSON object on its own line. This format is JSON Lines, or JSONL. The converter must turn the two numeric cells into integers. Once they’re JSON numbers, a later validator can detect a bad string, a missing field, or a value outside the agreed range.

3. Record where a label came from

A label of 80 in a cell is hard to trust if you don’t know which fee rule was used. Keep the source reference and the date beside the label. The record of where your evidence came from is called provenance.

  • SV-1#2. Section 2 of the approved Standard Savings policy in effect January 1 through June 30, 2026. The minimum was ₹4,000. An ₹80 monthly fee applied below that balance.
  • SV-2#2. Section 2 of the approved policy effective July 1, 2026. The minimum is ₹5,000. A ₹100 monthly fee applies below that balance.

Read the two policy dates before you read either amount. June 30 is the last day of SV-1. A balance of exactly ₹4,000 is at that policy’s minimum, so the expected fee is zero. Now try citing SV-2#2 instead. The section exists in the register, but its July start date rules it out for this question. A reference check can find a section. A reviewer still needs to check that it applied and supports the label.

4. Keep a record of changes

Save the original dataset as fees-v1 and the corrected copy as fees-v2. Store a short note with the new version listing its name, its parent, the schema version, what changed, and why. This note is a version manifest. For the June correction it should name FEE-001, the old value 80, the new value 0, and the source section that explains the change.

The original run belongs with the dataset and scorer it actually used. Keep it and add a separate report for scoring the same saved replies against the corrected labels. Saving new entries without rewriting past entries is called append-only. Keeping the artifacts separate lets a teammate answer two questions. What did we report then? What would those exact replies score with the corrected answer key?

In the two-case example, the June reply fails against 80 and the July reply passes against 100. That gives one pass out of two. Correct the June label to zero and both replies pass. The change from one of two to two of two comes from the label correction. Use one reviewed dataset version and one scoring rule for both assistants before trying to compare their performance.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Make a worksheet row readable by a program

User question. “Did a fee apply at a balance of ₹4,999 on July 15?” It appears in case FEE-002.

Approved reference. SV-2#2 gives a ₹100 fee below ₹5,000. The worksheet stores “4999” and “100” in its balance and expected-fee cells.

Actual LLM response. A saved reply says “A ₹100 monthly fee applies.”

Assessment. Start with the cell under the balance heading. The program reads it as the text "4999". Convert it to the integer 4999, then do the same for the expected fee so "100" becomes 100. Keep FEE-002, the question, its date, and SV-2#2 in the record. Write the full record as one JSONL line. The unquoted numbers let a reader check their types without guessing from their appearance.

Failure classification. Leaving the amounts as strings is a field-type error, even if the numbers look right on the screen. Fix the mapping before scoring. Correct conversion only shows that the row can be read under the contract.

Example 2. Find a problem that valid JSON can hide

User question. “Did a fee apply at exactly ₹4,000 on June 30?” It appears in case FEE-001.

Approved reference. SV-1#2 was in effect on that date. The team has an approved source register with that exact section reference.

Actual LLM response. The saved reply says “No below-minimum fee applies.” In a practice copy, a second case uses FEE-001 again and cites SV-X#9.

Assessment. Both records could parse as JSON and carry the fields you expect. Compare the case IDs and find that two rows use the same name. Look up the second source and find no matching reference. Stop before joining replies to those rows, because the scorer can’t choose a unique case or trace the second label.

Failure classification. Report a duplicate ID and unknown source. Determine whether the second row is a duplicate copy or a separate case. Remove a duplicate copy from the revision, or give a separate case its own ID and verified evidence. These checks don’t establish whether the surviving label agrees with policy.

Example 3. Explain a score change without a new reply

User question. Compare the saved June and July replies after auditing the answer key. The June balance is exactly ₹4,000 and the July balance is ₹4,999.

Approved reference. SV-1#2 gives zero at the June minimum. SV-2#2 gives ₹100 below the July minimum.

Actual LLM response. R-001 says “No below-minimum fee applies.” R-002 says “A ₹100 monthly fee applies.” The scorer uses amounts of 0 and 100 recorded from those replies.

Assessment. On fees-v1, compare 0 with the old June label of 80 and 100 with the July label of 100. Only July passes. Keep both replies and the same comparison rule. On fees-v2, change the June label to 0. The June comparison now passes, and July stays a pass.

Failure classification. The old label was wrong. Save the correction, publish the new manifest alongside the worksheet, and report the two counts with their dataset versions. The assistant’s replies did not change. If you want to compare two assistant versions, score both under the same reviewed dataset version.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Each example is a complete Python 3.10+ program with fictional data inside it. The worksheet slice is shown as text, so you can use it without spreadsheet software. The examples print JSONL or reports in the editor. They don’t call a model or change a file.

  1. Select Open Python Editor beside the activity to open the editor.
  2. Select Copy Code in the lesson and paste the entire block yourself, replacing whatever is already in the editor.
  3. Click Run and compare the result with the first Expected output.
  4. Predict the experiment result, make the specified edit, and run again. Check the second Expected output.

Keep indentation when you paste. If an edit causes an error, paste the original block and run it again before retrying the change.

Step 1 — Find a question after the sheet is reordered

You’ll compare a physical row number with a lookup by ID. Square brackets hold an ordered list. Each pair in parentheses contains the case ID and a short question. cases[0] reads the first item because Python starts counting positions at zero. A for loop visits each pair and names the two values. The comparison == checks whether the current ID matches the one you want.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

cases = [
    ("FEE-001", "June 30 boundary"),
    ("FEE-002", "July 15 fee"),
]
reverse_order = False
if reverse_order:
    cases.reverse()

print("First row:", cases[0][0])
for case_id, question in cases:
    if case_id == "FEE-001":
        print("Lookup:", case_id, question)
Expected output
First row: FEE-001
Lookup: FEE-001 June 30 boundary

The same case happens to be first and to match your ID.

Experiment. Change only reverse_order to True. Run again. reverse() flips the order of the list.

Expected output
First row: FEE-002
Lookup: FEE-001 June 30 boundary

The first row now points to July. The lookup still finds the June question because the ID travels with it.

Checkpoint. Which identifier belongs in a saved judgment? Keep the case ID with the response ID. A row number can change when someone sorts the sheet.

Step 2 — Convert worksheet cells to JSONL

The worksheet slice below is in CSV, text with a header row and comma-separated cells. Triple quotes hold the whole worksheet as one string. StringIO lets the CSV reader read that string as if it were an open sheet of text. csv.DictReader uses the header names as dictionary keys. The loop uses int() to convert the two numeric cells. json.dumps() makes JSON text from one record. Each print() writes one whole JSON object on a line.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

import csv
import json
from io import StringIO

sheet = """case_id,task,question,as_of,balance_rupees,source_ref,expected_fee_rupees
FEE-001,monthly_fee,June boundary fee?,2026-06-30,4000,SV-1#2,80
FEE-002,monthly_fee,July fee?,2026-07-15,4999,SV-2#2,100
"""

for row in csv.DictReader(StringIO(sheet)):
    row["balance_rupees"] = int(row["balance_rupees"])
    row["expected_fee_rupees"] = int(row["expected_fee_rupees"])
    print(json.dumps(row))
Expected output
{"case_id": "FEE-001", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "June boundary fee?", "as_of": "2026-06-30", "balance_rupees": 4000, "source_ref": "SV-1#2", "expected_fee_rupees": 80}
{"case_id": "FEE-002", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "July fee?", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "balance_rupees": 4999, "source_ref": "SV-2#2", "expected_fee_rupees": 100}

The balances and fees are JSON numbers without quotes. The source IDs and dates remain strings. Notice that the old June label is still present. The converter copies the values under the schema, so policy review is a separate step.

Experiment. Change only the last cell of the FEE-001 CSV line from 80 to 0. Run again.

Expected output
{"case_id": "FEE-001", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "June boundary fee?", "as_of": "2026-06-30", "balance_rupees": 4000, "source_ref": "SV-1#2", "expected_fee_rupees": 0}
{"case_id": "FEE-002", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "July fee?", "as_of": "2026-07-15", "balance_rupees": 4999, "source_ref": "SV-2#2", "expected_fee_rupees": 100}

Only the converted label changes. In a real review, save the corrected rows as a new version and record the evidence for the change.

Checkpoint. Does writing 0 without quotes prove the fee is zero? It shows the expected type. The June source is what supports the label.

Step 3 — Check field types and ranges

A row can contain every required field and still have values the scorer can’t use. Here you’ll check the two numeric fields. In type(fee) is int, type() looks up the kind of value and is int requires the exact whole-number type. That also excludes yes-or-no values, even though Python can count True as 1 in some comparisons. and makes Python check the range only after the value passes the type check. The <= comparison includes each endpoint.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

row = {"balance_rupees": 4000, "expected_fee_rupees": "80"}
balance = row.get("balance_rupees")
fee = row.get("expected_fee_rupees")

print("Balance valid:", type(balance) is int and 0 <= balance <= 1_000_000)
print("Fee valid:", type(fee) is int and 0 <= fee <= 1000)
Expected output
Balance valid: True
Fee valid: False

The balance is an integer within the allowed range. The quote marks around 80 make it a string. row.get(...) returns None for a missing key, which would also fail the type check. The underscore in 1_000_000 groups the digits for reading.

Experiment. Remove the quotes around "80" and leave the rest of the row alone. Run again.

Expected output
Balance valid: True
Fee valid: True

An integer 80 passes the format check. It is still the wrong label for the June boundary case. A schema can tell you which values the format accepts. Use the approved rule to judge the label.

Checkpoint. Would an integer fee of 1001 pass? It meets the type rule but falls outside the practice range.

Step 4 — Find duplicate IDs and unknown references

Here the list has two entries with the same case ID. Check that each ID appears only once and each source resolves to the supplied register. A set keeps distinct values. set() starts one with no items. case_id in seen tests whether the current ID has appeared and seen.add(case_id) remembers it. The other membership check looks up the source reference.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

sources = {"SV-1#2", "SV-2#2"}
rows = [
    ("FEE-001", "SV-1#2"),
    ("FEE-001", "SV-X#9"),
]
seen = set()

for case_id, source_ref in rows:
    if case_id in seen:
        print("Duplicate ID:", case_id)
    seen.add(case_id)
    if source_ref not in sources:
        print("Unknown source:", source_ref)
Expected output
Duplicate ID: FEE-001
Unknown source: SV-X#9

The second row repeats the ID, so it can't be reliably matched to a response. Its cited section is also missing from the source register.

Experiment. Change only "SV-X#9" to "SV-1#2". Run again.

Expected output
Duplicate ID: FEE-001

Now the source exists. The ID is still repeated, so the row remains blocked. In a real dataset, verify the date and policy meaning before accepting the new reference.

Checkpoint. Should you give the duplicate a new ID automatically? First check whether it’s an accidental copy. A genuinely different question needs its own ID.

Step 5 — Store a new reply without replacing the old one

Imagine you’re asked to explain a score from yesterday, but someone pasted today’s wording over the reply you scored. Even if both replies say there was no fee, you’ve lost the exact words behind the old score. Give the second capture its own ID, R-003, and keep both linked to FEE-001.

The dictionary uses a response ID as each key. If the proposed ID already exists, hold the incoming record. Otherwise, assignment to history[new_id] adds a new entry. The loop uses history.items() to read each ID with its record. It gives the four values in each record separate names so you can see the case, version, assistant, and exact reply.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

history = {
    "R-001": ("FEE-001", "fees-v1", "assistant-a", "No below-minimum fee applies."),
}
new_id = "R-003"
new_record = ("FEE-001", "fees-v1", "assistant-a", "No fee at that balance.")

if new_id in history:
    print("Refused duplicate response ID:", new_id)
else:
    history[new_id] = new_record
    print("Added:", new_id)

for response_id, record in history.items():
    case_id, version, assistant, reply = record
    print(response_id, case_id, version, assistant, "|", reply)
Expected output
Added: R-003
R-001 FEE-001 fees-v1 assistant-a | No below-minimum fee applies.
R-003 FEE-001 fees-v1 assistant-a | No fee at that balance.

Both records point to one question. The separate IDs keep the captures distinct, including their wording.

Experiment. Change only new_id to "R-001". Run again.

Expected output
Refused duplicate response ID: R-001
R-001 FEE-001 fees-v1 assistant-a | No below-minimum fee applies.

The guard catches the collision. Without it, assigning a value to an existing key would replace the original record.

Checkpoint. Is this a permanent audit log? The code checks the rule in memory. An actual team must keep the run artifacts somewhere that preserves old entries and their versions.

Step 6 — Rescore the same replies against two versions

The saved June amount is 0 and the July amount is 100. Compare each with the original labels. June fails and July passes, giving one of two. On the corrected copy, change just the June label to zero and both pass. The loop below counts those passes. A function is a named block of work. def score(labels, replies): accepts a label dictionary and a reply list. Each time the amount matches, add one to passes. return hands back the count.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

def score(labels, replies):
    passes = 0
    for case_id, amount in replies:
        if amount == labels[case_id]:
            passes = passes + 1
    return passes


replies = [("FEE-001", 0), ("FEE-002", 100)]
old_labels = {"FEE-001": 80, "FEE-002": 100}
new_labels = old_labels.copy()
new_labels["FEE-001"] = 0

print("fees-v1:", score(old_labels, replies), "of", len(replies))
print("fees-v2:", score(new_labels, replies), "of", len(replies))
Expected output
fees-v1: 1 of 2
fees-v2: 2 of 2

copy() makes a separate dictionary here, where both values are integers. len(replies) gives the size of the same saved reply list. Only the June label changes which comparison succeeds.

Experiment. Set new_labels["FEE-001"] to 80 instead of 0. Run again to simulate copying the worksheet without correcting the label.

Expected output
fees-v1: 1 of 2
fees-v2: 1 of 2

Both dictionaries now hold the same labels. A new version name alone changes no score. In a change log, distinguish a label correction from packaging a copy.

Checkpoint. If a score rises after a label correction, what would it take to show the assistant got better? Compare its old and new replies using the same reviewed dataset and rule.

Step 7 — Validate a revision and explain its score change

Start from two converted cases and two captured replies. Copy each case dictionary before editing the June label. Check required types and ranges, duplicate IDs, and whether every source reference is in the register. Save a manifest only for the valid revision. In this exercise the register is embedded in the program, and a reviewer has already checked the June policy.

In sorted(required - row.keys()), the minus sign finds required fields that are missing. Sorting makes the reported order predictable. continue moves to the next row if a field is missing, so the program doesn’t read it. errors.append(...) adds a message to the end of a list. A loop builds a lookup from case ID to expected fee, then the scorer compares only the numeric amounts supplied with the saved replies. It uses exactly the same replies for both versions.

Select Copy Code, paste the block into the editor, and click Run.

Open Python Editor

import json


def validate(rows, sources):
    required = {"case_id", "task", "question", "as_of", "balance_rupees",
                "source_ref", "expected_fee_rupees"}
    errors = []
    seen = set()
    for row in rows:
        missing = sorted(required - row.keys())
        if missing:
            errors.append("Missing fields: " + ", ".join(missing))
            continue
        case_id = row["case_id"]
        for field in ("case_id", "task", "question", "as_of", "source_ref"):
            if type(row[field]) is not str or not row[field].strip():
                errors.append("Expected non-empty text: " + field)
        if type(case_id) is str:
            if case_id in seen:
                errors.append("Duplicate case ID: " + case_id)
            seen.add(case_id)
        source_ref = row["source_ref"]
        if type(source_ref) is str and source_ref not in sources:
            errors.append("Unknown source: " + source_ref)
        for field, maximum in (("balance_rupees", 1_000_000),
                               ("expected_fee_rupees", 1000)):
            value = row[field]
            if type(value) is not int or not 0 <= value <= maximum:
                errors.append("Invalid whole-rupee field: " + field)
    return errors


def score(rows, captured):
    labels = {}
    for row in rows:
        labels[row["case_id"]] = row["expected_fee_rupees"]
    passes = 0
    for response_id, case_id, reply, amount in captured:
        if amount == labels[case_id]:
            passes = passes + 1
    return passes


sources = {"SV-1#2", "SV-2#2"}
original = [
    {"case_id": "FEE-001", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "June boundary fee?",
     "as_of": "2026-06-30", "balance_rupees": 4000, "source_ref": "SV-1#2",
     "expected_fee_rupees": 80},
    {"case_id": "FEE-002", "task": "monthly_fee", "question": "July fee?",
     "as_of": "2026-07-15", "balance_rupees": 4999, "source_ref": "SV-2#2",
     "expected_fee_rupees": 100},
]
captured = [
    ("R-001", "FEE-001", "No below-minimum fee applies.", 0),
    ("R-002", "FEE-002", "A ₹100 monthly fee applies.", 100),
]
revised = []
for row in original:
    revised.append(row.copy())
first = revised[0]
first["expected_fee_rupees"] = 0

errors = validate(original, sources) + validate(revised, sources)
if errors:
    for error in errors:
        print(error)
    print("Revision rejected before scoring")
else:
    old_passes = score(original, captured)
    new_passes = score(revised, captured)
    manifest = {
        "dataset": "fees-v2", "parent": "fees-v1", "schema": 1,
        "case_id": first["case_id"], "old_fee_rupees": original[0]["expected_fee_rupees"],
        "new_fee_rupees": first["expected_fee_rupees"], "source": first["source_ref"],
        "reason": "June boundary is at the minimum", "replay": "saved R-001 and R-002",
    }
    print(json.dumps(manifest))
    print("fees-v1:", old_passes, "of", len(captured))
    print("fees-v2:", new_passes, "of", len(captured))
Expected output
{"dataset": "fees-v2", "parent": "fees-v1", "schema": 1, "case_id": "FEE-001", "old_fee_rupees": 80, "new_fee_rupees": 0, "source": "SV-1#2", "reason": "June boundary is at the minimum", "replay": "saved R-001 and R-002"}
fees-v1: 1 of 2
fees-v2: 2 of 2

The manifest points to the original version, evidence, and saved replies. Both scores stay visible. Passing the field and reference checks allows this replay. The labels depend on the reviewer’s separate reading of the policy.

Experiment. Change only first["expected_fee_rupees"] = 0 to first["expected_fee_rupees"] = -1 and run again.

Expected output
Invalid whole-rupee field: expected_fee_rupees
Revision rejected before scoring

The integer −1 fails the range rule. The program stops before emitting a successful manifest or a revised score. Keep the old report and correct the proposed revision before comparing scores.

Checkpoint. What is the limit of this validator? It checks the named fields and references. It assumes the captured replies are correctly linked to known cases and leaves policy applicability and label accuracy to the reviewer.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Recover the case after a sort

A note says “row 2 failed.” In the old order row 2 was FEE-001. In the sorted sheet row 2 is FEE-002. R-001 and R-003 are two replies to FEE-001. Rewrite the note so a teammate can find the exact reply, assuming the reviewer meant the earlier capture. List the other records you need to reproduce the verdict.

Practice 2. Separate format errors from evidence errors

Assume two full rows exist. Both have case ID FEE-001. The second row has "balance_rupees": "4000" and a source reference of SV-X#9. Its expected fee is the number 0. List the errors a validator can find. What must a reviewer still establish after these errors are repaired?

Practice 3. Choose the applicable policy

A record says a customer with exactly ₹4,000 owed ₹80 on June 30, 2026. It cites SV-2#2, which exists in the register. Explain why the case can pass the reference check and still fail source review. Give the corrected source and label.

Practice 4. Explain a report that looks better

The same two captured amounts are 0 and 100. The original labels are 80 and 100. The revised labels are 0 and 100. Work out both scores, then write what belongs in the revision manifest. A teammate says the assistant improved. What comparison would let you test that claim?

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Write “R-001 for FEE-001 failed under fees-v1.” The case ID finds the June question and R-001 selects its first captured reply. Retrieve that exact reply and the amount the scorer used, the original dataset version and policy reference, and the original scoring rule. A different capture under R-003 could contain different wording or an amount that scores differently.

Solution 2

The duplicate ID prevents a unique case lookup. The balance is text where the contract requires an integer. The source reference doesn’t exist in the register. Check whether the duplicate is an accidental copy and convert the balance only after verifying the cell. Once it has a documented source, a reviewer still needs to verify that source covers the case’s account, date and fee question and supports the label of zero.

Solution 3

SV-2#2 is a real section in the practice register. It became effective July 1, so it doesn’t govern June 30. Use SV-1#2. The balance equals the minimum, and SV-1 charges only below it, so the correct expected fee is 0.

Solution 4

The original score is one of two because 0 differs from 80 and 100 equals 100. The corrected score is two of two because 0 now equals 0 and the July comparison stays the same. Record the version and parent, schema version, case ID, old and new values, applicable source, and reason for the correction. Keep the original report and say which replies were replayed. To test whether the assistant improved, use comparable captures of both assistant versions and score them against the same reviewed dataset and rule.

Knowledge Check

  1. A teammate renames FEE-001 when correcting just its label. What could happen to earlier response records?
  2. The expected-fee cell is “100” and its converted JSON still has quotes around 100. What should you check?
  3. Two rows have different wording but the same case ID. What must you establish before changing an ID?
  4. A reference exists, but the policy started one day after the case date. What can the validator conclude and what can the reviewer conclude?
  5. An assistant gives identical wording in two separate captures. Why keep two response IDs?
  6. The revised label is an integer −1. What should happen before any revised score is reported?
  7. The same replies score higher against a new answer key. Which artifact should you inspect before attributing the change to the assistant?
  8. What would you save so a teammate can reproduce yesterday’s score and also compare it with a corrected replay today?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Old captures still point to FEE-001. Renaming it could break the link and obscure that both versions test the same question. Keep the ID for a label correction.
  2. The value is still text. Check whether the converter turned that numeric field into an integer before serializing the row.
  3. Determine whether the rows are accidental duplicates or distinct cases. Distinct cases need unique IDs. Extra copies must not make one question count twice.
  4. The validator can confirm a source reference exists. The reviewer should reject its use for this date and check the policy effective when the case occurred.
  5. Each ID links to one capture. Its run metadata may differ even if the wording coincides.
  6. The range check should reject the revision before scoring. Keep the old report available while investigating the bad value.
  7. Inspect the manifest and case labels. If the capture and rule stayed the same, the score change reflects what the answer key accepts.
  8. Keep the original cases and labels, source section, exact captured replies with IDs, scoring rule and original report. Record the corrected dataset version and replay as separate artifacts.

Independent Assignment

A teammate corrected the June fee to zero and now needs to verify the source reference before releasing the revision. Keep the two original replies and all original rows unchanged. Use the code from Step 7.

  1. Paste Step 7 into a fresh editor. Insert the line first["source_ref"] = "SV-X#9" immediately after the assignment of the corrected fee. Run it. Record both output lines and explain what kept the replay from running.
  2. Change only that new line so it assigns "SV-2#2". Run again. Record the manifest and both scores. Decide whether you would accept the revision after reading the June case and the cited policy.
  3. Change the same line to assign "SV-1#2". Run again. Point to the date and policy wording that support zero. Keep both version names and scores in your note to the team. Explain that the replies and scoring rule stayed fixed, while the expected June fee changed from ₹80 to ₹0.
Check your assignment

The first run prints these lines.

  1. Unknown source: SV-X#9
  2. Revision rejected before scoring

The second run prints these lines.

  1. {"dataset": "fees-v2", "parent": "fees-v1", "schema": 1, "case_id": "FEE-001", "old_fee_rupees": 80, "new_fee_rupees": 0, "source": "SV-2#2", "reason": "June boundary is at the minimum", "replay": "saved R-001 and R-002"}
  2. fees-v1: 1 of 2
  3. fees-v2: 2 of 2

The reference exists, so the program reports a score. The cited policy applies from July 1 and doesn’t support the June label. Hold that revision. The last run prints the same three lines as the second run, with "source": "SV-1#2" replacing "source": "SV-2#2" in the manifest. Verify that section and keep the original report. The approved June boundary rule supports zero, and only the label changed the pass count. The same two replies were replayed in all comparisons that reached scoring.

Common Mistakes

  • Using row position as identity. Store stable case and response IDs before anyone sorts or filters the worksheet.
  • Treating valid JSON as a valid dataset. Check the fields, types, ranges, IDs, and references before scoring.
  • Treating a known source as the right source. Verify the account, effective date, and rule it supplies.
  • Replacing old records with corrected data. Preserve the earlier report and record the reason for the new version.
  • Calling a corrected score a model improvement. Compare assistants against the same reviewed answer key and scoring rule.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Use stable IDs to connect named cases with exact captured replies. Convert worksheet records under a clear data contract and validate the result before scoring. Keep each label traceable to its source. When a label changes, record why in a new manifest and preserve earlier reports and captures. Replaying the same replies makes the effect of the revision visible.
