Intermediate · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Write instructions for reviewers who label a case independently.
  • Resolve a disagreement using the full question, the applicable source, and a recorded reason.
  • Generate draft cases from a policy without treating proposed labels as reviewed truth.
  • Decide which drafts to accept, hold for review, or reject.
  • Record where a draft came from and what permission covers its reuse.

Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine you keep exactly the balance your bank asks for. The assistant says you won’t owe a fee, but the team’s test marks that reply wrong. At Harbor Leaf Bank, one reviewer filled in “fee due” in the answer key and another wrote “no fee.” Before anyone changes the assistant, check what the policy says about a balance right at the minimum.

The question is about a Standard Savings account with exactly ₹5,000 on July 15, 2026. Section 2 of the approved July policy, SV-2#2, says the monthly fee of ₹100 applies below ₹5,000. Put the customer’s balance beside that word. Exactly ₹5,000 is at the minimum. A label that says fee due would make a correct “no fee” reply fail the test.

The bank, policy, generated drafts, and reviewer records are fictional. The chapter builds on Rubrics and a first human evaluation. If you’re publishing reviewed cases to a versioned dataset, first use Golden schemas, provenance and versioning. Allow about six hours for demonstrations, Python experiments, and practice.

Beginner Explanation

1. Give reviewers the same question and the same rule

Imagine you hand someone a printed question and ask them to “mark it right.” They may judge the wording, while you wanted them to check the fee. Instead, tell each reviewer what decision the label represents. Supply the same case ID, account, date, balance if known, and policy excerpt.

Here the label describes what the correct answer should say for the case. It belongs to the case. A later verdict on a particular assistant reply belongs to that captured reply. Adding a label or evidence note to a case is annotation. These instructions keep everyone on the same task.

  • FEE_DUE. Use when the verified July Standard Savings balance is below ₹5,000. Record the approved fee of ₹100 per month.
  • NO_FEE. Use at ₹5,000 or above. Record that no below-minimum fee applies.
  • NEEDS_REVIEW. Use when the balance or applicable policy is missing or unclear. Record what would let you decide. Keep the case out of the scored set while it is unresolved.

Ask each reviewer to record a label and the words from the policy that support it before they see the other reviewer's decision. These are independent labels. They give you a record of where people could interpret the instructions differently. Independent reviewers can still make the same mistake, so agreement alone gives no guarantee that a label is correct.

2. Resolve the disagreement from the evidence

For case S-02 at ₹5,000, reviewer A reads “below” as “at or below” and chooses FEE_DUE. Reviewer B chooses NO_FEE and cites the strict cutoff. Show the full case and approved policy to a designated reviewer who can resolve the disagreement. Have them compare the notes, record a final label and reason, and keep the original labels.

This process is adjudication, sometimes called arbitration. The adjudicator should explain the decision by reference to the case and policy. When the source itself is unclear, keep the case unresolved and ask the policy owner. Two votes for one label can’t settle a policy that says something different.

If reviewers keep making the same mistake, change the instructions. Add a worked example at exactly ₹5,000. Keep a record of which instruction version was used and recheck any reviewed labels affected by the change.

3. Make more draft cases from one approved source

Start with the policy sentence and pick balances just below, at, and just above the cutoff. Use ₹4,999, ₹5,000 and ₹5,001. Write a customer question for each. Include the account, date, balance, source, and a proposed label in each draft. This is structured generation because you’re asking for the same fields every time. You can create drafts with a small program or ask a model for candidates. In this chapter Python supplies the fictional drafts.

Cases created deliberately for practice or testing are synthetic data. Three invented balances help test the edge of this rule. They don’t tell you how often actual customers ask those questions. A draft can introduce an invented source, a different account, or a wrong proposed label. A neat table is only the start of review.

Imagine S-01 comes back a month later with a note that says “from the bank’s website.” Another reviewer can’t tell which policy was used or whether the label was checked. Save SV-2#2, the effective date, how the case was made, and who reviewed it. That record of the case’s history is its provenance.

Then check what you’re allowed to reuse. A public policy could be readable while its reuse terms remain unclear. Record the permission or license, the terms that say what you can copy or share, and keep a reference to those terms alongside the case. Here the bank’s fictional permission covers these excerpts and derived questions for the practice set. If that record is missing, hold the draft while you check with the owner.

4. Decide what enters the scored set

A draft that meets the source and review requirements can be accepted. A draft with missing evidence or an unresolved label should be held. A draft that contradicts the approved rule should be rejected.

Keep held cases in a separate review area. This is quarantine. They stay available for investigation but don’t count toward a score. Keep the reason for a rejection too. If a reviewer later corrects a defective draft, go through review again before accepting a new version. Preserve the original decisions.

For the lab, accept a draft only if the source applies, the reuse permission is known, the balance is verified within the case, and the proposed label agrees with a reviewed, policy-backed final label. Run simple checks to catch missing fields or an inconsistent proposal. Human review still handles whether the source and language make sense for the question. These examples do not measure real assistant performance.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Label the same case before discussing it

User question. S-01 asks “Will I pay a monthly fee on a Standard Savings balance of ₹4,999 on July 15, 2026?”

Approved reference. SV-2#2 applies to Standard Savings on that date and charges ₹100 monthly below ₹5,000.

Actual LLM response. The draft generator proposed the label FEE_DUE and the reference reply “A ₹100 monthly fee applies.” This is a fictional draft.

Assessment. Reviewer A checks that ₹4,999 lies below ₹5,000 and chooses FEE_DUE. Reviewer B reads the applicable excerpt independently and records the same label and amount. Compare both notes only after they have been saved. The passage supports their shared answer.

Failure classification. Accept the row once source and permission checks are complete. The agreement supports the decision on S-01. It gives no estimate of how often reviewers will agree on other wording.

Example 2. Settle a dispute at exactly the minimum

User question. S-02 asks “If my Standard Savings balance is exactly ₹5,000 on July 15, 2026, do I pay the monthly fee?”

Approved reference. SV-2#2 charges the fee strictly below ₹5,000. The source and instructions are the same as for S-01.

Actual LLM response. The fictional draft answer says “No below-minimum fee applies.” Reviewer A chose FEE_DUE and reviewer B chose NO_FEE.

Assessment. Read A’s and B’s labels beside the case. A treated the cutoff as “at or below.” B used “below.” Check the date, then read SV-2#2 and compare the two numbers. ₹5,000 equals ₹5,000, so the balance does not meet the “below” condition. Write the resolution as “S-02, NO_FEE. The stated balance equals the minimum, and SV-2#2 charges only below it.” Keep A’s and B’s labels with that new entry. If the same mistake recurs, add the exact-cutoff example to the guide.

Failure classification. The first label used the wrong comparison. Resolve the label without changing the question or the policy. An unresolved policy conflict would need a different decision, to hold the case while the owner clarifies the rule.

Example 3. A plausible draft still needs review before it counts

User question. S-03 asks “Will I pay a fee on my July Standard Savings account?” and omits the balance. S-04 asks the same question with a verified balance of ₹5,001.

Approved reference. SV-2#2 is approved and reusable in the fictional practice set. The amount of the balance determines whether the fee applies.

Actual LLM response. Both fictional drafts say “A ₹100 monthly fee applies” and propose FEE_DUE. The wording reads like a real answer.

Assessment. S-03 gives no balance, so the reviewer can’t verify a fee. Mark NEEDS_REVIEW. S-04 gives an above-threshold balance, and both reviewers choose NO_FEE. Read the source to verify that decision. The draft’s proposed FEE_DUE contradicts the policy for S-04.

Failure classification. Hold S-03 outside scoring until the missing information is resolved. Reject S-04 as submitted and review any corrected draft again. Counting both as valid because they cite a real policy would make the set look bigger without making its labels more reliable.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Each block is a complete Python 3.10+ program using fictional inline data. You can run the blocks in any order. Python helps check the records and summarize the supplied decisions. The labels in the examples are not live model judgments.

  1. Use the Open Python Editor link beside each block.
  2. Select Copy Code and paste the entire block yourself. Replace any existing code in the editor.
  3. Click Run and check the first Expected output.
  4. Predict the experiment result, make the specified edit, then run again and compare with the second Expected output.

Keep indentation when pasting. If an edit causes an error, paste the original block and run it before trying the edit again.

Step 1 — Turn one policy sentence into an instruction

The approved July policy charges a fee below 5000. Try the instruction with a known balance. The equals sign stores a value in a named variable. The < comparison asks whether one number is less than the other. The indented line under if runs when the comparison is true. The else line selects the other outcome.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

balance = 4999
minimum = 5000

if balance < minimum:
    print("Proposed label: FEE_DUE")
else:
    print("Proposed label: NO_FEE")
Expected output
Proposed label: FEE_DUE

The balance is one rupee below the minimum, so the program takes the first branch.

Experiment. Change only balance to 5000 and run again.

Expected output
Proposed label: NO_FEE

Equal values don’t meet the less-than comparison. Include both values in the guide so reviewers can test how they interpret “below.”

Checkpoint. Does this rule apply to every account or date? It only models the supplied July Standard Savings rule. Check the account and effective date before using it.

Step 2 — Hold a case when a fact is missing

Try a July test case with no balance recorded. The braces make a dictionary. Use case["balance"] to read the value under that field name. None represents a missing fact in this exercise. Test it before comparing numbers. elif means “otherwise, check this next condition.”

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

case = {"id": "S-03", "balance": None}
balance = case["balance"]

if balance is None:
    label = "NEEDS_REVIEW"
elif balance < 5000:
    label = "FEE_DUE"
else:
    label = "NO_FEE"

print(case["id"], label)
Expected output
S-03 NEEDS_REVIEW

The missing value goes to review before any threshold test. Setting a missing balance to zero would create a different case.

Experiment. In this fictional record, supply a verified balance of 5000 in place of None. Run again.

Expected output
S-03 NO_FEE

With a balance available, Python can apply the comparison. It lands at the minimum and selects NO_FEE. A reviewer can now check the supplied evidence.

Checkpoint. Does finding a number in a draft make it verified? Check where the balance came from. This experiment supplies the verified value as part of the example.

Step 3 — Find disagreements by case ID

Two people recorded their labels in separate dictionaries. They used different orders. The loop takes each case ID from the first sheet and looks up the same ID in both sheets. == compares the two labels. This example assumes both sheets cover the same IDs.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

reviewer_a = {"S-01": "FEE_DUE", "S-02": "FEE_DUE"}
reviewer_b = {"S-02": "NO_FEE", "S-01": "FEE_DUE"}

for case_id in reviewer_a:
    first = reviewer_a[case_id]
    second = reviewer_b[case_id]
    if first == second:
        print(case_id, "AGREE")
    else:
        print(case_id, "DISAGREE:", first, "vs", second)
Expected output
S-01 AGREE
S-02 DISAGREE: FEE_DUE vs NO_FEE

S-01 compares correctly even though it appears in different positions. S-02 is the case you need to inspect.

Experiment. In a separate practice copy of reviewer A’s sheet, change only the S-02 label to "NO_FEE". Run again.

Expected output
S-01 AGREE
S-02 AGREE

The labels now match. The program didn’t check the policy. In a real review, keep the original sheets and store any later judgment separately.

Checkpoint. Which record should an adjudicator read first? Find S-02 by ID, then read its full question, source, and both evidence notes.

Step 4 — Record the adjudicator’s decision separately

Use S-02’s original two labels. An adjudicator has written a proposed decision and a reason. In this example the person records whether they confirmed the approved evidence. elif not evidence_confirmed asks whether that confirmation is missing. Print the final label only when the two labels differ and the evidence has been checked.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

first = "FEE_DUE"
second = "NO_FEE"
final_label = "NO_FEE"
reason = "SV-2#2 charges only below 5000."
evidence_confirmed = True

print("Original S-02 labels:", first, second)
if first == second:
    print("No disagreement to resolve")
elif not evidence_confirmed:
    print("HOLD: verify the applicable policy")
else:
    print("Adjudicated S-02:", final_label)
    print("Reason:", reason)
Expected output
Original S-02 labels: FEE_DUE NO_FEE
Adjudicated S-02: NO_FEE
Reason: SV-2#2 charges only below 5000.

The original two labels still appear. The adjudicator’s recorded decision is a separate entry.

Experiment. Change only evidence_confirmed to False. Run again.

Expected output
Original S-02 labels: FEE_DUE NO_FEE
HOLD: verify the applicable policy

The program now takes the hold branch. Even a plausible reason needs a verified source before it settles the disagreement.

Checkpoint. Did Python decide which source is right? It used the confirmation supplied by the human reviewer. The policy excerpt is the evidence behind the decision.

Step 5 — Generate drafts around a boundary

Start at ₹5,000 and move one rupee in either direction. Subtracting one gives ₹4,999, and adding one gives ₹5,001. Both readings of the rule agree at those balances. Add zero to test the only balance that separates “below” from “at or below.” Each list item holds a name and a number to add, called an offset. append() adds the exact-cutoff pair when you ask for it.

The loop builds a dictionary for each draft with the same fields. str(balance) converts the balance to text so it can be joined to the ID prefix. The f before the question string tells Python to insert the current balance where it sees {balance}.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

minimum = 5000
source = "SV-2#2"
include_boundary = False
offsets = [("below", -1), ("above", 1)]
if include_boundary:
    offsets.append(("at", 0))

for position, offset in offsets:
    balance = minimum + offset
    if balance < minimum:
        proposal = "FEE_DUE"
    else:
        proposal = "NO_FEE"
    draft = {
        "id": "JULY-" + str(balance),
        "question": f"Does a Standard Savings balance of {balance} rupees incur the monthly fee?",
        "date": "2026-07-15",
        "balance": balance,
        "source": source,
        "proposal": proposal,
    }
    print("DRAFT", draft["id"], position, draft["date"], draft["source"], draft["proposal"])
    print(draft["question"])
Expected output
DRAFT JULY-4999 below 2026-07-15 SV-2#2 FEE_DUE
Does a Standard Savings balance of 4999 rupees incur the monthly fee?
DRAFT JULY-5001 above 2026-07-15 SV-2#2 NO_FEE
Does a Standard Savings balance of 5001 rupees incur the monthly fee?

The two drafts cover opposite sides of the threshold. They leave out the balance where reviewers disagreed.

Experiment. Change only include_boundary to True. Run again.

Expected output
DRAFT JULY-4999 below 2026-07-15 SV-2#2 FEE_DUE
Does a Standard Savings balance of 4999 rupees incur the monthly fee?
DRAFT JULY-5001 above 2026-07-15 SV-2#2 NO_FEE
Does a Standard Savings balance of 5001 rupees incur the monthly fee?
DRAFT JULY-5000 at 2026-07-15 SV-2#2 NO_FEE
Does a Standard Savings balance of 5000 rupees incur the monthly fee?

The new pair adds a balance of exactly ₹5,000. It’s the one draft here that distinguishes “below” from “at or below.”

Checkpoint. Is the added case ready to score? It’s a draft generated from the same rule you’re checking. Have people verify the source, question, and proposed label independently.

Step 6 — Check provenance and permission before review

Try a draft that names the approved policy and records how it was created. It has no confirmed permission to reuse the source excerpt. != means “is different from.” In this example the first check compares the reported source with the supplied source ID. The second looks for the documented scope of permission.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

draft = {
    "id": "S-05",
    "source": "SV-2#2",
    "origin": "generated from July fee rule",
    "permission": None,
}

print(draft["id"], draft["source"], draft["origin"])
if draft["source"] != "SV-2#2":
    print("HOLD: confirm the source")
elif draft["permission"] != "practice-set reuse":
    print("HOLD: confirm reuse permission")
else:
    print("READY FOR LABEL REVIEW")
Expected output
S-05 SV-2#2 generated from July fee rule
HOLD: confirm reuse permission

You can trace the draft to the named excerpt. There is still no permission record for that use.

Experiment. Imagine the policy owner has provided permission for this practice set. Change only the value of "permission" to "practice-set reuse". Run again.

Expected output
S-05 SV-2#2 generated from July fee rule
READY FOR LABEL REVIEW

The second check now passes. The change represents a verified permission in the fictional exercise. In real work, retain the owner’s permission record and its scope.

Checkpoint. Does a permission string prove you can reuse real material? It records a claim for the checker to use. A reviewer must verify the permission and separately check the draft’s label.

Step 7 — Keep accepted, held, and rejected drafts separate

Start with four complete practice records for the July Standard Savings task. The reviewer pairs and the adjudicator’s decision are supplied human judgments. Each case must have the applicable July source, recorded reuse permission, a verified balance, and a supported decision before its draft can be accepted.

A function is a named group of instructions. def review(case): takes one draft and return hands back its first outcome. decisions.get(case_id) gives None when there’s no adjudication record. In final, note = decision, Python gives the two parts of the decision their own names. not note checks for an empty note here. For the known balances, compare the final label to the simple policy rule. A draft label is accepted only if it agrees with that final label.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

cases = [
    {"id": "S-01", "balance": 4999, "proposal": "FEE_DUE",
     "source": "SV-2#2", "permission": "practice-set reuse"},
    {"id": "S-02", "balance": 5000, "proposal": "NO_FEE",
     "source": "SV-2#2", "permission": "practice-set reuse"},
    {"id": "S-03", "balance": None, "proposal": "FEE_DUE",
     "source": "SV-2#2", "permission": "practice-set reuse"},
    {"id": "S-04", "balance": 5001, "proposal": "FEE_DUE",
     "source": "SV-2#2", "permission": "practice-set reuse"},
]
reviews = {
    "S-01": ("FEE_DUE", "FEE_DUE"),
    "S-02": ("FEE_DUE", "NO_FEE"),
    "S-03": ("NEEDS_REVIEW", "NEEDS_REVIEW"),
    "S-04": ("NO_FEE", "NO_FEE"),
}
decisions = {"S-02": ("NO_FEE", "SV-2#2 charges only below 5000.")}


def review(case):
    if case["source"] != "SV-2#2":
        return "HOLD: confirm applicable source"
    if case["permission"] != "practice-set reuse":
        return "HOLD: confirm reuse permission"
    balance = case["balance"]
    if balance is None:
        return "HOLD: verify balance"

    first, second = reviews[case["id"]]
    if first != second:
        decision = decisions.get(case["id"])
        if decision is None:
            return "HOLD: adjudicate disagreement"
        final, note = decision
        if not note:
            return "HOLD: record adjudication reason"
    else:
        final = first

    if final == "NEEDS_REVIEW":
        return "HOLD: resolve reviewer concern"
    if balance < 5000:
        expected = "FEE_DUE"
    else:
        expected = "NO_FEE"
    if final != expected:
        return "HOLD: recheck decision against policy"
    if case["proposal"] != final:
        return "REJECT: draft label contradicts reviewed label"
    return "ACCEPT: " + final


for case in cases:
    print(case["id"], review(case))
Expected output
S-01 ACCEPT: FEE_DUE
S-02 ACCEPT: NO_FEE
S-03 HOLD: verify balance
S-04 REJECT: draft label contradicts reviewed label

S-02 reaches acceptance after its disagreement has a recorded, policy-backed resolution. S-03 stops before scoring because the balance is unknown. S-04 has a supported review decision and a conflicting proposed label.

Experiment. Change only the permission value for S-02 from "practice-set reuse" to None. Run again.

Expected output
S-01 ACCEPT: FEE_DUE
S-02 HOLD: confirm reuse permission
S-03 HOLD: verify balance
S-04 REJECT: draft label contradicts reviewed label

S-02 now stops at the permission check. Its original reviewer labels and adjudication stay the same.

Checkpoint. Could this checker establish that a real dataset is ready to publish? It checks the supplied rows for this one fictional task. A real team still needs to verify evidence and permissions, review the actual text and policy scope, and preserve the case history before publication.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Write a guide another reviewer can follow

Write one sentence per label for verified balances of ₹4,999 and ₹5,000 and for an unknown balance. Give the approved monthly amount where the fee applies. Explain why a reviewer should record the policy’s effective date.

Practice 2. Resolve a disagreement without erasing it

S-02 is at ₹5,000 on July 15. Reviewer A wrote FEE_DUE and “balance is at the cutoff.” Reviewer B wrote NO_FEE and quoted “below ₹5,000.” Write a disagreement record. Include both original labels, the final label, and a reason. Say what you would do if you only had an undated copy of the policy.

Practice 3. Improve coverage without overstating it

A draft generator produces five questions about July balances below ₹5,000 and one about a balance above it. A teammate reports six draft cases and calls the coverage complete. Which test is missing for the difference between “below” and “at or below”? Write the new test with the source and expected label. Explain what the new count can tell you.

Practice 4. Choose what to accept, hold, or reject

Three drafts come with the following evidence. P cites SV-2#2 and has two matching labels but no verified reuse permission. Q uses a verified balance of ₹5,001 with an approved source and permission. Reviewers agree on NO_FEE, but the proposed label is FEE_DUE. R has verified source, permission, and balance of ₹4,999, and both reviewers and the draft say FEE_DUE. Decide what to do and what note to retain for each draft.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Label ₹4,999 FEE_DUE because it is one rupee below the July minimum. Record ₹100 per month. Label ₹5,000 NO_FEE because it equals the cutoff. Label an unknown balance NEEDS_REVIEW because you can’t compare an unknown value with ₹5,000. Record July 1, 2026, the effective date of SV-2, so another reviewer can check that it applied on July 15.

Solution 2

Keep the record for S-02 with A’s FEE_DUE and B’s NO_FEE. Record NO_FEE as the resolved label and cite SV-2#2. The balance equals the minimum and the fee applies only below it. With only an undated copy, hold the row and verify which approved policy applied on July 15 before resolving the disagreement.

Solution 3

The missing case is exactly ₹5,000. Use SV-2#2 on July 15 for Standard Savings and expect NO_FEE. Both versions of the rule agree at ₹4,999 and ₹5,001, so the exact threshold exposes the difference. The set now has seven drafts and includes the missing boundary. The count tells you nothing about how often customers ask each question or whether every draft label is right.

Solution 4

Hold P and record that reuse permission needs confirmation. Agreement does not provide permission. Reject Q as submitted and retain the reviewed NO_FEE label and the reason. ₹5,001 is above the minimum. Accept R for this fictional set and keep its source, recorded permission, and supporting labels. ₹4,999 is below the threshold, so the policy supports the proposed fee.

Knowledge Check

  1. A reviewer starts by reading another reviewer’s label. What would you change to collect independent judgments?
  2. Two reviewers mark FEE_DUE for exactly ₹5,000. Which evidence should you use before accepting the label?
  3. A dated source is missing for a disputed July question. What should the adjudicator record now?
  4. An assistant gives a wrong amount for a case whose expected label is correct. Which record should hold the verdict on that reply?
  5. Why should a draft with an unknown balance stay apart from a draft that asserts a fee at a verified ₹5,001?
  6. A generated case cites a real policy. What else should you check before reusing it?
  7. The draft generator and the validator apply the same cutoff. Why still ask a person to review the result?
  8. The team fixes the instructions and resolves an old disagreement. Which records would you keep to explain the change?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Give both reviewers the same case and source, then collect their labels and evidence notes separately before discussing either answer.
  2. Use the approved and applicable SV-2#2. It says below ₹5,000. At the cutoff, their shared label is wrong.
  3. Hold it in quarantine with both original judgments and the reason. Ask the policy owner for an approved source and effective date.
  4. Keep the expected label on the case. Store the verdict against the exact assistant response ID so other replies to the same question remain separate.
  5. The unknown balance prevents a decision and calls for more evidence. The verified balance and applicable policy let a reviewer contradict and reject the second draft.
  6. Confirm that the policy applies to the account and date, that reuse is permitted for the intended purpose, and that the question and proposed label agree with the source.
  7. Both could apply the same mistaken interpretation. A reviewer should check the original evidence and test a boundary independently.
  8. Keep the original labels and instruction version. Save the resolution, its evidence and reason, and the revised instructions separately. Recheck labels affected by the revised guide.

Independent Assignment

You’re preparing the bank’s fictional practice evaluation set. Start with Step 7. Submit a short labeling guide, a disagreement record for S-02, and a rule for admitting generated drafts. Keep the approved July policy, questions, and original reviewer labels fixed.

  1. In a fresh copy of Step 7, replace the decisions dictionary with {}. Run it. Which case must be held now? Write the adjudicator’s decision and reason from the full S-02 question and the approved source. Keep both original reviewer labels in your note.
  2. In a fresh copy of the original Step 7, revise S-04. First write the corrected reference answer in your notes and keep the old answer with its rejection reason. Confirm that ₹5,001 is above the minimum and that the two existing NO_FEE labels support your revision. In the code, change only S-04’s proposal to "NO_FEE" and run again. Which row can now be accepted, and which held row still needs evidence?
  3. Write a rule the bank can use to decide whether to accept, hold, or reject future drafts. Say what still needs a human check even when the program prints ACCEPT.
Check your assignment

Your guide should mark balances below ₹5,000 FEE_DUE with ₹100 per month, balances at or above ₹5,000 NO_FEE, and cases missing applicable evidence NEEDS_REVIEW. In S-02, keep A’s FEE_DUE and B’s NO_FEE. Record NO_FEE as the resolution because SV-2#2 charges the fee only below the minimum and the stated balance equals it.

The first run prints these lines.

  1. S-01 ACCEPT: FEE_DUE
  2. S-02 HOLD: adjudicate disagreement
  3. S-03 HOLD: verify balance
  4. S-04 REJECT: draft label contradicts reviewed label

The second run prints these lines.

  1. S-01 ACCEPT: FEE_DUE
  2. S-02 ACCEPT: NO_FEE
  3. S-03 HOLD: verify balance
  4. S-04 ACCEPT: NO_FEE

The corrected S-04 answer should say no below-minimum fee applies at ₹5,001. Accept after verifying the source, reuse permission, inputs, and reviewed label. Hold missing evidence or unresolved disagreements apart from the accepted set. Reject a draft that contradicts the reviewed label. The checker uses supplied fields. A human still needs to confirm the underlying source, permission, and question wording. Preserve rejected drafts and review notes when you release a corrected version.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing case labels and reply verdicts. Link verdicts to the exact responses judged and expectations to the cases.
  • Copying a first label. Record independent decisions before sharing them.
  • Using consensus as proof. Check the applicable source, especially at the threshold.
  • Counting unresolved drafts as coverage. Keep held drafts available for review and outside the scored set.
  • Dropping source and permission history. Save the evidence, permitted use, and review record for each case.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Compare a sample with the questions it is meant to represent and plan coverage by question group.
  • Keep a deliberate stress check separate from an estimate of everyday performance.
  • Spot duplicate questions and keep related cases together when separating development from final evaluation.
  • Protect a final check from tuning and explain how to refresh or retire cases after a policy change.
  • Validate a small split, trace a label to its source, and print a versioned dataset draft.

Why This Lesson Matters

You ask Harbor Leaf Bank whether you’ll be charged at exactly the required balance. The new assistant says you’ll owe ₹100. The approved July rule says there’s no charge at that balance. At the release meeting, both versions have the same headline score, nine out of ten. Before the bank moves ahead, you want to know whether the new answer is the mistake that score is hiding.

In the fictional review, eight questions are ordinary July fee lookups. Two ask about the balance right at the Standard Savings minimum. The old version passed seven ordinary cases and both cutoff cases. The new version passed all eight ordinary cases and only one cutoff case. Add each version’s passes. Both reach nine, but the new version got worse on the exact balance where a customer needs to know whether a charge applies.

You’ll prepare questions for the next check, protect the final review set, and plan what to do when the bank changes its policy. All data, policies, and verdicts in this chapter are fictional. Allow about 5.5 hours. The required background is Golden schemas, provenance and versioning. The earlier Annotation, adjudication and synthetic data chapter helps with deciding which drafted cases to accept.

Beginner Explanation

1. Check which customers your sample represents

Suppose ten customer questions arrive. Eight are ordinary fee questions and two ask about the cutoff. If you read five questions and all five are ordinary lookups, you have learned how the assistant handled those five. A sample is a subset you examine. A representative sample should resemble the population you want to describe on the characteristics that matter. Here the population is the set of eligible questions in the time window you picked.

Write down a target of four ordinary questions and one cutoff question before reading any answers. Four out of five is 80% and one out of five is 20%, the same mix as eight and two out of ten. Put the eligible IDs into two piles and draw from each pile. This is stratified sampling, and each pile is a stratum. Draw without checking which cases passed. If all five selected cases still come from one date or account, report that limitation alongside the matched proportions.

2. Check hard cases more often for a different decision

One sampled cutoff question is easy to miss. Suppose an audit asks you to check four ordinary cases and four cutoff cases. In that audit half the cases are cutoff questions, compared with two in ten in the target traffic. Deliberately including more cases from a rare group is oversampling. A stress set is an evaluation set designed to probe difficult or high-consequence cases.

For the new assistant in the opening example, all eight ordinary answers passed, and one of two cutoff answers passed. Imagine applying those same group rates to a different mix. In ten cases with the everyday mix, you would expect eight ordinary passes and one cutoff pass, or nine of ten. In an eight-case stress mix with four of each, the same rates would give four ordinary passes and two cutoff passes, or six of eight. The group rates stayed fixed in this calculation. Only how much each group contributes to the overall score changed.

This stress mix gives cutoff failures more influence. Report the stress score under its own name. For an estimate of everyday performance, use a representative sample or trustworthy group rates combined using the actual traffic proportions. With only two cutoff observations, the true rate for that group is still uncertain.

Try changing just one important detail, such as the balance from ₹4,999 to ₹5,000. An adversarial edge case here is a deliberately difficult test chosen to surface a likely error. The bank could set a practice requirement before testing. Include at least one verified exact-minimum case and pause release if any such case applies a charge. A reviewer still needs to verify each label against the policy. Passing the small set answers that release check and gives little evidence about rare failures outside it.

3. Protect questions used for the final check

A team can use some saved questions to improve its prompts or examples. Call those its development set. Reserve a separate set for checking how those changes work on unseen cases. That set is a holdout. If you tune using answers from the holdout, the final score can reward familiarity with that material. This is leakage, a form of train/test contamination. It can happen during prompt tuning or case selection even when no model weights are changed.

Consider “Do I pay a fee at ₹5,000?” and “Is there a charge at the ₹5,000 minimum?” If both were made from the same fee guide, you could put them in different sets by mistake. Group cases by the policy or document family that links them. Give the whole family one destination. This is a grouped split. Preserve the source and family IDs so someone else can verify which cases travelled together.

Put “What fee applies below ₹5,000?” beside “What fee applies above ₹5,000?” If you remove the second just because most words match, you lose a useful check. Now put two paraphrases of the exact same question side by side. Keeping both as separate cases can double the weight of one underlying test. Deduplication means finding repeated material and deciding whether to keep one copy or group related cases. Use similarity to flag pairs, then read both questions and their sources before deciding. Settle the family assignments before drawing samples for each side. If the available families leave a gap in coverage, report the gap and find suitable data.

4. Refresh the evaluation when policy changes

For this chapter, SV-2#2 sets the July Standard Savings minimum at ₹5,000. A ₹100 monthly fee applies below it. Imagine the bank approves a new fee guide, SV-3#2, for August 1, 2026 onward. Its minimum is ₹6,000 and its fee is ₹120 per month below that balance. Both are fictional policy excerpts for this lesson.

Keep the frozen July holdout and its results. A question explicitly about July can still be correct as a historical case. If you’re checking the current policy, move July-only coverage out of that current check and keep it in the historical set. This is retirement from a specific evaluation. Add reviewed August cases in a new version. This is a refresh. Record the parent version, additions and retirements, their reasons, and who can see the new holdout.

For this unseen-family check, give developers practice cases from other families. Keep the reserved guide, questions, labels, and close variants behind the review boundary. If developers need the August guide for tuning, record that use and reserve a different family for an unseen-family check. Preserve the old benchmark so you can replay it. A split check can catch some paths for leakage. You still need access controls and a record of what was actually used to tune.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Read the group scores before trusting the total

User question. The bank asks whether it can release the new assistant after both versions get nine of ten July questions right.

Approved reference. The fictional question mix is eight ordinary lookups and two cutoff questions. SV-2#2 charges ₹100 only below ₹5,000. A charge at exactly ₹5,000 is a cutoff failure.

Actual LLM response. In the illustrative review, the old assistant passed seven ordinary cases and both cutoff cases. The new assistant passed eight ordinary cases and one cutoff case. In the failed cutoff example it says, “A ₹100 monthly fee applies at ₹5,000.”

Assessment. Verify the failed claim against “below.” Add seven and two for the old total, then eight and one for the new total. Both are nine. Compare the cutoff results separately and the change is visible. For a practice stress mix with four cases of each kind, applying the same new-assistant group rates gives four ordinary successes and two cutoff successes, six of eight.

Failure classification. Investigate the cutoff regression before approving release. Keep the everyday and stress summaries labeled separately. Neither figure establishes a precise live failure rate on this small fictional set.

Example 2. Detect related cases on both sides of the split

User question. A reviewer wants to know whether a final check is independent of the material used to tune the assistant.

Approved reference. The July fee guide supports no charge at exactly ₹5,000. The team keeps all cases derived from that guide in one document family.

Actual LLM response. A saved reply says no charge for the held-out prompt “Is there a charge at the ₹5,000 minimum?” Development already contains “Do I pay a fee at exactly ₹5,000?”

Assessment. Compare the full texts. The wording differs, but the balance, rule, and intended answer match. Check the source records and find the same fee-guide family in both sets. Move the family together if the split is still being planned. If developers already used one case to tune, record the exposure and choose a different family for an unseen final check.

Failure classification. The split cannot support an unseen-family claim. The held-out answer can still be correct for the policy. The problem is the evidence behind the benchmark claim.

Example 3. Keep a policy refresh traceable

User question. A new fee guide takes effect on August 1. The team wants to check the new rule without losing the old benchmark.

Approved reference. July’s SV-2#2 charges ₹100 below ₹5,000. August’s SV-3#2 charges ₹120 below ₹6,000. These versions are in the same fee-guide family.

Actual LLM response. A saved July reply says, “At ₹5,999, no below-minimum fee applies.” The team drafts an August case at the same balance.

Assessment. Check July against its own policy and keep the old verdict. Use the August source for the new case. Since 5999 is one below 6000, the expected new fee is ₹120. Have reviewers verify that label. Keep the new question in the reviewer-only fee-guide family and record the transition in a new version manifest. Keep July rows available for historical testing.

Failure classification. Replacing July’s labels in place would make old results hard to explain. Report August as a distinct check. For a fair comparison, rescore both versions on the same reviewed set under the same access rules.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Each block is a complete Python 3.10+ program with fictional inline examples. You’ll examine samples, compare simulated scores, and check a proposed dataset. There are no local files or model calls.

  1. Select Open Python Editor beside the block.
  2. Select Copy Code and paste the entire block into the editor yourself.
  3. Click Run and check the first Expected output.
  4. Predict the result of the experiment, make the specified edit, and compare the new result with the second Expected output.

Keep the spaces at the start of lines. If an experiment produces an error, paste the original code and run it before trying the edit again.

Step 1 — Count the kinds of questions you sampled

The practice queue starts with eight ordinary lookups and ends with two cutoff questions. A list holds values in order. The expression queue[start:start + 5] takes five positions starting at start. Python counts from zero and stops before the second position. sample.count(...) counts how many entries equal a value.

Copy the entire block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

queue = ["ordinary"] * 8 + ["cutoff"] * 2
start = 0
sample = queue[start:start + 5]

print("Ordinary:", sample.count("ordinary"))
print("Cutoff:", sample.count("cutoff"))
Expected output
Ordinary: 5
Cutoff: 0

Multiplying the list repeats its item. The plus sign joins the two lists. The first five positions all come from the ordinary group.

Experiment. Change only start to 5. Run again.

Expected output
Ordinary: 3
Cutoff: 2

The sample now reaches both cutoff questions. Picking five consecutive rows can change the mix whenever the queue is ordered.

Checkpoint. Did moving to a different part of the queue produce a representative sample? The new mix is three ordinary cases and two cutoff cases. The whole queue has eight and two. Inspect the mix before interpreting a score.

Step 2 — Select questions within each group

The bank has eight ordinary questions and four drafted cutoff questions available for this exercise. The target traffic card is still eight ordinary for every two cutoff questions. Use that card to plan a sample of five. import random loads Python’s standard random tools. random.Random(7) starts a local generator from seed 7. sample(pool, count) chooses distinct items from that pool. len() counts the selected IDs.

Copy the entire block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

import random

ordinary = ["R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5", "R6", "R7", "R8"]
cutoff = ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4"]
cutoff_target = 1
rng = random.Random(7)

ordinary_sample = rng.sample(ordinary, 4)
cutoff_sample = rng.sample(cutoff, cutoff_target)

print("Ordinary selected:", len(ordinary_sample))
print("Cutoff selected:", len(cutoff_sample))
print("Total selected:", len(ordinary_sample) + len(cutoff_sample))
Expected output
Ordinary selected: 4
Cutoff selected: 1
Total selected: 5

The groups are selected separately. Their combined proportion matches the traffic card for question type.

Experiment. Change only cutoff_target from 1 to 4. Run again.

Expected output
Ordinary selected: 4
Cutoff selected: 4
Total selected: 8

The cutoff group now has half the slots. Save the selected IDs and rule for real evaluations. This exercise checks the mix. It gives no evidence that these questions cover every account, date, or wording.

Checkpoint. Would you present the eight-case stress set as typical traffic? Its cutoff share is four of eight, while the target share is two of ten.

Step 3 — Compare scores under two mixes

Use the new assistant’s group results from the worked example. Eight of eight ordinary cases passed. One of two cutoff cases passed. Dividing gives 1.0 and 0.5. Multiply each rate by the number of slots for that group and add the results. In a ten-slot everyday mix, eight ordinary slots contribute eight expected passes and two cutoff slots contribute one.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run. In f"{projected_score:.0%}", the f lets Python insert a value and .0% formats a fraction as a percentage with no decimal places.

Open Python Editor

ordinary_rate = 8 / 8
cutoff_rate = 1 / 2
total_slots = 10
cutoff_slots = 2
ordinary_slots = total_slots - cutoff_slots

projected_passes = ordinary_slots * ordinary_rate + cutoff_slots * cutoff_rate
projected_score = projected_passes / total_slots

print("Mix:", ordinary_slots, "ordinary and", cutoff_slots, "cutoff")
print("Illustrative score:", f"{projected_score:.0%}")
Expected output
Mix: 8 ordinary and 2 cutoff
Illustrative score: 90%

This is a calculation using the observed group rates from the fictional report. It gives no new test results.

Experiment. Change only cutoff_slots to 5. Run again.

Expected output
Mix: 5 ordinary and 5 cutoff
Illustrative score: 75%

Five ordinary slots contribute five expected passes and five cutoff slots contribute two and a half. A fractional expected count is possible because this is a projection, not a count of actual replies. The five cutoff slots give the weaker group more influence. Both group rates stayed fixed.

Checkpoint. Does the lower figure mean the assistant changed? The example changed only the weighting. Compare two assistants under the same mix if you want to study a change in the system.

Step 4 — Flag wording that deserves a closer look

Compare two draft questions. Strip a question mark with replace(), fold letter case with casefold(), and split at whitespace with split(). A set keeps each word once. The & operator finds words both sets contain. The | operator finds words used in either set. Five shared words out of five distinct words give a score of 1.00. This ratio is called Jaccard similarity. The sample questions are both non-empty.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

def words(question):
    return set(question.casefold().replace("?", "").split())


first = "What fee applies below 5000?"
second = "What fee applies below 5000?"
left = words(first)
right = words(second)
overlap = len(left & right)
total = len(left | right)
similarity = overlap / total

print("Second question:", second)
print("Shared and distinct:", overlap, "of", total)
print("Similarity:", f"{similarity:.2f}")
if similarity >= 0.60:
    print("REVIEW: similar wording")
Expected output
Second question: What fee applies below 5000?
Shared and distinct: 5 of 5
Similarity: 1.00
REVIEW: similar wording

Both questions use the same words, so they are worth checking for duplication.

Experiment. Change only second to "What fee applies above 5000?". Run again.

Expected output
Second question: What fee applies above 5000?
Shared and distinct: 4 of 6
Similarity: 0.67
REVIEW: similar wording

“Below” and “above” appear on different sides. Four other words are shared. The score still clears the review threshold, but the expected fee can differ. A sensible next step is to read the source and labels together.

Checkpoint. Would you delete the second case? It checks a different condition. Keep both if they are useful, and keep their shared document family from crossing the split.

Step 5 — Detect a document family on both sides

The first two rows are different questions from the same fee guide. A dictionary maps case IDs to family IDs. A second dictionary records which side each case is on. In for case_id, family in families.items():, the loop reads each key and value together. Add each family to the set for its side. Use sorted() to keep the overlap report in a predictable order.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

families = {"F-01": "fee-guide", "F-02": "fee-guide", "S-01": "statements"}
split = {"F-01": "development", "F-02": "holdout", "S-01": "holdout"}
groups = {"development": set(), "holdout": set()}

for case_id, family in families.items():
    groups[split[case_id]].add(family)

overlap = sorted(groups["development"] & groups["holdout"])
print("Shared families:", overlap)
if overlap:
    print("HOLD: split crosses a family")
else:
    print("PASS: no recorded family overlap")
Expected output
Shared families: ['fee-guide']
HOLD: split crosses a family

The fee family is present on both sides. A unique case ID for each question did not prevent that overlap.

Experiment. In the proposed split only, change F-02 from "holdout" to "development". Run again.

Expected output
Shared families: []
PASS: no recorded family overlap

Both fee questions now stay on the development side, leaving the distinct statements family for the final check. The recorded families are separated, though the holdout may now lack fee coverage. Check coverage before using it to decide release. This edit is suitable for a proposed split, before a holdout is frozen.

Checkpoint. Does the pass prove the holdout was unseen? The check only uses the recorded family assignments. Confirm the lineage of near-duplicates and check the access records.

Step 6 — Preserve a frozen holdout after exposure

Imagine the access log shows someone copied a fee guide from the final check into the tuning notes. Keep the original holdout so you can replay its report. For the next unseen-family check, set aside every row from that guide. In the program, None means no exposure was recorded. The loop uses append() to place each ID in one of two lists. The bracketed expression in the first print gathers the original IDs into a separate list.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

frozen = [("H-01", "fee-guide"), ("H-02", "statements")]
exposed_family = None
eligible = []
retire = []

for case_id, family in frozen:
    if family == exposed_family:
        retire.append(case_id)
    else:
        eligible.append(case_id)

print("Frozen v1 IDs:", [case_id for case_id, family in frozen])
print("Eligible for next check:", eligible)
print("Retire from unseen-family check:", retire)
Expected output
Frozen v1 IDs: ['H-01', 'H-02']
Eligible for next check: ['H-01', 'H-02']
Retire from unseen-family check: []

The frozen list and the eligible list contain the same IDs. In this toy log, neither family is recorded as exposed. Actual eligibility still depends on the completeness of the access and tuning history.

Experiment. Change only exposed_family to "fee-guide". Run again.

Expected output
Frozen v1 IDs: ['H-01', 'H-02']
Eligible for next check: ['H-02']
Retire from unseen-family check: ['H-01']

H-01 still belongs to the original version. It moves out of the next unseen-family check. Find replacement coverage from an unexposed family, review it, and record the retirement reason and replacement in a new manifest.

Checkpoint. Can you replay the old evaluation? Yes, using the saved original version. Record the exposure when reporting what that version can still support.

Step 7 — Check a draft refresh before using it

Use two frozen rows and a reviewed August draft. H-01 and H-03 belong to the same fee-guide family even though their policies have different effective dates. The first row belongs to a separate statements family. The supplied fictional evidence for ST-1#1 is “Monthly statements are available as PDF.” A reviewer checks its expected answer against that excerpt. For H-03, the reviewer uses SV-3#2 and confirms a balance of exactly ₹6,000 equals the new minimum, so no fee applies.

A function groups the rows and finds problems before printing the new version. The source register maps each reference to its family. continue skips the rest of a row after the split or source check fails. The + operator builds a new list from the frozen rows and the draft. This program reads the old rows without editing them. json.dumps() writes one JSON object at a time, so the case lines are JSON Lines, or JSONL.

Copy the block into the editor and click Run.

Open Python Editor

import json


def audit(rows, source_families):
    groups = {"development": set(), "holdout": set()}
    seen = set()
    errors = []
    for row in rows:
        case_id = row["id"]
        if case_id in seen:
            errors.append("Duplicate ID: " + case_id)
        seen.add(case_id)
        side = row["split"]
        if side not in groups:
            errors.append("Unknown split: " + side)
            continue
        family = source_families.get(row["source"])
        if family is None:
            errors.append("Unknown source: " + row["source"])
            continue
        groups[side].add(family)
    for family in sorted(groups["development"] & groups["holdout"]):
        errors.append("Shared family: " + family)
    return errors


sources = {"ST-1#1": "statements", "SV-2#2": "fee-guide", "SV-3#2": "fee-guide"}
frozen = [
    {"id": "D-01", "split": "development", "source": "ST-1#1",
     "question": "What format are monthly statements available in?", "expected": "PDF"},
    {"id": "H-01", "split": "holdout", "source": "SV-2#2",
     "question": "Is a fee due at 5000 on July 15, 2026?", "expected": "NO_FEE"},
]
candidate = {
    "id": "H-03", "split": "holdout", "source": "SV-3#2",
    "question": "Is a fee due at 6000 on August 1, 2026?", "expected": "NO_FEE",
}
proposed = frozen + [candidate]

print("Frozen v1 rows:", len(frozen))
errors = audit(proposed, sources)
if errors:
    for error in errors:
        print(error)
    print("HOLD: do not use draft split")
else:
    manifest = {
        "version": "fees-v2-draft", "parent": "fees-v1",
        "added": [candidate["id"]], "holdout_access": "reviewer-only",
        "scope": "July history and August review reported separately",
    }
    print("Manifest:", json.dumps(manifest))
    for row in proposed:
        print(json.dumps(row))
Expected output
Frozen v1 rows: 2
Manifest: {"version": "fees-v2-draft", "parent": "fees-v1", "added": ["H-03"], "holdout_access": "reviewer-only", "scope": "July history and August review reported separately"}
{"id": "D-01", "split": "development", "source": "ST-1#1", "question": "What format are monthly statements available in?", "expected": "PDF"}
{"id": "H-01", "split": "holdout", "source": "SV-2#2", "question": "Is a fee due at 5000 on July 15, 2026?", "expected": "NO_FEE"}
{"id": "H-03", "split": "holdout", "source": "SV-3#2", "question": "Is a fee due at 6000 on August 1, 2026?", "expected": "NO_FEE"}

The printed manifest names the parent and the new row. The old July case stays in the historical coverage, and the draft adds August to the reviewer-only split. The manifest records the intended access rule. An actual system has to enforce it.

The August source belongs to the same family as the July holdout row. The split check blocks the draft before it prints a manifest. Keep the family on one side. Prepare unrelated development examples or reserve a fresh, unexposed family for a future check.

Checkpoint. Could this audit check the correctness of every label? It checks IDs, split names, recorded sources, and family separation. Reviewers still need to check the labels and confirm that the recorded sources and access history are accurate.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Choose a sample for the decision

The bank has a target mix of eight ordinary questions and two cutoff questions. You have room for five cases. Plan a sample that matches the mix by question type. Your teammate suggests using the first five rows of the ordered queue from Step 1. What would their sample miss, and how would you choose cases within each group?

Practice 2. Explain different scores for the same assistant

Use the new assistant’s group rates from Example 1. Calculate the expected score under an eight-slot stress mix with four ordinary and four cutoff slots. A report compares that stress score with the nine of ten everyday score and says the assistant got worse. Explain the mistake.

Practice 3. Repair a split before and after exposure

F-01 and F-02 come from one fee-guide family. F-01 is in development and F-02 is in holdout. S-01 comes from a separate statements family. Explain a valid proposed split that keeps the fee cases in holdout. Then explain what to do if a developer already used F-01 to tune the assistant.

Practice 4. Plan a refresh without rewriting the past

A frozen July question asks about a balance of ₹5,999. Add a case with the same balance for August 1. Tell a teammate where the two expected answers come from, which scope each case belongs to, and what should go in the manifest. Explain what developers should get to practise the new policy.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Use four ordinary cases and one cutoff case. Four of five is 80% and one of five is 20%. The first five rows are all ordinary because the queue is ordered by type. Select from within each group without looking at its verdict, for example with a saved random selection. Report the group mix and note the other characteristics you haven’t checked.

Solution 2

All ordinary slots are expected to pass, so four slots contribute four. Half of the four cutoff slots are expected to pass, so they contribute two more. Six of eight is 75%. The nine of ten everyday score gives the stronger group eight slots instead of four. The different weights are enough to explain the two numbers. Compare assistants under the same mix and report the stress result separately.

Solution 3

In a proposed split, move F-01 to holdout with F-02 and keep S-01 in development. The two families are separated. If F-01 already influenced tuning, moving its row cannot make the family unseen. Record the exposure, preserve the old split for replay, and reserve another unexposed family for a new holdout. Check whether the replacement still covers the fee risk.

Solution 4

Under SV-2#2, ₹5,999 is above ₹5,000, so no fee applies in July. Under SV-3#2, ₹5,999 is below ₹6,000, so ₹120 per month applies in August. Retain July in the historical evaluation. Add a dated August case in a new version and record its source, reviewed label, parent version, access scope, and why coverage changed. Give developers cases from separate families for this unseen-family check. If they tune on the August guide, reserve a different family before making an unseen-family claim. Use dated scores when reporting the refresh.

Knowledge Check

  1. A review pulls five questions from an ordered queue and none are about the cutoff. What can you conclude?
  2. Two assistants both pass nine out of ten. One fails a cutoff question the other passes. What evidence should you ask for before release?
  3. Your report says a stress set passes six of eight. Why can’t you use 75% as the everyday score?
  4. Two questions share only one changed word, “below” versus “above.” How should a duplicate check handle them?
  5. A holdout and development set have no exactly equal strings. What other check can reveal related examples?
  6. A team already tuned on a source family that it later moves into holdout. What claim must it give up about those examples?
  7. A policy changes and an old benchmark row asks explicitly about July. How should you handle that row?
  8. The split audit passes for a new version. What evidence would you still need before trusting a release score?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. You can describe the five reviewed cases. You have no cutoff observations. Check the sampling method and add the coverage needed for the decision.
  2. Ask for the group counts and read the cutoff failure against the policy. The unchanged total can hide a loss in the affected group.
  3. The stress set gives cutoff cases more weight than ordinary traffic does. Report its score for the stress purpose or use appropriate traffic weights and defensible group estimates.
  4. Flag the pair and review the full questions, sources, and labels. The changed word can change the answer, so preserving both may be useful. Keep related cases within one side of the split.
  5. Check for paraphrases and shared documents or derivation history. Compare recorded source-family IDs across the two sides.
  6. It can no longer call the family unseen for that comparison. Preserve the earlier reports, record the exposure, and plan a fresh final check.
  7. Keep the old version and the July label for historical testing. If the current policy report retires that case, record the retirement and review the new August case separately.
  8. Confirm source and group assignments, check for near-duplicates and access or tuning history, and verify labels and coverage. The audit applies to the fields it was given.

Include the split for each row and a short review note citing the August rule and showing how you verified the label.

  2. In a fresh copy of the original block, replace the draft H-03 with a new holdout case, H-04. Use source SV-3#2 and the question “What fee is due at 5999 on August 1, 2026?” Before typing FEE_120 as the expected label, write down why NO_FEE would be right for that balance in July and wrong in August. Keep the two frozen rows in place and run the code. Check that the manifest adds only H-04.
  3. Explain which resources developers can see, which cases the reviewers should keep reserved, and how you would report July and August results. Name a condition that would make you retire a case from an unseen evaluation.

The new label follows from SV-3#2. ₹5,999 is one below ₹6,000, so the monthly fee is ₹120. Both fee versions stay in one family on the holdout side. For this unseen-family check, give developers cases from other families and keep the reserved guide, prompts, and labels within the review boundary. Report the July history and August results separately. If the team tunes on a reserved family, record the exposure and retire that family from the next unseen check. The printed draft is a reproducible fixture. A real release needs reviewed sources, coverage, and actual access control.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a convenient sample as typical. Record the question mix and how you selected within groups.
  • Comparing aggregate scores under different weights. Compare like with like and show the difficult group.
  • Removing near-duplicates by score alone. Read the full meaning and evidence before merging or grouping.
  • Reshuffling an exposed family. Save the exposure history and reserve truly unexposed material.
  • Updating a frozen set in place. Preserve the previous benchmark and explain the refresh or retirement in a new version.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Select the everyday check and stress check to answer different questions. Inspect group scores and the case sources. Keep related examples together and preserve the final review boundary. When a source changes or a family is exposed, preserve the old evidence and record the decision in a new version.
