Intermediate · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Count repeated words fairly and use the counts to explain token precision, recall, and F1.
  • Compare overlap of single words, neighboring words, and words that stay in order across gaps.
  • Explain how BLEU handles short replies and why a score over a set differs from an average of reply scores.
  • Use several approved phrasings, identify the scale of each metric, and spot a wrong summary that earns a high score.

Why This Lesson Matters

You check your balance before payday. It is ₹5,500, and you want to know whether Harbor Leaf Bank will charge its monthly savings fee. One draft says you’ll pay below ₹6,000. Another says you’ll pay below ₹5,000. At your balance, the two drafts give you opposite answers. Before putting either draft on the help page, the bank needs to see which one follows the July rule.

The bank and replies are fictional. Read the approved summary first: “monthly fee applies below 5000.” Now compare “monthly fee applies below 6000” and “balances under 5000 incur a monthly charge.” The first shares four words with the approved line. The second shares only two. If you ranked them by the number of matching words, which would win? Keep that ranking beside your own reading of the policy. We'll work out why they disagree.

From Ground truth, references and benchmarks, bring the habit of checking an answer against approved evidence. Exact match, normalization and rules is a useful refresher on writing checks with clear rules. Here the approved rule is the July savings policy, SV-2#2. Amounts are in rupees, and the task is only to describe when the monthly fee applies.

Beginner Explanation

Count what the two lines share

Put the approved line above the draft “fee fee applies.” Cross off the first “fee” in each line. When you reach the draft’s second “fee,” there’s no uncrossed “fee” left on the approved line. Cross off “applies” in both lines and you have two matches. That limit on how often a repeated word can count is called clipping.

The bank has written a short line that is acceptable under the approved policy. That line is the reference. The reply we want to score is the candidate. In this lesson every piece between spaces is a token. That's a convenient way of splitting these lowercase examples. A shared scoring tool might split punctuation differently, so record how you split the text when comparing scores.

Now look at “monthly fee applies.” All three of its tokens appear in the five-token reference. Token precision is the fraction of candidate tokens that match, so precision is 3 ÷ 3 = 1. Token recall is the fraction of reference tokens recovered, so recall is 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60. The reply gets full precision even though it leaves out the condition customers need.

F1 balances those two fractions. With the same clipped match count on both sides, double the three matches and divide by the total length of the two lines: 6 ÷ (3 + 5) = 0.75. This is the usual F1 calculation written using counts. That 0.75 is a text overlap score. It gives no special weight to the missing cutoff. Keep both precision and recall visible during review. A reply that contains every approved word and three extra words also gets a similar F1, 10 ÷ 13 ≈ 0.77. You’d investigate the missing condition in the first case and the added wording in the second.

Compare neighbors and words in order

Try a draft that puts the first two words in the opposite order, “fee monthly applies below 5000.” You still have all five words, but “monthly fee” is gone as a pair. Count one word at a time and you get all five matches. Slide a two-word window along each line and you find only two shared pairs, “applies below” and “below 5000.” A neighboring run of n tokens is an n-gram. A one-token run is a unigram and a two-token run is a bigram.

ROUGE-N compares n-gram overlap against a reference. For instance ROUGE-2 counts bigrams. Reports can include precision, recall, and F1, so write down which one you used. Both lines above contain four pairs, and two match. The ROUGE-2 precision and recall are each 2 ÷ 4, so the F1 is 0.50. ROUGE-1 F1 is still 1.00. Original ROUGE paper

Try removing “applies” instead. The line “monthly fee below 5000” shares four words that stay in the same order, even though the reference has a gap between “fee” and “below.” The longest list you can trace in both lines while preserving order is the longest common subsequence. ROUGE-L uses its length. Here its F1 is 2 × 4 ÷ (4 + 5) = 0.889. The gap is allowed, but reversing the line would prevent those same four words from all staying in order. When shared wording matters, the two methods tell you different things about the change. Original ROUGE paper

Ask whether a reply got a high score by saying very little

“Monthly fee” has perfect one-word and two-word precision against the reference. It could earn full credit if you only considered the words it used. Yet a customer still wouldn't know when they pay. BLEU measures clipped n-gram precision across several lengths and reduces the score when the candidate is too short compared with the reference. This multiplier is the brevity penalty. If the candidate is two tokens and the reference is five, the multiplier is about 0.22. With perfect precision for the lengths we count, a teaching BLEU-2 score on a 0–100 scale falls from 100 to about 22.

For BLEU-2, multiply the one-word precision by the two-word precision and take the square root. For example, with 0.80 and 0.75, multiply to get 0.60, then take the square root to get about 0.775. This is the geometric mean. BLEU-4 does the same with four precisions and a fourth root. Multiply by the brevity penalty, then by 100 for the scale used in this chapter.

A sentence can share several individual words and still share zero pairs. The product then becomes zero. Some settings use a small substitute for an observed zero precision to make short sentences easier to compare. This is smoothing. The first missing order under the library setting used here counts as half a match for calculation purposes. The next missing order counts as a quarter. Keep the raw count visible so nobody mistakes a substitute for a match that occurred. Original BLEU paper · SacreBLEU implementation

If you score two replies separately, then average their scores, each reply gets equal weight. Corpus BLEU, calculated over the whole set, adds match counts and possible counts first. It uses the total candidate and reference lengths for the brevity penalty. A five-word reply can contribute more possible pairs than a two-word reply. Record whether you used corpus BLEU or the mean of sentence BLEU before comparing reports.

Allow more than one acceptable wording

Ask two policy reviewers to write a short summary independently. If both summaries preserve the same rule, you can approve both and keep them with the benchmark. With multiple references, BLEU clips each n-gram against the largest count seen in any one reference and uses the closest reference length, preferring the shorter length on a tie. In rouge-score, the multiple-reference operation selects the best F1 separately for each requested metric. Our token F1 report similarly takes the best score against an individual approved line. Joining the approved lines into one long reference would describe a different scoring task. SacreBLEU implementation · Google Research rouge-score

If you need to compare close spellings or forms of the same word, you can also count neighboring characters. For “fee,” the two-character pieces are “fe” and “ee.” “Fees” adds “es” while keeping both pieces. chrF is an optional metric that compares character runs of several lengths using precision and recall. It can give partial credit where whole words differ. Similar spellings can still express different facts. Original chrF paper

Freeze the input, references, scoring options and implementation version before comparing two releases. When a review adds new acceptable wording, record that as a new reference version and rescore both releases with it. If both of the assistant’s replies are unchanged, a higher score after that edit tells you the scoring rule changed. To see whether a new assistant improved, first score both versions against the same approved references, then review the replies against the policy.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. A reply that leaves out the condition

User question. When does the Standard Savings monthly fee apply?

Approved reference. The July policy says “monthly fee applies below 5000.”

Actual LLM response. The fictional saved reply is “monthly fee applies.”

Assessment. First write down the three matching words. All three candidate words match, giving 3 ÷ 3 = 1.00 precision. Only three of the five reference words match, giving 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 recall. F1 is 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75. Read the reply as a customer and try to decide whether a balance of 4900 incurs the fee. The reply does not give you enough information.

Failure classification. Mark the reply incomplete based on the policy question. Use the recall result to flag it for inspection. A low recall score alone would also flag some valid paraphrases, so use the policy itself to decide which information is missing.

Example 2. Same words, different order

User question. Write a clean one-line summary of the July fee trigger.

Approved reference. “monthly fee applies below 5000.”

Actual LLM response. The fictional saved reply is “fee monthly applies below 5000.”

Assessment. Underline the matching words first. All five match. Next list the four candidate pairs: “fee monthly,” “monthly applies,” “applies below,” and “below 5000.” Only the last two appear as pairs in the reference. That gives ROUGE-2 F1 of 0.50. You can keep “monthly applies below 5000” in order in both lines, so the longest common subsequence has four tokens. ROUGE-L F1 is 8 ÷ 10 = 0.80.

Failure classification. Send the line back for a wording edit. The awkward order broke two pairs, but you can still read the cutoff as 5000. If a second draft scored just as low, you would still read it against the policy before deciding whether to fix its wording or correct a factual error.

Example 3. The scoring winner gets the policy wrong

User question. Summarize when a Standard Savings customer pays the monthly fee.

Approved reference. Keep the July rule fixed: “monthly fee applies below 5000.” The approved evidence says an exact balance of 5000 does not trigger the fee.

Actual LLM response. Two fictional saved replies are A, “balances under 5000 incur a monthly charge,” and B, “monthly fee applies below 6000.”

Assessment. Score both against the same approved line. A shares two tokens, giving F1 of 4 ÷ 12 = 0.3333. B shares four and gives 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8000. B also leads on bigram and in-order overlap. Now test the claim at a balance of 5500. B says a fee applies there. The July rule says it does not. A preserves the correct rule.

Failure classification. Record a wrong cutoff for B. Accept A on the supplied policy criterion and keep B as a case to inspect whenever a scoring rule changes. The evidence covers these two examples. It does not tell you how often the assistant gets the policy wrong.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Use Copy Code on each program, open the Python editor beside it, paste the entire program into the editor, and select Run. Compare the result with the lesson before making the experiment's one change. Start from a fresh copy of the code for each activity. The replies and reviewer decisions are fictional, and all inputs are included in the programs. The programs compare text and report saved labels. They never call a model.

Step 1 — Count repeated words fairly

Check how often a reply repeats “fee.” split() turns each line into a list of words. Counter (included with Python) counts how many times each word occurs. Putting & between two counters keeps the smaller count for each shared word. values() gets just the counts, and sum() adds them. The from ... import ... line makes Counter available in this program.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000"
candidate = "fee fee applies"
counts = Counter(candidate.split()) & Counter(reference.split())

print("Matched:", sum(counts.values()))
print("Candidate tokens:", len(candidate.split()))
Expected output
Matched: 2
Candidate tokens: 3

The reference gives credit for one “fee” and for “applies.” Experiment. Set candidate = "monthly fee applies" and run again.

Expected output
Matched: 3
Candidate tokens: 3

“Monthly” earns the match the repeat could never earn, without changing candidate length. Checkpoint. Would a third “fee” earn another match? No, the reference has only one copy. When an overlap report rewards repetition, inspect its clipping rule before trusting it.

Step 2 — Find what a short reply leaves out

Measure the short reply from Example 1. len() counts the words on each side. / divides. The :.2f inside an f"..." print string shows the value inside braces with two digits after the decimal point.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
candidate = "monthly fee applies".split()
matched = sum((Counter(candidate) & Counter(reference)).values())

print(f"Precision: {matched / len(candidate):.2f}")
print(f"Recall: {matched / len(reference):.2f}")
print(f"F1: {2 * matched / (len(candidate) + len(reference)):.2f}")
Expected output
Precision: 1.00
Recall: 0.60
F1: 0.75

Experiment. Replace the candidate text inside the quotes with monthly fee applies below 5000. Keep the .split() and the reference as they are.

Expected output
Precision: 1.00
Recall: 1.00
F1: 1.00

The same three words still match, and both added words match. The number of reference words stays five, so recall rises to five out of five. Checkpoint. Why did precision stay at 1.00? Before and after your edit, every word the candidate used was in the reference. Inspect missing policy conditions when precision is high and recall is low. Check the wording first when you see paraphrases.

Step 3 — Compare neighboring words

Score Example 2 by sliding a window along the words. words[start:start + size] takes the words from start up to the position before start + size. range(len(words) - size + 1) gives every starting position where a full window fits. tuple() makes an ordered group that a Counter can use as a key. In the loop, sequence takes the values 1 and 2 in turn. def gives the window-counting steps the name runs, and return passes the finished count back. counts[group] += 1 adds one for the current window.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter

def runs(words, size):
    counts = Counter()
    for start in range(len(words) - size + 1):
        group = tuple(words[start:start + size])
        counts[group] += 1
    return counts

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
candidate = "fee monthly applies below 5000".split()
for sequence in (1, 2):
    expected = runs(reference, sequence)
    actual = runs(candidate, sequence)
    matched = sum((actual & expected).values())
    total = sum(actual.values()) + sum(expected.values())
    print(f"ROUGE-{sequence} F1: {2 * matched / total:.2f}")
Expected output
ROUGE-1 F1: 1.00
ROUGE-2 F1: 0.50

Experiment. Change just the candidate to monthly fee applies below 5000, keeping .split().

Expected output
ROUGE-1 F1: 1.00
ROUGE-2 F1: 1.00

The swap never changed the word counts. Fixing the order gives back the missing pairs “monthly fee” and “fee applies.” Checkpoint. Which score would an evaluator use to notice this swap? ROUGE-2 sees it. Use a separate readability review before deciding what the swap means for a customer.

Step 4 — Keep words in order across a gap

Follow “monthly” with your finger in both lines. In “monthly fee” the next word is “fee.” In “monthly below fee” you have to move past “below” to reach it. Your fingers moved forward in both lines, so the shared sequence still has two words. The program keeps track of how far that kind of match has gone as it reads longer beginnings of each line.

In the function, one row of numbers records the best length so far for each beginning of right. enumerate(right, 1) supplies each word and its position starting at one. A matching word extends the answer for the two shorter beginnings by one, using previous[j - 1]. If words differ, max() chooses the better result from dropping one end word or the other. current[-1] means the last count built for this row, and append() adds a new count to it.

Open Python Editor

def shared_order(left, right):
    previous = [0] * (len(right) + 1)
    for word in left:
        current = [0]
        for j, other in enumerate(right, 1):
            if word == other:
                length = previous[j - 1] + 1
            else:
                length = max(previous[j], current[-1])
            current.append(length)
        previous = current
    return previous[-1]

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
candidate = "monthly fee below 5000".split()
length = shared_order(candidate, reference)
print("Shared in order:", length)
print(f"ROUGE-L F1: {2 * length / (len(candidate) + len(reference)):.4f}")
Expected output
Shared in order: 4
ROUGE-L F1: 0.8889

Experiment. Change only the candidate text to 5000 below fee monthly. The words are the same as before.

Expected output
Shared in order: 1
ROUGE-L F1: 0.2222

The original four words can all be traced in order if you step over “applies.” After reversing them, any one word can match, but no pair stays in order. Checkpoint. Would token F1 change? No. The same four words still appear once each. A low ROUGE-L tells you that shared words moved or disappeared. Read the reply before attributing a meaning change.

Step 5 — See how BLEU treats short and unusual replies

Try a reply with four of the five reference words and no matching pairs. The scoring example uses up to two words at a time, so this is BLEU-2. zip(words, words[1:]) lines up each word with its next neighbor. sqrt() takes a square root. exp(x) raises a fixed mathematical number, about 2.718, to the power x. For a short reply, the multiplier is exp(1 - reference length / candidate length). With four versus five words, its input is −0.25, giving about 0.7788. Replies at least as long as the reference use a multiplier of 1. In the code, min(0, ...) keeps that exponent at or below zero. The if line changes the pair count used in the calculation only when smoothing is on and there were zero shared pairs.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter
from math import exp, sqrt

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
candidate = "fee monthly below applies".split()
use_smoothing = False

one = sum((Counter(candidate) & Counter(reference)).values())
pairs = Counter(zip(candidate, candidate[1:]))
ref_pairs = Counter(zip(reference, reference[1:]))
two = sum((pairs & ref_pairs).values())
pair_count = sum(pairs.values())
adjusted = two
if use_smoothing and two == 0:
    adjusted = 0.5
penalty = exp(min(0, 1 - len(reference) / len(candidate)))
score = 100 * penalty * sqrt((one / len(candidate)) * (adjusted / pair_count))
print(f"Word matches: {one}/{len(candidate)}")
print(f"Pair matches: {two}/{pair_count}")
print(f"Brevity multiplier: {penalty:.4f}")
print(f"BLEU-2: {score:.2f}")
Expected output
Word matches: 4/4
Pair matches: 0/3
Brevity multiplier: 0.7788
BLEU-2: 0.00

Experiment. Change use_smoothing = False to use_smoothing = True. Keep the two lines of text fixed.

Expected output
Word matches: 4/4
Pair matches: 0/3
Brevity multiplier: 0.7788
BLEU-2: 31.79

The score was zero because the two-word precision was zero. With smoothing, the calculation uses 0.5 ÷ 3 in its place. The square root is now about 0.4082 and multiplying by 0.7788 and 100 gives about 31.79. Checkpoint. Did this change create a matching pair? No, the counts were unchanged. When a score moves after a settings change, rerun both candidates with one shared setting before comparing them.

Step 6 — Score a set instead of averaging replies

Score a short reply and a longer reply separately, then score the same pair as a collection. stats() returns five values in a fixed order. The names on the left of = receive those values in that same order. When a score is calculated for the whole collection, sum(row[i] for row in rows) adds the same field from every row. score(*totals) passes the five values from totals as five inputs to score. += adds a number to a running total. The expression in square brackets repeats the sum once per field. rows[0] is the first row, which tells Python how many fields to add.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter
from math import exp, sqrt

def stats(candidate, reference):
    words = sum((Counter(candidate) & Counter(reference)).values())
    pairs = Counter(zip(candidate, candidate[1:]))
    ref_pairs = Counter(zip(reference, reference[1:]))
    pair_matches = sum((pairs & ref_pairs).values())
    return len(candidate), len(reference), words, pair_matches, sum(pairs.values())

def score(length, ref_length, words, pair_matches, pairs):
    penalty = exp(min(0, 1 - ref_length / length))
    return 100 * penalty * sqrt((words / length) * (pair_matches / pairs))

reference = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
candidates = ["monthly fee", "monthly fee applies below 6000"]
rows = []
score_sum = 0
for number, text in enumerate(candidates, 1):
    row = stats(text.split(), reference)
    rows.append(row)
    value = score(*row)
    score_sum += value
    print(f"Reply {number}: {value:.2f}")

totals = [sum(row[i] for row in rows) for i in range(len(rows[0]))]
print(f"Mean of reply scores: {score_sum / len(rows):.2f}")
print(f"Collection score: {score(*totals):.2f}")
Expected output
Reply 1: 22.31
Reply 2: 77.46
Mean of reply scores: 49.89
Collection score: 53.94

Experiment. In candidates, change monthly fee applies below 6000 to monthly fee applies below 5000. Leave the first reply as it is.

Expected output
Reply 1: 22.31
Reply 2: 100.00
Mean of reply scores: 61.16
Collection score: 65.14

In the first run, the collection has six matching words out of seven and four matching pairs out of five. Its length multiplier uses seven candidate words and ten reference words. In the second run, the longer reply gains a word match and a pair match. It keeps its length, so the multiplier stays the same. Checkpoint. Why did the collection's score differ from the average? The collection combines counts and lengths before applying the score. Confirm which calculation a report used before investigating a difference between reports. Both calculations can hide a wrong cutoff in a single reply.

Step 7 — Compare two replies against approved wording

Put the measurements beside a reviewer's policy verdict. The programs above count shared words and runs. This one uses those same operations and also reads a label supplied by a reviewer who checked the cutoff independently. Both replies and labels are fictional. Both starting examples have enough words to count up to four at a time. The assignment also tries a shorter reply. The BLEU calculation follows the library settings described below for these inputs, and the ROUGE calculations report F1.

Counter() starts an empty count. caps |= runs(reference, size) keeps the largest count for each run across the approved references. min(..., key=...) chooses a length by the rule supplied in key. The lambda is a short, unnamed function. It returns two numbers to compare in order. The first is the distance from the candidate’s length, which abs() makes positive or zero. The second is the length itself, so a tie goes to the shorter one. prod() multiplies the precisions, and ** raises the product to the power that gives the requested root. Four precisions give a power of one-quarter. smoothing *= 2 doubles the divisor at each missing order. The loop returns zero if even the single words have no matches. In the print string, :g drops unnecessary decimal zeros, and .4f prints four decimal places.

Open Python Editor

from collections import Counter
from math import exp, prod

def runs(words, size):
    return Counter(tuple(words[i:i + size])
                   for i in range(len(words) - size + 1))

def run_f1(candidate, reference, size):
    actual = runs(candidate, size)
    expected = runs(reference, size)
    matched = sum((actual & expected).values())
    return 2 * matched / (sum(actual.values()) + sum(expected.values()))

def ordered_f1(candidate, reference):
    row = [0] * (len(reference) + 1)
    for word in candidate:
        next_row = [0]
        for j, other in enumerate(reference, 1):
            if word == other:
                next_row.append(row[j - 1] + 1)
            else:
                next_row.append(max(row[j], next_row[-1]))
        row = next_row
    return 2 * row[-1] / (len(candidate) + len(reference))

def bleu4(candidate, references):
    length = len(candidate)
    lengths = [len(reference) for reference in references]
    closest = min(lengths, key=lambda size: (abs(size - length), size))
    multiplier = exp(min(0, 1 - closest / length))
    smoothing = 1
    precisions = []
    for size in range(1, min(4, length) + 1):
        actual = runs(candidate, size)
        caps = Counter()
        for reference in references:
            caps |= runs(reference, size)
        matches = sum((actual & caps).values())
        if matches == 0 and size == 1:
            return 0.0
        if matches == 0:
            smoothing *= 2
            matches = 1 / smoothing
        precisions.append(matches / sum(actual.values()))
    return 100 * multiplier * prod(precisions) ** (1 / len(precisions))

first = "monthly fee applies below 5000".split()
second = "balances under 5000 incur a monthly charge".split()
use_second_reference = False
references = [first]
if use_second_reference:
    references.append(second)

replies = [
    ("A", "balances under 5000 incur a monthly charge", "CORRECT"),
    ("B", "monthly fee applies below 6000", "WRONG CUTOFF"),
]
print("Approved wordings:", len(references))
for name, text, policy_label in replies:
    candidate = text.split()
    token = max(run_f1(candidate, ref, 1) for ref in references)
    rouge2 = max(run_f1(candidate, ref, 2) for ref in references)
    rouge_l = max(ordered_f1(candidate, ref) for ref in references)
    bleu = bleu4(candidate, references)
    print(f"{name} | token F1 {token:.4f} | BLEU {bleu:.4f}")
    print(f"  ROUGE-2 {rouge2:.4f} | ROUGE-L {rouge_l:.4f} | {policy_label}")
Expected output
Approved wordings: 1
A | token F1 0.3333 | BLEU 7.8098
  ROUGE-2 0.0000 | ROUGE-L 0.1667 | CORRECT
B | token F1 0.8000 | BLEU 66.8740
  ROUGE-2 0.7500 | ROUGE-L 0.8000 | WRONG CUTOFF

With one reference, B leads in all four columns, but a reviewer comparing the meaning with the policy sees the changed cutoff. The program prints that judgment from the label supplied with each reply.

Experiment. Change only use_second_reference = False to use_second_reference = True. The second approved wording encodes the same policy and was supplied separately for this teaching example. Both candidate replies and labels stay fixed.

Expected output
Approved wordings: 2
A | token F1 1.0000 | BLEU 100.0000
  ROUGE-2 1.0000 | ROUGE-L 1.0000 | CORRECT
B | token F1 0.8000 | BLEU 66.8740
  ROUGE-2 0.7500 | ROUGE-L 0.8000 | WRONG CUTOFF

A matches an approved wording exactly. B gains no new matching runs that raise its scores, and its cutoff is still wrong. Checkpoint. Could you claim the assistant got better after that edit? No reply changed. You changed which phrasings the scorer accepts. Freeze the new approved wording before using it to judge different replies, and label the reference change in the report.

Compare with the library definitions

Keep the July reference and both summaries exactly as printed. For SacreBLEU, the comparable configuration is case sensitive, with tokenizer none (use the supplied spaces), smoothing method exp, maximum order 4 and effective order enabled. Effective order stops at the number of token positions a short candidate actually has. With these first two candidates, orders one through four are available. For rouge-score, use rouge2 and rougeL with stemming (reducing words such as “applies” to a common base) turned off, and read the fmeasure returned by score(reference, candidate). For the second run use score_multi(references, candidate). The fixture is deliberately lowercase and has simple spacing, so the two libraries see the same words as the lab. SacreBLEU v2.5.1 · Google Research rouge-score

The printed values were cross-checked against SacreBLEU 2.5.1 and rouge-score 0.1.2. With both approved wordings, the libraries also give A BLEU 100.0000 and both ROUGE F1 scores 1.0000. You can finish the lab by comparing these results, with no additional setup. If you already have the prepared metric environment, use BLEU(tokenize='none', smooth_method='exp', effective_order=True).sentence_score(candidate, references).score and RougeScorer(['rouge2', 'rougeL'], use_stemmer=False).score_multi(references, candidate) on the same lines. Put the approved lines in a list of strings and pass the reply as one string. For B, BLEU's four raw precision fractions are 4/5, 3/4, 2/3, and 1/2. Their product is 0.20, there is no brevity penalty, and the fourth root times 100 gives 66.8740. The reference has four pairs and B matches three, giving ROUGE-2 F1 of 0.7500. B has four words shared in order out of the ten combined words, giving ROUGE-L F1 of 0.8000. For A, the same calculation starts with two unigram matches and no matches for the longer orders, so the BLEU value uses smoothing at each of those orders. Report BLEU on its 0–100 scale and the lab's token and ROUGE F1 values on 0–1. A comparison across releases also needs the same settings, tokenization rules, and approved texts.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Audit a surprising precision result

A reviewer scores “fee fee below” against “monthly fee applies below 5000” and reports perfect token precision. Count by hand, calculate precision, recall and F1, and state what you would check before accepting the report.

Practice 2. Choose an order-sensitive measurement

Compare “monthly fee below 5000” and “5000 below fee monthly” against “monthly fee applies below 5000.” Both use the same four words. Calculate each token F1 and ROUGE-L F1. Explain which value helps diagnose a reversal, and what you still need to read.

Practice 3. Decide whether two reports can be compared

One report lists 49.89 as the mean of per-reply BLEU-2. A second lists 53.94 as aggregate BLEU-2 over the same two replies from Step 6. It reports six word matches out of seven and four pair matches out of five with a brevity multiplier of about 0.6514. Reconstruct its score and explain whether the two reported numbers demonstrate an improvement.

Practice 4. Recommend a next check with incomplete evidence

A new assistant was given 0.80 token F1 for “monthly fee applies below 6000.” An older assistant was given 0.33 for “balances under 5000 incur a monthly charge.” The report shows one July reference, but omits the original question and says nothing about which policy was supplied to either assistant. What can you say about the scores? Which missing evidence would you request, and what decision would it support?

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Match one “fee” and one “below.” The second “fee” gets no credit because there is no second “fee” in the reference. Precision is 2 ÷ 3, about 0.667. Recall is 2 ÷ 5 = 0.40. F1 is 4 ÷ 8 = 0.50. Inspect whether the scorer allowed repeats to exceed reference counts. Read the candidate for the missing amount before accepting the reply.

Solution 2

Each candidate has four shared words out of nine words across the two lines, so token F1 is 8 ÷ 9, about 0.889 for both. In the first candidate all four shared words stay in reference order, giving ROUGE-L F1 of 8 ÷ 9, about 0.889. In the reversal at most one stays in order with the reference, giving 2 ÷ 9, about 0.222. ROUGE-L shows the order change. Read the summary to decide whether the new order affects meaning or only readability.

Solution 3

Multiply 6 ÷ 7 by 4 ÷ 5 to get about 0.686. Its square root is about 0.828. Multiply by 0.6514 and by 100 to get about 53.94, using the more precise values in Step 6. The quoted scores describe the same replies with different ways of combining them. To assess improvement, freeze the scoring method, the cases, and reference version, then score the two sets of candidate replies using the same settings.

Solution 4

Under the stated word rule, the reply containing 6000 overlaps more with the July reference. It would be wrong if both replies were meant to describe that July rule. Request the original question, the product and policy version that applied when it was asked, and the actual policy text supplied to each assistant. That evidence lets you judge whether the replies answered the same task and decide whether to inspect policy selection or the assistant's use of the supplied policy. The two overlap values cannot identify the cause.

Knowledge Check

  1. A candidate adds a second copy of “below.” The reference has one. How do clipped matches and candidate length change?
  2. A reply keeps three of the five reference words and adds no other words. A teammate says perfect precision means the reply is complete. What would you check?
  3. If two summaries contain identical words shuffled into different positions, which measurements might change and which stays fixed?
  4. Two sentences have some word matches, but every two-word match count is zero. A smoother raises BLEU-2 above zero. What actually changed?
  5. A two-word candidate and a five-word candidate each get their own BLEU score. Why might the mean differ from the score for both together?
  6. A valid paraphrase gets a high score after you add an approved reference. What evidence do you need before saying a new model improved?
  7. Which reply should a customer get if the exact-looking line changes a cutoff and a lower-scoring paraphrase keeps the policy correct? What additional checks still matter?
  8. A report puts BLEU 66.8740 next to ROUGE-L F1 0.8000. Can you rank those two values as measurements of the same kind of success?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. The match count for “below” stays one. Candidate length rises by one, which can lower precision.
  2. Check recall and then the meaning of the missing words. The short reply in Example 1 omits the cutoff even though every word it uses matches.
  3. Token F1 stays fixed if word counts stay fixed. The shuffle can break adjacent pairs and common ordered sequences, changing ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, or BLEU.
  4. The calculation uses a substitute for a zero precision. No observed match appeared. Keep the raw counts so readers can tell which orders needed smoothing.
  5. An average gives each reply one vote. The collection score combines length and match counts first, so the longer reply contributes more possible words and pairs.
  6. Rescore the old and new replies under the same frozen set of approved references, using identical scoring options. Check policy accuracy independently of overlap.
  7. Prefer the paraphrase for the stated policy question. Still check that it is clear, complete for the original question, and based on the version the customer should receive.
  8. No. BLEU here has a 0–100 scale and measures a blend of clipped precision and length. ROUGE-L F1 has a 0–1 scale and measures shared order. Rescaling the numbers would leave the two scoring rules different.

Independent Assignment

You are reviewing summaries before Harbor Leaf publishes a new savings help page. Use a fresh copy of Step 7 for each variant and keep use_second_reference = False. Keep reply B fixed as a comparison. Review each new A against the July policy first, then make the edit and run it. Copy the score lines into your notes. Write two sentences per variant explaining whether you would approve each candidate and whether using overlap alone would have led you there.

  1. Replace the whole A row with ("A", "monthly fee", "INCOMPLETE"),. This is a short reply to the same question. Decide whether it tells a customer with a balance of 4900 what will happen.
  2. Start again from Step 7. Replace the A row with ("A", "monthly fee applies below 5000", "CORRECT"),. Ask whether the four overlap measures now agree with the approved judgment, and what else you'd need before publishing a collection of answers.
Answer key

For variant 1 the report prints Approved wordings: 1, then A | token F1 0.5714 | BLEU 22.3130, followed by two spaces and ROUGE-2 0.4000 | ROUGE-L 0.5714 | INCOMPLETE. For variant 2 it prints Approved wordings: 1, then A | token F1 1.0000 | BLEU 100.0000, followed by two spaces and ROUGE-2 1.0000 | ROUGE-L 1.0000 | CORRECT. Both runs end with B | token F1 0.8000 | BLEU 66.8740, then two spaces and ROUGE-2 0.7500 | ROUGE-L 0.8000 | WRONG CUTOFF.

In variant 1, A leaves the customer with ₹4,900 guessing, and B would wrongly tell a customer with ₹5,500 to expect a charge. Hold both drafts. In variant 2, approve A for the July question. It copies the approved wording, so all four scores reach their maximum. You still have the same wrong cutoff in B. Before publishing a collection of replies, add reviewed cases at ₹4,999 and ₹5,000 and include a paraphrase you approved without looking at its score.

Common Mistakes

A percentage-looking score can hide a serious error. Before clearing a draft, check decision-critical details such as the amount, which account it applies to, and what happens at the boundary.

A high precision with low recall can mean a reply left something out. It may also mean the approved line and the reply used different words. Read the pair before treating a recall drop as an omission.

BLEU can change when smoothing, tokenization, or aggregation changes. Keep the raw counts and the settings beside a score. If a report omits those details, rerun the comparison under one shared setup.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Start with the approved evidence. Token F1 measures shared counts, ROUGE-2 measures neighboring pairs, ROUGE-L follows shared words in order, and BLEU combines clipped precision at different lengths with a penalty for short answers. Use these measurements to flag a difference worth reading. Record which replies, references, settings and scale you used before comparing results. When a customer's decision depends on a fact such as a cutoff, check the fact independently.

What You Will Learn

  • Explain how a pretrained encoder turns a sentence into a vector and why its individual numbers usually need no human-readable labels.
  • Calculate cosine similarity for two short vectors and recognize when there is no usable score.
  • Compare paraphrases, wrong deadlines, and reversed policy claims without treating a similarity score as a verdict.
  • Test two thresholds on held-out replies, report their trade-offs, and identify which claims need a direct policy check.

Why This Lesson Matters

Imagine you ordered a jacket online from Harbor Leaf Market. It arrived 20 days ago, and you haven't worn it. You type “Can I get my money back?” The help page calls this “requesting a refund.” A person reading both phrases can see what you mean. A computer that only counts matching words has less to go on.

Then the team sees “You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery.” It is nearly a word-for-word copy of the approved answer, except the store allows 30 calendar days, including day 30. A customer on day 45 would get the wrong impression from the 90-day reply.

The store, policy, replies, and numerical vectors in this lesson are fictional. The store accepts refund requests for unused online purchases within 30 calendar days of delivery. The question we score is about that deadline for an eligible item. From Ground truth, references and benchmarks, bring an approved source for each fact. Token F1, BLEU, ROUGE and reference metrics explains why matching words can miss a paraphrase. Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance is useful here and required before building your own held-out split for threshold tuning.

Beginner Explanation

Start with the words you can see

Put “You may request a refund within 30 days of delivery” above “Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives.” With case and punctuation set aside, the lines share just “days.” Read again without counting. “Money back” means a refund here, “arrives” marks delivery, and thirty is 30. Both give the same instruction for the same eligible purchase. A restatement that preserves the meaning is a paraphrase. Comparing the meanings rather than the written words is called semantic similarity.

Watch what happens with “a refund is available during the first month.” It sounds close, but “first month” can be read in more than one way. A calendar month can have more or fewer than 30 days. When the deadline matters, send this wording for clarification. Being about the same event is a weaker claim than preserving the rule.

Give the computer something it can compare

Mark a starting point on a sheet of paper. Move three squares right and one up, then draw an arrow to that spot. Write the directions as (3, 1). Swap them to (1, 3) and the arrow turns. This ordered group of numbers is a vector, and each number is a component. You needed two directions to draw the arrow, so the vector has two dimensions. A model can keep track of more dimensions than you can draw.

For the demonstration, imagine that someone has already placed the approved reply at (4, 0) and the paraphrase at (3, 1). These are hand-authored positions. An embedding is a numerical representation made by a model for text or another input. A sentence encoder is a model that takes text in and returns a vector. A pretrained encoder has already learned from examples before you use it here. Depending on what it learned, sentences about similar things can end up pointing in similar directions. Sentence-BERT research paper

Real encoders often return many numbers so they can represent more patterns than our two-position sketch. You generally cannot point to one learned position and call it “refund” or “truth.” The positions work together. Even in this lesson we leave the two teaching positions unnamed. An evaluator compares the whole vectors and checks how well the scores work on reviewed examples.

Compare the directions

Draw an arrow from the origin, where both coordinates are zero, to (4, 0). Now draw one to (8, 0). The second goes twice as far, but both point straight right. The length of an arrow is its magnitude. If you want to know whether arrows point the same way, their lengths alone won't help.

Try a third arrow to (3, 1). Multiply the numbers in matching positions and add the results. With (4, 0), that gives (4 × 3) + (0 × 1) = 12. This is the dot product. Doubling one arrow doubles that number even when its direction stays fixed.

To account for length, find the magnitude of each arrow. Square each component by multiplying it by itself, add the squares, then take the square root. The square root of 9 is 3 because 3 × 3 = 9. The reference length is √(16 + 0) = 4. The paraphrase length is √(9 + 1) = √10. Divide 12 by 4 × √10 and you get about 0.949. This is cosine similarity, the dot product divided by the product of the two magnitudes. It compares the angle between the arrows. SciPy cosine distance definition

Cosine runs from −1 to 1 for nonzero vectors. A score of 1 means the same direction, 0 means a right angle, and −1 means opposite directions. These are directions in the model’s numbers. A score of −1 does not label a contradiction, and 0.949 does not mean a 94.9% chance the reply is correct. A vector of all zeros has no direction, so dividing by its length would be undefined. Record the score as unavailable. Also treat unequal vector lengths or vectors from different encoders as a setup problem, even when the scores would be convenient to compare.

Check the parts a score can miss

Read these three lines against the store's rule.

  • “Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives” preserves the refund request, deadline, and starting event.
  • “You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery” changes the deadline. The topic remains the same and the numerical fact is wrong.
  • “You cannot request a refund within 30 days of delivery” keeps the number and reverses the permission. A small word changes whether the rest of the statement is allowed. That reversal is negation. Here it creates a contradiction with the policy.

“You may request a refund” is also about the right topic, but leaves the customer without a deadline. A related statement can be incomplete, wrong, or opposite in meaning. Another useful question is whether the policy actually guarantees the claim. That relationship is called entailment. The right to request a refund does not guarantee it will be approved. Cosine gives a direction comparison. Check the approved policy for facts, dates, conditions, and whether the reply says enough to answer the question.

You can implement some factual checks as direct rules. For example, once the text has been reliably read as allowing a request within 90 days of delivery, 90 and 30 can be compared with an exact number check. Confirm the event and the unit before comparing the numbers. If the reply says “month,” mixes two deadlines, or leaves out the event, ask a reviewer to inspect the original text. The lesson's code is given reviewed facts as inputs. It does not extract them from a sentence.

Choose which replies need attention

Suppose you have ten replies and enough time to read only a few right away. You can use the score to sort replies into a likely-match group and a group for closer reading. That first sorting step is called triage. A number you use to divide the groups is a threshold. Here we shortlist when the unrounded cosine is at least the threshold. Policy mismatches can still block a reply before that shortlist is used.

To pick a threshold, start with a labeled practice set. The labels come from people who read the approved source and reply. Try more than one cutoff. Then test both on a separate, held-out set that wasn't used to choose those cutoffs. Choosing a cutoff for the task using labeled examples is threshold calibration. If you choose a new cutoff after seeing the held-out results, get a fresh set for the next independent check.

For a small development example, imagine four replies scored 0.96 (equivalent), 0.85 (equivalent), 0.93 (wrong deadline), and 0.84 (missing deadline). A cutoff of 0.90 shortlists two replies, one correct and one wrong, and misses one valid reply. A cutoff of 0.80 shortlists all four. It recovers the valid reply and adds one more false shortlist. A false shortlist here means a reply the score shortlisted that the reviewer did not consider equivalent. A missed match is an equivalent reply the score left out. The lab tests these same two preset cutoffs on a different set. Do not treat either number as a universal standard.

When using real embeddings, save the encoder name and exact version, how you prepared the text, the reference wording, the scores or vectors, and the threshold alongside your labels. If the encoder changes, encode both sets of texts with the new encoder and compare the two scoring setups on the same reviewed cases. For example, a new encoder could give the same paraphrase 0.84 where the old one gave 0.93. Test both versions before reusing the old cutoff. An equal number of components does not make vectors from two models comparable. Keep actual failed requests, which produced no reply, in a separate count so they neither earn zero similarity nor inflate the number of wrong answers.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. A paraphrase loses on word overlap

User question. How long after delivery can I ask for a refund on my unused online purchase?

Approved reference. “You may request a refund within 30 days of delivery.” The policy counts calendar days and includes day 30.

Actual LLM response. The fictional saved reply says “Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives.”

Assessment. Lowercase the two lines, remove the final periods, and cross off the words they share. Only “days” matches, so the reference coverage is 1 ÷ 10 = 0.10. The supplied teaching vectors are (4, 0) and (3, 1). Their cosine is 12 ÷ (4 × √10), about 0.949. Next check the text itself. “Ask for” preserves the permission, “thirty calendar days” preserves the deadline, and “after it arrives” preserves the starting event.

Failure classification. The reply fits the policy, so a rule that rejects it for low word overlap would make a mistake. Use this pair to test whether a new scoring setup can find equivalent wording. The invented cosine explains how the approach could help. It gives no measured result for a real encoder.

Example 2. Compare direction before comparing length

User question. Would a longer vector make a candidate seem more similar to the approved refund reply?

Approved reference. Keep the same reply and its teaching vector (4, 0). Compare only the numbers in this example.

Actual LLM response. Use a fictional measurement for the same saved line before and after scaling. Its vector changes from (3, 1) to (6, 2). This isolates length from changes in the reply.

Assessment. The dot product goes from 4 × 3 + 0 × 1 = 12 to 4 × 6 + 0 × 2 = 24. The original length is √10. The second is √(36 + 4) = √40 = 2 × √10. The reference length stays 4. The new cosine is 24 ÷ (4 × 2 × √10), which is the original 0.949. If you instead turn the candidate arrow up to (0, 3), the dot product becomes zero and cosine becomes 0.

Failure classification. Ranking these two scaled copies by dot product alone would reward a longer arrow even though it points the same way. The angle comparison avoids that effect. This deliberate scaling test does not tell you why a real encoder might produce a longer vector.

Example 3. The wrong deadline leads the ranking

User question. On day 45 after delivery, can I still request a refund for an eligible item under the standard policy?

Approved reference. Use the same 30-day policy statement as evidence. Since 45 is greater than 30, the ordinary request window has closed.

Actual LLM response. One fictional reply restates the correct rule as “Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives.” A second says “You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery.”

Assessment. The paraphrase scores 12 ÷ (4 × √10) ≈ 0.949. The 90-day reply uses the supplied vector (4, 1) and scores 16 ÷ (4 × √17) ≈ 0.970. Both clear a cutoff of 0.90. Now put the customer's day 45 next to the two deadlines. It is past day 30, but still inside day 90. Following the higher-scoring reply would lead this customer to think the window was still open.

Failure classification. Block the 90-day reply for a policy mismatch. The paraphrase preserves the standard deadline, although a direct “the window has closed” would answer this customer's specific question more completely. Keep the refund deadline check even if the similarity ranking looks strong across the rest of the set.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

For each step choose Copy Code, open the editor next to the program, paste the full code into the editor yourself, and choose Run. Compare the console with the first expected output. Make the one specified edit and run the program again. Each program starts from an empty editor and includes its own data. The numbers are hand-authored teaching fixtures, saved beside fictional replies so you can rerun a comparison. No program calls an encoder or measures a real assistant.

Step 1 — Count the words before checking what they mean

Measure how many distinct words in the approved line reappear in two drafts. lower() makes the letters lowercase. rstrip(".") removes final periods, and split() breaks the line at whitespace. set() keeps one copy of each distinct word. & keeps only the words in both sets. This coverage measure uses the number of distinct reference words as its denominator.

Open Python Editor

def words(text):
    return set(text.lower().rstrip(".").split())

reference = "You may request a refund within 30 days of delivery."
paraphrase = "Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives."
wrong = "You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery."
reference_words = words(reference)

for label, reply in [("Paraphrase", paraphrase), ("Wrong deadline", wrong)]:
    shared = len(reference_words & words(reply))
    print(f"{label}: {shared} of {len(reference_words)} reference words")
Expected output
Paraphrase: 1 of 10 reference words
Wrong deadline: 9 of 10 reference words

Experiment. Replace the text of paraphrase with Request a refund no later than 30 days after delivery.. Keep the reference and the wrong reply fixed.

Expected output
Paraphrase: 6 of 10 reference words
Wrong deadline: 9 of 10 reference words

The approved and revised lines share “request,” “a,” “refund,” “30,” “days,” and “delivery.” The score rises even though the paraphrase still gives the same deadline. Checkpoint. Which line would this counter rank first? The 90-day reply. Use the count to inspect wording changes and read the policy to make the decision.

Step 2 — Store two positions for a sentence

Look at the numbers attached to the approved line and its paraphrase. Parentheses and commas make a fixed ordered group, a tuple. Python starts counting positions at zero, so [0] reads the first component and [1] reads the second. len() counts components. The plotting values are supplied by hand in this program, independently of the words.

Open Python Editor

reference = (4, 0)
paraphrase = (3, 1)

print(f"Reference: {reference}")
print(f"Paraphrase: x={paraphrase[0]}, y={paraphrase[1]}")
print(f"Dimensions: {len(paraphrase)}")
Expected output
Reference: (4, 0)
Paraphrase: x=3, y=1
Dimensions: 2

Experiment. Change the second component of paraphrase from 1 to 3, giving (3, 3). Predict which printed fields will change.

Expected output
Reference: (4, 0)
Paraphrase: x=3, y=3
Dimensions: 2

The point moves up but stays three steps to the right. It still has two components. Checkpoint. Could the change be interpreted as “more refund”? The coordinates provide no such label. In an evaluation, record how the vectors were made so a manually altered pair is never mistaken for output from an encoder.

Step 3 — Measure the length of an arrow

Use a supplied point for a refund reply to see what doubling the whole arrow does. At (3, 4), the squares are 9 and 16, which add to 25. The square root gives 5. ** 2 squares a number. sqrt() comes from Python's math module. In x, y = point, Python gives the two components the names on the left in order.

Open Python Editor

from math import sqrt

point = (3, 4)
scale = 1
x, y = point
x = x * scale
y = y * scale
squared_length = x ** 2 + y ** 2

print(f"Vector: ({x}, {y})")
print(f"Sum of squares: {squared_length}")
print(f"Magnitude: {sqrt(squared_length):.3f}")
Expected output
Vector: (3, 4)
Sum of squares: 25
Magnitude: 5.000

Experiment. Change scale = 1 to scale = 2.

Expected output
Vector: (6, 8)
Sum of squares: 100
Magnitude: 10.000

The two components double, each square quadruples, and the square root doubles the length. Checkpoint. What happened to the direction? It stayed fixed, because both components changed by the same positive factor. An evaluator who compares only length could report a change even though direction stays fixed.

Step 4 — Compare direction and handle a missing score

Multiply corresponding components to get the dot product. zip(left, right) supplies pairs of corresponding components, and sum(a * b for a, b in ...) adds their products. hypot(*left) passes the separate components to Python's length function. None represents a missing result. The check for different lengths keeps zip() from quietly dropping an unmatched component.

Open Python Editor

from math import hypot

def compare(left, right):
    if len(left) != len(right):
        return None
    product = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(left, right))
    lengths = hypot(*left) * hypot(*right)
    if lengths == 0:
        return None
    return product, product / lengths

reference = (4, 0)
candidate = (3, 4)
dot, score = compare(reference, candidate)
print(f"Dot product: {dot}")
print(f"Cosine: {score:.3f}")
if compare(reference, (0, 0)) is None:
    print("Zero vector: unavailable")
Expected output
Dot product: 12
Cosine: 0.600
Zero vector: unavailable

Experiment. Change candidate to (0, 5). Its length is still 5. Leave the separate zero-vector check alone.

Expected output
Dot product: 0
Cosine: 0.000
Zero vector: unavailable

The reference arrow points right and the changed candidate points straight up. Both still have a length, so the division is 0 ÷ (4 × 5) = 0. Checkpoint. Why does the last line still say “unavailable”? Its separate test uses (0, 0), an arrow with no length at all. That would require dividing by zero, so the function returns no score. Keep these outcomes separate when counting low scores.

Step 5 — Rank saved replies and read the policy labels

Score three fictional refund replies with the same reference vector. A asks for money back within thirty days, B changes the window to 90 days, and C says “From delivery, you have 30 days to ask for your money back.” The reviewed policy judgment is already attached to each reply. The list ranked collects a tuple with the score first. sort(reverse=True) orders those tuples from highest to lowest, comparing the score before the other fields. There are no tied scores in this exercise. :.3f displays three decimal places.

Open Python Editor

from math import hypot

def cosine(left, right):
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(left, right)) / (hypot(*left) * hypot(*right))

reference = (4, 0)
replies = [
    ("A", (3, 1), "correct paraphrase"),
    ("B", (4, 1), "wrong deadline"),
    ("C", (4, 3), "correct reordering"),
]
ranked = []
for name, vector, policy_label in replies:
    ranked.append((cosine(reference, vector), name, policy_label))

ranked.sort(reverse=True)
for score, name, policy_label in ranked:
    print(f"{name}: {score:.3f} | {policy_label}")
Expected output
B: 0.970 | wrong deadline
A: 0.949 | correct paraphrase
C: 0.800 | correct reordering

Experiment. Imagine a different teaching setup records (8, 1) for reply C, “From delivery, you have 30 days to ask for your money back.” Change just C's vector in the list and leave its policy label fixed.

Expected output
C: 0.992 | correct reordering
B: 0.970 | wrong deadline
A: 0.949 | correct paraphrase

C's arrow now points closer to the reference direction, so its rank rises. It is still the same reply. Checkpoint. Has the wrong deadline improved? B is unchanged. Keep reviewed labels and fixed replies when comparing scoring setups, and compare whole sets if you change encoders. This activity assumes valid nonzero vectors of equal length, as supplied.

Step 6 — Check the deadline independently

Change the number printed in a hypothetical reply. Keep its teaching vector fixed so you can see the difference between a similarity calculation and a deadline check. Both drafts allow a request and use the same starting event and units. The code inserts the reviewed day count into the text using braces in an f"..." string. == compares the reported and approved values. This exact comparison can run after those facts have been verified.

Open Python Editor

from math import hypot

policy_days = 30
reported_days = 90
reply = f"You may request a refund within {reported_days} days of delivery."
reference = (4, 0)
vector = (4, 1)
product = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(reference, vector))
score = product / (hypot(*reference) * hypot(*vector))

print(reply)
print(f"Cosine: {score:.3f}")
if reported_days == policy_days:
    print(f"Deadline: MATCH ({reported_days} == {policy_days})")
else:
    print(f"Deadline: WRONG ({reported_days} != {policy_days})")
Expected output
You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery.
Cosine: 0.970
Deadline: WRONG (90 != 30)

Experiment. Change only reported_days = 90 to reported_days = 30.

Expected output
You may request a refund within 30 days of delivery.
Cosine: 0.970
Deadline: MATCH (30 == 30)

The displayed number changes and the rule now passes. Cosine is identical because the program was given the same numbers for both runs. Checkpoint. Would a real encoder have to give both replies the same score? You would have to measure that. This controlled example shows why a direct check is valuable even if a similarity change is small. The check here covers the verified deadline, so a separate permission check is still needed before accepting “cannot.”

Step 7 — Try two thresholds on held-out refund replies

The refund team chose 0.90 and 0.80 using the earlier practice records. This program uses a different collection of frozen replies to compare what those choices would do. The team already read each reply and recorded whether it was equivalent to the approved answer. It also wrote down the day count and whether the reply allows or denies the request. Treat those supplied facts and labels as separate evidence. The toy vectors cannot supply either of them. Think of the rows as a saved snapshot from the scoring stage: you can compare the near misses again without regenerating the numbers. In a real experiment the snapshot would contain cached outputs from a named encoder. Here it contains hand-authored teaching values.

The approved reference is “You may request a refund within 30 days of delivery.” Each record holds the case ID, the captured text, the teaching vector, the reviewed deadline in calendar days from delivery, the permission, and the equivalence label. If the trigger or units are unclear, the reviewer leaves the deadline missing. A request that produced no reply has None in its reply field. If a saved reply has no vector, the cosine function returns a missing result. The program uses continue to skip the rest of the loop for that record. score is not None and ... checks that a score exists before comparing it with a number. A missing score stays out of the shortlist counts, while a known policy mismatch can still block the reply. In above = score >= threshold, the result is True when the score meets or exceeds the cutoff. += 1 adds one to a count. The route CHECKED MATCH means the supplied policy facts matched and the cosine met this illustrative cutoff.

Open Python Editor

from math import hypot

def cosine(left, right):
    if right is None or len(left) != len(right):
        return None
    lengths = hypot(*left) * hypot(*right)
    if lengths == 0:
        return None
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(left, right)) / lengths

reference = (4, 0)
policy_days = 30
threshold = 0.90
cases = [
    ("H1", "Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives.",
     (3, 1), 30, "allows", True),
    ("H2", "You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery.",
     (4, 1), 90, "allows", False),
    ("H3", "You cannot request a refund within 30 days of delivery.",
     (4, -1), 30, "denies", False),
    ("H4", "From delivery, you have 30 days to ask for your money back.",
     (4, 3), 30, "allows", True),
    ("H5", "You may request a refund.",
     (3, 2), None, "allows", False),
    ("H6", None, None, None, None, None),
    ("H7", "Track the parcel in Orders.",
     (3, 4), None, None, False),
]

scored = shortlisted = false_shortlist = missed = no_reply = 0
print(f"Threshold: {threshold:.2f}")
for case_id, reply, vector, days, permission, equivalent in cases:
    if reply is None:
        no_reply += 1
        print(f"{case_id}: no reply | REQUEST ERROR")
        continue

    score = cosine(reference, vector)
    above = score is not None and score >= threshold
    score_text = "unavailable"
    if score is not None:
        score_text = f"{score:.3f}"
        scored += 1
        if above:
            shortlisted += 1
            if not equivalent:
                false_shortlist += 1
        elif equivalent:
            missed += 1

    if permission == "denies":
        route = "BLOCK (permission)"
    elif days is None or permission != "allows":
        route = "REVIEW (missing facts)"
    elif days != policy_days:
        route = f"BLOCK (expected {policy_days}, found {days})"
    elif score is None:
        route = "REVIEW (vector)"
    elif above:
        route = "CHECKED MATCH"
    else:
        route = "REVIEW (low cosine)"
    print(f"{case_id}: {score_text} | {route}")

print(f"Score only: {shortlisted}/{scored} shortlisted | "
      f"false shortlists: {false_shortlist} | missed matches: {missed}")
print(f"Request errors: {no_reply}")
Expected output
Threshold: 0.90
H1: 0.949 | CHECKED MATCH
H2: 0.970 | BLOCK (expected 30, found 90)
H3: 0.970 | BLOCK (permission)
H4: 0.800 | REVIEW (low cosine)
H5: 0.832 | REVIEW (missing facts)
H6: no reply | REQUEST ERROR
H7: 0.600 | REVIEW (missing facts)
Score only: 3/6 shortlisted | false shortlists: 2 | missed matches: 1
Request errors: 1

Experiment. Change only threshold = 0.90 to threshold = 0.80. Keep the saved text, approved facts, vectors, and reviewer labels fixed.

Expected output
Threshold: 0.80
H1: 0.949 | CHECKED MATCH
H2: 0.970 | BLOCK (expected 30, found 90)
H3: 0.970 | BLOCK (permission)
H4: 0.800 | CHECKED MATCH
H5: 0.832 | REVIEW (missing facts)
H6: no reply | REQUEST ERROR
H7: 0.600 | REVIEW (missing facts)
Score only: 5/6 shortlisted | false shortlists: 3 | missed matches: 0
Request errors: 1

At 0.90, the score alone would shortlist H1, H2, and H3. At 0.80, H4 meets the cutoff exactly and H5 also clears it. H4 preserves the required facts, so it moves out of the low-cosine review queue. H5 stays in review because it omits the deadline. H2 and H3 stay blocked. The summary counts errors from using the score alone, while each printed route also uses the supplied policy facts. To express the score-only error as a share of the shortlist, use 2 of 3 at 0.90 and 3 of 5 at 0.80. Quote the counts too. The lower cutoff adds one false shortlist even though the fraction of shortlists that are false falls.

Checkpoint. What can you report to the team? On these six scored replies, the lower cutoff recovered one reviewed match and added one false shortlist. The independent rule caught that extra shortlist and kept the two explicit mismatches blocked. Report the failed request separately. Neither cutoff is validated for live traffic by these six hand-authored cases.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Find the actual paraphrase

The approved rule allows a request up to and including calendar day 30 after delivery. Which is an equivalent restatement: “Ask for your money back up to thirty calendar days after it arrives,” “A refund is available during the first month,” or “You cannot request a refund within 30 days of delivery”? Give the reason for your choice and the next action for the other two.

Practice 2. Compare arrows by hand

The approved vector is (4, 0). One supplied vector is (3, 4) and another is (6, 8). Find the dot product, candidate length, and cosine for each comparison. Which ranks higher? What would a dot-product-only ranking show?

Practice 3. Diagnose a false shortlist

A reply to an eligible customer on day 40 says “You may request a refund within 90 days of delivery” and scores 0.970. Another says “You may request a refund” and scores 0.832. With a 0.80 cutoff, which replies reach the shortlist? Use the policy to decide their individual routes and explain why they differ.

Practice 4. Choose evidence before raising a cutoff

Your team has labeled 80 practice replies and has 25 held-out replies it has never read. The practice set includes correct paraphrases and wrong deadlines but no reversed permissions. A new encoder calls many short replies more similar than the earlier encoder did. Describe what to keep fixed, how to compare the two encoders and candidate thresholds, and what evidence the team still needs.

Independent Assignment

You own the refund queue for this trial. Use the approved reference, eligibility and deadline from the setup and all seven captured records, vectors, and labels in Step 7. Before running anything, pick H4 and H5 and decide which should be eligible for a checked match. Then write down which cases need a numeric check, a permission check, a closer read, or a separate retry.

The full executable answer key is the Step 7 program. Use Copy Code on that block for each variant. Make a fresh copy each time, keep the same reference and evidence, and change only threshold. Use 0.95 for variant A and 0.60 for variant B. Predict each route and record the number of false shortlists, missed matches, and request errors. Compare both variants with 0.90 and 0.80. These are trial cutoffs for inspecting the fixture. Spending the held-out set on further tuning would call for another independent test.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The first choice preserves the event, the 30-day limit, and the permission to request. Ask a policy reviewer to clarify “first month” because the wording may move the cutoff or describe approval rather than a request. Block the third choice because the denial directly conflicts with permission. Shared words are compatible with both a correct answer and a denial of the right.

Solution 2

The reference length is 4. For (3, 4), the dot product is 4 × 3 + 0 × 4 = 12 and length is √(9 + 16) = 5. Cosine is 12 ÷ (4 × 5) = 0.60. For (6, 8), the dot product is 24 and the length is √(36 + 64) = 10. Cosine is 24 ÷ (4 × 10) = 0.60. The scores tie because the arrows point the same way. The raw dot products would give the second arrow a higher rank because it is longer.

Solution 3

Both scores clear 0.80. The first reply should be blocked. A 90-day window permits a request on day 40, but the approved 30-day window has closed. Send the second for review or revision because it omits the deadline. A missing deadline is different evidence from an explicit wrong deadline, even though neither reply should be published to this customer.

Solution 4

Run both versions on the same practice replies and reference text. Within each run, use that version to encode both sides of every comparison. Pick the cutoffs from the practice results, then open the 25 held-out replies and count both kinds of mistake. Read the replies where the versions disagree. The practice set never asked either encoder to distinguish “you can” from “you cannot.” Add reviewed examples of that contrast to future practice and test sets, and keep the direct permission and deadline checks while you collect that evidence.

Assignment answer key

H4 states the correct deadline and qualifies when its score meets the cutoff. H5 never provides a deadline and always needs review. The two explicit mismatches are H2 (days) and H3 (permission). Review H7 as an off-topic reply that does not provide the facts, and investigate H6 as a failed request separately.

For variant A, the exact changed lines from the 0.90 run are Threshold: 0.95, H1: 0.949 | REVIEW (low cosine), and Score only: 2/6 shortlisted | false shortlists: 2 | missed matches: 2. Every other line is as printed for 0.90, including Request errors: 1. The raw shortlist is just H2 and H3. The higher bar leaves both correct replies in review and does not remove either explicit error from the raw shortlist.

For variant B, the exact changed lines from the 0.90 run are Threshold: 0.60, H4: 0.800 | CHECKED MATCH, and Score only: 6/6 shortlisted | false shortlists: 4 | missed matches: 0. Every other line is as printed for 0.90, including Request errors: 1. Now even H7 clears the raw threshold. The policy route still sends it to review. If reviewer time is scarce, the extra score-only candidates matter. This tiny fixture supports comparing routes and writing more tests. It gives no estimate of live performance.

Knowledge Check

  1. Two encoders both output vectors of length 384. Can you score a reply from one against a reference from the other? How would you compare the setups fairly?
  2. You change (3, 1) to (3, 3). What changed about the arrow, and why does the vector still have two dimensions?
  3. Why can the dot product increase when a candidate arrow points exactly the same way as before?
  4. What is the magnitude of (0, -5)? Why does a component with a negative sign still add to length?
  5. Two nonzero arrows point at right angles. A third vector is all zeros. Which comparison can legitimately produce a cosine of zero?
  6. A valid paraphrase falls from 0.93 to 0.84 when evaluated with a new encoder. What should the team check before calling the reply worse?
  7. A reply says “You cannot request a refund within 30 days of delivery” and scores 0.970. Which piece of the reply needs a separate check, and why is the number insufficient?
  8. In Step 7, you read the held-out results and then choose a third cutoff. Can you use the same held-out cases to report an independent result for that new choice?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Equal length gives the same number of positions, but the positions were learned in different models. Score complete pairs with each encoder separately, then compare where their rankings and decisions differ on the same reviewed examples.
  2. The first component stays at 3 and the second rises from 1 to 3. The arrow turns upward. There are still two component positions, since the repeated value 3 occupies both positions. The lesson assigns neither component a meaning such as “refund.”
  3. Doubling the candidate doubles each matching-position product and therefore their sum. Its magnitude doubles too, so the cosine ratio remains the same.
  4. Square 0 and −5 to get 0 and 25. Their sum is 25 and its square root is 5. Squaring makes the contribution nonnegative.
  5. The right-angle pair has valid lengths and a dot product of zero, so its cosine is zero. The all-zero vector makes the denominator zero and leaves the score undefined.
  6. Confirm the reply and approved evidence were held fixed, and score both texts with each version. Reread the paraphrase against the policy. The score may reflect the change of encoder rather than a change in the text or its correctness.
  7. Check permission. “Cannot” denies an action the approved policy permits. Both lines can contain 30 and still give opposite instructions.
  8. The revised choice has already seen those cases through the results, so they now serve as development evidence. Report the tuning honestly and test the revised cutoff on new held-out cases.

Common Mistakes

A large score can make it tempting to clear a reply immediately. Read the deadline, permission, and event first. If you cannot verify a fact from the text and the approved source, route it to review.

Avoid comparing scores from different model versions as if the vectors shared one set of directions. Freeze and record the settings. When a setup changes, score a common set of reference and reply pairs with each version.

Count failures to capture a reply separately. A missing response cannot tell you whether two answers use similar wording or preserve the same rule. Giving it a score of zero would mix operational reliability with text comparison.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

A sentence encoder represents text as a vector. Cosine compares the direction of two vectors, which can help you find paraphrases worth inspecting. An approved source and direct checks still decide whether a reply preserves the policy. Use reviewed cases to choose a trial cutoff, hold back separate examples for comparison, and report how many replies enter the review queue along with the types of error you observed.

Next, Combining evaluators and handling uncertainty uses several checks together and asks what to do when their results disagree.
