Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Match independent reviewer and judge labels to frozen response IDs and calculate exact agreement.
  • Use the approved policy to check whether agreement reflects a justified outcome.
  • Read a confusion matrix and calculate Cohen’s kappa from observed agreement and each reviewer’s label frequencies.
  • Clarify rubric anchors, investigate style preferences, and report held-out errors, sample sizes, and unresolved cases.

Why This Lesson Matters

Your parcel arrived 45 days ago. Harbor Leaf Market’s assistant tells you the store gives you 90 days to request a refund. Two reviewers and an automated judge approve the reply. Then someone opens the policy and finds a 30-day deadline. The customer is already too late. Before trusting the next round of ratings, the team needs to understand how three matching judgments missed the same fact.

The store, messages, labels, and replay outputs in this chapter are fictional. Policy refund-1 says “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included. Each customer in the fixture has an eligible unused online order and asks for the deadline and what they need to request a refund. The approved clause is the reference for those answers.

Allow about six hours. Start with Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge. Annotation, adjudication and synthetic data and Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance are recommended background. Use the latter before building your own calibration and holdout sets. This chapter supplies separate case IDs and replays so you can inspect both sets entirely offline.

Beginner Explanation

Start with two independent reads

Nia and Omar each receive the same policy, question, and saved replies. They record their labels without seeing each other’s work or the judge’s output. This is independent review. A rubric is their shared scoring guide. Version v1 says PASS for “sufficient refund guidance,” FAIL for wrong or insufficient guidance, and REVIEW for a material doubt. It does not say clearly whether omitting the receipt makes a reply insufficient. A rubric anchor is a concrete example showing which label to assign and why.

Preparation skills
IDFrozen replyNiaOmarJudge replay v1
AYou may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.PASSPASSPASS
BYou can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.PASSPASSPASS
CAsk for a refund during the first month after delivery if you have proof of purchase.REVIEWPASSPASS
DYou can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.FAILPASSPASS
EContact our support team for assistance.FAILFAILFAIL

Put a check mark next to each row where Nia and Omar gave the same label. You’ll mark A and B for matching PASS labels, and E for matching FAIL labels. C and D get no mark. You have three marks across five rows that both people rated. Divide 3 by 5 to get 60%. That is exact agreement. It counts matches, so on a five-point scale a 4 versus a 5 is a mismatch just as a 1 versus a 5 is.

The judge matches Nia on three cases and Omar on all five. Nia and Omar use different interpretations of the receipt rule. Matching one person more often does not tell you whose interpretation is supported. Check each disagreement using the frozen reply and the source. Then inspect some agreements too. B is where all three labels miss the same fact.

Confirm what the policy supports

Put B’s “90 calendar days” beside the approved “through calendar day 30.” At day 45, the two statements give different instructions. The written policy provides stronger evidence than the three matching labels. An independent reviewer can now record FAIL for this specific claim.

A person who resolves a disputed judgment by reading the evidence and applying an agreed rule is doing adjudication. Keep their reason alongside their decision. For D, the updated rubric can make the omission rule explicit and support FAIL. For C, there is no exact day count and no clear confirmation of a valid receipt. Leave its adjudicated label open and route it for clarification. REVIEW describes the next action. A pending reference means the team has yet to establish a binary outcome for this report.

Report judge agreement with each reviewer separately. Then compare valid judge labels against adjudicated labels when available. The second comparison estimates correctness against a documented reference on those cases. A reference label is as trustworthy as the evidence and rule used to establish it. A judge output that cannot be read under the required format is invalid. In Step 7 that format is one label, so the illustrative raw value “{broken” cannot be scored. Keep it out of agreement and report it separately.

Read the types of mistakes

Imagine testing a held-out group with two adjudicated PASS cases and two adjudicated FAIL cases. The saved judge gets one of each right. Write the reference labels down the side and judge labels across the top. This count table is a confusion matrix.

Course hours by track
Adjudicated labelJudge PASSJudge FAIL
PASS11
FAIL11

The PASS/PASS and FAIL/FAIL cells give 2 matches out of 4. The FAIL row has one false pass out of two known FAIL replies. The PASS row has one false fail out of two known PASS replies. A judge that passes every reply can look strong on a set dominated by correct replies. Read each row before trusting the total. Report the number of cases, the number with both valid binary labels, and the cases excluded because of missing or invalid evidence.

Notice how the choice of labels affects agreement

Picture eight new refund replies. Nia and Omar both use PASS six times and FAIL twice. They match on six replies, giving observed agreement of 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75. If you shuffled each reviewer’s labels independently while keeping their label counts, you would still expect many PASS labels to land together. The expected agreement under this independence calculation is the product of the two PASS frequencies plus the product of the two FAIL frequencies. Here it is (6/8 × 6/8) + (2/8 × 2/8) = 0.625.

Cohen’s kappa compares the observed agreement to that baseline. The observed result is 0.75 − 0.625 = 0.125 above it. The best possible agreement is 1, so the available room was 1 − 0.625 = 0.375. Divide 0.125 by 0.375 to get 0.333. In symbols, κ = (observed − expected) ÷ (1 − expected). A kappa of 0 means the match rate equals this baseline. A negative value means fewer matches than the baseline expects. If expected agreement is 1, kappa is undefined. Cohen, A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales

If both reviewers used PASS and FAIL equally often with the same 75% observed agreement, expected agreement would be 0.50, and kappa would be 0.50. The frequency of a category in the set is its prevalence. Show the label counts, sample size, raw agreement, and kappa together. Kappa describes agreement under a particular baseline. It cannot tell you whether either person applied the refund policy correctly.

Calibrate the rule, then test it on fresh cases

Choose practice cases that cover clear answers, wrong deadlines, missing receipts, and ambiguous replies. Have the reviewers label them independently. Compare their ratings and read the disputed text against the policy. Write down which part of the guide caused the disagreement. For instance, replace “sufficient refund guidance” with examples of a complete answer, a missing receipt, and an uncertain date. Save the resolved labels and any pending cases alongside a new rubric version. This is calibration in this lesson.

Keep a separate set for evaluation. A holdout is a set you keep away from the examples used to revise the rubric or judge prompt. Keep near-duplicate replies from the same question family in the same partition. Reviewers can prepare reference labels independently, while the people revising the rubric avoid reading the holdout cases or scores until the rules are frozen. Opening the same outcomes after each edit lets you tailor the rule to those particular replies. Using held-out examples to pick a rule moves information into the design process. That is data leakage. If you revise the rules after reading the results, treat those cases as development evidence and use a fresh holdout.

Test a suspected preference without changing the facts

Take a correct short reply and a longer version with the same facts. Give both the same question, policy, rubric, and judge settings. If the longer wording repeatedly gets a better verdict, investigate a possible preference for verbosity. Try adding “Definitely” to a wrong reply to test confidence. Show the same two policy facts once in a paragraph and once as a numbered list to test formatting. Compare a plain reply with a polished paraphrase that keeps the deadline and receipt unchanged. Change one property at a time. Keep the review focused on the refund requirements unless the rubric explicitly includes style. A slice is a subgroup, such as short or long replies, whose errors you report separately.

An evaluator may also favor replies generated by its own model family. This is model self-preference. For example, the judge may pass its own model family’s replies more often than equally accurate replies written by another family. Keep model identities hidden when possible and compare independently labeled examples from several sources. Check whether the pattern persists after matching on facts and controlling presentation. If you present multiple answers together, their order may affect judgments. Here each replay rates one reply independently. For pointwise repeat consistency, rerun that same reply with the same inputs and count how often the verdict changes. Repeat agreement can coexist with a repeated mistake. Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

A report should keep each case ID, frozen reply, policy, dataset version, split, reviewer IDs and labels, raw judge output, rubric version, disagreement reason, adjudicated outcome, and calibration action. Include the counts and denominators behind each summary. Save each new run alongside the earlier one. This report computes agreement from the saved per-case labels so a colleague can reproduce the calculation.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Count the matches before asking why

User question. How long after delivery can I ask for a refund, and what do I need?

Approved reference. Under refund-1 the window ends on calendar day 30 and a valid receipt is required.

Actual LLM response. D says “You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.” Read D with A, B, C, and E in the calibration table.

Assessment. Nia and Omar each labeled all five replies separately. A, B, and E match, giving 3/5 or 60% agreement. C and D differ. On D, Omar treated the deadline as sufficient guidance, while Nia considered the receipt a required part of the answer.

Failure classification. Keep both original labels. Record an omission under the clarified rubric and add an anchor that names the missing receipt as a failure for this question. The 60% describes this table and cannot explain the disagreement by itself.

Example 2. Find an error inside unanimous agreement

User question. How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?

Approved reference. The approved source allows a request through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.

Actual LLM response. B says “You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.”

Assessment. Nia, Omar, and the judge replay all use PASS. Read the cutoff directly from the reply and the source. At day 45, B says the request is within the window, but the approved clause says the window has ended. Record an adjudicated FAIL under the same ID.

Failure classification. Write two lines for B. On the agreement line, all three pairs of raters matched: Nia and Omar, Nia and the judge, Omar and the judge. On the policy line, all three PASS labels conflict with the 30-day rule. Keep the original labels, block the reply, and record the evidence for FAIL. Use B in calibration to show why a similar format and a correct receipt condition cannot rescue a wrong deadline.

Example 3. Investigate which answers earned undeserved credit

User question. For the same eligible order, how long do I have and what do I need to request a refund?

Approved reference. Use refund-1. A PASS answers both required facts. A wrong deadline is FAIL even when the answer is polished.

Actual LLM response. The frozen holdout has F and G, short and long versions of a correct answer for a blender order, and H and I, short and long versions of the same wrong 90-day answer for a jacket order. J is ambiguous. K has an invalid replay output. The exact texts and outputs are in Step 7.

Assessment. The first replay labels F and H FAIL and G and I PASS. Among comparable cases it scores 1/2 on short replies and 1/2 on long replies. The short error is a false fail and the long error is a false pass. Revise the prompt on the separate calibration set, then check saved holdout outputs for the revised guide. The fictional replay changes F to PASS and I to FAIL and leaves G and H correct. Comparable cases rise from two correct out of four to four out of four. J and K stay outside that comparison.

Failure classification. The first replay is consistent with a possible length preference on these pairs. The second reduces the observed errors in this teaching set. Keep the two runs, fixtures, and evidence notes linked to their versions. Test the pattern on more matched examples before claiming a general preference or better performance from a live judge.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Select Copy Code, open the editor next to the program, paste the full block, and select Run. Check the first output before making the one specified change. Each activity starts in a fresh editor, uses inline data, and runs on standard Python. The human and judge labels are fictional saved records. The programs calculate comparisons and never call a model.

Step 1 — Compare two human reviewers by response ID

Match the labels for the same frozen reply before counting agreements. The list holds tuples, ordered groups of three values. The for line gives those values names in the order they appear. == tests whether two labels are equal. The conditional expression picks “match” if the labels agree and “disagree” otherwise.

Open Python Editor

rows = [
    ("A", "PASS", "PASS"),
    ("B", "PASS", "PASS"),
    ("C", "REVIEW", "PASS"),
    ("D", "FAIL", "PASS"),
    ("E", "FAIL", "FAIL"),
]

for case_id, nia, omar in rows:
    result = "match" if nia == omar else "disagree"
    print(f"{case_id}: Nia {nia} | Omar {omar} | {result}")
Expected output
A: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
B: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
C: Nia REVIEW | Omar PASS | disagree
D: Nia FAIL | Omar PASS | disagree
E: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match

Experiment. In D’s row only, change Omar’s label, the last value, from PASS to FAIL.

Expected output
A: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
B: Nia PASS | Omar PASS | match
C: Nia REVIEW | Omar PASS | disagree
D: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match
E: Nia FAIL | Omar FAIL | match

The D comparison changes because both labels are now FAIL. Checkpoint. Which input would justify that change in an actual review? Record the missing receipt alongside the rubric rule, and keep Omar’s earlier label. This experiment changes a copy of a rating.

Step 2 — Calculate exact agreement

Count matches out of all comparable pairs in the first table. In this activity REVIEW counts as a recorded label, and every case has both ratings. When Python adds comparisons with sum(), each True counts as one. len() counts pairs. In an f"..." string, :.1f displays one decimal place.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("PASS", "PASS"), ("PASS", "PASS"), ("REVIEW", "PASS"),
         ("FAIL", "PASS"), ("FAIL", "FAIL")]
matches = sum(nia == omar for nia, omar in pairs)
total = len(pairs)

print(f"Matches: {matches}/{total}")
print(f"Exact agreement: {100 * matches / total:.1f}%")
Expected output
Matches: 3/5
Exact agreement: 60.0%

Experiment. Change Omar’s PASS to FAIL only in the pair ("FAIL", "PASS").

Expected output
Matches: 4/5
Exact agreement: 80.0%

One additional pair matches and the denominator stays five. Checkpoint. Does removing a disputed row give the same result? Removing D instead would give 3/4, or 75%, on a different set. Document exclusions rather than using them to raise the headline percentage.

Step 3 — Compare the judge with each human

Use the fictional v1 judge labels. Each dictionary stores labels keyed by case ID, so judge[case_id] retrieves the matching row regardless of insertion order. Loop over the reviewer IDs and compare all five cases.

Open Python Editor

nia = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "REVIEW", "D": "FAIL", "E": "FAIL"}
omar = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "PASS", "D": "PASS", "E": "FAIL"}
judge = {"A": "PASS", "B": "PASS", "C": "PASS", "D": "PASS", "E": "FAIL"}

for reviewer, labels in [("Nia", nia), ("Omar", omar)]:
    matches = sum(judge[case_id] == labels[case_id] for case_id in labels)
    print(f"Judge vs {reviewer}: {matches}/{len(labels)} ({100 * matches / len(labels):.1f}%)")
Expected output
Judge vs Nia: 3/5 (60.0%)
Judge vs Omar: 5/5 (100.0%)

Experiment. In judge, change C from PASS to REVIEW.

Expected output
Judge vs Nia: 4/5 (80.0%)
Judge vs Omar: 4/5 (80.0%)

Look at C’s row after the edit. The judge gains one match with Nia and loses one with Omar. Both totals land at four, but nobody changed the customer’s reply or found new policy evidence. Checkpoint. Which result tells you what “first month” means for the customer? Neither match count answers that. Give an adjudicator the frozen reply and the applicable policy so they can check the date and receipt wording.

Step 4 — Check the claim behind a unanimous label

Compare a controlled teaching reply with the policy. Both versions use calendar days after delivery and include the receipt, so the direct rule can check the exact number. all() returns true when every comparison is true. The numbers in the program are supplied inline. It does not extract facts from chat text.

Open Python Editor

policy_days = 30
stated_days = 30
labels = ["PASS", "PASS", "PASS"]
reference = "PASS" if stated_days == policy_days else "FAIL"

print(f"Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day {stated_days} after delivery with a valid receipt.")
print(f"Unanimous: {all(label == labels[0] for label in labels)}")
print(f"Checked deadline: {reference}")
print(f"Labels matching the deadline check: {labels.count(reference)}/{len(labels)}")
Expected output
Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Unanimous: True
Checked deadline: PASS
Labels matching the deadline check: 3/3

Experiment. Change only stated_days = 30 to stated_days = 90. This controlled example holds old labels fixed to show how consensus can hide an error.

Expected output
Reply: Refund requests are allowed through day 90 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Unanimous: True
Checked deadline: FAIL
Labels matching the deadline check: 0/3

All three labels still match each other. The number contradicts the policy. Checkpoint. What would you do with the saved labels in a real audit? Keep them with the exact reply they were recorded against, and add a new evidence-backed decision for that reply. Never attach old ratings to an edited response as though they had reviewed it.

Step 5 — Adjust agreement for label frequency

Use the eight fresh examples from the kappa calculation. The four counts say how often each pair of labels occurred. The sum gives the number of pairs. Divide the row and column totals by that number to find each reviewer’s label frequencies. Multiply matching frequencies to get expected agreement, then subtract it from observed agreement before dividing by the remaining room.

Open Python Editor

both_pass = 5
nia_pass_omar_fail = 1
nia_fail_omar_pass = 1
both_fail = 1

total = both_pass + nia_pass_omar_fail + nia_fail_omar_pass + both_fail
observed = (both_pass + both_fail) / total
nia_pass = (both_pass + nia_pass_omar_fail) / total
omar_pass = (both_pass + nia_fail_omar_pass) / total
expected = nia_pass * omar_pass + (1 - nia_pass) * (1 - omar_pass)

print(f"Observed agreement: {observed:.3f}")
print(f"Expected agreement: {expected:.4f}")
if expected == 1:
    print("Kappa: undefined")
else:
    print(f"Kappa: {(observed - expected) / (1 - expected):.3f}")
Expected output
Observed agreement: 0.750
Expected agreement: 0.6250
Kappa: 0.333

Experiment. Reassign one pair from Nia FAIL/Omar PASS to both FAIL, leaving eight cases. Replace the four consecutive count assignments with both_pass, nia_pass_omar_fail, nia_fail_omar_pass, both_fail = 5, 1, 0, 2.

Expected output
Observed agreement: 0.875
Expected agreement: 0.5625
Kappa: 0.714

The reassignment keeps Nia at six PASS labels and moves Omar from six to five. The two expected contributions become 30/64 and 6/64. Observed agreement is 7/8, so kappa is (0.875 − 0.5625) ÷ 0.4375 ≈ 0.714. Checkpoint. If both reviewers use only PASS, what does the program print? Expected agreement becomes 1, so kappa is undefined even with unanimous PASS. Record the raw counts and inspect the sample mix.

Step 6 — Look for a preference on matched replies

Replay the fictional judge on two matched pairs from Harbor Leaf. Within each pair, the short and long reply state the same facts. One pair is correct and the other gives the wrong deadline. Count the number of times the long version alone passes. The word counts help identify the style contrast. The final tally uses three saved runs for F. It uses the first as the comparison label and counts the first run as a match, so one of the two subsequent runs differs.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [
    ("correct", "With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 30 from delivery.",
     "For an eligible order, please make your request within 30 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
     "FAIL", "PASS"),
    ("wrong deadline", "With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 90 from delivery.",
     "For an eligible order, please make your request within 90 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
     "FAIL", "PASS"),
]
long_only = 0
for case, short, long, short_label, long_label in pairs:
    long_only += short_label == "FAIL" and long_label == "PASS"
    print(f"{case}: short {len(short.split())} words {short_label} | long {len(long.split())} words {long_label}")

repeats_f = ["FAIL", "PASS", "FAIL"]
matches = repeats_f.count(repeats_f[0])
print(f"Long-only passes: {long_only}/{len(pairs)}")
print(f"F repeats matching the first verdict: {matches}/{len(repeats_f)}")
Expected output
correct: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
wrong deadline: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
Long-only passes: 2/2
F repeats matching the first verdict: 2/3

Experiment. In the pair named "wrong deadline", change only the final judge label from "PASS" to "FAIL".

Expected output
correct: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words PASS
wrong deadline: short 11 words FAIL | long 24 words FAIL
Long-only passes: 1/2
F repeats matching the first verdict: 2/3

The judge now fails both versions of the wrong answer. The correct pair still shows a style-related difference, and the separate repeat tally stays fixed. Checkpoint. Can two pairs isolate length as the cause? The long drafts also change sentence structure. Try more matched paraphrases and vary formatting, confidence, and length separately before attributing a pattern.

Step 7 — Replay the calibration and audit report

Use frozen cases and two dictionaries of fictional replay labels. Each key is a case ID. A through E were available during calibration. F through K are the holdout. Both replay versions use identical candidate texts and independent human ratings. The fictional v2 guide explicitly requires the deadline and receipt, fails contradictions and material omissions, sends ambiguity to REVIEW, and asks the judge to ignore tone and length. The v2 labels are supplied for comparison. The Python code does not generate them.

Each case row contains the reply, style, two original human labels, a reviewed day count when available, and any adjudicated binary label. F/G and H/I share a ticket within each pair. The ticket check keeps both versions of each answer in the same split. A reason is stored even when adjudication remains pending. set(calibration_ids).isdisjoint(holdout_ids) checks that no ID belongs to both groups. A set comparison checks that all cases are assigned. In the report, the tuple key (reference, judge) keeps the two axes of the confusion matrix in that order.

For judge-human agreement, a valid REVIEW counts as a label when comparing raw ratings. For the binary confusion matrix, a case needs both an adjudicated PASS or FAIL and a valid judge PASS or FAIL. Missing sources, unresolved references, valid judge abstentions, and malformed verdicts need their own counts or reasons. The policy check uses day counts already checked for unit and starting event. The omitted receipt on D is recorded in the adjudicator’s note.

Open Python Editor

policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
question = "How long after delivery can I request a refund, and what do I need?"
ticket = {"F": "blender-01", "G": "blender-01", "H": "jacket-01", "I": "jacket-01"}
holdout_questions = {
    "blender-01": "My unused blender arrived last week. When is the last day to ask for a refund, and what do I need?",
    "jacket-01": "When does the refund window close for my unworn jacket, and what do I need to ask?",
    "J": "Does the refund window start when I place my order or when the item arrives, and what do I need?",
    "K": "Can I ask for a refund on day 30 after delivery of my unused headphones, and what should I bring?",
}
dataset = "refund-eval-1"
rubric = "v1"
calibration_ids = ("A", "B", "C", "D", "E")
holdout_ids = ("F", "G", "H", "I", "J", "K")
labels = ("PASS", "FAIL", "REVIEW")
binary = ("PASS", "FAIL")

# Text, style, Nia, Omar, verified day count, adjudicated label, evidence note.
cases = {
    "A": ("You may request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "B": ("You can request a refund within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "C": ("Ask for a refund during the first month after delivery if you have proof of purchase.",
          "short", "REVIEW", "PASS", None, None, "date and receipt wording need clarification"),
    "D": ("You can request a refund within 30 calendar days after delivery.",
          "short", "FAIL", "PASS", 30, "FAIL", "receipt omitted"),
    "E": ("Contact our support team for assistance.",
          "short", "FAIL", "FAIL", None, "FAIL", "neither requested fact stated"),
    "F": ("With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 30 from delivery.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "G": ("For an eligible order, please make your request within 30 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
          "long", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
    "H": ("With your valid receipt, ask by calendar day 90 from delivery.",
          "short", "FAIL", "FAIL", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "I": ("For an eligible order, please make your request within 90 calendar days after delivery. Please have a valid receipt when you make the request.",
          "long", "FAIL", "PASS", 90, "FAIL", "deadline contradicts policy"),
    "J": ("Bring a valid receipt and apply within thirty days of placing or receiving the order, whichever date applies.",
          "short", "REVIEW", "REVIEW", None, None, "starting event for the 30 days is unclear"),
    "K": ("With a valid receipt, you can ask for a refund up to and including day 30 after delivery.",
          "short", "PASS", "PASS", 30, "PASS", "both facts present"),
}
replays = {
    "v1": dict(zip("ABCDEFGHIJK", ("PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "PASS", "FAIL",
                                    "FAIL", "PASS", "FAIL", "PASS", "PASS", "{broken"))),
    "v2": dict(zip("ABCDEFGHIJK", ("PASS", "FAIL", "REVIEW", "FAIL", "FAIL",
                                    "PASS", "PASS", "FAIL", "FAIL", "REVIEW", "{broken"))),
}

assert set(calibration_ids).isdisjoint(holdout_ids)
calibration_tickets = {ticket.get(case_id, case_id) for case_id in calibration_ids}
holdout_tickets = {ticket.get(case_id, case_id) for case_id in holdout_ids}
assert calibration_tickets.isdisjoint(holdout_tickets)
assert set(calibration_ids) | set(holdout_ids) == set(cases) == set(replays[rubric])
audit = {}
for case_id, (reply, style, nia, omar, days, reference, note) in cases.items():
    raw_judge = replays[rubric][case_id]
    judge = raw_judge if raw_judge in labels else None
    gate = "UNKNOWN" if days is None else ("PASS" if days == 30 else "FAIL")
    assert gate != "FAIL" or reference == "FAIL"
    audit[case_id] = {
        "id": case_id, "dataset": dataset, "policy_version": "refund-1", "source": policy,
        "rubric": rubric, "split": "calibration" if case_id in calibration_ids else "holdout",
        "ticket": ticket.get(case_id, case_id),
        "question": holdout_questions.get(ticket.get(case_id, case_id), question),
        "candidate": reply, "style": style, "Nia": nia, "Omar": omar,
        "raw_judge": raw_judge, "judge": judge, "deadline_check": gate,
        "adjudicated": reference, "reference_note": note,
        "human_dispute": nia != omar,
        "calibration_action": "add anchors for deadline, receipt, and ambiguity",
    }

print(f"{dataset} | rubric {rubric}")
for group, ids in [("Calibration", calibration_ids), ("Holdout", holdout_ids)]:
    rows = [audit[case_id] for case_id in ids]
    valid = [r for r in rows if r["judge"] is not None]
    comparable = [r for r in valid if r["adjudicated"] in binary and r["judge"] in binary]
    human_matches = sum(r["Nia"] == r["Omar"] for r in rows)
    judge_nia = sum(r["judge"] == r["Nia"] for r in valid)
    judge_omar = sum(r["judge"] == r["Omar"] for r in valid)
    matches = sum(r["judge"] == r["adjudicated"] for r in comparable)
    unresolved = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["adjudicated"] is None]
    invalid = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["judge"] is None]
    disputes = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["human_dispute"]]
    print(f"{group} n={len(rows)}: human {human_matches}/{len(rows)} | judge vs Nia {judge_nia}/{len(valid)} | judge vs Omar {judge_omar}/{len(valid)}")
    print(f"  valid {len(valid)}/{len(rows)} | adjudicated matches {matches}/{len(comparable)}")
    print(f"  disputed {','.join(disputes)} | unresolved {','.join(unresolved)} | invalid {','.join(invalid) or 'none'}")
    if group == "Holdout":
        matrix = {(ref, pred): 0 for ref in binary for pred in binary}
        for r in comparable:
            matrix[r["adjudicated"], r["judge"]] += 1
        for ref in binary:
            print(f"  ref {ref}: judge PASS {matrix[ref, 'PASS']} | judge FAIL {matrix[ref, 'FAIL']}")
        for ref, pred, error in [("FAIL", "PASS", "False passes"), ("PASS", "FAIL", "False fails")]:
            total = sum(matrix[ref, label] for label in binary)
            count = matrix[ref, pred]
            rate = f"{count}/{total} ({100 * count / total:.1f}%)" if total else "unavailable (0 comparable)"
            print(f"  {error}: {rate}")
        for style in ("short", "long"):
            members = [r for r in comparable if r["style"] == style]
            correct = sum(r["judge"] == r["adjudicated"] for r in members)
            print(f"  {style}: {correct}/{len(members)} adjudicated matches")

for case_id in ("B", "I"):
    r = audit[case_id]
    print(f"Audit {case_id}: refund-1 | deadline {r['deadline_check']} | judge {r['judge']} | adjudicated {r['adjudicated']} | {r['reference_note']}")

F and I now match their adjudicated labels, while the number of comparable replies stays four. K still needs a valid replay. J still needs clarification. Notice that the calibration agreement with Omar fell. The reference-based check improved because it tests the confirmed facts with an explicit rule. Checkpoint. Could you report perfect held-out reliability? You can report four matches among four comparable teaching cases, with two cases outside that comparison and five valid judge outputs in six attempts. This replay does not measure live behavior.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Read the ratings before calculating

From A through E, list the cases where Nia and Omar agree. For the remaining cases, write what would need to be checked to resolve the difference. Explain why B deserves a policy check even if no one flagged it.

Practice 2. Compare two denominators

On five replies, both reviewers label three identically. One reviewer then withdraws the label on one of the two disputed replies pending evidence. Compute agreement first on all five recorded pairs and then on the four remaining comparable pairs. How should the report describe the change?

Practice 3. Find the false pass

A saved judge and both reviewers pass a 90-day reply. The approved policy states 30 calendar days after delivery. The holdout also includes another known FAIL that the judge fails, and two known PASS replies, one of which the judge fails. Fill the four confusion-matrix cells and calculate the false-pass and false-fail rates.

Practice 4. Design a calibration comparison

A judge passes a short correct reply and a long correct reply. For a wrong deadline, it fails the short version and passes the long version. A colleague concludes it is biased toward length. Explain what the four results support. Propose a revised anchor and a held-out comparison that could test the hypothesis while controlling for the facts.

Independent Assignment

Harbor Leaf wants an audit of the holdout report. Include human agreement, judge agreement with each reviewer, adjudicated agreement, class-specific errors, short and long style slices, unresolved cases, and invalid outputs. Use the policy, frozen candidates, human ratings, and two replay versions in Step 7. First reconcile A through E by hand. Then explain why both B and I are wrong when the replay says PASS. For C and J, write what would need clarification. For K, explain why the raw verdict cannot be counted as a substantive disagreement.

Use the full Step 7 program as the runnable answer key. Copy it afresh for each variant. In both variants choose rubric = "v2". In variant A, simulate a successful new replay for K by changing just the last value of the v2 tuple from "{broken" to "PASS". In variant B, use the original v2 tuple and change I, the ninth verdict, from "FAIL" to "PASS". In a real audit, save the retry or changed judge run separately. Tabulate what changed and recommend a calibration action backed by the policy and the disagreement pattern.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

A, B, and E match. Check whether C’s wording fixes the exact day, starting event, and valid receipt requirement before choosing a binary label. For D, confirm that the question asks for both requirements. The receipt is missing, so the clarified rubric records FAIL for the omission. B did not trigger a human dispute. Comparing 90 with the approved 30 reveals why a policy check is still needed on agreements.

Solution 2

Before the withdrawal, there are 3 matches out of 5 pairs, or 60%. With one disagreement missing a rating, three of four comparable pairs match, or 75%. Record both the change in agreement and the decrease in coverage from 5/5 to 4/5. No rating was improved by removing a row. The case still needs evidence.

Solution 3

Put one in each matrix cell. Of the two adjudicated FAIL replies, one was passed and one was failed. The false-pass rate is 1/2, or 50%. Of the two adjudicated PASS replies, one was passed and one was failed. The false-fail rate is also 1/2, or 50%. The policy, rather than the three matching judgments, establishes which row contains the 90-day reply.

Solution 4

Start with the two 90-day replies. Both give the same wrong deadline, and only the longer one passed. That is a reason to investigate. To make the next check fair, write a rule that says an explicitly wrong deadline earns FAIL. Set aside new pairs with the same day count, starting event, and receipt requirement in both versions. Change length first. Record how often wrong answers pass, then try separate changes to tone or formatting. If the long answers add a missing policy fact, the comparison can no longer tell you what length contributed.

Assignment answer key

The calibration human agreement is 3/5. In v1 the judge agrees with Nia on 3/5 and Omar on 5/5. B’s 90-day claim contradicts the source on the calibration set. I independently makes the same mistake in the holdout. C needs a definite date and proof that the receipt condition is covered. J needs the answer to name delivery as the start of the window. K’s malformed verdict needs a retry and remains outside the binary matrix until a valid rating is available.

For variant A, the changed lines from v2 are Holdout n=6: human 5/6 | judge vs Nia 6/6 | judge vs Omar 5/6, valid 6/6 | adjudicated matches 5/5, disputed I | unresolved J | invalid none, ref PASS: judge PASS 3 | judge FAIL 0, False fails: 0/3 (0.0%), and short: 3/3 adjudicated matches. Indent the lines after the heading with two spaces, as in the report. The retry increases valid coverage without resolving J.

For variant B, the changed lines from v2 are Holdout n=6: human 5/6 | judge vs Nia 4/5 | judge vs Omar 5/5, valid 5/6 | adjudicated matches 3/4, ref FAIL: judge PASS 1 | judge FAIL 1, False passes: 1/2 (50.0%), long: 1/2 adjudicated matches, and Audit I: refund-1 | deadline FAIL | judge PASS | adjudicated FAIL | deadline contradicts policy. Indent the summary rows under Holdout as before. The judge now agrees perfectly with Omar on valid holdout outputs while making a confirmed policy error. Keep the contradiction anchor and investigate the long incorrect replies on separate paired examples. Keep unresolved and invalid cases visible in both variants.

Knowledge Check

  1. Omar sees Nia’s labels before recording his own. What does a high match rate fail to tell you about their independent judgment?
  2. Six of eight comparable ratings match. What is exact agreement, and does it describe how far mismatched scores were apart?
  3. All reviewers pass a 90-day reply and the policy gives 30. What action follows from each piece of evidence?
  4. Why can agreement with one reviewer go down after a rubric change while agreement with the adjudicated labels goes up?
  5. Both reviewers always say PASS. What happens to raw agreement and kappa, and what would you check next?
  6. A longer version gets PASS, but it added the valid-receipt requirement. Is this enough evidence of verbosity bias?
  7. You see a holdout result and revise the prompt specifically to fix it. What should you call that set now?
  8. The judge’s verdict is corrupt for K. A human reference is known. How does that affect coverage, agreement, and the audit record?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Omar may have been influenced by the visible marks. Preserve independent rating conditions so their match rate reflects separately reached decisions.
  2. It is 6/8, or 75%. Exact agreement counts every unequal pair once and does not encode the size of an ordinal difference.
  3. The unanimous rating tells you the reviewers and judge gave the same label. The documented rule supports a FAIL for the reply. Record the adjudication and investigate the shared miss.
  4. One reviewer may have treated the old ambiguous language as permission to overlook a missing receipt. A clearer rule can move the judge away from that reviewer and closer to evidence-backed decisions.
  5. Raw agreement is 100%. Expected agreement is 1, so kappa is undefined. Check whether the case mix includes instructive FAIL examples and independently verify the approved criteria.
  6. The extra receipt changes the factual content. To investigate length, keep policy facts fixed within each pair before rewriting style.
  7. Call the exposed cases development evidence and keep a new set sealed for evaluation. Retain the earlier result and connect each later run to its own prompt and data version.
  8. Count a failed attempt in coverage, but omit the invalid output from substantive agreement and the matrix. Store the raw output, case ID, verdict failure reason, and retry or review action.

Common Mistakes

Read some cases where everyone agreed. Shared assumptions or an overlooked fact can make all three labels wrong together.

Keep REVIEW, an unresolved reference, and an invalid judge output visible. Each has a different implication for the next action and the denominator.

Record which texts, reviewers, policy, and rubric produced each result. Keep calibration and holdout groups separate, and preserve earlier judgments when a new rubric changes the decision.

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Apply a policy-first rubric when comparing two saved answers.
  • Record a winner, a tie, or a request for review and map display choices back to stable response IDs.
  • Replay each pair in reverse order, preserve disagreements, and count a supported pair once.
  • Build a win/loss/tie table and explain how coverage, cycles, and judge disagreement limit a ranking.
  • Explain the intuition behind Bradley–Terry and when a ranking still needs a separate factual check.

Why This Lesson Matters

Your Harbor Leaf Market parcel arrived 45 days ago. One draft says you still have time to request a refund because it allows 90 days. The other gives the store’s real 30-day deadline and asks for a receipt. If you’re reviewing the drafts side by side, the policy gives you a clear reason to choose. The harder question comes when two drafts get the facts right and the reviewer still has to decide whether either one is better.

All responses, sources, judges, and outcomes in this chapter are fictional. We keep the earlier Harbor Leaf policy refund-1: “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included. Assume an eligible unused online purchase throughout. The saved question is “Can I get a refund for something I bought?” Four fictional systems produced one frozen reply each. The judge sees display slots, and the report uses stable IDs A through D to track the replies.

Allow about 5.5 hours. The required background is Rubrics and a first human evaluation. Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge and Human agreement, calibration and bias help with evidence and judge disagreement. Complete the pointwise lesson first if you add a live judge later. This lesson uses offline replays only.

Beginner Explanation

Compare the same answers in two ways
Course hours by track
Stable IDFrozen response
AYes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
BAbsolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.
CBring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.
DPlease contact customer support about refunds.

Give A to a reviewer on its own. Ask whether it states the deadline, the starting event, and the receipt rule correctly. This is pointwise evaluation. It answers an absolute question such as whether a reply passes a policy check.

Now put A beside B and ask which reply gives the customer better refund guidance. This is pairwise evaluation. It can be easier to see why one draft is better than to decide whether a draft deserves 3 or 4 on a scale. The two approaches answer different questions. A reply can win a recorded preference and still fail the independent policy check.

Write the rule before showing the pair

Give both candidates the same saved question, approved policy, and rubric. Give the judge the same instructions in every position under rubric pairwise-v1 and ask it to return A, B, TIE, or REVIEW, plus a brief reason quoting the relevant reply and policy words. In this output format A and B are display slots. Keep the stable candidate IDs in the audit record, where they remain the same between displays.

  • Correctness first. A reply that follows the policy wins over one with a confirmed critical contradiction. Check the exact number, calendar-day unit, delivery event, and receipt requirement.
  • Completeness next. When the two replies preserve the facts, prefer the one that answers more of the question. A generic referral can avoid giving wrong advice while leaving the requested guidance missing.
  • Clarity and conciseness last. Compare how easy the replies are to follow and whether extra words help the customer. A confident tone or polished formatting cannot rescue a wrong rule.
  • TIE means you compared both answers with sufficient evidence and found no meaningful difference under the rubric. For A and C, both give day 30 and require a valid receipt. A reviewer can tie them if both are equally usable.
  • REVIEW means a winner or tie cannot be justified yet. If a reply says “first month” and no approved source gives that phrase a clear meaning, leave the comparison unresolved. A tie would imply the evidence had already supported equivalence.
Swap the displays and follow the stable IDs

Hide system names and use a recorded random assignment to choose the first display order across cases. This is blind randomization. Then show each selected pair in the opposite order in a separate judging pass. With two displays per pair, each candidate appears once in each slot. Preserve both records. Keep the question, policy, rubric, judge, and answer text fixed so you can inspect what changed.

Write the stable ID under each slot before you read a saved verdict. In the first display, slot A contains candidate A. After the swap, slot B contains that same answer. A judge that picks slot A first and slot B after the swap has followed the answer. A judge that picks slot A both times has followed the position in this replay, and its stable winner changes. Flag a tie that becomes a win as well. Keep REVIEW and malformed results visible. Under this lesson’s rule, two matching displays support one pair on one question. Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

For other presentation checks, hold the policy facts fixed. Put the same terms in a list or a paragraph to test formatting. Add “Certainly” without changing the facts to test confidence. Vary length separately from extra useful information. A result on one imagined pair tells you which comparison to inspect next. Repeat across several matched cases and saves before describing a preference as systematic.

Two judges can each be consistent under the swap and still prefer different answers. Keep their normalized outcomes separately. That is multi-model uncertainty when the judges are different models. Compare their cited evidence and ask a human reviewer to resolve important disagreements. Several judges can miss the same policy fact, so a majority still needs a factual check.

Count supported pairs and show the coverage

Start with one point for a win, half a point per candidate for a tie, and zero for a loss. This chapter uses these points as a simple summary. Take two wins and a tie. The points are 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5, the win rate is 2/3, and the points per scored pair are 2.5/3. The two fractions answer different questions because the second gives partial credit for ties.

With four candidates, there are six possible unordered pairs. If you can score four of them, coverage is 4/6. Say which pairs were absent and which were attempted but unresolved. A candidate with two wins from three pairs can have more raw points than one with one win from one pair. Report both the pair counts and the points per pair. Normalizing helps expose unequal exposure. It cannot correct for different opponents, missing hard cases, or a player with no scored pairs. Report an unavailable rate for a zero denominator. Avoid treating a tied points total as a head-to-head tie.

Separate a summary from a defensible ranking

Draw an arrow from each winner to the loser. If A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A, the arrows form a cycle. A wins against B and loses to C, so no ordering puts every observed winner ahead of every loser. This pattern is called non-transitivity. Keep the cycle visible even if a points table has a top row. With incomplete comparisons, explain which extra pair would help before releasing a ranking.

A model such as Bradley–Terry tries to explain repeated decisive comparisons using one positive strength per candidate. If two fitted strengths were 2 and 1, the model would give the first candidate a win probability of 2 ÷ (2 + 1), about 0.67, for that matchup. The strengths come from a fit to many comparisons and need not equal raw points. The basic model handles wins and losses. Ties and abstentions need an explicitly chosen policy or extension. A single strength cannot reproduce all directions in a cycle, and disconnected groups lack evidence for a common ranking. Paired replays also share a question and need appropriate treatment as dependent observations. This chapter teaches the intuition and uses transparent points for its own report. Bradley and Terry, Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs

Keep the raw comparison ID, order, judge identity, question, frozen candidates, policy, rubric version, outcome, evidence, and reverse result. Record which results entered the aggregation, the ranking method, and all open review flags. A relative preference can put B above D even though B fails the critical refund gate. Keep that gate alongside the preference report before deciding which answers a customer can see.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. A plausible draft loses on the policy

User question. Can I get a refund for something I bought?

Approved reference. Harbor Leaf allows eligible requests through calendar day 30 after delivery. A valid receipt is required.

Actual LLM response. A says “Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” B says “Absolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.”

Assessment. Check the starting event, date, and receipt first. A preserves all three. In B, “90 calendar days” contradicts the 30-day limit and “a receipt is optional” contradicts the requirement. A wins. The word “Absolutely” cannot change either fact. If you reviewed B pointwise, it would independently fail the refund-policy check.

Failure classification. Save A as the winner and record B’s two contradictions. The comparison supports a preference for this question. It gives no ranking of the systems on other refund questions.

Example 2. Follow the answer through the swap

User question. Can I get a refund for something I bought?

Approved reference. Use the same refund-1 policy and the pairwise-v1 rubric above in each display.

Actual LLM response. Compare the frozen A/B and B/C pairs. The fixture gives saved choices for two displays per pair.

Assessment. For A/B, order A,B selects slot A and order B,A selects slot B. Both normalize to candidate A. For B/C, order B,C selects slot B and order C,B also selects slot B. Those choices normalize to C and B respectively. The second pair changes winner when the slot changes, although no candidate text or policy changed.

Failure classification. Enter one win for A on A/B. Keep B/C out of the points table until a reviewer reads both displays and their reasons. In one display the judge rewards C for preserving the deadline. In the reverse it rewards B for sounding decisive. Ask the reviewer to put the two quoted deadlines next to the policy. The two fictional displays show where to investigate. A larger controlled replay would be needed to establish a persistent bias.

Example 3. Rank a complete table, then test a missing pair

User question. Which answer should be sent for this eligible refund question?

Approved reference. Use refund-1, and prefer the correct deadline and receipt condition before style.

Actual LLM response. Use the four frozen candidates. For this worked example, use independently resolved teaching outcomes for all six pairs. The raw audit in Step 7 is a different snapshot that retains open disagreements.

Assessment. Read the six results below. Give A 1 for each of two wins plus 0.5 for its tie. C also earns 2.5. D has one win and earns 1. B earns 0. Now remove B/C because its two displays disagree. C drops to 1.5 points across two scored pairs, and B has only two scored pairs. Coverage drops from 6/6 to 5/6. A’s 2.5 from three pairs and C’s 1.5 from two pairs come from different opponents.

Failure classification. Report A and C as tied by points in the complete snapshot. In the incomplete snapshot, report the difference as provisional and ask for B/C to be adjudicated. Confirm B independently fails policy, even if another replay ranks it above a generic referral.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Select Copy Code, use the editor link next to the example, paste the whole program, and select Run. Compare the output, make the one specified edit, and run again in the same editor. Start each activity with a fresh copy. All data are inline and the comparisons use standard Python. The saved judgments are invented examples. None of the programs calls a model.

Step 1 — Record a comparison and the reason

Store what was shown before interpreting the result. A dictionary maps names to values. The tuple "order" shows slot A first and slot B second. The nested candidate dictionary stores the texts by stable ID.

Open Python Editor

record = {
    "id": "P-AC-1", "rubric": "pairwise-v1", "order": ("A", "C"),
    "candidates": {
        "A": "Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.",
        "C": "Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.",
    },
    "judge": "J1", "choice": "A",
}
print(f"{record['id']} | {record['rubric']} | judge {record['judge']}")
for slot, candidate in zip(("A", "B"), record["order"]):
    print(f"Slot {slot} / ID {candidate}: {record['candidates'][candidate]}")
print(f"Recorded choice: {record['choice']}")
Expected output
P-AC-1 | pairwise-v1 | judge J1
Slot A / ID A: Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Slot B / ID C: Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.
Recorded choice: A

Experiment. Change only "choice": "A" to "choice": "TIE".

Expected output
P-AC-1 | pairwise-v1 | judge J1
Slot A / ID A: Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.
Slot B / ID C: Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.
Recorded choice: TIE

Only the saved choice changes. In a real audit, keep the previous record and attach the evidence for a new verdict. Checkpoint. What would justify this tie? Both answers must be compared against the rubric with enough evidence to conclude that neither is meaningfully better.

Step 2 — Let a critical check take priority

Use a controlled variant of B that requires a valid receipt in both versions, so the deadline is the only policy fact whose value changes. The numbers and clarity ratings are reviewed inputs for the exercise. The Boolean result from == is true if the reviewed count matches 30. The if branches use the clarity preference only when both policy checks pass.

Open Python Editor

approved_days = 30
a_days = 30
b_days = 90
clarity_a, clarity_b = 3, 4
a_ok = a_days == approved_days
b_ok = b_days == approved_days
print(f"B says: Ask within {b_days} calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.")
print(f"Deadline check: A {a_ok} | B {b_ok}")
if a_ok != b_ok:
    winner = "A" if a_ok else "B"
elif not a_ok:
    winner = "REVIEW"
elif clarity_a == clarity_b:
    winner = "TIE"
else:
    winner = "A" if clarity_a > clarity_b else "B"
print(f"Fixture choice: {winner}")
Expected output
B says: Ask within 90 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.
Deadline check: A True | B False
Fixture choice: A

Experiment. Change only b_days = 90 to b_days = 30.

Expected output
B says: Ask within 30 calendar days after delivery with a valid receipt.
Deadline check: A True | B True
Fixture choice: B

With both deadline checks passing and the receipt held fixed, the clarity rating can decide the comparison. Checkpoint. Would this program catch a waiver of the receipt rule? The fixture assumed a valid receipt for both replies. Free-text answers still need evidence for the amount, unit, event, and receipt.

Step 3 — Normalize the two display choices

Map the first display slot to index 0 and the second to index 1. If the raw label is TIE or REVIEW, preserve it. Compare the two resulting values only after translating display labels to stable IDs.

Open Python Editor

def normalize(order, choice):
    if choice == "A":
        return order[0]
    if choice == "B":
        return order[1]
    return choice

first_order = ("B", "C")
reverse_order = ("C", "B")
first_choice = "B"
reverse_choice = "B"
first = normalize(first_order, first_choice)
reverse = normalize(reverse_order, reverse_choice)
print(f"Forward: slot {first_choice} -> ID {first}")
print(f"Reverse: slot {reverse_choice} -> ID {reverse}")
print("Supported pair" if first == reverse and first != "REVIEW" else "Send to review")
Expected output
Forward: slot B -> ID C
Reverse: slot B -> ID B
Send to review

Experiment. Change only reverse_choice from "B" to "A".

Expected output
Forward: slot B -> ID C
Reverse: slot A -> ID C
Supported pair

The reversed display now points to C as well. Checkpoint. How many supported pairs did the change produce? One. You used two displays of the same evidence to check sensitivity to order.

Step 4 — Count wins, losses, and ties

Use the complete resolved table from the worked demonstration. Count only rows involving A. The tuple stores both IDs and the winner, or TIE. continue skips a row involving neither slot. The win rate uses every scored appearance, including ties, in its denominator.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("A", "B", "A"), ("A", "C", "TIE"), ("A", "D", "A"),
         ("B", "C", "C"), ("B", "D", "D"), ("C", "D", "C")]
wins = losses = ties = 0
for left, right, result in pairs:
    if "A" not in (left, right):
        continue
    if result == "TIE":
        ties += 1
    elif result == "A":
        wins += 1
    else:
        losses += 1

total = wins + losses + ties
points = wins + 0.5 * ties
print(f"A: {wins} wins | {losses} losses | {ties} ties | {total} scored")
print(f"Win rate: {100 * wins / total:.1f}%")
print(f"Points: {points:.1f} | points per pair: {points / total:.3f}")
Expected output
A: 2 wins | 0 losses | 1 ties | 3 scored
Win rate: 66.7%
Points: 2.5 | points per pair: 0.833

Experiment. Change the A/B result from "A" to "TIE".

Expected output
A: 1 wins | 0 losses | 2 ties | 3 scored
Win rate: 33.3%
Points: 2.0 | points per pair: 0.667

A loses one full win and gains a half-point tie. Three pairs still count. Checkpoint. If A/B instead needed REVIEW, should it count in the denominator? No. Keep the attempt in the audit and leave it out of the scored win rate.

Step 5 — Rank by points without breaking ties

Add one point for each winner and half a point per side for each tie. set(points.values()) keeps each distinct points total. sorted(..., reverse=True) visits those totals from highest to lowest. ' = '.join(...) displays every candidate in a tied group.

Open Python Editor

pairs = [("A", "B", "A"), ("A", "C", "TIE"), ("A", "D", "A"),
         ("B", "C", "C"), ("B", "D", "D"), ("C", "D", "C")]
points = {"A": 0.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0, "D": 0.0}
for left, right, result in pairs:
    if result == "TIE":
        points[left] += 0.5
        points[right] += 0.5
    else:
        points[result] += 1

for score in sorted(set(points.values()), reverse=True):
    group = [name for name in points if points[name] == score]
    print(f"{' = '.join(group)}: {score:.1f} points")
Expected output
A = C: 2.5 points
D: 1.0 points
B: 0.0 points

Experiment. Change C/D’s result from "C" to "D".

Expected output
A: 2.5 points
D: 2.0 points
C: 1.5 points
B: 0.0 points

A keeps 2.5. One point moves from C to D. Checkpoint. Did the edited verdict prove D gives better policy advice? It changed the recorded points only. Inspect D’s generic referral and check the evidence before releasing it.

Step 6 — Find a cycle and show missing pairs

Represent a win as a tuple (winner, loser). combinations(ids, 2) gives each unordered pair once. tuple(sorted(edge)) puts both directions of a pair under the same key for coverage. For a three-way cycle, test the two directions starting at the earliest ID in each group of three. This small check detects three-candidate cycles.

Open Python Editor

from itertools import combinations

ids = ("A", "B", "C", "D")
edges = {("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")}
all_pairs = set(combinations(ids, 2))
scored = {tuple(sorted(edge)) for edge in edges}
cycles = []
for a, b, c in combinations(ids, 3):
    for x, y in ((b, c), (c, b)):
        if {(a, x), (x, y), (y, a)} <= edges:
            cycles.append(f"{a}>{x}>{y}>{a}")

missing = [a + b for a, b in sorted(all_pairs - scored)]
print(f"Scored pairs: {len(scored)}/{len(all_pairs)}")
print(f"Missing: {', '.join(missing)}")
print(f"Three-way cycles: {', '.join(cycles) or 'none'}")
Expected output
Scored pairs: 3/6
Missing: AD, BD, CD
Three-way cycles: A>B>C>A

Experiment. Remove only ("C", "A") from edges.

Expected output
Scored pairs: 2/6
Missing: AC, AD, BD, CD
Three-way cycles: none

Cross out the arrow from C to A. The two remaining arrows still say A beat B and B beat C, but you lost the direct comparison between A and C. Checkpoint. Which new result would bring the cycle back? A supported C win against A. Report the missing pair beside the cycle check so a reader can see what the program had enough evidence to find.

Step 7 — Build an auditable pairwise report

Replay all six unordered pairs. The first and reversed rows keep their display order, raw choice, and saved reason. These are stored examples of a balanced schedule, with one display in each order per pair. J1 is the primary fictional model judge. J2 is a different fictional model that supplies only a comparison on B/D. A reversal that changes the stable winner, or an abstention in either display, sends the pair to review. The baseline points summarize supported J1 results. It flags a stable J2 disagreement separately. A sensitivity check can withhold that pair from the table.

The program checks the reviewed policy facts separately. A confirmed wrong claim is FAIL, and missing facts need REVIEW. These values are supplied by a policy reader. The program neither interprets free text nor runs a judge. Its cycle check uses only decisive results included in the points table. It tries each possible path through a group of candidates once per starting ID. permutations() provides the possible orders after the first ID. path[1:] + path[:1] shifts the path by one step and wraps back to its start, so zip() pairs every stop with the next.

The dictionary audit preserves each pair and its two displays. The list rankable contains only candidates with a scored appearance. A missing reverse stays open. [::-1] reverses a tuple so the two orders can be checked before counting anything. A sorted set of their scores makes the report deterministic. Group equal points together and keep a total ranking provisional if coverage, cycles, or judge disagreements leave open questions.

Open Python Editor

from itertools import combinations, permutations

question = "Can I get a refund for something I bought?"
policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
policy_version = "refund-1"
rubric = "pairwise-v1"
aggregation = "primary"
# Frozen text, verified day count, and whether a valid receipt is required.
candidates = {
    "A": ("Yes, you may request a refund through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.", 30, True),
    "B": ("Absolutely. You have 90 calendar days after delivery to request a refund, and a receipt is optional.", 90, False),
    "C": ("Bring your valid receipt and ask for your money back up to and including calendar day 30 after your order arrives.", 30, True),
    "D": ("Please contact customer support about refunds.", None, None),
}
# Each row keeps order, raw slot choice, and the saved judge's reason.
primary = {
    "AB": [(("A", "B"), "A", "chosen answer preserves the 30-day limit and receipt"),
           (("B", "A"), "B", "chosen answer preserves the 30-day limit and receipt")],
    "AC": [(("A", "C"), "TIE", "both preserve the required facts"),
           (("C", "A"), "TIE", "both preserve the required facts")],
    "AD": [(("A", "D"), "A", "chosen answer provides the deadline and receipt"),
           (("D", "A"), "B", "chosen answer provides the deadline and receipt")],
    "BC": [(("B", "C"), "B", "C preserves the 30-day limit"),
           (("C", "B"), "B", "B sounds decisive")],
    "BD": [(("B", "D"), "A", "B gives more detail"),
           (("D", "B"), "B", "B gives more detail")],
    "CD": [(("C", "D"), "REVIEW", "no supported comparison supplied"),
           (("D", "C"), "REVIEW", "no supported comparison supplied")],
}
secondary = {
    "BD": [(("B", "D"), "B", "D avoids giving the wrong deadline"),
           (("D", "B"), "A", "D avoids giving the wrong deadline")],
}

def normalize(order, choice):
    if choice in ("A", "B"):
        return order[0 if choice == "A" else 1]
    return choice if choice in ("TIE", "REVIEW") else "INVALID"

def supported(pair, views):
    if len(views) != 2:
        return "REVIEW", "missing reverse"
    first, reverse = views
    if set(first[0]) != set(pair) or reverse[0] != first[0][::-1]:
        return "REVIEW", "invalid display orders"
    outcomes = [normalize(order, choice) for order, choice, reason in views]
    if any(result in ("REVIEW", "INVALID") for result in outcomes):
        return "REVIEW", "abstention or invalid"
    if outcomes[0] != outcomes[1]:
        return "REVIEW", "order conflict"
    return outcomes[0], "supported"

def gate(days, receipt):
    if (days is not None and days != 30) or receipt is False:
        return "FAIL"
    if days is None or receipt is None:
        return "REVIEW"
    return "PASS"

ids = sorted(candidates)
counts = {name: dict(wins=0, losses=0, ties=0) for name in ids}
audit, edges, open_pairs, judge_disputes = {}, set(), [], []
scored = 0
print(f"{policy_version} | {rubric} | aggregation {aggregation}")
for a, b in combinations(ids, 2):
    pair = a + b
    views = primary.get(pair, [])
    result, reason = supported(pair, views)
    other_views = secondary.get(pair, [])
    other, _ = supported(pair, other_views)
    dispute = result != "REVIEW" and other != "REVIEW" and result != other
    if dispute:
        judge_disputes.append(pair)
    if dispute and aggregation == "exclude-disputes":
        result, reason = "REVIEW", "judge disagreement"
    audit[pair] = {
        "id": "P-" + pair, "question": question, "source": policy, "policy_version": policy_version,
        "rubric": rubric, "aggregation": aggregation, "stable_ids": (a, b),
        "candidate_texts": {name: candidates[name][0] for name in (a, b)},
        "J1_displays": views, "J2_displays": other_views, "judge_dispute": dispute,
        "table_result": result, "reason": reason,
    }
    choices = "/".join(normalize(order, choice) for order, choice, _ in views) or "none"
    print(f"P-{pair}: J1 {choices} | table {result} ({reason})")
    if result == "REVIEW":
        open_pairs.append(pair)
        continue
    scored += 1
    if result == "TIE":
        counts[a]["ties"] += 1
        counts[b]["ties"] += 1
    else:
        loser = b if result == a else a
        counts[result]["wins"] += 1
        counts[loser]["losses"] += 1
        edges.add((result, loser))

points, rankable, cycles = {}, [], []
for name, row in counts.items():
    wins, losses, ties = row["wins"], row["losses"], row["ties"]
    total = wins + losses + ties
    points[name] = wins + 0.5 * ties
    rate = f"{points[name] / total:.3f}" if total else "unavailable"
    if total:
        rankable.append(name)
    print(f"{name}: {wins}W {losses}L {ties}T | {points[name]:.1f} pts | {rate} per pair | policy {gate(*candidates[name][1:])}")

for length in range(3, len(ids) + 1):
    for group in combinations(ids, length):
        start = group[0]
        for tail in permutations(group[1:]):
            path = (start,) + tail
            next_nodes = path[1:] + path[:1]
            if set(zip(path, next_nodes)) <= edges:
                cycles.append(">".join(path + (start,)))
groups = ["=".join(name for name in rankable if points[name] == score)
          for score in sorted({points[name] for name in rankable}, reverse=True)]
attempted = sum(bool(entry["J1_displays"]) for entry in audit.values())
print(f"Attempted coverage: {attempted}/{len(audit)}")
print(f"Scored coverage: {scored}/{len(audit)} | open: {','.join(open_pairs) or 'none'}")
print(f"Cross-judge disputes: {','.join(judge_disputes) or 'none'}")
print(f"Cycles: {','.join(cycles) or 'none'}")
print("Points groups: " + (" > ".join(groups) or "unavailable"))
print("Total ranking: withheld" if open_pairs or judge_disputes or cycles else "Total ranking: points groups")
Expected output
refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation primary
P-AB: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-AC: J1 TIE/TIE | table TIE (supported)
P-AD: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-BC: J1 C/B | table REVIEW (order conflict)
P-BD: J1 B/B | table B (supported)
P-CD: J1 REVIEW/REVIEW | table REVIEW (abstention or invalid)
A: 2W 0L 1T | 2.5 pts | 0.833 per pair | policy PASS
B: 1W 1L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy FAIL
C: 0W 0L 1T | 0.5 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy PASS
D: 0W 2L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW
Attempted coverage: 6/6
Scored coverage: 4/6 | open: BC,CD
Cross-judge disputes: BD
Cycles: none
Points groups: A > B > C > D
Total ranking: withheld

Experiment. In the B/C reverse row, replace (("C", "B"), "B", "B sounds decisive") with (("C", "B"), "A", "C preserves the 30-day limit"). This is a replacement replay of one display. Save the earlier replay separately in a real audit.

Expected output
refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation primary
P-AB: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-AC: J1 TIE/TIE | table TIE (supported)
P-AD: J1 A/A | table A (supported)
P-BC: J1 C/C | table C (supported)
P-BD: J1 B/B | table B (supported)
P-CD: J1 REVIEW/REVIEW | table REVIEW (abstention or invalid)
A: 2W 0L 1T | 2.5 pts | 0.833 per pair | policy PASS
B: 1W 2L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.333 per pair | policy FAIL
C: 1W 0L 1T | 1.5 pts | 0.750 per pair | policy PASS
D: 0W 2L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW
Attempted coverage: 6/6

Cross-judge disputes: BD
