Points groups: A > C > B > D
Total ranking: withheld

The two displays now support C on B/C, adding one scored pair and a loss for B. A still has one more scored opponent than C. J1’s two stable B/D results are sufficient for this table under the primary rule. J2 picks D in both orders, so the report keeps their disagreement visible. Checkpoint. Would you release B because it won a supported pair? B independently fails on the deadline and receipt. Inspect the saved reasons for B/D, get another review of C/D, and keep the points groups provisional.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Apply the policy-first rubric

Compare A with B using refund-1. Then compare A with C. Decide when you have a supported winner and when a tie is justified. Name the evidence for each result.

Practice 2. Read the reversed display

The first display puts C in slot A and D in slot B. The judge chooses A. The second display puts D in slot A and C in slot B. The judge chooses A again. Translate both choices and decide what goes in the scored table.

Practice 3. Calculate points when two candidates tie

In the complete resolved snapshot, A halves its A/C pair with C and beats B and D. C beats B and D. D beats B. Calculate each points total and the points-per-pair of the two leaders. Do the totals establish a unique winner?

Practice 4. Read a cycle with missing evidence

In a small replay, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. D has no comparisons. Compute coverage over all four candidates and identify which claims would be defensible in an audit. What should the team compare next?

Independent Assignment

Use the full Step 7 program as the standalone answer key. First read the four frozen answers and record each policy status using refund-1. Normalize every display. List which pairs came from repeated displays of the same evidence, which are open, and where the two judges disagree. Verify the table counts, coverage, and points groups by hand. Write a release recommendation supported by the critical facts as well as the preferences.

For variant A, start from the Step 7 experiment, where B/C consistently supports C. Replace the two C/D rows with (("C", "D"), "B", "D gives an escalation path") and (("D", "C"), "A", "D gives an escalation path"). The revised replay prefers D in both orders. For variant B, start from the baseline and change only aggregation = "primary" to aggregation = "exclude-disputes". Keep all text, evidence, and display choices fixed. In both variants save a review recommendation and explain when the ranked points fail to settle it.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

A wins A/B. Both replies count from delivery, but B says 90 instead of 30 and makes the receipt optional. These two contradictions outweigh B’s confident wording. A and C both give the 30-day rule and require a valid receipt. If both are similarly clear for the customer, record TIE. An ambiguous “first month” version of C would need clarification before deciding whether it satisfies the same cutoff.

Solution 2

The first displayed A means candidate C. The reversed displayed A means candidate D. The stable winner changes from C to D. Log both raw outcomes and leave the pair unresolved. Inspect whether the judge anchored on the first slot or had another reason before asking for adjudication.

Solution 3

A and C each earn 1 + 1 + 0.5 = 2.5 over three pairs, or 0.833 points per pair. D has one win and two losses, so it earns 1. B loses every pair and earns 0. The two leaders are tied by points. This fixture also records a supported head-to-head tie between them. Another dataset can give equal totals even without a head-to-head tie.

Solution 4

List all six pairs first: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. Three contain a scored result, giving 50% coverage. Try putting A first. The C-over-A result immediately conflicts with that choice. Starting with B or C has the same problem. D has no scored comparison, so its rate is unavailable. Ask for both display orders on A/D, B/D, and C/D. Review the three existing reasons before proposing an order for all four.

Assignment answer key

The baseline has 4/6 coverage, with B/C and C/D in review. A and C pass the policy, B fails it, and D lacks the facts. B/D is supported by J1 in both orders. J2 points to D both times. Keep both records. The policy failure means the team should hold B even if a scoring method raises it above D.

For variant A, the changed lines from the Step 7 experiment are P-CD: J1 D/D | table D (supported), C: 1W 1L 1T | 1.5 pts | 0.500 per pair | policy PASS, D: 1W 2L 0T | 1.0 pts | 0.333 per pair | policy REVIEW, Scored coverage: 6/6 | open: none, Cycles: B>D>C>B, and Points groups: A > C > B=D. Keep every other line. Ask a reviewer to inspect the three edges in the cycle and the raw B/D disagreement. Complete coverage does not make these preferences transitive.

For variant B, the changed lines from the baseline are refund-1 | pairwise-v1 | aggregation exclude-disputes, P-BD: J1 B/B | table REVIEW (judge disagreement), B: 0W 1L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy FAIL, D: 0W 1L 0T | 0.0 pts | 0.000 per pair | policy REVIEW, Scored coverage: 3/6 | open: BC,BD,CD, and Points groups: A > C > B=D. The disagreement is still listed, and the total ranking is withheld. Reducing coverage exposes how much the baseline placement depended on one disputed win.

Knowledge Check

  1. A reply beats a vague referral but tells the customer the receipt is optional. Which separate evaluation answers whether it can be sent?
  2. Both replies satisfy the rules and one is shorter. When should conciseness influence the result?
  3. The policy page is missing and the judge cannot check either deadline. Which output should it return and why?
  4. Why start from a blind randomized display order and collect the reverse as well?
  5. Stable A is in slot B and wins. In the swapped display it is in slot A and wins. How many supported pair outcomes go into the table?
  6. A candidate wins twice, ties once, and loses once. Give its wins-per-scored-pair and points-per-scored-pair.
  7. A points summary puts a candidate first even though its preference arrows form a cycle. What should the audit say?
  8. Two model judges each agree with their own reversed replay but disagree with one another. What evidence is needed before deciding which answer to send?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Apply a pointwise policy check to that reply. It fails because refund-1 requires a valid receipt, regardless of its relative preference.
  2. Check completeness and clarity first. If both are adequate and the shorter wording is easier to use without losing a needed detail, use the conciseness criterion. A small difference can still justify a tie.
  3. Return REVIEW. A tie needs evidence that the compared answers are equivalent under the rubric.
  4. Blinding reduces influence from knowing the source system. Randomization spreads initial slot placement, and the reverse exposes choices that change when the stable texts swap slots.
  5. One. Both display choices normalize to the same stable answer on a single pair.
  6. The win rate is 2/4, or 50%. The points are 2 + 0.5 = 2.5, so the points rate is 2.5/4 = 0.625.
  7. Show the cycle alongside the points and report that the ordering cannot satisfy every observed preference. Include coverage and review the conflicting comparisons.
  8. Inspect both reasons, the original question, the exact responses, and the source. Apply the independent critical checks and ask a human reviewer to adjudicate the disputed comparison.

Common Mistakes

Map each display label back to the stable answer before comparing the outcomes. A raw slot label can point to a different answer after a swap.

Track ties, unresolved attempts, absent pairs, and cross-judge disputes separately. These outcomes change the evidence available to a ranking.

Always check each answer against the approved policy before release. Ranking points summarize relative choices on the collected pairs.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

A pairwise comparison answers which of two frozen responses serves the customer better under a stated rule. Keep stable IDs and normalize reversed display choices. Report counts, coverage, cycles, and open disputes alongside any points groups. An independent check is needed for the facts a customer will act on.

Next, Variance, repetition and score aggregation examines what repeated evaluations tell you about variation and how to combine results across cases.

Intermediate · Core

Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Design controlled repeats and identify whether the response, judge, case set, or effective settings changed.
  • Calculate mean, median, range, population variance, and standard deviation from saved scores.
  • Separate variation within one case from differences between cases, and explain why repeated draws do not add distinct cases.
  • Calculate per-run, per-case, and pooled summaries. Show how slice weights, missing rows, and policy failures affect the interpretation.
  • Reproduce a report from its saved inputs and state what further evidence a decision needs.

Why This Lesson Matters

The first time Harbor Leaf Market tests its refund assistant, nine out of ten judged answers pass. Someone puts 90% in the release notes. Then the next two runs return 70% and 80%. Before the team edits the headline, it needs to find out whether the assistant gave different answers, the judge rated the same answers differently, or a different set of questions was counted.

The examples are fictional. Harbor Leaf keeps the policy used in the earlier lessons, refund-1: “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” Day 30 is included for eligible unused online purchases. The opening numbers are run-level pass percentages. Later, the audit uses presentation scores on a 0–100 scale and a separate policy check.

Allow about 5.5 hours. Start with Objectives, dimensions and failure taxonomy. Inference, sampling and repeatability, Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance, and Combining evaluators and handling uncertainty are useful refreshers.

Beginner Explanation

Find what changed before repeating

Read the 90%, 70%, and 80% alongside their run logs. First identify what was measured. If a run answered ten questions, 90% can mean nine passed judgments out of ten valid binary results. Check the counts and the criteria before comparing that score with another percentage.

  • To investigate assistant variation, ask the same questions again under the same generation procedure. Keep the judge and scoring rule fixed. Save each answer so you can see which wording changed.
  • To investigate judge variation, replay the exact same frozen answers against the same rubric and judge configuration. Compare the individual verdicts on each answer.
  • To investigate the effect of the questions sampled, freeze the settings and document which case IDs were selected. A set with more deadline questions can score differently even without a change to the assistant or judge.
  • To evaluate a configuration change, choose which factor to change and record both versions. A different rubric, judge, or aggregation rule can move the score even when every reply stays fixed.

A seed is a value used to initialize a random procedure. Record it, or the planned seed sequence, along with the model version, prompt, sampling settings, and scoring versions. The effective configuration is what actually ran, including resolved defaults. Check whether a requested setting was applied. Preserve the dataset and generation procedure or exact response records, judge, rubric, aggregation, and run ID. A seed can help reproduce a sampling procedure without guaranteeing that a live service produces the same result.

If the evaluation uses a service that loads work lazily, record whether each run started cold, before a first request warmed it, or warm, after a documented warm-up. Compare like starts when measuring latency. A timeout can also change which scores enter a quality mean. Record it before trying to explain a change in the mean.

Running the same arithmetic twice is a deterministic repeat. Replaying saved judge outcomes verifies the report and the decisions that follow from those outcomes. Generating fresh live replies or asking a live judge to score again measures another source of variation. The Python in this lesson replays invented data.

Read the observed scores before summarizing

Suppose two more runs return 80% and 80%. The five scores are 70, 80, 90, 80, 80. Put them on a number line and place one mark at 70, three at 80, and one at 90. This pattern of observed scores is their distribution.

Add the five values to get 400. Divide by the five runs to get 80. This arithmetic mean describes the center of the observed scores. It leaves the spread out of view.

Sort the scores to get 70, 80, 80, 80, 90. The middle score is 80, the median. With an even number of scores, average the middle two. If the 90 were instead a 20, the sum would fall to 330 and the mean to 66. The middle score would still be 80. Inspect the 20. It could be a real failure or a run with a configuration change.

The minimum is 70 and the maximum is 90. Their difference is 20 percentage points, the range. It shows the distance between the observed extremes. It does not tell how many runs were near either end.

Measure distance from the mean

Put 70 and 90 on either side of the mean, 80. They are both ten points from the center. If you subtract 80 from each of the scores 70, 80, 90, you get −10, 0, 10. Adding those differences would give zero and hide both ten-point gaps. Square each difference and the two gaps both contribute 100. The middle score contributes zero. The total is 200.

Divide 200 by all three observed runs to get 66.67, the population variance of these three saved scores. Its units are squared percentage points because the distances were squared. Take the square root to get population standard deviation, about 8.16 percentage points. It summarizes observed spread in the same units as the scores. It gives no guaranteed bound on a future run.

If you wanted to estimate a wider population’s variance from a suitable sample under the usual assumptions, the standard sample variance calculation would divide by one less than the number of observations. For these three, it would give 100. This lesson uses population variance throughout to describe the complete lists on screen. Repeated scores from the same case do not automatically satisfy the independence assumptions for inference.

Choose what counts as one observation

If you read Q1 twice and Q2 twice, you have four recorded observations and two distinct questions. An analysis unit is what you count as one observation for a particular statement. Use the case to report question coverage. Use a repeated attempt within that case to describe how its scores changed.

Here is a small case-by-setting plot. Each cell uses the same 50–100 scale. Read left to right, with each character advancing two points. An asterisk marks each observed score. The exact scores are printed beside the marks. The numbers are presentation scores. Both settings saw the same case IDs and a fixed rubric.

Course hours by track
Case and sliceSetting X, two observationsSetting Y, two observations
R, routine......................*.*. 94, 98....................*.*... 90, 94
H, deadline....*.*................... 58, 62...........*.*............ 72, 76

Within-case variation is the spread of repeats on the same question and setting. For X on R, the scores differ by four points. For X, the case means are 96 and 60. Their difference shows between-case variation, the change in the center from one question to another. Here is the variance version of the same comparison. Within either X case the two distances from its mean are −2 and 2, giving population variance (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4. Compare the two case means, 96 and 60, around their own center of 78. Their population variance is (324 + 324) ÷ 2 = 324. Keep the unit next to each result. Repeats on R share whatever makes R easy or hard, so four observations across R and H still give you only two distinct questions.

A slice is a group of questions that share a trait. With equal weight on routine and deadline, X scores (96 + 60) ÷ 2 = 78 and Y scores (92 + 74) ÷ 2 = 83. Now give routine 90% of the weight and deadline 10%, using the same weights for both settings. X scores 0.90 × 96 + 0.10 × 60 = 92.4. Y scores 0.90 × 92 + 0.10 × 74 = 90.2. The order reverses even though every saved score stays fixed. Choose and document slice weights before comparing. These two weighting plans answer different questions.

Choose an aggregation and show its denominator

To summarize one case across runs, average its eligible repeat scores. To summarize one run across cases, average its eligible scores across the cases in that run. An equal-run mean gives every run the same weight, even when one run scored fewer rows. This is a macro mean over runs. A pooled micro mean gives every valid, scorable row the same weight. Weighting each run mean by its number of scored rows reproduces the micro result. An equal-case macro mean is another option if each distinct case should contribute equally.

A missing result can come from a skipped case or a timeout. If failures are more likely on deadline questions, excluding those rows can make a mean look better by changing the case mix. An invalid result might be unreadable. A valid abstention is readable and says no numeric judgment was made. Set these aside with reasons rather than filling in zero. In the audit report below, attempted / planned includes timeouts, valid / attempted counts usable verdict records including abstentions, and scorable / valid counts numeric verdicts. Also show scorable / planned as end-to-end coverage. Keep denominators visible and use “unavailable” when there is nothing to divide by.

A critical policy failure remains a failure even if its presentation score is high or missing. Count it separately and keep its case ID. A consistent presentation score can be useful if predictable wording matters. Stable bad advice still needs to be fixed. A small set of repeats helps find cases to inspect. It cannot establish live reliability or justify a precise confidence claim.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Replace a headline with the observed spread

User question. What should the team conclude after the first 90% refund-policy test?

Approved reference. Use the same refund-1 cases and pass rule for the saved repeats.

Actual LLM response. The fictional batch of five runs yields 90%, 70%, 80%, 80%, and 80%.

Assessment. The total is 400 and there are five results, so the mean is 80%. Sort them to see that the median is also 80%. The lowest and highest are 70% and 90%, giving a range of 20 percentage points.

Failure classification. Treat 90% as one observed result. Review the 70% run by case ID, and compare the effective configuration and scorable counts before attributing the difference to generation or judging.

Example 2. Compare runs with the same center

User question. Which setting gives more predictable presentation scores in these saved runs?

Approved reference. The rubric, judge and refund questions are fixed for this toy comparison. Policy is verified separately.

Actual LLM response. The saved scores are 78, 80, 82 for the steadier setting and 70, 80, 90 for the wider setting.

Assessment. Both means are 80. The first series has distances −2, 0 and 2. The squared distances total 8, so population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and standard deviation is about 1.63. The second series has squared distances totaling 200. Population variance is 200/3 ≈ 66.67 and standard deviation is about 8.16.

Failure classification. The first setting varied less in these runs. Open the 70-point run for the second setting and look for the cases that pulled it down. Then open the policy checks for the steadier setting too. If it repeatedly tells customers they get 90 days, its consistent presentation is no reason to release it.

Example 3. Count what each average leaves out

User question. Has setting X produced enough evidence to release the refund assistant?

Approved reference. A request for an eligible item must be made through calendar day 30 after delivery and with a valid receipt. Presentation scores measure how the advice is communicated.

Actual LLM response. In X1, Q1 earns 90, Q2 earns 70, and Q3 earns 90 while promising a 90-day deadline. Q4 is skipped. In X2, Q1 earns 100, Q2 returns an invalid verdict, Q3 has a valid abstention, and Q4 times out.

Assessment. X1’s mean is 250/3 ≈ 83.33 and X2’s is 100/1 = 100. Equal run weight gives 91.67. Pooling the scored rows gives (250 + 100) ÷ (3 + 1) = 87.50. Report 7/8 attempted, 5/7 valid, 4/5 scorable, and 4/8 scorable end to end. The 90-day reply still fails the policy even though its presentation scored 90.

Failure classification. Block release on the verified critical violation. Inspect the invalid verdict and timeout, and repeat only after identifying the failed stage. If the question is how results change with a different case mix, test declared slice weights on fixed cases, as in the case-by-setting plot above. Do not compare the averages without their denominators.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Choose Copy Code, open the editor next to the activity, paste the entire program, and select Run. Compare the output before making the one described change. Start each step in a fresh editor. All programs use standard Python and inline fictional records. None runs a live model or judge.

Step 1 — Record the first three runs

Keep the run IDs next to the percentages so you can trace an unusual result. Each tuple groups an ID and a score. The for loop assigns each pair’s values to run_id and score. An f"..." string places those values where you see braces.

Open Python Editor

runs = [("R1", 90), ("R2", 70), ("R3", 80)]
for run_id, score in runs:
    print(f"{run_id}: {score}%")
print(f"Recorded runs: {len(runs)}")
Expected output
R1: 90%
R2: 70%
R3: 80%
Recorded runs: 3

Experiment. Add ("R4", 60) at the end of runs.

Expected output
R1: 90%
R2: 70%
R3: 80%
R4: 60%
Recorded runs: 4

The fourth run adds a lower observed value and leaves the earlier values intact. Checkpoint. What would you inspect before deciding R4 was worse? Check case IDs, raw verdicts, coverage, and versions. A changed result is a starting point for investigation.

Step 2 — See what an extreme value changes

The first five percentages cluster around 80. Import mean and median from Python’s statistics module. These functions return the arithmetic average and the middle of the sorted values. :.1f prints one decimal place.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, median

scores = [70, 80, 90, 80, 80]
print(f"Sorted: {sorted(scores)}")
print(f"Mean: {mean(scores):.1f}")
print(f"Median: {median(scores):.1f}")
Expected output
Sorted: [70, 80, 80, 80, 90]
Mean: 80.0
Median: 80.0

Experiment. Replace only the 90 in scores with 20.

Expected output
Sorted: [20, 70, 80, 80, 80]
Mean: 66.0
Median: 80.0

The sum lost 70 points, so the mean fell by 70/5 = 14. The middle position still holds 80. Checkpoint. Would you discard the 20 because the median stayed at 80? Keep it and trace the run. The median and the unusual value each tell you something the other misses.

Step 3 — Measure spread around a fixed mean

Construct three run percentages around 80. The variable offset sets how far the two outside scores are from the middle. min() and max() find the extremes. The p in pvariance() and pstdev() denotes population. These functions describe the complete three-value list using division by three before the square root.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, pvariance, pstdev

center = 80
offset = 2
scores = [center - offset, center, center + offset]
print(f"Scores: {scores} | mean {mean(scores):.2f}")
print(f"Min {min(scores)} | max {max(scores)} | range {max(scores) - min(scores)}")
print(f"Population variance: {pvariance(scores):.2f}")
print(f"Population SD: {pstdev(scores):.2f}")
Expected output
Scores: [78, 80, 82] | mean 80.00
Min 78 | max 82 | range 4
Population variance: 2.67
Population SD: 1.63

Experiment. Change offset = 2 to offset = 10.

Expected output
Scores: [70, 80, 90] | mean 80.00
Min 70 | max 90 | range 20
Population variance: 66.67
Population SD: 8.16

The center stayed fixed and the squared distances rose from 8 in total to 200. Checkpoint. What would using the sample formula change? It would divide 200 by 2 and give 100. Label the variance convention so readers can reproduce the result.

Step 4 — Compare average and stability separately

Compare the earlier two example settings. A dictionary groups the repeated scores under their setting IDs. items() gives each ID with its list. Report mean and population standard deviation together.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, pstdev

scores = {"X": [78, 80, 82], "Y": [70, 80, 90]}
for name, runs in scores.items():
    print(f"{name}: mean {mean(runs):.2f} | population SD {pstdev(runs):.2f}")
Expected output
X: mean 80.00 | population SD 1.63
Y: mean 80.00 | population SD 8.16

Experiment. Replace X’s last score, 82, with 88.

Expected output
X: mean 82.00 | population SD 4.32
Y: mean 80.00 | population SD 8.16

X’s center increased, while the new score also spread its values further apart. Checkpoint. Which setting had the smaller observed spread after the edit? X. Check the policy results and compare more matched cases before treating this score summary as a release decision.

Step 5 — Give runs or scored rows equal weight

Start with two presentation scores for each of two runs. The dictionary under a run ID stores case IDs and scores. set().union(*runs.values()) collects distinct case IDs from all nested dictionaries. sorted() gives them a stable output order. The list expression after values = collects a case’s score from every run that has one.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean

runs = {"R1": {"Q1": 90, "Q2": 70}, "R2": {"Q1": 100, "Q2": 80}}
case_ids = sorted(set().union(*runs.values()))
for name in case_ids:
    values = [run[name] for run in runs.values() if name in run]
    print(f"{name}: mean {mean(values):.2f} ({len(values)} scored)")

run_means, pooled = [], []
for run_id, run in runs.items():
    run_means.append(mean(run.values()))
    pooled.extend(run.values())
    print(f"{run_id}: mean {run_means[-1]:.2f} ({len(run)} scored)")
print(f"Equal-run mean: {mean(run_means):.2f}")
print(f"Pooled score mean: {mean(pooled):.2f}")
Expected output
Q1: mean 95.00 (2 scored)
Q2: mean 75.00 (2 scored)
R1: mean 80.00 (2 scored)
R2: mean 90.00 (2 scored)
Equal-run mean: 85.00
Pooled score mean: 85.00

Experiment. Add "Q3": 100 only inside R2’s dictionary.

Expected output
Q1: mean 95.00 (2 scored)
Q2: mean 75.00 (2 scored)
Q3: mean 100.00 (1 scored)
R1: mean 80.00 (2 scored)
R2: mean 93.33 (3 scored)
Equal-run mean: 86.67
Pooled score mean: 88.00

Draw five boxes for the scores after the edit. Two belong to R1 and three to R2. A pooled mean gives each box one vote, so R2 gets three votes. An equal-run mean gives each run one vote. Checkpoint. Which case has only one score behind its mean? Q3. Say so in the report, especially if someone wants to compare its mean with Q1 or Q2, where each was scored twice.

Step 6 — Keep missing, invalid, and abstained results visible

Four cases were planned. None means no usable response arrived. "ABSTAIN" is a valid verdict with no numeric rating. type(raw) is int prevents a true/false flag from being counted as a numeric score. 0 <= raw <= 100 tests both bounds.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean

rows = {"Q1": 90, "Q2": "bad", "Q3": None, "Q4": "ABSTAIN"}
scores = []
missing = invalid = abstained = 0
for raw in rows.values():
    if raw is None:
        missing += 1
    elif raw == "ABSTAIN":
        abstained += 1
    elif type(raw) is int and 0 <= raw <= 100:
        scores.append(raw)
    else:
        invalid += 1
print(f"Valid: {len(scores) + abstained} | missing: {missing} | invalid: {invalid}")
print(f"Abstentions: {abstained} | scorable coverage: {len(scores)}/{len(rows)}")
print(f"Valid numeric mean: {mean(scores):.2f}" if scores else "Valid numeric mean: unavailable")
Expected output
Valid: 2 | missing: 1 | invalid: 1
Abstentions: 1 | scorable coverage: 1/4
Valid numeric mean: 90.00

Experiment. Replace Q2’s "bad" with the number 70.

Expected output
Valid: 3 | missing: 1 | invalid: 0
Abstentions: 1 | scorable coverage: 2/4
Valid numeric mean: 80.00

A previously excluded case is now scorable. Coverage rises and the mean falls because the new 70 is below 90. Checkpoint. Did Q1 get worse? Its score stayed at 90. Trace the lower mean to newly available evidence before crediting or blaming a change in the assistant.

Step 7 — Reproduce a score report and its release decision

Compare two fictional sampling settings on the same four planned questions and the same presentation rubric. The reply records include wording and a separate policy decision supplied by a human reviewer. A row is a planned run–case pair. The report saves the case, reply ID and text, original and replayed verdict values, effective settings, policy result, and action. A policy failure takes priority over an unscorable verdict. Keep all observed rows and the score filters so another evaluator can reconstruct the report.

observed holds the historical fixture. The changes dictionary describes independent replay variants. Looking up a replacement with .get() leaves the historical rows intact. Check the original raw value beside the replayed value in the audit. For the spread of both per-run means and pooled scores we use population standard deviation, using all the saved values in the corresponding list.

Open Python Editor

from statistics import mean, median, pvariance, pstdev

policy = "Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt."
dataset = "refund-eval-1"
rubric = "presentation-v1"
judge = "fictional-judge-r1 | temperature 0"
judge_replay = "saved-verdicts-1"
revision = "baseline"
questions = {
    "Q1": "What is the refund deadline?",
    "Q2": "Do I need a receipt for an eligible refund?",
    "Q3": "Can I still request a refund 45 days after delivery?",
    "Q4": "Can I ask for a refund on day 30 with my receipt?",
}
# Text and independently reviewed policy result.
replies = {
    "deadline": ("Ask through calendar day 30 after delivery.", "PASS"),
    "receipt": ("You need a valid receipt.", "PASS"),
    "wrong": ("You can still request a refund. You have 90 days after delivery with a valid receipt.", "FAIL"),
    "expired": ("Day 45 is outside the 30-calendar-day refund window after delivery.", "PASS"),
    "boundary": ("Yes. Day 30 after delivery is included, with a valid receipt.", "PASS"),
}
generation = {"X": "refund-assistant-r1 | temperature 0.7", "Y": "refund-assistant-r1 | temperature 0.2"}
# Setting, generation seed, start state. These are saved, effective fixture values.
runs = {
    "X1": ("X", 41, "warm"), "X2": ("X", 42, "warm"),
    "Y1": ("Y", 41, "warm"), "Y2": ("Y", 42, "warm"),
}
# Captured reply ID, attempt flag, raw result. An absent row was never attempted.
observed = {
    "X1": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 90), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 70), "Q3": ("wrong", True, 90)},
    "X2": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 100), "Q2": ("receipt", True, "bad"), "Q3": ("expired", True, "ABSTAIN"),
           "Q4": (None, True, None)},
    "Y1": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 88), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 76), "Q3": ("expired", True, 84),
           "Q4": ("boundary", True, 82)},
    "Y2": {"Q1": ("deadline", True, 90), "Q2": ("receipt", True, 78), "Q3": ("expired", True, 80),
           "Q4": ("boundary", True, 82)},
}
changes = {"baseline": {}, "rescore": {("X1", "Q3"): 60},
           "repair": {("X2", "Q2"): 80}, "abstain": {("Y2", "Q4"): "ABSTAIN"}}

def status(attempted, reply, raw):
    if not attempted:
        return "SKIPPED"
    if reply is None:
        return "TIMEOUT"
    if raw == "ABSTAIN":
        return "ABSTAIN"
    if type(raw) is int and 0 <= raw <= 100:
        return "SCORED"
    return "INVALID"

def fraction(count, total):
    return f"{count}/{total}" if total else "unavailable"

audit = []
for run, (setting, seed, start) in runs.items():
    for case, question in questions.items():
        reply, attempted, original = observed[run].get(case, (None, False, None))
        raw = changes[revision].get((run, case), original)
        text, gate = replies.get(reply, (None, "UNKNOWN"))
        validity = status(attempted, reply, raw)
        action = "BLOCK" if gate == "FAIL" else ("REVIEW" if validity != "SCORED" or gate == "UNKNOWN" else "CHECKED")
        audit.append({
            "run": run, "setting": setting, "dataset": dataset, "policy": policy,
            "policy_version": "refund-1", "generation": generation[setting],
            "seed": seed, "start": start, "rubric": rubric, "judge": judge, "judge_replay": judge_replay,
            "case": case, "question": question, "reply": reply, "text": text,
            "attempted": attempted, "original": original, "raw": raw,
            "status": validity, "gate": gate, "review": action, "revision": revision,
            "aggregation": "pooled scorable rows and equal-run mean",
        })

print(f"{dataset} | {rubric} | {judge_replay} | revision {revision}")
for setting, effective in generation.items():
    print(f"Setting {setting}: {effective}")
    rows = [row for row in audit if row["setting"] == setting]
    scores = [row["raw"] for row in rows if row["status"] == "SCORED"]
    run_means = []
    for run in runs:
        if runs[run][0] != setting:
            continue
        values = [row["raw"] for row in rows if row["run"] == run and row["status"] == "SCORED"]
        average = f"{mean(values):.2f}" if values else "unavailable"
        print(f"  {run}: {average} ({len(values)} scored)")
        if values:
            run_means.append(mean(values))

    attempted = sum(row["attempted"] for row in rows)
    valid = sum(row["status"] in ("SCORED", "ABSTAIN") for row in rows)
    print(f"  attempted {fraction(attempted, len(rows))} | valid {fraction(valid, attempted)} | "
          f"scorable {fraction(len(scores), valid)} | end-to-end {fraction(len(scores), len(rows))}")
    if scores:
        print(f"  micro mean {mean(scores):.2f} | median {median(scores):.2f} | "
              f"min {min(scores)} | max {max(scores)} | range {max(scores) - min(scores)}")
        print(f"  row population variance {pvariance(scores):.2f} | row population SD {pstdev(scores):.2f}")
        print(f"  macro run mean {mean(run_means):.2f} | run-mean population SD {pstdev(run_means):.2f}")
    else:
        print("  score summaries unavailable")

    gaps = [f"{row['run']}/{row['case']}:{row['status']}" for row in rows if row["status"] != "SCORED"]
    failures = [f"{row['run']}/{row['case']}" for row in rows if row["gate"] == "FAIL"]
    print("  gaps " + (", ".join(gaps) or "none"))
    print("  critical " + (", ".join(failures) or "none observed"))
    needs_review = any(row["review"] == "REVIEW" for row in rows)
    decision = "BLOCK" if failures else ("REVIEW" if needs_review else "CONTINUE EVALUATION")
    print(f"  decision {decision}")

sample = next(row for row in audit if (row["run"], row["case"]) == ("X1", "Q3"))
print(f"Audit X1/Q3: {sample['reply']} | original {sample['original']} | "
      f"replay {sample['raw']} | policy {sample['gate']} | decision {sample['review']}")
Expected output

Setting Y: refund-assistant-r1 | temperature 0.2
  Y1: 82.50 (4 scored)
  Y2: 82.50 (4 scored)

  micro mean 82.50 | median 82.00 | min 76 | max 90 | range 14
  row population variance 19.75 | row population SD 4.44

  gaps none

  decision CONTINUE EVALUATION

The new presentation judgment lowers X’s mean and increases its observed spread. Its release decision stays BLOCK because the candidate still contradicts the policy. Checkpoint. How can Y have zero spread across its run means and nonzero spread across its rows? Different case scores can sum to the same total. State the unit before interpreting stability. Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Calculate the center of three repeats

Three fictional pass rates are 90%, 70%, and 80%. Calculate their mean. Explain what evidence you would inspect before attributing the 70% result to the assistant.

Practice 2. Calculate range and population standard deviation

Three presentation scores are 74, 80, and 86. Find the mean, range, variance, and standard deviation using all three observed values. Explain the units of the last two results.

Practice 3. Compare steadiness and average quality

Setting X has scores 78, 80, 82. Setting Y has scores 70, 80, 90. Show the mean and population standard deviation for each. Suppose the reviewer finds a critical failure in X and none in these three Y scores. Explain what can be concluded and what evidence is still needed.

Practice 4. Audit a missing-heavy average

X1 has three scorable rows, 90, 70, 90, one skipped case, and a critical failure on the last scored row. X2 has 100, one invalid verdict, one valid abstention, and one timeout. Each run planned four rows. Calculate equal-run and pooled means, all four coverage ratios, and the release decision. Name the minimum facts someone would need to reproduce the report.

Independent Assignment

You are reviewing the four saved runs and four questions in Step 7. First write down the dataset, rubric, judge replay, effective generation settings, and the independent policy rule. Recalculate each run mean and compare pooled means and medians, ranges, population variances, and population standard deviations for X and Y. Explain why neither repeated attempts nor matching seed values make the individual rows independent questions. Use the audit record to show which critical case blocks release. Give a plan for investigating each kind of missing score.

Use the complete Step 7 program as the executable answer key. Select Copy Code and start from a fresh copy for each variant. For variant A set revision = "repair" to replay a valid 80 for X2/Q2. For variant B instead set revision = "abstain" to replay a valid abstention on Y2/Q4. Each replay keeps the original response and historical raw score. Report which coverage ratio and spread change, whether policy evidence changes, and whether to block, review, or continue evaluating. Finish by explaining why the same weights and comparable case coverage matter if someone wants to use these configurations for a comparative decision.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

Add 90 + 70 + 80 = 240. Divide by three to get 80%. Open the 70% run and check the case IDs, saved replies, and verdicts. Verify the effective generation and judge settings, rubric, and scorable counts before interpreting the drop.

Solution 2

The mean is (74 + 80 + 86) ÷ 3 = 80. Range is 86 − 74 = 12 points. Deviations are −6, 0, and 6. Their squares sum to 36 + 0 + 36 = 72. Population variance is 72 ÷ 3 = 24 squared points. Standard deviation is √24 ≈ 4.90 points.

Solution 3

Both means are 80. X has squared deviations totaling 8, giving population variance 8/3 and standard deviation 1.63. Y has squared deviations totaling 200, giving population variance 200/3 and standard deviation 8.16. X is steadier on these scores and still fails the policy gate. Investigate that failure before release. Check more matched cases and separate sources of variation before making a claim about either setting’s live reliability.

Solution 4

Give X1 and X2 one vote each and you get (250/3 + 100) ÷ 2, about 91.67. Give the four scored rows one vote each and you get 350 ÷ 4 = 87.50. Now account for the other rows. Seven of eight were attempted, including the timeout. Five of those seven produced a valid record, and four of those five gave a number. So end-to-end coverage is 4/8. Block the 90-day reply using the policy evidence. Save the case and run IDs, raw outcomes, effective settings, policy decisions, versions, and weighting rule so another reviewer can reconstruct both averages and the block.

Assignment answer key

X has the higher baseline pooled presentation mean and greater row spread, but only four of eight planned rows contribute scores. Y’s two run means match, and its rows still vary. Review X’s missing or unusable evidence and block its verified 90-day reply. Continue evaluating Y on more distinct cases rather than treating complete coverage of this small fixture as approval.

For variant A, replace the baseline version line with refund-eval-1 | presentation-v1 | saved-verdicts-1 | revision repair. In X, the exact changed lines are X2: 90.00 (2 scored), attempted 7/8 | valid 6/7 | scorable 5/6 | end-to-end 5/8, micro mean 86.00 | median 90.00 | min 70 | max 100 | range 30, row population variance 104.00 | row population SD 10.20, macro run mean 86.67 | run-mean population SD 3.33, and gaps X1/Q4:SKIPPED, X2/Q3:ABSTAIN, X2/Q4:TIMEOUT. These six lines each have two leading spaces. Every other line stays as in the baseline. The below-mean 80 increases scored coverage. X remains blocked.

For variant B, replace the baseline version line with refund-eval-1 | presentation-v1 | saved-verdicts-1 | revision abstain. In Y, the exact changed lines are Y2: 82.67 (3 scored), attempted 8/8 | valid 8/8 | scorable 7/8 | end-to-end 7/8, micro mean 82.57 | median 82.00 | min 76 | max 90 | range 14, row population variance 22.53 | row population SD 4.75, macro run mean 82.58 | run-mean population SD 0.08, gaps Y2/Q4:ABSTAIN, and decision REVIEW. These seven lines each have two leading spaces. Every other line stays as in the baseline. The valid abstention changes the score mix and calls for review even though a policy failure was not observed.

Knowledge Check

  1. Two runs disagree on the same saved reply. What would you fix in the experiment to investigate judge variation?
  2. What does an 80% mean tell you about a series with scores 70%, 80%, and 90%?
  3. In the list 70, 80, 80, 80, 90, replace 90 with 20. Why does the median stay fixed?
  4. Two lists have the same minimum and maximum. What facts about their distribution could still differ?
  5. When would you divide by the number of values for variance, and what does the square root give you?
  6. One run has twice as many scored cases as another. How does the pooled mean weight the two runs?
  7. A judge output is a valid abstention. Which coverage counts include it and which score count excludes it?
  8. A setting consistently gives polished but wrong deadline advice. What should the engineering decision use?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Keep each captured reply, reference, rubric, effective judge configuration, and scoring rule fixed. Compare repeated judge verdicts by case rather than regenerating the reply.
  2. The observed center is 80%. The mean gives no count of distinct cases and no explanation for the low or high runs.
  3. Sorting yields 20, 70, 80, 80, 80. The middle position still holds 80. The mean changes because the sum changes.
  4. The values inside the extremes could be clustered in the middle or near the edges. Their means, medians, and standard deviations may differ.
  5. Divide by the full count to describe the population variance of the saved list. Its square root is population standard deviation, in the same units as the original scores.
  6. The run with twice as many scored cases contributes twice as many rows, so it receives twice the weight in the pooled mean. An equal-run mean gives each run half.
  7. Count the attempt and valid record. Leave it out of the scorable count and numeric mean. Report the abstention as its own status.
  8. Apply the independent policy rule and block the confirmed contradiction. Use the score series to understand presentation stability and collect more paired evidence after correcting the policy behavior.

Common Mistakes

When percentages move, open the run and case records first. Identify which settings applied, which answers were reused or generated anew, and which judge outputs were valid.

Repeated values on one question reveal what happened on that question. Keep the number of distinct questions separate.

Publish score coverage and the policy gate beside any average. Missing scores change the denominator, and a high presentation score can accompany a wrong policy claim.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Replay saved outcomes to reproduce the math. Use controlled repeats to investigate response or judge variability. Keep the analysis unit, variance convention, weights, and coverage clear. Inspect critical facts and missing evidence before drawing a release conclusion.

What You Will Learn

  • Translate pass rates into counts and distinguish a percentage-point change from a relative change.
  • Use Wilson intervals to describe uncertainty around a binary pass rate and understand how sample size and confidence level affect precision.
  • Compare two configurations on matched cases with an exact paired test and a whole-pair bootstrap.
  • Plan a comparison around a meaningful effect, then combine statistical evidence, coverage, and critical policy checks in a release recommendation.

Why This Lesson Matters

At Harbor Leaf Market, someone brings two numbers to the release meeting: 80% for the current refund assistant, A, and 85% for the proposed upgrade, B. Before voting, ask for the case list. If both assistants faced twenty questions, one extra pass could explain the whole gain. Find that extra pass, look for cases B got worse, and check whether either reply would send a customer past the real refund deadline.

The company, replies, verdicts, and thresholds in this lesson are fictional. We keep the earlier policy refund-1: “Refund requests are allowed through calendar day 30 after delivery with a valid receipt.” The item is an eligible unused online purchase, and day 30 is included. The statistic we measure is the fraction of judged cases that pass the case rubric.

Allow about 6.5 hours. Start with Variance, repetition and score aggregation. Sampling, holdouts, leakage and maintenance helps you plan a fair set of cases.

Beginner Explanation

Ask what each percentage counted

Suppose A passed 16 of 20 and B passed 17 of the same 20. One more pass is enough to move from 80% to 85%. Subtract 80 from 85 to get five percentage points. Divide that gain by A’s 80% to get a 6.25% relative improvement in the pass rate. These are two ways to describe the observed effect size, the size of the measured difference.

If you sampled a new group of customers, the questions and outcomes could differ. This is sampling variability. An observed 85% describes the cases counted in one evaluation. It estimates performance for a target population only to the extent that those cases and their labels represent it. Rerating a frozen reply tells you how the judge behaves on that reply. It does not add another sampled customer or question.

If A and B use different case sets, differences in question difficulty can move the rates. Ask for the case IDs, planned and valid counts, response records, and rubric version before comparing the headline results. Repeated variants from one customer or conversation can be correlated. In that setting, count and resample the independent groups, keeping their replies together.

Give the single pass rate an interval

Three teams each report 80%. One counted 8 of 10, another 80 of 100, and the third 800 of 1,000. Each has a different number of independent binary observations. That number is its sample size. Eight passes give a rougher picture than eight hundred if both sets are sampled well. A large set drawn from easy cases can still miss the kinds of question you need to judge.

Imagine a new Harbor Leaf team taking a fresh sample each week. Each team draws the same number of suitable cases and marks two limits around its observed rate. Those limits form a confidence interval. If you could draw one line at the fixed underlying rate, some of the weekly intervals would cross that line and others would miss it. The 95% label describes how often the procedure aims to cross that line over many such samples, under its assumptions. Wilson coverage is approximate. The two limits in this week’s report are already fixed.

Here is how we get the two endpoints. Let k be the number of passes, n the number of scored cases, and p = k/n the observed fraction. Let z be the normal cutoff chosen for the confidence level, for example 1.96 for 95%. A normal cutoff is measured in standard deviations from zero under a standard bell-shaped reference curve. For 90% it is about 1.645, and for 99% about 2.576. The larger cutoff reaches farther into the tails of that curve.

For 8 of 10, p is 0.8 and z²/n is about 0.384. The Wilson center shifts inward to about 0.717. Its half-width is about 0.227. Subtract and add that half-width to get about 0.490 and 0.943. Keep full precision until the end. The calculation adjusts both the center and width and gives useful limits even when a small sample has zero or all passes. NIST, Wilson confidence limits

In symbols, the common divisor is d = 1 + z²/n. The center is (p + z²/(2n)) / d. The half-width is z × sqrt(p(1−p)/n + z²/(4n²)) / d. The term p(1−p) reflects how much 0/1 outcomes can vary and sqrt turns squared uncertainty back into pass-rate units. The extra terms come from solving the Wilson score rule. They keep the two limits meaningful when p is near zero or one. Predict what happens to the width when n grows at the same observed rate. Then check it in Step 2.

At the same sample size, a higher confidence level usually makes the interval wider. A 99% procedure aims to miss the underlying rate less often, so it leaves itself more room. Compare the actual widths in Step 3. Confidence levels describe the interval method. They do not account for bias in deciding which questions go into the evaluation.

Pair the answers before counting changes
Course hours by track
CaseABWhat changed
C01PASSPASSNeither wins this case.
C02FAILPASSB gains one pass.
C03PASSFAILB loses one pass.
C04FAILFAILNeither wins this case.

The matched case is the unit. Rows where the outcomes agree are concordant. Rows that differ are discordant. The B-only and A-only rows give the direction of the changes. B gained one and lost one. Its observed effect on these four cases is (1 − 1) ÷ 4 = 0. A paired comparison keeps this match. An independent-samples test would discard it by treating the observations as if A and B got separate, unrelated cases. Use that analysis only when the sampling design actually supports it.

Keep the same small example in mind when estimating uncertainty in the difference. Write the case IDs on four cards. A draw might be C01, C02, C02, C04. Take both outcomes each time you draw a card. That draw has two B-only passes and no A-only passes, for an effect of +50 points. Another draw, C01, C03, C03, C04, gives −50 points. Returning the card after every draw is called sampling with replacement.

Repeat this draw many times, always drawing the same number of whole pairs as in the original sample. Sort the new differences and use the 2.5% and 97.5% positions for an approximate 95% paired bootstrap interval. This estimates uncertainty by resampling the observed cases. It needs representative independent case units and can be unreliable with very small or nearly degenerate data. In the lab, independently drawing A and B would break the link between outcomes on the same case. You will calculate that independent-design approximation as a contrast, with its different assumptions printed beside it.

Ask how unusual the discordant counts are

Suppose three discordant cases favor B and two favor A. If neither configuration has an advantage, each discordant direction should be equally likely. This is the null hypothesis of equal marginal pass probabilities. The two-sided alternative allows either configuration to win more often on discordant cases. Conditional on five discordant cases under the null, imagine five independent fair flips giving the direction. This is the case-level swap intuition of a paired test. A tied case adds no evidence about direction.

Use the smaller discordant count, two, as the test statistic. Of the 32 equally likely flip sequences, 1 has zero B wins, 5 have one, and 10 have two. The opposite tail has the same size. The two-sided exact McNemar test adds both tails to get 2 × (1 + 5 + 10)/32 = 1. A p-value is the probability, under the null and test assumptions, of results at least as extreme as the one observed. It gives no probability that the null is true. Statsmodels, exact binomial McNemar test

Choose the significance level, often written alpha, before seeing results. This fictional plan uses 0.05. Reject the equal-probability null when the exact p-value is at most 0.05. If you do not reject, the test may have little information. It gives no guarantee of equality. With no discordant pairs the code reports p = 1 and flags that there was no directional evidence. The test assumes independent pairs, consistent binary scoring, and an analysis fixed before looking at outcomes.

The Wilson intervals describe each configuration’s rate. The whole-pair interval describes the gain. The exact paired test asks how unusual the direction count is under equality. Comparing two marginal interval pictures for overlap does not perform this test. A percentile bootstrap and an exact probability test may also differ near a threshold because they use different procedures.

Plan for a useful result

Suppose a one-point gain would only prevent one error per 100 questions, while changing the system would add manual review on ten. Decide whether that is worthwhile and which error types matter. For Harbor Leaf, getting a deadline wrong can outweigh gains on routine replies. Set a practical threshold for an observed gain before testing and require a separate critical policy review. A small p-value alone says little about business value or safety.

For planning, write down the baseline pass rate, a plausible improvement, the desired false-positive level, and the chance you want of detecting a specified real improvement. That chance is power. The minimum detectable effect is the smallest effect the proposed design is intended to detect with that power. It depends on sample size and expected variability. For paired tests, estimate how often changes go in both directions. A five-point gain could come from 7% B-only and 2% A-only cases, or 22% B-only and 17% A-only. The same net gain then comes with different disagreement rates. Use estimates from separate pilot cases and plan using the paired design.

If a pilot suggests 10% discordance and a net gain of 5 points, that implies 7.5% B-only and 2.5% A-only. Simulate many paired samples at a candidate size using those probabilities, run the exact test on each sample, and count how often it rejects at the planned alpha. Increase the size until that fraction meets your power goal, checking other plausible disagreement rates as well. This is planning under explicit assumptions, not a guarantee.

Step 6 does a narrower job. It finds the first sample size on a declared grid that gives a single-rate Wilson interval with a target width, assuming the observed rate stays at 80%. It is a precision calculation, with no promise of a particular power for the paired test. More distinct cases can improve precision under good sampling. More copies of old cases cannot replace a representative evaluation set.

If ten unrelated null comparisons each have a 5% false-positive chance, the chance at least one triggers is 1 − 0.95¹⁰, about 40%. That illustration assumes independent comparisons which real model trials may not satisfy. Choose the primary comparison and decision rules in advance, record the configurations tried, and validate any selected model on a fresh holdout. If several claims are primary, plan how to handle the family of tests before drawing conclusions.

Even a good calculation cannot correct changing rubrics, judge mistakes, correlated cases, or an unrepresentative sample. Repeated use of a holdout can tune you to it. Model settings or live generation can also change between runs. Report invalid outcomes, missing slices, version differences, and deployment risks the evaluation did not cover.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Same rate, different precision

User question. Which 80% report gives the tighter estimate for refund-case performance?

Approved reference. Each report uses the same binary refund rubric and a sample of distinct cases drawn from the same target population in this teaching example.

Actual LLM response. The saved pass/fail counts are 8/10, 80/100, and 800/1,000.

Assessment. Each numerator divided by its denominator is 0.80. For 8/10 the Wilson center is about 0.717 and the half-width about 0.227. For 80/100 they are about 0.789 and 0.078. For 800/1,000 they are about 0.799 and 0.025. Using the unrounded values, the 95% intervals are 49.02–94.33%, 71.12–86.66%, and 77.41–82.36%.

Failure classification. The widths shrink from 45.32 to 15.55 to 4.95 percentage points. Repeating a cached reply 1,000 times would not supply the distinct cases needed for the third claim. Check the case mix as well as the count.

Example 2. Count gains and losses on the same questions

User question. Do the first 20 paired cases support a difference between A and B?

Approved reference. Each configuration faces the same cases and the same binary refund rubric. The exact paired test uses a two-sided 0.05 threshold fixed in advance.

Actual LLM response. Both pass on C01–C14, A alone passes on C15–C16, B alone passes on C17–C19, and both fail on C20. All labels are illustrative.

Assessment. A passes 14 + 2 = 16/20. B passes 14 + 3 = 17/20. The observed gain is (3 − 2)/20 = 5 percentage points. Use only the five discordant directions for the exact test. The smaller tail through two has 16 of the 32 null sequences, and doubling it yields p = 1.00000.

Failure classification. The evidence is inconclusive about an underlying difference. It also cannot establish equivalence. Collect more matched cases and check whether the expected benefit and policy risk warrant a larger study.

Example 3. A supported gain still hits a critical gate

User question. Can Harbor Leaf release B after the larger paired evaluation?

Approved reference. The lab’s fictional release plan requires at least 99% matched coverage, a positive gain of at least 3 percentage points, exact p ≤ 0.05, and completed critical review with zero verified critical failures for B.

Actual LLM response. Of 202 planned cases, two have one invalid verdict, leaving 200 complete pairs. Both pass on 156, A alone on 4, B alone on 14, and neither on 26. B’s captured C157 reply wrongly promises 90 days.

Assessment. A passes (156 + 4)/200 = 80%. B passes (156 + 14)/200 = 85%. Their marginal Wilson intervals are 73.91–84.95% and 79.39–89.29%. The paired effect is (14 − 4)/200 = +5 points. The null gives 2¹⁸ equally likely discordant direction sequences. The tail through four has 1 + 18 + 153 + 816 + 3060 = 4048. Doubling and dividing by 262,144 gives p ≈ 0.03088. Coverage is 200/202 = 99.01%.

Failure classification. Write HOLD on the release sheet and attach reply C157. At day 45, the 90-day reply says to go ahead, even though the store’s window closed on day 30. The paired test and the observed gain clear their respective rules, so keep those results too. The team needs both records to understand why a promising gain still leaves a customer-facing error to fix.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

Use Copy Code, open the editor next to a block, paste the whole program, and select Run. Compare the output with the first disclosure. Predict the experimental result before making the single described change. Start every exercise in a fresh editor. All inputs are fictional and inline. Each program uses standard Python with no live service.

Step 1 — Count passes and failures by case ID

Start from the existing assistant’s 20 clean binary verdicts. A dictionary gives each verdict a stable case ID. range(1, 21) yields the numbers 1 through 20. The formatting code 02d prints each number with at least two digits. Adding Boolean comparisons counts the number of true ones.

Open Python Editor

outcomes = {f"C{i:02d}": "PASS" if i <= 16 else "FAIL" for i in range(1, 21)}
passes = sum(result == "PASS" for result in outcomes.values())
failures = sum(result == "FAIL" for result in outcomes.values())
total = passes + failures
print(f"Sample size: {total} | passes: {passes} | failures: {failures}")
print(f"Accuracy: {passes / total:.1%}")
Expected output
Sample size: 20 | passes: 16 | failures: 4
Accuracy: 80.0%

Experiment. Insert outcomes["C17"] = "PASS" below the first line. Predict how many percentage points one change buys.

Expected output
Sample size: 20 | passes: 17 | failures: 3
Accuracy: 85.0%

One case changes out of twenty. Checkpoint. Does this prove new customers will have exactly five points fewer errors? It only describes these twenty outcomes. Compare a fresh or larger representative paired sample to learn about future cases.

Step 2 — Calculate the Wilson interval

Use 8 of 10 and compute the divisor, center, and half-width from the worked numbers. ** 2 squares a value, sqrt() takes the square root, and return sends the two limits back together. The two names before = receive the lower and upper limits in that order.

Open Python Editor

from math import sqrt

def wilson(passes, n, z):
    p = passes / n
    z2 = z ** 2
    divisor = 1 + z2 / n
    center = (p + z2 / (2 * n)) / divisor
    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z2 / (4 * n ** 2)) / divisor
    return center - half, center + half

passes, n = 8, 10
low, high = wilson(passes, n, 1.959963984540054)
print(f"Observed: {passes}/{n} ({passes / n:.2%})")
print(f"Wilson 95%: {low:.2%} to {high:.2%}")
print(f"Width: {100 * (high - low):.2f} pp")
Expected output
Observed: 8/10 (80.00%)
Wilson 95%: 49.02% to 94.33%
Width: 45.32 pp

Experiment. Change the whole count pair to passes, n = 80, 100. Keep 80% fixed and predict the width.

Expected output
Observed: 80/100 (80.00%)
Wilson 95%: 71.12% to 86.66%
Width: 15.55 pp

The rate stays 80% while the extra independent cases narrow the interval. Width is computed before rounding the endpoints. Checkpoint. Would duplicating the ten rows ten times justify this output? The formula would print it, but the claimed sample size would be wrong.

Step 3 — Change confidence on the same dataset

Keep 80/100 fixed. The table supplies precomputed two-sided normal cutoffs. A dictionary connects the requested confidence level to its cutoff. The loop prints all three widths for inspection before reporting one selected interval.

Open Python Editor

from math import sqrt

def wilson(passes, n, z):
    p = passes / n
    z2 = z * z
    divisor = 1 + z2 / n
    center = (p + z2 / (2 * n)) / divisor
    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z2 / (4 * n * n)) / divisor
    return center - half, center + half

critical_values = {90: 1.6448536269514722, 95: 1.959963984540054, 99: 2.5758293035489004}
level = 90
for confidence, z in critical_values.items():
    lower, upper = wilson(80, 100, z)
    print(f"{confidence}% width: {100 * (upper - lower):.2f} pp")
low, high = wilson(80, 100, critical_values[level])
print(f"Selected {level}%: {low:.2%} to {high:.2%}")
Expected output
90% width: 13.08 pp
95% width: 15.55 pp
99% width: 20.30 pp
Selected 90%: 72.67% to 85.75%

Experiment. Change level = 90 to level = 99. Predict which limits move.

Expected output
90% width: 13.08 pp
95% width: 15.55 pp
99% width: 20.30 pp
Selected 99%: 67.98% to 88.28%

The wider selected interval goes with a higher confidence procedure. Checkpoint. Did the release evidence get stronger by changing the line? The data stayed fixed. Choose the level in the plan and report it with the result.

Step 4 — Count each matched outcome

Read the four rows from the pairing table. The dictionary key is a tuple holding both labels. counts[a, b] += 1 adds one to its category. The agree categories describe overall performance, while A-only and B-only determine the net improvement.

Open Python Editor

rows = [
    ("C01", "PASS", "PASS"), ("C02", "FAIL", "PASS"),
    ("C03", "PASS", "FAIL"), ("C04", "FAIL", "FAIL"),
]
counts = {("PASS", "PASS"): 0, ("PASS", "FAIL"): 0,
          ("FAIL", "PASS"): 0, ("FAIL", "FAIL"): 0}
for case_id, a, b in rows:
    counts[a, b] += 1
both, a_only, b_only, neither = counts.values()
print(f"Both pass {both} | A only {a_only} | B only {b_only} | both fail {neither}")
print(f"A passes {both + a_only}/{len(rows)} | B passes {both + b_only}/{len(rows)}")

A passes 2/4 | B passes 2/4

Experiment. Change only B’s C03 label from "FAIL" to "PASS". Predict which two categories change.

Both pass 2 | A only 0 | B only 1 | both fail 1
A passes 2/4 | B passes 3/4
Paired B-A: +25.0 pp

C03 moves from A-only into both pass, reducing B’s losses by one. Checkpoint. Did the number of questions change? It stayed four. A large-looking effect can come from a single case in a tiny sample.

Step 5 — Test the discordant directions

Use the twenty-case demonstration. Keep the number of pairs, A-only passes, and both-fail cases fixed. Changing B-only replaces some both-pass rows, leaving B’s number of passes fixed. comb(m, k) counts the ways to choose k of m positions for one direction. The loop adds the counts through the smaller observed direction. There are 2 ** m possible sequences.

Open Python Editor

from math import comb

def exact_p(a_only, b_only):
    m = a_only + b_only
    if m == 0:
        return 1.0
    tail = sum(comb(m, k) for k in range(min(a_only, b_only) + 1))
    return min(1.0, 2 * tail / (2 ** m))

n = 20
a_only, b_only, neither = 2, 3, 1
both = n - a_only - b_only - neither
assert both >= 0
p_value = exact_p(a_only, b_only)
print(f"Both pass {both} | A only {a_only} | B only {b_only} | both fail {neither}")
print(f"Discordant: {a_only + b_only} | effect {100 * (b_only - a_only) / n:+.1f} pp")
print(f"Exact two-sided p: {p_value:.5f}")
print("Reject equality at 0.05" if p_value <= 0.05 else "Do not reject equality at 0.05")
Expected output
Both pass 14 | A only 2 | B only 3 | both fail 1
Discordant: 5 | effect +5.0 pp
Exact two-sided p: 1.00000
Do not reject equality at 0.05

Experiment. Replace the three counts with a_only, b_only, neither = 2, 10, 1. Seven former both-pass cases now have a hypothetical A failure. Predict the direction of the p-value change.

Expected output
Both pass 7 | A only 2 | B only 10 | both fail 1
Discordant: 12 | effect +40.0 pp
Exact two-sided p: 0.03857
Reject equality at 0.05

Compare the discordant rows before and after the edit. B goes from winning three of five to winning ten of twelve. Under the fair-flip assumption, only 79 of the 4,096 sequences put two or fewer wins in one specified direction. Count the other tail too, giving 158 of 4,096. Checkpoint. What would you inspect before acting on the smaller p-value? Read the failed replies and the release rules. The edited counts illustrate the test, while the source and actual replies supply evidence about the service.

Step 6 — Plan for a target interval width

Assume a fixed observed rate of 80%. Try planning sizes in steps of ten so that four fifths gives a whole pass count. The // 5 operation gives the integer quotient. next() returns the first matching row in the search, or None if the grid never reaches the target. Keep 95% confidence for both runs.

Open Python Editor

from math import sqrt

def width(n):
    p = (4 * n // 5) / n
    z = 1.959963984540054
    z2 = z * z
    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z2 / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z2 / n)
    return 2 * half

for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"n={n}: width {100 * width(n):.2f} pp")

target = 0.10
chosen = next((n for n in range(10, 2001, 10) if width(n) <= target), None)
print(f"Target width: {100 * target:.1f} pp")
print(f"First grid size: {chosen} | width {100 * width(chosen):.2f} pp" if chosen else "Target not reached")
Expected output
n=10: width 45.32 pp
n=100: width 15.55 pp
n=1000: width 4.95 pp
Target width: 10.0 pp
First grid size: 250 | width 9.88 pp

Experiment. Change target = 0.10 to target = 0.06.

Expected output
n=10: width 45.32 pp
n=100: width 15.55 pp
n=1000: width 4.95 pp
Target width: 6.0 pp
First grid size: 690 | width 5.96 pp

The narrower target needs more independent cases under the 80% planning assumption. Checkpoint. Does this plan show you can detect a five-point gain between A and B? This search tells you about the width of one rate’s interval on the chosen grid. A power calculation needs the paired design and anticipated counts of changes in both directions.

Step 7 — Reproduce a release report

Use the twenty scored pairs from the small demonstration and one planned case with an invalid B verdict. The rows contain saved values, not live model calls. dict.get() can look up an adjudication for one case and retain its original status otherwise. all() tests whether both labels belong to the binary scale. Both A-only pairs enter the statistical table because both binary labels are valid. Their separate critical review can still be pending.

Open Python Editor

from math import comb, sqrt

dataset, rubric = "refund-small-1", "refund-binary-v1"
config_a, config_b = "A/current", "B/proposed"
revision = "baseline"
z = 1.959963984540054
raw = {}
for i in range(1, 22):
    a = "PASS" if i <= 16 or i == 21 else "FAIL"
    b = "PASS" if i <= 14 or 17 <= i <= 19 else "FAIL"
    raw[f"C{i:02d}"] = (a, "INVALID" if i == 21 else b, "PENDING" if i == 15 else "CLEAR")
adjudications = {"baseline": {}, "confirmed": {"C15": "FAIL"}}

def wilson(k, n):
    p = k / n
    z2 = z * z
    d = 1 + z2 / n
    center = (p + z2 / (2 * n)) / d
    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z2 / (4 * n * n)) / d
    return center - half, center + half

audit = {case: (a, b, original, adjudications[revision].get(case, original))
         for case, (a, b, original) in raw.items()}
paired = [row for row in audit.values() if all(label in ("PASS", "FAIL") for label in row[:2])]
n = len(paired)
a_pass = sum(row[0] == "PASS" for row in paired)
b_pass = sum(row[1] == "PASS" for row in paired)
a_only = sum(row[:2] == ("PASS", "FAIL") for row in paired)
b_only = sum(row[:2] == ("FAIL", "PASS") for row in paired)
m = a_only + b_only
p = min(1.0, 2 * sum(comb(m, k) for k in range(min(a_only, b_only) + 1)) / (2 ** m))
effect = (b_pass - a_pass) / n
critical = [case for case, row in audit.items() if row[3] == "FAIL"]
pending = [case for case, row in audit.items() if row[3] == "PENDING"]
excluded = [case for case, row in audit.items() if not all(label in ("PASS", "FAIL") for label in row[:2])]
if critical:
    decision = "HOLD"
elif pending or n / len(raw) < 0.99 or p > 0.05 or effect < 0.03:
    decision = "REVIEW"
else:
    decision = "RELEASE"

print(f"{dataset} | {rubric} | {config_a} vs {config_b} | {revision}")
print(f"Paired coverage: {n}/{len(raw)} | excluded: {', '.join(excluded)}")
for name, count in [("A", a_pass), ("B", b_pass)]:
    low, high = wilson(count, n)
    print(f"{name}: {count} pass, {n-count} fail | {count/n:.1%} | Wilson 95% {low:.2%} to {high:.2%}")
print(f"Effect B-A: {effect*100:+.1f} pp | A only {a_only} | B only {b_only} | exact p {p:.5f}")
print("Statistical threshold: " + ("met" if p <= 0.05 else "not met"))
print("Observed practical floor (+3 pp): " + ("met" if effect >= 0.03 else "not met"))
print(f"B critical: {', '.join(critical) or 'none'} | B pending: {', '.join(pending) or 'none'}")
print(f"Audit C15: original gate {raw['C15'][2]} | replay gate {audit['C15'][3]}")
print(f"Recommendation: {decision}")
Expected output
refund-small-1 | refund-binary-v1 | A/current vs B/proposed | baseline
Paired coverage: 20/21 | excluded: C21
A: 16 pass, 4 fail | 80.0% | Wilson 95% 58.40% to 91.93%
B: 17 pass, 3 fail | 85.0% | Wilson 95% 63.96% to 94.76%
Effect B-A: +5.0 pp | A only 2 | B only 3 | exact p 1.00000
Statistical threshold: not met
Observed practical floor (+3 pp): met
B critical: none | B pending: C15
Audit C15: original gate PENDING | replay gate PENDING
Recommendation: REVIEW

Experiment. Set revision = "confirmed". The independent reviewer checked the frozen C15 reply “You have 90 days after delivery if you have a valid receipt” against refund-1, and recorded a critical failure. Leave both original verdicts and the reply fixed.

Expected output

Paired coverage: 20/21 | excluded: C21

The raw audit still shows PENDING. The new evidence strengthens the reason to block deployment without changing a rate or the p-value. Checkpoint.
