Link to topic

What You Will Learn

  • Turn a policy document into searchable passages and trace each passage back to its source and version.
  • Retrieve and rank passages, then explain what the score can miss.
  • Hand-score two lists, reproduce the results in Python, and use a controlled replay to diagnose a retrieval failure.
  • Report missing, partial, stale, duplicate, or unauthorized evidence before evaluating a generated answer.

Why This Lesson Matters

A customer bought something from Northstar Support 45 days ago and asks, “Can I still get a refund?” Imagine you can send the assistant just one of the three notes below.

  • Refunds. Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.
  • Shipping. After 45 days without a receipt, contact us for shipping delays.
  • Warranty. Start a warranty claim from your order.

Choose the note you would send. The shipping note repeats the customer’s number, but the refund note is the one that sets the deadline. A search that rewards shared words can make the opposite choice.

Imagine an assistant sees only the shipping passage. A reply about refunds may still sound plausible, but the log would show that the necessary evidence was missing before the assistant wrote anything. In this lesson you’ll inspect that log, reproduce why the shipping page wins, and test a change against other questions so you can see what it fixes.

All Northstar records, policy details, replies, and results are fictional. Budget about 6.5 hours. Complete Ground truth, references and benchmarks first. Golden schemas, provenance and versioning and Embeddings and semantic similarity are recommended. Complete the similarity lesson before changing a dense retriever’s encoder or interpreting its scores. The code here uses ordinary text search.

Beginner Explanation

Get the policy into the request

An assistant has patterns learned during training, stored as numbers called parameters. Northstar can also put a policy directly in the prompt, the information supplied for the current request. Copying an entire handbook into every prompt wastes room and makes updates hard to track. Looking up a few passages for this question is retrieval. Giving the model those passages before it writes is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. If the search misses a rule or the model ignores it, the answer can still be wrong.

Follow the 45-day request through the system.

  1. Ingest and parse. Take in the refund page, read its fields, and separate its text from its title and version. Keep the original wording.
  2. Clean and chunk. Make a consistent search copy. Divide the page into passages small enough to inspect or send to the assistant.
  3. Index. Make a lookup from a term such as refund to the IDs of passages containing it.
  4. Process the query. Use the same rules to turn the customer’s question into searchable terms.
  5. Retrieve, rank, and select. Find eligible candidate passages, give each a score, and take the first few. These become the selected context, the evidence the writer gets.
  6. Generate and evaluate. The assistant writes an answer. Inspect the passages it received first, then compare its claims with the approved policy.
Keep track of where a sentence came from

The current refund document has ID RF, title “Refund eligibility,” source kb/refunds, and version 2. The title helps a person find it, the source identifies the policy page, and the version identifies the revision. Text, publication status, and the access rule travel with that record. Check required fields and duplicate IDs at ingestion. If two different records use RF, a replay could point at the wrong policy.

For search, REFUND, 45 days? can become refund, 45, days. Lowercase both the text and the query. Turn tabs and runs of spaces into single spaces. Ignore sentence punctuation when finding words, while keeping 30 and 45 distinct. Making those consistent changes is normalization, and turning the text into searchable pieces is tokenization. A model can use a different tokenizer. Removing all digits would erase the policy distinction. Splitting 3.5 into 3 and 5 or merging 2025-03-01 into 20250301 can also change which texts match. Save the original text for review.

If the exact same passage enters through two copies of one policy source and version, it can occupy two result slots. Keep one searchable copy and preserve its provenance. Different sources, versions, permissions, or subtle wording can change the answer, so do not merge passages merely because they look similar. If you deduplicate, keep a trace of any source or evidence IDs you collapse in real evaluations.

Give the search a useful passage

Suppose one sentence says, “Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition.” The next says, “Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.” A one-sentence passage can point the search toward the damaged-product rule while leaving the deadline and photos behind. A two-sentence passage can carry both.

Put sentences 1 and 2 on one card and sentence 3 on another. A search for “damaged product refund” may return just the first card. The customer would hear that a separate condition exists without learning the deadline or what to send. Copy sentence 2 onto the second card and it can now travel with the seven-day instruction.

Each card represents a chunk. The place where a card starts or ends is its boundary. Chunk size is how much text a card can hold. Overlap is the text printed on neighboring cards. With size 2 and overlap 1, the two cards hold sentences 1–2 and 2–3. If both are selected, the assistant sees sentence 2 twice. Larger chunks keep rules together but take up more of the model’s input space, called its context budget. Smaller chunks can be precise but lose conditions. A production splitter may count words or model tokens instead of sentences. For example, six tokens at a time with two repeated tokens means starting each new window four tokens later. Test boundaries against real policies and keep each chunk’s ID, source document ID and version.

Find candidates, then put them in order

If a catalog says refund → RF-v2:c01, RF-v2:c02 and receipt → RF-v2:c01, a query containing both words can look up two lists and combine them. This term-to-passage catalog is an inverted index. A set stores each matching ID once. The index points to passages and the separate document records still carry the source wording.

Start by awarding one point per distinct shared term. A ranking score orders the candidates. top-k means the first k positions, for example three passages when k = 3. Set an explicit rule for equal scores, such as comparing chunk IDs, so a rerun produces the same order. A lexical search compares words, so proof of purchase may miss a source that says only receipt. This gap is a lexical mismatch. The opposite also happens. A shared phrase such as 45 days can point to the wrong subject.

A refinement weights terms by how common they are in the collection. Suppose refund appears in one of two chunks and days appears in both. Give days weight 1. Give refund weight 1 + ln(3/2) ≈ 1.405, where ln is the natural logarithm, a function that grows slowly as its input rises. Both matches together score about 2.405. The rule we’ll use is 1 + ln((N + 1)/(df + 1)), where N is the number of eligible chunks and df is the number containing the term. The added ones keep the ratio defined at zero counts. Each matching term counts once per chunk. This is a simplified term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF) style weight with binary term presence. Adding a document can change scores for existing documents because the collection counts change.

A term index is sparse retrieval because most vocabulary terms are absent from any one passage. Dense retrieval compares learned number vectors, called embeddings, that can help recognize related phrasing. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and dense signals, for example by merging two ranked lists using a documented rule. Freeze the collection, permissions, queries, labels, and cutoff when comparing a ranking method. If you change the dense encoder, record its model version and rebuild its index with that encoder. Similarity still needs a relevance check. The lesson’s executable examples use lexical scoring only.

Decide what evidence counts

Write down the policy evidence each test question needs before running the search. These reviewed answers are gold relevance judgments. Use stable source IDs and sentence IDs to say which wording supports a claim. A chunk can contain one needed sentence and still leave out another. When you change chunking, map gold sentence IDs to the new chunk IDs. Compare sentence coverage across both versions because the number of relevant chunks can change.

Take a query with two relevant chunks. If the top three are [shipping, refund, receipt], there is a hit in the first three, two of the three slots are relevant, and both of the two relevant chunks were found. That gives Hit@3 = 1, Precision@3 = 2/3, and Recall@3 = 2/2. If the first relevant chunk is second, its reciprocal rank is 1/2. The mean reciprocal rank (MRR) is the average of those fractions across scored queries. A query with known relevant evidence that retrieves none gets reciprocal rank 0. This lesson computes MRR from the full returned ranking before the top-k cut. If you use only the first k results, label the metric MRR@k. Precision here always divides by k, including any empty slots.

One chunk can answer the policy question directly while another can help only with one detail. Give those grades 2 and 1. A reviewed irrelevant passage gets 0. If the complete policy appears first, the writer sees it sooner than if a partial answer appears first. Normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) rewards that ordering. At rank 1, grade 2 earns (2² − 1)/log₂(2) = 3/1 = 3. At rank 2, grade 1 earns (2¹ − 1)/log₂(3) ≈ 0.631. Here log₂ is a logarithm with base 2. As the rank number increases, so does the divisor, which reduces the credit. For this lesson each contribution is (2^grade − 1)/log₂(rank + 1). Sum the contributions through k to get DCG. Divide by the DCG of the ideal order of the known grades at the same cutoff to get nDCG. A value of 1 means the list earned as much credit as that ideal order.

An unlabeled passage has yet to be judged. Queue it for review and disclose judgment coverage. For example, if two of the top three are judged, record 2/3 judged. Treat a calculation that temporarily gives the unknown passage zero credit as provisional. A query with no positive gold judgments cannot support ordinary recall or normalized gain. If a reviewer confirms the corpus lacks an answer, test that separately. If the query is simply unjudged, label that gap and keep it out of the scored mean. Always report the number scored.

Diagnose before changing the system

Open the saved query, eligible source versions, chunk boundaries, ranked list, and context actually sent to the writer. If the needed refund policy is absent from that context, start with retrieval or selection. If the full policy is present and the answer says “45 days is fine,” investigate generation, the step that wrote the answer. Record both if both are supported by the trace.

  • Wrong subject at the top. Compare matched terms and weights for that passage and the gold passage.
  • Needed evidence absent from the full ranking. Check that the current source was ingested, indexed, authorized, and reachable with the query’s wording.
  • Needed evidence ranked below the cutoff. Try a ranking change or a larger top-k on the same queries. Measure the extra noise and context.
  • Condition separated from the rule. Read neighboring chunks. Try overlap or a policy-section boundary.
  • Repeated passages crowd the list. Compare the original source and version, and inspect deduplication before rebuilding.
  • Stale wording appears. Check the approved version and index refresh. Remove stale versions from eligible search.
  • Restricted material is visible. Treat as a critical failure. Filter by verified access before ranking, context selection, or display.

A passage can be useful and still be unauthorized. The public replay in this chapter builds the index for the allowed role and approved current versions, so restricted text never appears in any public result. Production permissions must come from a trusted identity and access system. For a real change, also check search latency, freshness after policy updates, and the total input space used by the chosen passages. Freeze the query set and judgments while varying one setting. Use new reviewed queries before generalizing.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Preserve the condition while changing chunk boundaries

Read the fictional current policy RF v2, from kb/refunds. It contains these three sentences.

  1. “Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.”
  2. “Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition.”
  3. “Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.”

User question. “What do I send for a damaged product refund, and when?”

Approved reference. Sentences 2 and 3 establish the subject, seven-day deadline measured from delivery, and photo requirement.

With size 2 and overlap 0, RF-v2:c01 covers sentences 1–2 and RF-v2:c02 covers sentence 3. Both keep source kb/refunds, version 2, and document ID RF. Predict which chunk contains the product type and the photo requirement together. There is no such chunk. With overlap 1, RF-v2:c01 still covers 1–2 and RF-v2:c02 now covers 2–3. The chunk IDs are local to a build, so log its settings alongside them. The stable sentence IDs RF-v2:s02 and RF-v2:s03 make the evidence comparable.

Actual LLM response. Fictional replay fixture, “Check with support for the required documents,” after only the original c01 was selected.

Assessment. The selected text refers to a separate condition but never states it. The overlap supplies a passage with both sentences for a later ranking test.

Failure classification. Required evidence split at the chunk boundary. Check whether the new chunk is selected, and measure how much repeated text overlap sends to the writer.

Example 2. Find why a shipping passage beats the refund policy

User question. “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?”

Approved reference. RF-v2:s01 requires a valid receipt and filing within 30 days of purchase.

Score one point per distinct shared term, using these three fictional single-sentence passages.

  • SH. “After 45 days without a receipt, contact us for shipping delays.” The shared terms are after, 45, days, without, a, and receipt. Score 6.
  • RF. “Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.” The shared terms are refund, a, receipt, and days. Score 4.
  • WA. “Start a warranty claim from your order.” The only shared term is a. Score 1.

Ranking is SH, RF, WA. Predict the new result if a match on refund is worth four points instead of one. RF earns three extra points, so it takes first place with 7. SH stays at 6 and WA at 1.

Actual LLM response. Fictional fixture, “Contact us about your refund after 45 days,” after top-1 search sent only SH.

Assessment. Look at the words that earn SH points. It gets credit for both “45” and “after,” but those words describe a shipping delay. Open RF and read “within 30 days of purchase.” That line is the evidence the writer needed. Giving “refund” more weight changes which passage arrives first, without changing any policy wording.

Failure classification. Wrong subject first and required evidence cut from the writer’s context. Replay the weighting change on the same collection and include a shipping query before adopting it.

Example 3. Hand-score two ranked lists

User question. Q1 asks about the refund window and proof. Q2 asks where to start a warranty claim.

Approved reference. The fictional reviewer gives Q1 R (complete refund rule) grade 2 and M (receipt help) grade 1. For Q2 only W (warranty claim instructions) earns grade 2. Every other item in these lists is judged 0. A positive grade counts as relevant for binary metrics.

  • Q1 ranks S, R, M, X. The first slot has no relevant result, so Hit@1 is 0. Hit@3 is 1 because R and M appear inside three slots. Precision@3 is 2/3 and Recall@3 is 2/2. R is the first relevant result at rank 2, giving reciprocal rank 1/2.
  • Q2 ranks W, U, X. W is the only relevant result and appears first, so Hit@1 and Hit@3 are both 1. Precision@3 is 1/3, Recall@3 is 1/1, and reciprocal rank is 1.

Across the two queries, mean Hit@1 is (0 + 1)/2 = 0.5. Mean Hit@3 and Recall@3 are both 1. Mean Precision@3 is (2/3 + 1/3)/2 = 0.5. MRR is (1/2 + 1)/2 = 0.75. For Q1, DCG@3 is 0 + 3/log₂(3) + 1/log₂(4) ≈ 2.393. The ideal DCG is 3 + 1/log₂(3) ≈ 3.631. Divide to get nDCG@3 ≈ 0.659. Q2 has its best passage first, so its nDCG@3 is 1.

Actual LLM response. Fictional Q1 fixture, “File a refund within 30 days of purchase and include a valid receipt,” after all three selected passages were delivered.

Assessment. At three slots Q1 can receive both relevant chunks despite the first result being wrong. Move M below the cutoff and Recall@3 drops to 1/2 for Q1, while the rank of R remains 2 and MRR stays 0.75.

Failure classification. Q1 has poor first-position retrieval. A stable MRR after moving M cannot tell you whether supporting material has been lost. Inspect coverage at the cutoff the writer actually uses, and verify the claims in its answer separately.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

For each step select Copy Code, open the Python editor link, replace the starter text with the complete program, and click Run. Open each expected-output disclosure after running. Predict the result of the experiment, make only the named edit, and run again. Reload the original block before moving on. Each Python program starts from its own inline data.

Step 1 — Ingest documents

Check which policy records can enter the catalog. Python dictionaries store a name and value together. A list holds multiple records, and a set remembers IDs you have seen. The expression key not in doc detects a missing field before you try to read it. any is true as soon as one required key is missing. continue moves to the next record. The f in an f-string lets the braces insert values into the printed line.

Open Python Editor

docs = [
    {"id": "RF", "title": "Refund eligibility", "source": "kb/refunds",
     "version": 2, "text": "Refund requests require a valid receipt."},
    {"id": "SH", "title": "Shipping delays", "source": "kb/shipping",
     "version": 1, "text": "Contact us after 45 days for shipping delays."},
]
add_duplicate = False
if add_duplicate:
    docs.append(docs[0])

required = ["id", "title", "source", "version", "text"]
seen = set()
for doc in docs:
    if any(key not in doc for key in required):
        print("Rejected: missing metadata")
        continue
    doc_id = doc["id"]
    if doc_id in seen:
        print(f"Rejected: duplicate {doc_id}")
        continue
    seen.add(doc_id)
    print(f"Loaded {doc_id} v{doc['version']} from {doc['source']}")
Expected output
Loaded RF v2 from kb/refunds
Loaded SH v1 from kb/shipping

Experiment. Set add_duplicate from False to True. Predict whether the two original records will still load.

Expected output
Loaded RF v2 from kb/refunds
Loaded SH v1 from kb/shipping
Rejected: duplicate RF

The last row carries an ID already in seen, so the check rejects it while the two original rows remain. Give conflicting source records distinct IDs or resolve them before indexing. A unique ID alone cannot establish that the record is current.

Checkpoint. If another record has an unused ID but no source field, will it load? No. The missing-field check runs before the duplicate check.

Step 2 — Clean and tokenize text

Try matching a query to a policy sentence. split() without an argument cuts on whitespace and ' '.join(...) puts one space between the pieces. import re makes Python’s pattern tools available. re.findall collects the pieces that match a pattern, and the r before the pattern keeps the backslashes available to those tools. The pattern reads runs of letters or numbers, allowing inward dots, slashes, or hyphens between digit groups to keep a decimal or a numeric date together. & takes the common items in two sets. sorted gives a predictable reading order.

Open Python Editor

import re

def tokens(text):
    cleaned = " ".join(text.lower().split())
    return re.findall(r"[a-z]+|\d+(?:[./-]\d+)*", cleaned)

policy = "REFUND\twithin 30 days. Reference date: 2025-03-01."
query = "REFUND, 45 DAYS?"
print("Policy:", " ".join(tokens(policy)))
print("Query:", " ".join(tokens(query)))
print("Shared:", ", ".join(sorted(set(tokens(policy)) & set(tokens(query)))))
Expected output
Policy: refund within 30 days reference date 2025-03-01
Query: refund 45 days
Shared: days, refund

Experiment. Change query = "REFUND, 45 DAYS?" to query = "REFUND, 30 DAYS?". Predict which token joins the shared list.

Expected output
Policy: refund within 30 days reference date 2025-03-01
Query: refund 30 days
Shared: 30, days, refund

Changing the number adds one shared token. Uppercase and punctuation around the words no longer matter, while the day number still does. This matcher can help diagnose a search. It cannot tell you whether a customer meets the deadline.

Checkpoint. Would refund match refunded here? No. They are separate tokens under these rules.

Step 3 — Create chunks with source IDs

Start with the three refund-policy sentences you read in Example 1. In sentences[start:start + size] the first number is included and the end is excluded. range uses the third argument as the step. enumerate(..., 1) numbers the starts beginning at 1, while Python list positions begin at 0. In an f-string, :02d prints an integer with at least two digits.

Open Python Editor

sentences = [
    "Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.",
    "Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition.",
    "Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.",
]
size = 2
overlap = 0
doc_id = "RF"
version = 2
if size < 1 or not 0 <= overlap < size:
    raise ValueError("Choose a positive size and overlap smaller than size")
for number, start in enumerate(range(0, len(sentences), size - overlap), 1):
    window = sentences[start:start + size]
    print(f"{doc_id}-v{version}:c{number:02d} ({doc_id}, v{version}): {' '.join(window)}")
    if start + size >= len(sentences):
        break
Expected output
RF-v2:c01 (RF, v2): Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase. Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition.
RF-v2:c02 (RF, v2): Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.

Experiment. Set overlap from 0 to 1. Before running, point to the sentence that should appear twice.

Expected output
RF-v2:c01 (RF, v2): Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase. Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition.
RF-v2:c02 (RF, v2): Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition. Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.

With a step of two, the second chunk starts at sentence 3. With a step of one, it starts at sentence 2. The second chunk can now carry both the damaged-product label and its instructions. Track the build settings because the same chunk ID can represent a different span after rebuilding.

Checkpoint. Why does c02 change without changing the source ID? The source is the same revision. The settings change where its second window begins.

Step 4 — Build an inverted index

Make a lookup for the words in short searchable copies of the Northstar passages. .items() gives each chunk ID and its text. setdefault(term, set()) supplies an empty set when a term first appears. .add(chunk_id) puts one ID into that set.

Open Python Editor

chunks = {
    "RF": "refund receipt",
    "SH": "shipping delay",
}
add_warranty = False
if add_warranty:
    chunks["WA"] = "warranty claim"
index = {}
for chunk_id, text in chunks.items():
    for term in text.split():
        index.setdefault(term, set()).add(chunk_id)
for term in sorted(index):
    print(f"{term}: {', '.join(sorted(index[term]))}")
print("Warranty lookup:", sorted(index.get("warranty", set())))
Expected output
delay: SH
receipt: RF
refund: RF
shipping: SH
Warranty lookup: []

Experiment. Set add_warranty to True. Predict which lookup keys appear and which stay the same.

Expected output
claim: WA
delay: SH
receipt: RF
refund: RF
shipping: SH
warranty: WA
Warranty lookup: ['WA']

Adding WA creates two lookups and changes the warranty query from an empty set to a match. The text here is already clean. In a full search, normalize the query and passages identically and rebuild or update postings when the corpus changes.

Checkpoint. Why use a set for each lookup? Repeating receipt in one chunk should still point to that chunk once.

Step 5 — Rank eligible chunks with rare-term weights

Compare refund and warranty passages using the simplified TF–IDF-style rule above. sum(term in words for words in passages.values()) adds one per chunk containing a term. math.log computes the natural logarithm. The sorting function returns a tuple of two keys, putting larger scores first by negating them, then ordering equal scores by ID.

Open Python Editor

from math import log

texts = {
    "R": "Refund requests close within 30 days.",
    "W": "Warranty claims close after 60 days.",
}
add_shipping = False
if add_shipping:
    texts["S"] = "Ask shipping after 45 days."

def terms(text):
    return set(text.lower().replace(".", "").split())

passages = {key: terms(text) for key, text in texts.items()}
query = terms("refund after 45 days")
scores = {}
for key, words in passages.items():
    score = 0
    for term in sorted(query & words):
        df = sum(term in other for other in passages.values())
        score += 1 + log((len(passages) + 1) / (df + 1))
    if score:
        scores[key] = score

def sort_key(key):
    return (-scores[key], key)

for key in sorted(scores, key=sort_key):
    print(f"{key}: {scores[key]:.3f}")
Expected output
R: 2.405
W: 2.405

Experiment. Set add_shipping to True. Can a new chunk change scores for the existing ones?

Expected output
S: 3.981
R: 2.693
W: 2.288

The shipping passage matches after, 45 and days. The unique 45 gains extra weight. The collection counts also changed, so the original scores move. Inspect shared terms before assuming the most highly scored passage supports the policy.

Checkpoint. What breaks the baseline tie? R comes before W by ID. The tie rule promises reproducibility and says nothing about either passage’s policy evidence.

Step 6 — Score two ranked lists

Reproduce Example 3. enumerate(..., 1) gives each passage its rank. grades.get(chunk, 0) returns the grade or zero because the exercise explicitly judges every unlisted passage irrelevant. 2 ** grade raises 2 to the grade’s power. A list slice [:k] takes the first k items. statistics.mean averages one value per query. next(..., 0) takes the first matching reciprocal rank or uses zero. At the end, zip(*rows) groups the first value from each row, the second value from each row, and so on. map(mean, ...) averages each group. A zero grade would require an explicit judgment. In this fixed example, the grades dictionaries list only positive grades.

Open Python Editor

from math import log2
from statistics import mean

k = 3
ranking1 = ["S", "R", "M", "X"]
cases = [
    ("Q1", ranking1, {"R": 2, "M": 1}),
    ("Q2", ["W", "U", "X"], {"W": 2}),
]

def dcg(grades):
    return sum((2 ** grade - 1) / log2(rank + 1)
               for rank, grade in enumerate(grades, 1))

rows = []
for name, ranked, grades in cases:
    top_grades = [grades.get(chunk, 0) for chunk in ranked[:k]]
    hits = sum(grade > 0 for grade in top_grades)
    first_hit = int(bool(ranked) and ranked[0] in grades)
    hit = int(hits > 0)
    precision = hits / k
    recall = hits / len(grades)
    rr = next((1 / rank for rank, key in enumerate(ranked, 1) if key in grades), 0)
    ideal = dcg(sorted(grades.values(), reverse=True)[:k])
    ndcg = dcg(top_grades) / ideal
    rows.append((first_hit, hit, precision, recall, rr, ndcg))
    print(f"{name}: H@1={first_hit} H@3={hit} P@3={precision:.3f} R@3={recall:.3f} RR={rr:.3f} nDCG@3={ndcg:.3f}")

h1, h3, p, r, mrr, ndcg = map(mean, zip(*rows))
print(f"Mean: H@1={h1:.3f} H@3={h3:.3f} P@3={p:.3f} R@3={r:.3f} MRR={mrr:.3f} nDCG@3={ndcg:.3f}")
Expected output
Q1: H@1=0 H@3=1 P@3=0.667 R@3=1.000 RR=0.500 nDCG@3=0.659
Q2: H@1=1 H@3=1 P@3=0.333 R@3=1.000 RR=1.000 nDCG@3=1.000
Mean: H@1=0.500 H@3=1.000 P@3=0.500 R@3=1.000 MRR=0.750 nDCG@3=0.830

Experiment. Change ranking1 to ["S", "R", "X", "M"]. Predict which metric will keep the same value.

Expected output
Q1: H@1=0 H@3=1 P@3=0.333 R@3=0.500 RR=0.500 nDCG@3=0.521
Q2: H@1=1 H@3=1 P@3=0.333 R@3=1.000 RR=1.000 nDCG@3=1.000
Mean: H@1=0.500 H@3=1.000 P@3=0.333 R@3=0.750 MRR=0.750 nDCG@3=0.761

Read the two Q1 lists side by side. R is second in both, so Q1 still contributes 1/2 to MRR and the two-query mean stays at 0.750. M moves from third to fourth. The writer gets only the first three, so Q1 recall falls from 2/2 to 1/2. Q1 also loses M’s grade-1 gain at rank 3, which is why its nDCG falls from 0.659 to 0.521. Check both how quickly useful evidence appears and how much of it actually reaches the writer.

Checkpoint. Why does Q1 keep Hit@3 of 1? R still appears in the first three. A hit equals 1 as soon as any relevant chunk appears there.

Step 7 — Diagnose what was ranked too low

Use the full question from Example 2, now with stable chunk IDs. re.findall finds lowercase letters and numbers. weights.get(term, 1) returns the specified weight or one for an ordinary term. sorted orders score and ID pairs. sum(key in gold ...) counts matches by adding 1 for true and 0 for false.

Open Python Editor

import re

query_id = "Q1"
query = "Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?"
chunks = {
    "RF-v2:c01": "Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.",
    "SH-v1:c01": "After 45 days without a receipt, contact us for shipping delays.",
}
gold = {"RF-v2:c01"}
refund_weight = 1
weights = {"refund": refund_weight}

def terms(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+|\d+", text.lower()))

scored = [(key, sum(weights.get(term, 1) for term in terms(query) & terms(value)))
          for key, value in chunks.items()]
ranked = sorted(scored, key=lambda row: (-row[1], row[0]))
hits = sum(key in gold for key, score in ranked[:1] if score > 0)
print(f"{query_id}: {query}")
print("Gold:", ", ".join(sorted(gold)))
print("Ranked:", ", ".join(f"{key}={score}" for key, score in ranked))
print(f"Hit@1={int(hits > 0)} Recall@1={hits / len(gold):.2f}")
if hits:
    print("PASS: required evidence selected; check generation separately")
else:
    print("FAIL: gold ranked below top 1; investigate term weights")
Expected output
Q1: Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?
Gold: RF-v2:c01
Ranked: SH-v1:c01=6, RF-v2:c01=4
Hit@1=0 Recall@1=0.00
FAIL: gold ranked below top 1; investigate term weights

Experiment. Set refund_weight from 1 to 4. Predict which candidate gains three points.

Expected output
Q1: Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?
Gold: RF-v2:c01
Ranked: RF-v2:c01=7, SH-v1:c01=6
Hit@1=1 Recall@1=1.00
PASS: required evidence selected; check generation separately

Only the refund passage matches the weighted word, so it moves ahead. A lambda is a short unnamed function; here it gives the sorter the negative score followed by the ID. The evidence now reaches the writer in this case. Replay other queries before adopting the weight.

Checkpoint. Did the program verify a written answer? It only verified that the policy would be selected. Answer validation would inspect the actual reply against the policy.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Accept or reject an import

The catalog already has RF v2 at kb/refunds. An incoming record has id=RF, title="Refund eligibility", version=3 and the new text, but no source reference. The published-version list still says 2. List the import problems and say what you would check before updating search.

Practice 2. Predict the boundaries

Use refund sentences 1, 2 and 3 from Example 1. Start with a size of 2 and an overlap of 0. Write the two spans and identify whether any chunk contains both pieces of the damaged-product rule. Repeat with overlap 1. Name the stable evidence IDs you would keep when comparing the outputs.

Practice 3. Rank three candidates

Use Example 2’s matched terms. Give refund weight 3 and every other matching term weight 1. Calculate all scores. For equal scores use the source IDs RF, SH and WA in alphabetical order. Predict the top-1 result and say why its position alone cannot establish the policy.

Practice 4. Explain a misleading improvement

Use the two lists in Example 3. A teammate replaces Q1’s list with [R, S, X, M] and claims the search delivers more evidence because MRR improves. Calculate MRR and mean Recall@3. For Q1, a new independent review finds that M answers a required proof-of-purchase subquestion directly. Add grade 2 for M, keeping R at grade 2. Using the original Q1 ranking, calculate the revised nDCG@3 and explain how to report the new judgment. A fifth candidate Y is added but has no review. Say whether it should be written down as grade 0.

Independent Assignment

Audit the fictional Northstar collection in the guided lab. Use the ten supplied records, published-version list, five queries, and adjudicated gold spans. For each run, submit the layout and cutoff, eligible chunk IDs, ranking and score for each test query, selected evidence IDs, Hit/Precision/Recall at the cutoff, full-list MRR, decision, and cause. Explain why Q5 does not have a normal numeric score. Show that both the staff-only and archived sources are missing from the customer-visible results and that the duplicate import does not occupy a result slot.

Start with the baseline. Normalize the text and query consistently and check the postings for refund and warranty by hand. Reuse the complete standalone lab program as your answer key. Run the following variants independently, restoring the original code between runs. Write a three-sentence report that explains what each change improves, its cost or unresolved failure, and your next controlled test. Try the assignment before opening the worked solutions.

  1. Variant A increases the number of selected slots. Change only k = 1 to k = 3. Predict what the writer gains on Q1 and what extra text it sees on Q4.
  2. Variant B reconstructs the refund chunks. Change only layout = (1, 0) to layout = (2, 1). Predict the exact two refund spans in the new build and whether Q2 can pass while its chunk recall stays below 1.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The source is missing, so nobody can trace or verify the proposed revision. The incoming document also repeats the ID already present in the ingestion batch. Verify the source and approval with the owner, then give the versioned record a unique import ID or follow the catalog’s controlled replacement procedure. The version registry still approves 2. Keep v2 searchable until the publication record authorizes a verified v3 and the new index is ready.

Solution 2

Without overlap, the passages contain 1–2 and 3. Neither carries both pieces of the damaged-product rule. With one sentence of overlap, the passages contain 1–2 and 2–3. The second can now provide the complete rule. Keep RF-v2:s02 and RF-v2:s03 as gold and map them to the appropriate chunk IDs in each build.

Solution 3

RF has four shared terms and one of those terms, refund, now receives two extra points. Its total becomes 6. SH also has 6, and WA has 1. The resulting order is RF, SH, WA because RF comes before SH by ID. RF wins the tie. To establish what the customer should do, read and verify the policy text that RF carries.

Solution 4

Q1’s first relevant result rises from rank 2 to 1, while Q2’s stays first. MRR becomes (1 + 1)/2 = 1. Q1 loses M from the first three, so Q1 recall is 1/2 and Q2 recall remains 1. Mean Recall@3 falls to 0.75. The first piece got easier to find while another needed piece went missing.

On the original Q1 ranking, grades [0, 2, 2] give DCG 3/log₂(3) + 3/log₂(4) ≈ 3.393. The ideal grades [2, 2, 0] give 3 + 3/log₂(3) ≈ 4.893. The new nDCG is approximately 0.693. Save the revised judgment with a new label version and use the same version when comparing rankings. Y is unknown until reviewed. Record it as unjudged, even if a provisional metric calculation gives it zero credit.

Lab and assignment answer key

Start with the matched terms in Example 2. The baseline lookup for refund points to RF-v2:c01 and RF-v2:c02. The lookup for warranty points to WA-v1:c01. On Q1 the baseline selects SH, and weighting refund as four points puts RF first with 7. Q2 still lacks sentence 3 in the selected context, Q3 and Q4 pass, and Q5 needs an answerability check. The lab’s two output disclosures provide the complete reproductions. A search report may recommend advancing the weighting change to a wider evaluation. A launch decision would need that wider search test and a separate check of generated answers.

For Variant A the only header change is k=3. Q1 selects SH-v1:c01, RF-v2:c01, RF-v2:c02 and reports Hit=1 P=0.333 R=1.000 RR=0.500 with REVIEW because its first relevant chunk is second. Q2 selects RF-v2:c02, DM-v1:c01, RF-v2:c01 and reports Hit=1 P=0.333 R=0.500 RR=1.000 with REVIEW because it still misses sentence 3. Q3 and Q4 remain PASS, each with Hit=1 P=0.333 R=1.000 RR=1.000. Q4 sends two passages, the warranty result and the refund damage instruction. Q5 stays unscored. The last line is Scored 4/5 | Mean Hit=1.000 P=0.333 R=0.875 MRR=0.875.

For Variant B the header shows size/overlap=(2, 1) and the index has eight chunks. The refund spans are RF-v2:c01 ← RF-v2:s01, RF-v2:s02 and RF-v2:c02 ← RF-v2:s02, RF-v2:s03. Q1 is still FAIL. Q2 selects RF-v2:c02 at score 4 and reports Hit=1 P=1.000 R=0.500 RR=1.000 with PASS. Both required sentences are present, even though only one of the two chunks with any relevant material is selected. Q3 and Q4 remain PASS with all four metrics equal to 1. Q5 stays unscored. The last line is Scored 4/5 | Mean Hit=0.750 P=0.750 R=0.625 MRR=0.875. The two variants change different parts of the system. They support different fixes.

Knowledge Check

  1. An assistant has never seen the latest refund policy. At which step can current approved wording enter its request, and which stage turns it into a customer-facing reply?
  2. An import names two different pages RF. One is a verified update and the other is a duplicate upload. What evidence should you inspect before deduplicating?
  3. A two-sentence policy says refunds require a receipt and next gives an exception. Which boundaries would you test, and what could go wrong after increasing overlap?
  4. What does an inverted index return for a term absent from all eligible chunks? What would you check if the reviewer knows there is good evidence for that query?
  5. A refund query ranks a shipping passage first. What logged detail lets you test whether a shared deadline caused the behavior?
  6. At k=3, one relevant chunk is found and two slots are empty. There are two relevant chunks in the eligible index. Under this lesson’s convention, what are Hit@3, Precision@3 and Recall@3?
  7. Q1’s first relevant passage stays at rank 2, but another relevant passage moves from rank 3 to 4. Why might MRR stay unchanged when Recall@3 changes?
  8. A reply says 45 days. Its saved context has the approved refund rule with the 30-day limit and receipt requirement. What do you investigate first? How would the diagnosis differ if the context contained only a shipping passage?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. Retrieval can find the current approved page and selection can place it in the prompt. Generation is the separate step where the assistant writes.
  2. Compare source, publication approval, revision, permissions, and original content. Fix the conflicting import IDs and retain the approved version and its trace. Matching titles or text alone cannot resolve approval.
  3. Try keeping both sentences in one policy section or overlapping adjacent windows. Verify that rule and exception both reach the writer. Measure repeated text and lost result slots after increasing overlap.
  4. The lookup gives an empty set. Check whether the source is authorized and present in the index, then compare the search terms with the source wording to find a mismatch.
  5. Compare the shared terms and their per-term weights for the shipping and refund chunks. Replay one ranking change with cases, permissions, and cutoff fixed, then check other shipping and refund queries for regressions.
  6. Hit@3 is 1. Precision@3 is 1/3 because the denominator is three slots. Recall@3 is 1/2 because half the relevant chunks were found.
  7. Reciprocal rank uses the first relevant position, so this query still contributes 1/2 to MRR. The second needed chunk moves beyond the cutoff, so recall decreases.
  8. Start with generation given the saved policy evidence. If only the shipping passage was supplied, start with retrieval or context selection and verify that the approved evidence reaches the writer on replay.

Guided Engineering Lab

Can Our RAG System Find the Correct Refund Policy?

Northstar wants the public assistant to receive enough evidence to answer “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?” Your task is to audit the search from source records to the selected passages. You will show why a shipping passage wins the baseline and test one ranking change. You will also identify a damaged-product question that still needs a separate change.

All data is inline and fictional. RF v2 holds the approved refund deadline and damaged-product procedure. SH mentions 45 days about shipping. RFO is archived, RX represents a staff-only record with placeholder content, and ZZ repeats the policy in a duplicate import. Warranty, missing receipt, damaged products, account access and escalation records round out the public collection. The program reports only eligible chunks. The fixture contains a placeholder because a real restricted policy must never be copied into a learner-facing script or public trace.

The five gold judgments appear directly alongside their queries. Verify Q1 against sentence 1 of RF v2. Q2 needs both the damaged-product label in sentence 2 and the seven-day deadline and photos in sentence 3. Q3 and Q4 each have one gold sentence giving the action to take. Q5 is a negative control, a query intentionally chosen with no relevant evidence in this corpus. Its metrics are N/A. Confirmed-absent and unlabeled evidence are different cases. These fixtures stipulate all relevant spans for Q1–Q4, so chunks containing none of their gold spans receive no credit.

Hand-work the first question before running the code. SH matches six distinct words. RF-v2:c01 matches four, including refund. With one selected slot the baseline shows only SH. The gold chunk appears in the full list at rank 2, so reciprocal rank is 1/2 even though Hit, Precision and Recall at 1 are zero. Predict which number will be 7 after changing the weight.

The program validates import records first. Then build walks documents in ID order, screens for approved version and role, creates passage windows and records their source spans. isinstance checks a value’s kind. raise ValueError stops the run with a readable message on bad input. The regular-expression lookbehind (?<=[.!?]) allows sentence splits only after punctuation followed by whitespace. This splitter is designed for the simple fixtures here. Check abbreviations and structured source formats before reusing it. The tuple fingerprint groups exact cleaned copies within the same source, version and role. *layout passes the two layout numbers as separate arguments. In assess, evidence.update(...) accumulates the stable gold spans from every chosen chunk. The report uses the same index for ranking and judging chunk relevance.

The toy rubric checks retrieval only. PASS means the selection includes every required span and its first relevant chunk ranks first. FAIL means required evidence is entirely absent from the selection or a critical restriction is violated. Unauthorized and unapproved records are excluded before indexing, so the intentional failure is about relevance. REVIEW means only part of the evidence appeared, complete evidence starts below rank 1, or no gold supports ordinary scoring. Report binary chunk recall and read the stable spans separately. All output metrics named Hit, P and R use the current k; RR and MRR use the uncut rankings.

Select Copy Code, open the editor, paste the full program into the editing pane, and click Run. Compare the report with the baseline below.

Open Python Editor

import re
from statistics import mean

refund_weight = 1
layout = (1, 0)  # (size in sentences, overlap)
k = 1

def document(key, title, source, version, text, status="published", role="public"):
    return dict(id=key, title=title, source=source, version=version,
                text=text, status=status, role=role)

refund = "Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase."
refund_page = (refund + " Damaged product refund claims have a separate condition."
               + " Report the damage claim within seven days of delivery and attach photos.")
docs = [
    document("RF", "Refund eligibility", "kb/refunds", 2, refund_page),
    document("RFO", "Old refund eligibility", "kb/refunds", 1,
             "Refund requests were accepted within 45 days.", status="archived"),
    document("RX", "Internal exception", "kb/internal", 1,
             "Placeholder for a staff-only refund exception.", role="staff"),
    document("ZZ", "Duplicate import", "kb/refunds", 2, refund_page),
    document("SH", "Shipping delays", "kb/shipping", 1,
             "After 45 days without a receipt, contact us for shipping delays."),
    document("WA", "Warranty claims", "kb/warranty", 1,
             "Start a warranty claim from your order."),
    document("MR", "Missing receipts", "kb/receipts", 1,
             "Missing receipt: download your receipt in Orders."),
    document("DM", "Damaged products", "kb/damage", 1,
             "Keep the product packaging until Support replies."),
    document("AC", "Account access", "kb/account", 1,
             "Reset your password from the sign-in page."),
    document("ES", "Escalations", "kb/escalate", 1,
             "Send unresolved shipping issues to Support."),
]
published = {
    "kb/refunds": 2, "kb/internal": 1, "kb/shipping": 1,
    "kb/warranty": 1, "kb/receipts": 1, "kb/damage": 1,
    "kb/account": 1, "kb/escalate": 1,
}
queries = [
    ("Q1", "Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?", {"RF-v2:s01"}),
    ("Q2", "damaged product refund claim", {"RF-v2:s02", "RF-v2:s03"}),
    ("Q3", "missing receipt", {"MR-v1:s01"}),
    ("Q4", "warranty claim", {"WA-v1:s01"}),
    ("Q5", "retired loyalty discount", set()),
]

def validate(documents):
    seen = set()
    for row in documents:
        for field in ("id", "title", "source", "text", "status", "role"):
            if not isinstance(row.get(field), str) or not row[field].strip():
                raise ValueError(f"Missing or blank {field}")
        if type(row.get("version")) is not int or row["version"] < 1:
            raise ValueError("Version must be a positive integer")
        if row["status"] not in {"published", "archived"} or row["role"] not in {"public", "staff"}:
            raise ValueError("Unknown status or role")
        if row["id"] in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"Duplicate ID {row['id']}")
        seen.add(row["id"])

def terms(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+|\d+(?:[./-]\d+)*", text.lower()))

def build(documents, versions, roles, size, overlap):
    validate(documents)
    if type(size) is not int or type(overlap) is not int or size < 1 or not 0 <= overlap < size:
        raise ValueError("Use a positive size and overlap from zero to size minus one")
    chunks, index, fingerprints = {}, {}, set()
    for row in sorted(documents, key=lambda doc: doc["id"]):
        if row["role"] not in roles or row["status"] != "published":
            continue
        if row["version"] != versions.get(row["source"]):
            continue
        prefix = f"{row['id']}-v{row['version']}"
        sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", " ".join(row["text"].split()))
        for number, start in enumerate(range(0, len(sentences), size - overlap), 1):
            end = min(start + size, len(sentences))
            body = " ".join(sentences[start:end])
            fingerprint = (row["source"], row["version"], row["role"], body.casefold())
            if fingerprint not in fingerprints:
                fingerprints.add(fingerprint)
                key = f"{prefix}:c{number:02d}"
                chunks[key] = {
                    "doc": row["id"], "title": row["title"], "source": row["source"],
                    "version": row["version"], "role": row["role"], "text": body,
                    "spans": {f"{prefix}:s{i + 1:02d}" for i in range(start, end)},
                }
                for term in terms(body):
                    index.setdefault(term, set()).add(key)
            if end == len(sentences):
                break
    return chunks, index

def rank(query, index, weight):
    scores = {}
    for term in terms(query):
        for key in index.get(term, set()):
            scores[key] = scores.get(key, 0) + (weight if term == "refund" else 1)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda row: (-row[1], row[0]))

def assess(ranked, chunks, gold, cutoff):
    if type(cutoff) is not int or cutoff < 1:
        raise ValueError("Use a positive cutoff")
    top = ranked[:cutoff]
    relevant = {key for key, chunk in chunks.items() if chunk["spans"] & gold}
    if not gold:
        return None, "REVIEW: no positive gold; check answerability separately"
    if not relevant:
        return None, "FAIL: known evidence absent from the eligible chunks"
    chosen = {key for key, _ in top}
    hits = len(chosen & relevant)
    evidence = set()
    for key in chosen:
        evidence.update(chunks[key]["spans"] & gold)
    rr = next((1 / i for i, (key, _) in enumerate(ranked, 1) if key in relevant), 0)
    metrics = (int(hits > 0), hits / cutoff, hits / len(relevant), rr)
    if not evidence:
        decision = "FAIL: required evidence absent from selection"
    elif evidence != gold:
        decision = "REVIEW: only part of the required evidence selected"
    elif rr != 1:
        decision = "REVIEW: full evidence selected but first relevant chunk ranks below 1"
    else:
        decision = "PASS: full evidence selected and relevant chunk ranks first"
    return metrics, decision

public_roles = {"public"}
chunks, index = build(docs, published, public_roles, *layout)
print(f"Northstar kb-v2 | gold-v1 | public | size/overlap={layout} | k={k} | refund weight={refund_weight}")
print(f"Indexed {len(chunks)} chunks")
for key, chunk in chunks.items():
    print(f"  {key} <- {chunk['source']} v{chunk['version']} | {', '.join(sorted(chunk['spans']))}")
rows = []
for query_id, query, gold in queries:
    ranked = rank(query, index, refund_weight)
    metrics, decision = assess(ranked, chunks, gold, k)
    evidence = ", ".join(sorted(gold)) or "none"
    ranking = ", ".join(f"{key}={score}" for key, score in ranked) or "none"
    selected = ", ".join(key for key, _ in ranked[:k]) or "none"
    print(f"{query_id}: {query}")
    print(f"  Gold: {evidence} | Ranked: {ranking} | Selected: {selected}")
    if metrics is None:
        print(f"  Metrics N/A | {decision}")
    else:
        hit, p, r, rr = metrics
        rows.append(metrics)
        print(f"  Hit={hit} P={p:.3f} R={r:.3f} RR={rr:.3f} | {decision}")
if rows:
    hit, p, r, mrr = map(mean, zip(*rows))
    print(f"Scored {len(rows)}/{len(queries)} | Mean Hit={hit:.3f} P={p:.3f} R={r:.3f} MRR={mrr:.3f}")
else:
    print(f"Scored 0/{len(queries)} | Metrics N/A")

If a validation error appears, check the copied records and required fields. If the first order looks different, check the layout, k and weight shown on the first line. Confirm that neither RFO nor RX is in the indexed list. Check the duplicate against RF’s source, role and version. If you get an indentation error, copy the full block before reapplying the one-line change.

A sample report reads, “On kb-v2 with gold-v1, the public top-1 replay moved Q1 from FAIL to PASS. The current refund chunk went from score 4 and rank 2 to score 7 and rank 1. Published versions, access, chunking, and queries stayed fixed. Q2 still retrieves the sentence that announces a separate condition and misses the one that specifies seven days and photos. Test overlap against the same gold sentences, then add more shipping and refund questions before deciding whether to keep the weight.” Mark the lab complete when you can reproduce both outputs, explain the Q1 rank change and Q2’s remaining evidence gap, and show that filtered records are absent. Improvements on a few fictional cases are evidence about this replay. You still need a separate test of generated answers and performance on broader queries.

An instructor replacing the fixtures can keep the same record structure. Capture query ID, text, verified caller role, document and chunk IDs, policy versions, selected context, and the eventual model reply in separate fields. Ask reviewers to mark required spans against those specific source versions. Replay saved retrieval traces offline or substitute an approved corpus and index. Compare the retrieval selections before using captured replies for an answer-quality review.

Common Mistakes

  • Scoring results before verifying who can access their text. Filter by approved version and access before building the rankable list.
  • Checking the ranked list without checking the exact context sent for the answer. A retrieved passage can be cut by top-k or by a later context limit.
  • Comparing chunk recall across builds without remapping the gold spans. The number of relevant chunks can change even when the underlying policy does not.
  • Treating unjudged passages as confirmed irrelevant or counting an empty gold set as zero recall. Show what was judged and how many queries were scored.
  • Increasing k or overlap without measuring cost. Read which passages were added and count repeated text and input space used.

Lesson Summary and Next Step

Ingestion keeps policy text and its origin available for review. Chunking decides which parts can travel together. The index finds lexical candidates and ranking decides which ones fit into the supplied context. Gold spans show whether that context covers the actual policy, and rank metrics tell you which parts appeared early. Use the raw evidence to explain the defect before changing the system.

Next is Context sufficiency, answer correctness and citations. There you’ll examine what happens after selected context reaches the assistant.
