What You Will Learn

  • Decide whether the passages actually supplied contain enough authorized evidence for a specific question.
  • Check the answer against the governing policy and trace each factual claim to its evidence.
  • Diagnose missing, fabricated, stale, and misleading citations, and judge when an assistant should abstain.
  • Report the failing stage, calculate rates with visible denominators, and preserve the original result when testing a repair.

Why This Lesson Matters

A customer asks Northstar Support, “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?” Read the one passage placed in the assistant’s prompt. “Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.” Before reading the saved reply, decide what you would tell the customer.

The assistant replies, “Yes, refunds are available within 90 days.” You can point to two problems with that decision. Day 45 is outside the 30-day window, and the customer has no receipt. The saved prompt shows that the necessary evidence reached the assistant. Start by investigating how it used that evidence.

All Northstar records, policy details, annotations, and replay results are fictional. Allow about 6.5 hours. Complete Ingestion, chunking and ranked retrieval first. Rubrics and a first human evaluation and Pointwise LLM-as-a-Judge are recommended. Complete the judging lesson before replacing manual claim review with a model judge. The programs in this lesson use reviewer-supplied labels and run offline.

Beginner Explanation

Look at the passage before the answer

The shipping page from the previous chapter mentions 45 days. That overlap can move it up the search ranking. Imagine the retriever instead returned the refund help desk passage, “Refund requests are handled by the customer-support department.” It is about refunds, so it is relevant. Could you tell this customer whether their request qualifies? The passage gives neither the deadline nor the proof requirement.

Ask what a complete answer needs. The review sheet lists the deadline measured from purchase and the requirement for a valid receipt. Read the exact context, the authorized passages delivered to the assistant for this request. Mark which facts those passages establish, then assign a context sufficiency label.

  • Sufficient. The context establishes both requirements. Day 45 is outside the 30-day window and the customer lacks the required receipt.
  • Partial. The context gives the deadline alone. It can explain why day 45 misses the deadline. This exercise also requires the response to address the receipt, so the context cannot support the complete answer.
  • Insufficient. The context only tells you which department handles refunds. Neither required fact is available.
  • Contradictory. Two eligible current passages disagree about a required fact and the writer has no approved rule for resolving their disagreement. Record the disagreement even if one passage alone would appear complete.

Predict how the deadline-only passage would score if the question asked just “What is the deadline?” It would be sufficient. Judge against the requested task, using the actual passages shown to the assistant. A gold passage, the correct source named on the review sheet, may appear high in the search results and still be cut from the delivered context.

Read the answer against two different sources of evidence

Consider a correct reply in your inbox. It says a refund request is due within 30 days of purchase and requires a valid receipt. Open the signed policy and you can verify both facts. Now open the saved prompt. Its only passage is about shipping delays. Nothing in the prompt can justify either refund claim.

The first check is correctness against the authoritative policy in effect for this customer and date. The second is groundedness, sometimes called faithfulness, against the supplied context. For an applied answer such as “Your request is outside the window,” check the inference too. Day 45 is later than the stated deadline of day 30. Finding 30 in the passage gives you a fact to use, and you still have to apply it to the customer’s question.

Compare six small replays. In the first four the correct refund passage and the unrelated shipping passage are both available. DOC-REFUND-01 and DOC-SHIPPING-02 are display IDs for those source documents. The full lab uses versioned passage IDs.

  • A. “Yes, refunds are available within 90 days.” The policy contradicts the answer. No citation was supplied.
  • B. “No. The policy requires a valid receipt and a request within 30 days.” The decision and both requirements are correct and supported. Required citations are missing.
  • C. “No. The refund period is 30 days, and a receipt is required. [DOC-REFUND-01]” The refund passage supports the claims and the decision follows from the customer’s stated facts.
  • D. “No. The refund period is 30 days, and a receipt is required. [DOC-SHIPPING-02]” The refund passage still supports the claims, but the cited shipping passage does not.
  • C with shipping context alone. The same reply stays correct against approved policy. The retrieved context lacks support, and the cited refund passage was never supplied.
  • Warranty reply backed by a stale guide. “Email Support to start a warranty claim.” The old policy supports this wording. The current order-page rule makes the answer wrong and the citation stale.

In B through D, the term “refund period” is understood from the purchase date in the question and supplied rule. In a standalone answer, prefer “within 30 days of purchase.” Answer C gives the reader a way to verify both facts. D can fail the citation check even when its wording is identical and authorized support exists elsewhere.

Use correct when the answer establishes every required fact and makes no wrong or unverifiable factual additions. A partially correct answer gets some required facts right while omitting or mishandling others. An incorrect answer gives a wrong policy value and establishes none of the required facts. An unverifiable claim concerns something the available governing record cannot establish. If the reply makes only claims you cannot verify, label it unverifiable. If it gives verified but irrelevant facts and omits everything asked for, label it incomplete. Separately record any critical violation, including 90 days in place of 30. The lab marks that error as blocking regardless of anything else the response gets right.

Check a multi-claim reply one statement at a time

Read “Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase, require a valid receipt, and are processed within two hours.” Underline the deadline, the receipt requirement, and the processing time. Each can be checked on its own. This is an atomic claim, a statement small enough for one evidence judgment. Keep conditions, units, and starting points in the claim. “30 days” without “of purchase” could match the wrong rule.

For each claim, copy the relevant wording and note its passage ID and version. A claim can be supported, unsupported, or unknown if part of the investigation record is missing. Where available, record whether an unsupported claim contradicts the text or adds something absent from it. For the reply above, the approved evidence supports two claims out of three. The two-hour promise may be an invented detail, often called a hallucination. The evidence establishes that the reply lacked support for it. You would need a governing processing-time source to decide whether the promise is false.

Follow each citation to the exact claim

Read a citation as a pointer. First ask whether the answer gave a reference. Then ask whether the ID resolves to a known source, whether the source is authorized and was supplied, and whether its version is approved for this question. Now read the cited wording. If it establishes the claim, the link provides entailment, meaning you can justify the claim from that wording and any explicit case facts. A shipping passage may be a real, accessible source and still fail this check for a refund deadline.

A document-level link names a whole policy, a passage-level link names an exact span such as RF-v2:s01, and a claim-level link attaches the evidence to the specific statement it supports. The last two can be used together. A document link can suffice in a short unambiguous policy. In a long policy with changing rules, a span and version make the result reproducible.

Suppose RF-v2:s01 gives only the deadline and RF-v2:s02 gives only the receipt requirement in a teaching variant. Cite the first for the deadline and the second for the receipt. If one claim needs both, link both and record how the two passages together support it. Two citations attached to a paragraph do not establish which statement either supports. Citation completeness, or coverage in this lab, is the share of claims with valid supporting citations. Citation precision, reported as citation validity rate here, is the share of supplied claim–reference links that pass all the link checks. Repeated copies of a link get one vote and a duplicate diagnostic.

Resolve source authority and decide when to stop

A current warranty policy says to start from the order page. An archived copy says to email Support. Northstar’s signed policy register identifies the governing clause for the policy snapshot and who may read it. A newly uploaded FAQ can be older in substance or lower in authority than the approved policy. Inspect the effective period and precedence rule for the specific question. If there is a clear winner for the reviewer but the assistant received two competing active passages with no resolution instructions, record the delivery conflict and make the precedence rule visible to the assistant. If the evidence cannot be resolved for either party, route to review.

A staff-only note can contain helpful wording. It remains outside the public evidence set. A trace that supplied or cited it to a public caller flags a critical authorization failure. Record the alert without reproducing the restricted passage in a customer-facing report.

If the question asks whether a particular parcel arrived and the supplied context has only a general shipping policy, “I can’t verify this parcel’s status from the information I have” is abstention, an explicit choice to withhold an unsupported answer. It is appropriate here. Giving the same response when the user asked for a deadline and the approved deadline was supplied would be unnecessary. An empty reply is a missing answer to investigate. It gives no evidence of deliberate abstention. Track how many answers and abstentions you could score so that a high score on a small answered subset cannot hide routine refusal.

Turn the observations into a diagnosis
  • Required evidence exists but was missing from the prompt. Check the retrieval ranking and the later context selection. If the case genuinely has no authorized evidence in the corpus, test abstention rather than treating the gap as a search defect.
  • Sufficient evidence was present and the answer misapplied it. Inspect how the writer used the rule. Preserve the exact question, delivered context, and reply.
  • The answer is correct and the reference points to the wrong passage. Check how citations are attached to claims.
  • Eligible passages disagree. Investigate context resolution. Record stale passages independently and compare them with the approved version.
  • Restricted text was supplied or cited. Record an authorization failure even if the public policy happens to agree with the reply. Check access controls before tuning relevance.

A single result can have several causes or symptoms. Annotate the evidence for each, and avoid inferring the system’s hidden reasoning from a final answer. In a controlled replay, keep the question, authoritative policy snapshot, rubric, and all unrelated inputs fixed. A repair of a saved annotation or citation proves the checker responds to that edit. You need new captured responses to measure a change to the generator.

Count with the right denominators

Suppose you reviewed four cases and three had sufficient context. Two cases had annotated factual answers and one was fully correct. The other two explicitly abstained and one refusal was appropriate. Suppose those answers made four claims, three supported by the context, and only one answer had every claim supported. They supplied three distinct claim–reference links. Two were valid and each supported a different claim.

  • Context sufficiency is 3/4 known context judgments.
  • Answer correctness is 1/2 annotated factual answers. Grounded-answer rate is 1/2 annotated answers with scorable context.
  • Claim support is 3/4 scorable claims, with one unsupported claim.
  • Citation validity is 2/3 supplied links. Citation coverage is 2/4 claims with at least one valid link.
  • Appropriate abstention is 1/2 judged explicit abstentions. Report the actual number of abstentions as well.
  • If a case promised 90 days, report one critical refund-policy failure. Count affected cases, even if multiple wrong refund claims appear in one reply.

Notice how an unanswered case and an unsupported claim enter different denominators. In the lab, missing reply text and missing annotations are reported for review and excluded from answer metrics. A missing context record is unknown for sufficiency and support. When zero items qualify for a measure, print N/A and the zero denominator. Do not treat missing evidence as a passing score. The fictional decision policy gives PASS for a complete, correct, supported, cited answer with adequate context, or for a justified abstention on a reviewed unanswerable case. FAIL blocks confirmed critical refund or authorization failures and unsupported factual claims. REVIEW is for unresolved contradictions, incomplete records, noncritical defects, and cases that need another look. One blocking case makes the lab suite FAIL.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Is the context sufficient?

User question. “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?”

Approved reference. “Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.” The evaluation requires the deadline and receipt rule.

Consider three alternative contexts before reading the verdicts.

  1. RF-v2:s01 contains the complete policy. Point to “within 30 days of purchase” and “valid receipt.” Both are available, so label sufficient.
  2. A teaching variant RF-TIME-v1:s01 contains only “Refund requests must be filed within 30 days of purchase.” The learner can evaluate the time limit but lacks evidence for the proof requirement. Label partial.
  3. REF-HELP-v1:s01 reads “Refund requests are handled by the customer-support department.” It confirms the topic but neither fact. Label insufficient.

Actual LLM response. In the third fictional replay, the assistant says, “I can’t verify the conditions from this information.”

Assessment. With that context the assistant should abstain. It makes no factual policy claim, so there are no answer claims or citations to score. The approved policy is known to exist and did not reach the writer.

Failure classification. Missing required context, with appropriate abstention. Inspect the top-k results and prompt assembly before editing the answer prompt.

Example 2. Is the answer supported?

User question. “How long do I have to request a refund, what proof is required, and how fast will it be processed?”

Approved reference. RF-v2:s01 establishes the purchase-based deadline and valid receipt rule. The approved record supplied for review gives no processing-time promise.

Actual LLM response. “Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase, require a valid receipt, and are processed within two hours.” The fictional capture shows RF-v2:s01 as its only context.

  1. “Within 30 days of purchase” → RF-v2:s01, “within 30 days of purchase.” Supported and correct.
  2. “Require a valid receipt” → RF-v2:s01, “require a valid receipt.” Supported and correct.
  3. “Processed within two hours” → no supporting span. Unsupported and unverifiable against the approved record.

Assessment. Put a check beside the deadline and another beside the receipt requirement. Leave the processing-time row unconfirmed. That gives 2 supported claims / 3 factual claims. The context is partial for the three-part question. If Northstar has no approved processing-time source, the response can explain the two documented requirements and say it cannot confirm processing time. The saved two-hour promise fails the unsupported-claim gate. Compare a second fictional reply from the warranty case: “Email Support to start a warranty claim.” The supplied WA-v1:s01 says exactly that, so the claim is supported, but the signed register now points to WA-v2:s01, which directs customers to their order page. That reply is wrong against current policy.

Failure classification. In the refund example, inspect the unsupported addition and request a governing processing-time source or abstention on that part. In the warranty example, investigate stale context and citation as well as the wrong policy result. A high groundedness score would hide the issue.

Example 3. Do the citations support the claims?

User question. “What is the refund deadline and what proof must I keep?”

Approved reference. RF-v2:s01 gives 30 days from purchase with a valid receipt. The delivered SH-v1:s01 gives a 45-day shipping-contact threshold.

Actual LLM response. Three fictional captures used the same context: “You have 30 days from purchase with a valid receipt [RF-v2:s01].” “You have 30 days from purchase with a valid receipt [SH-v1:s01].” “You have 90 days from purchase [RF-v2:s01].”

  1. Capture one’s reference resolves to the current supplied policy. Mark both deadline and receipt claims supported and link each to that passage. There are two valid claim–reference links.
  2. Capture two’s reference also resolves. Read the text. Shipping supports neither refund claim. The reply remains correct and grounded by the refund passage, but valid citation coverage is 0/2.
  3. Capture three’s reference exists and is current, but it says 30, not 90. The answer is wrong and unsupported. The citation is invalid for that claim, and the critical refund-policy gate fails.

Assessment. Changing just the second capture’s citation to RF-v2:s01 changes citation validity and coverage without changing the answer claims. A fabricated ID would fail earlier, at resolution.

Failure classification. Capture two has a citation attachment problem. Capture three has a policy and answer-use failure as well as a citation error. Repair each failure separately and rerun the checks.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

For each activity select Copy Code, open the editor link, replace the editor’s starter text with the full program, and click Run. Open the expected output after you run it. Predict the experiment result, make just the named edit, then click Run again. Reload the original code between activities. Each program is standalone. All claims and evidence links are annotations supplied by a fictional reviewer, so no program needs to interpret live model text.

Step 1 — Check whether the context is sufficient

Place the two requirements for the refund question in a set. A Python set holds each item once. A dictionary holds named values, which you read with square brackets. The expression required - found keeps the items still missing, & finds items in both sets, and sorted gives predictable output. if and elif evaluate the cases in order.

Open Python Editor

question = {
    "id": "Q1",
    "required": {"deadline", "receipt"},
}
retrieved = {"deadline", "receipt"}
required = question["required"]
missing = required - retrieved

if not missing:
    label = "SUFFICIENT"
elif required & retrieved:
    label = "PARTIAL"
else:
    label = "INSUFFICIENT"

print(question["id"], label)
print("Missing:", ", ".join(sorted(missing)) or "none")
Expected output
Q1 SUFFICIENT
Missing: none

Experiment. Remove "receipt" from retrieved. Predict which requirement remains unmet.

Expected output
Q1 PARTIAL
Missing: receipt

The deadline remains available, so the context is partial. These field names are human annotations of text. Retrieve the missing requirement or decline to give a complete eligibility answer.

Checkpoint. Would the deadline-only context work for a deadline-only question? Yes, because the required set would contain only the deadline.

Step 2 — Check the answer against policy

Check the deadline and receipt statements independently against the approved values. .items() gives each field and its value, .get() returns the value stored for a key, and == compares values. A dictionary comprehension makes one verdict for each required fact. sum adds 1 for a true check and 0 for a false one.

Open Python Editor

policy = {"deadline": 30, "receipt": "required"}
claims = {"deadline": 30, "receipt": "required"}
matches = {key: claims.get(key) == value for key, value in policy.items()}
for key, matches_policy in matches.items():
    print(key, "matches" if matches_policy else "wrong or missing")
count = sum(matches.values())
if count == len(policy) and all(key in policy for key in claims):
    verdict = "CORRECT"
elif count:
    verdict = "PARTIALLY CORRECT"
else:
    verdict = "INCORRECT"
print(verdict)
Expected output
deadline matches
receipt matches
CORRECT

Experiment. Change the deadline inside claims from 30 to 90. Keep policy fixed.

Expected output
deadline wrong or missing
receipt matches
PARTIALLY CORRECT

The receipt statement remains correct, so the narrow completeness rubric says partially correct. The false 90-day promise still blocks release. A case label and a critical gate can carry different information.

Checkpoint. If only the correct receipt statement remains, is the answer complete? No. The required deadline is still missing.

Step 3 — Count support claim by claim

Treat the claim and its value as a pair, or tuple, written with parentheses. An annotated passage can contain a set of these pairs. Python checks exact pair membership with in. This rolls up a manual evidence worksheet and does no language interpretation.

Open Python Editor

context = {("deadline", 30), ("receipt", "required")}
claims = [("deadline", 30), ("receipt", "required")]
extra_claim = False
if extra_claim:
    claims.append(("processing_hours", 2))

supported = 0
for claim in claims:
    found = claim in context
    supported += int(found)
    print(claim[0], "supported" if found else "unsupported")

print(f"Support: {supported}/{len(claims)}")
print("Unsupported:", len(claims) - supported)
Expected output
deadline supported
receipt supported
Support: 2/2
Unsupported: 0

Experiment. Change extra_claim from False to True. Predict both the numerator and denominator.

Expected output
deadline supported
receipt supported
processing_hours unsupported
Support: 2/3
Unsupported: 1

The deadline and receipt still have evidence. The two-hour promise adds one claim without adding support. Review that claim rather than averaging it away.

Checkpoint. Does no support for the two-hour promise prove it is false? No. It shows what this supplied evidence can establish.

Step 4 — Resolve a citation and test its support

Check a known policy claim against a claim-to-passage map. Empty text represents no citation in this exercise. An elif runs only when the branches above it did not apply. The final membership check asks whether the resolved passage supports this exact claim, after confirming it was supplied.

Open Python Editor

sources = {
    "RF-v2:s01": {("deadline", 30), ("receipt", "required")},
    "SH-v1:s01": {("shipping_delay", 45)},
    "RF-v1:s01": {("deadline", 90)},
}
supplied = {"RF-v2:s01", "SH-v1:s01"}
reference = "RF-v2:s01"
claim = ("deadline", 30)

for citation in (reference, "", "RF-unknown", "RF-v1:s01"):
    if not citation:
        label = "MISSING"
    elif citation not in sources:
        label = "UNKNOWN"
    elif citation not in supplied:
        label = "NOT SUPPLIED"
    elif claim not in sources[citation]:
        label = "DOES NOT SUPPORT"
    else:
        label = "VALID"
    print(citation or "(empty)", label)
Expected output
RF-v2:s01 VALID
(empty) MISSING
RF-unknown UNKNOWN
RF-v1:s01 NOT SUPPLIED

Experiment. Replace reference = "RF-v2:s01" with reference = "SH-v1:s01". Predict whether the identifier will still resolve.

Expected output
SH-v1:s01 DOES NOT SUPPORT
(empty) MISSING
RF-unknown UNKNOWN
RF-v1:s01 NOT SUPPLIED

The shipping passage exists and was supplied, but its 45 days refer to shipping. Inspect the actual span tied to the claim even when the link opens.

Checkpoint. Can a link to an approved but unsupplied passage pass this replay’s rule? No. It must identify evidence the assistant was actually given.

Step 5 — Keep authority separate from retrieved wording

Read the retrieved deadline values, then check the approved version published in the policy register. The loop uses version and days to unpack the two items in each row. The comparison filters the approved rows. A list can carry more than one value so the report can expose disagreement.

Open Python Editor

approved_version = 2
include_old = False
passages = [(2, 30)]
if include_old:
    passages.append((1, 90))

seen_days = []
approved_days = []
for version, days in passages:
    seen_days.append(days)
    if version == approved_version:
        approved_days.append(days)

print("Retrieved deadline values:", sorted(set(seen_days)))
print("Approved deadline values:", sorted(set(approved_days)))
print("Conflict in retrieved text:", len(set(seen_days)) > 1)
Expected output
Retrieved deadline values: [30]
Approved deadline values: [30]
Conflict in retrieved text: False

Experiment. Change include_old to True. Predict which of the two lists will change.

Expected output
Retrieved deadline values: [30, 90]
Approved deadline values: [30]
Conflict in retrieved text: True

The older wording makes the raw context disagree. The explicit authority rule resolves this example. If two approved sources conflict and no rule resolves them, send the case to review.

Checkpoint. If version 3 appears without approval, does its larger version number make it governing? No. Check the signed policy register.

Step 6 — Check a decision to abstain

An assistant abstains when it explicitly declines to decide from its context. Each fixture pairs a human context label with a recorded response type and a support flag. and requires both conditions. The branches check abstention first, then whether a substantive answer lacks the evidence it needs.

Open Python Editor

guess = False
cases = [
    ("Q1", False, "ANSWER" if guess else "ABSTAIN", False),
    ("Q2", True, "ABSTAIN", False),
    ("Q3", True, "ANSWER", True),
]
for case_id, sufficient, reply, supported in cases:
    if reply == "ABSTAIN":
        label = "UNNECESSARY ABSTENTION" if sufficient else "APPROPRIATE ABSTENTION"
    elif not sufficient or not supported:
        label = "UNSUPPORTED ANSWER"
    else:
        label = "ANSWER WITH SUPPORT"
    print(case_id, label)
Expected output
Q1 APPROPRIATE ABSTENTION
Q2 UNNECESSARY ABSTENTION
Q3 ANSWER WITH SUPPORT

Experiment. Set guess to True. The context stays incomplete. Predict what happens to Q1.

Expected output
Q1 UNSUPPORTED ANSWER
Q2 UNNECESSARY ABSTENTION
Q3 ANSWER WITH SUPPORT

The recorded behavior changes from admitting the gap to making a claim without support. Measure answer coverage alongside safe abstention so a system cannot hide a retrieval problem by refusing every question.

Checkpoint. Would a blank output count as abstention? No. The response must say it cannot determine the answer from its evidence.

Step 7 — Report a citation repair without erasing the failure

Evaluate one complete case with a two-claim answer and an unrelated citation. A set comprehension lists the fields in the retrieved evidence. frozenset is a set that cannot be edited, and a tuple holds the original citation sequence. The repair creates a new tuple. The comparison table shows sufficiency, correctness, support and decision side by side. Each audit row records the case, supplied IDs, answer, citation decisions, and gate result.

Open Python Editor

query = "How long do I have and what proof do I need?"
policy = {"deadline": 30, "receipt": "required"}
claims = (("deadline", 30), ("receipt", "required"))
sources = {
    "RF-v2:s01": frozenset(claims),
    "SH-v1:s01": frozenset({("shipping_delay", 45)}),
}
retrieved = ("RF-v2:s01", "SH-v1:s01")
evidence = frozenset().union(*(sources[key] for key in retrieved))
original = ("RF-v2:s01", "SH-v1:s01")
repair = False

def evaluate(run, refs):
    sufficient = policy.keys() <= {key for key, value in evidence}
    correct = dict(claims) == policy
    supported = sum(claim in evidence for claim in claims)
    labels = tuple("VALID" if claim in sources.get(ref, ()) and ref in retrieved
                   else "INVALID" for claim, ref in zip(claims, refs))
    critical = any(key == "deadline" and value != policy[key] for key, value in claims)
    if critical or supported < len(claims):
        decision = "FAIL"
    elif sufficient and correct and all(label == "VALID" for label in labels):
        decision = "PASS"
    else:
        decision = "REVIEW"
    return (run, refs, sufficient, correct, supported, labels, critical, decision)

history = (evaluate("original", original),)
if repair:
    history += (evaluate("repair", (original[0], "RF-v2:s01")),)

print("Q1:", query)
print("Retrieved:", ", ".join(retrieved))
print("Claims:", claims)
print("Run | Context sufficient | Correct | Claim support | Decision")
for run, refs, sufficient, correct, supported, labels, critical, decision in history:
    print(f"{run} | {sufficient} | {correct} | {supported}/2 | {decision}")
print("Citation audit:")
for run, refs, sufficient, correct, supported, labels, critical, decision in history:
    print(f"{run}: {refs} -> {labels}")
    print(f"  sufficient={sufficient} correct={correct} support={supported}/2")
    print(f"  abstention=N/A critical={critical} decision={decision}")
Expected output
Q1: How long do I have and what proof do I need?
Retrieved: RF-v2:s01, SH-v1:s01
Claims: (('deadline', 30), ('receipt', 'required'))
Run | Context sufficient | Correct | Claim support | Decision
original | True | True | 2/2 | REVIEW
Citation audit:
original: ('RF-v2:s01', 'SH-v1:s01') -> ('VALID', 'INVALID')
  sufficient=True correct=True support=2/2
  abstention=N/A critical=False decision=REVIEW

Experiment. Set repair to True. Predict which check will change and whether the original entry will still print.

Expected output
Q1: How long do I have and what proof do I need?
Retrieved: RF-v2:s01, SH-v1:s01
Claims: (('deadline', 30), ('receipt', 'required'))
Run | Context sufficient | Correct | Claim support | Decision
original | True | True | 2/2 | REVIEW
repair | True | True | 2/2 | PASS
Citation audit:
original: ('RF-v2:s01', 'SH-v1:s01') -> ('VALID', 'INVALID')
  sufficient=True correct=True support=2/2
  abstention=N/A critical=False decision=REVIEW
repair: ('RF-v2:s01', 'RF-v2:s01') -> ('VALID', 'VALID')
  sufficient=True correct=True support=2/2
  abstention=N/A critical=False decision=PASS

Read the original line and the repair line together. The receipt link changes from shipping to the quoted refund policy and its label changes from INVALID to VALID. Both factual claims were already correct and supported. The second row passes because its evidence links now pass, and the first row stays in the audit so a teammate can reproduce the failure.

Checkpoint. If a user asked whether the repaired citation changed factual accuracy, what would you show? Both audits report the same claims and correctness.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Label the context

Northstar asks the assistant to give both the time limit and acceptable proof. The delivered passage lists a 30-day window measured from purchase. It says nothing about proof. Write a label and the missing evidence. Repeat for a question asking the time limit alone.

Practice 2. Grade the extra claim

The approved account passage says “Reset your password from the sign-in page.” The reply says “Reset your password from the sign-in page. The link will arrive by SMS within five minutes.” Split it into checkable claims. Classify the support for each and give the policy correctness and gate result using the lesson rubric. The account passage is the only evidence and official reference.

Practice 3. Resolve three citations

Two supplied current passages say RF-v2:s01 “Requests must be filed within 30 days of purchase” and RF-v2:s02 “A valid receipt is required.” A reply correctly states both. The annotated deadline claim cites RF-v2:s01 and RF-v2:s99. The annotated receipt claim cites RF-v2:s01. The registry contains only the two supplied spans. Calculate validity and coverage, then repair the faulty links.

Practice 4. Explain the first repair to try

R08 receives WA-v2:s01, which explains how to start a warranty claim, but the assistant says it cannot tell. Separately, R05 correctly tells the customer how to reset a password though it saw only a shipping note. Explain the failure in each case, what to fix first, and which test result would show that the fix addressed your diagnosis.

Independent Assignment

Use the complete runnable program in the guided lab as the answer key for this assignment. Start with mode baseline and fill a worksheet with one row per case. Record the question ID, the reference policy and version, the context actually supplied, the sufficiency label, each atomic claim, supporting quote and versioned source ID, citation resolution and claim support, abstention decision, and any critical gate. When a claim has no support, write which record you inspected and whether it was absent, contradicted or excluded by permissions.

  1. Work R01, R02, R03 and R04 on paper first. Check every logged passage ID against the manifest. Treat the recorded response type and claim annotations as a human review that you can challenge. Score the other cases and compare your totals with the exact baseline transcript.
  2. Replay mode = "stale-context" starting from the original code. Change only delivered warranty context in R03. The old email answer is still in the capture. Explain why a better context can make the unchanged answer look less grounded.
  3. Restore the original program, then replay mode = "answer-warranty". Replace the unnecessary R08 abstention with the supplied cited answer, keeping its question and context fixed. Explain which denominators change and why.
  4. Submit a short engineering handoff. For each variant name the evidence that changed, which gate still blocks PASS, and the next data or test you would need. Give separate remedies for the wrong refund promise and the restricted source.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The two-part task has partial context. The passage gives the deadline but does not establish acceptable proof. With the deadline-only question the same passage is sufficient, because “within 30 days of purchase” establishes everything that task asks for.

Solution 2

Score three claims. The reset starts at the sign-in page. The link is delivered by SMS. It arrives within five minutes. The passage supports only the first claim, so claim support is 1/3. The other two facts are unverifiable against this record. The answer gets the required route right but makes two unverifiable additions, so it is partially correct. The unsupported-claim gate fails. Ask for the delivery evidence or remove the extra assertions. If the annotations combined SMS and five minutes into one claim, they would conceal two separately checkable promises.

Solution 3

The first link on the deadline resolves to current supplied text and supports the claim. The second is an unknown citation ID. The receipt claim’s link resolves but does not establish proof. Validity is 1/3 supplied links. Coverage is 1/2 claims. Remove the unknown link and cite RF-v2:s02 for the receipt. Both measures become 2/2. The facts and their support from the supplied context are unchanged.

Solution 4

R08’s context is sufficient and its refusal is unnecessary. Investigate the answer behavior with the same question and passage. A newly captured answer should give the order-page route, cite the supplied span, and show no unsupported claims. R05 is correct against approved account policy but unsupported in the capture. First inspect whether AC-v1:s01 was absent from the ranking or cut during context assembly. A retrieval or assembly fix should put that current public passage in the delivered context. Then replay with a newly captured reply and verify both support and citation. The existing R05 reply alone cannot show how it arrived at the right fact.

  • supplied public: WA-v2:s01
  • warranty_route: MATCH, SUPPORTED, WA-v2:s01=VALID
  • diagnostic: none | critical: none
  • Audit entries: 9; active cases: 8
  • Rates: context=3/8 | correct=4/6 | grounded=3/6 | support=4/7 | citations=2/7 | citation coverage=2/7 | abstention=2/2
  • Coverage: cases=8 context scored=8 answers scored=6 support claims scored=7
  • Counts: unsupported=3 refund policy failures=1 authorization failures=1
  • Suite decision: FAIL

R08 now answers with a supported, correctly cited route. The number of scored factual answers rises from five to six, claims from six to seven, and scorable abstentions fall from three to two. R02 still makes the false 90-day claim and R06 still breaches authorization. The suite stays FAIL in both assignment variants.

Knowledge Check

  1. A page says who handles refund requests but gives no policy requirements. How can it be relevant and insufficient at the same time?
  2. A reply cites only a shipping passage but gives the correct password-reset instructions. What records do you need to judge correctness and groundedness separately?
  3. How many claims would you annotate in “Refund requests are due in 30 days from purchase and refunds arrive within two hours”? What makes splitting them useful?
  4. A citation opens the archived warranty guide. Why is existence alone an inadequate test?
  5. One passage gives the refund window and another gives the receipt rule. How would you cite a sentence that contains both facts?
  6. A new FAQ contradicts an older signed policy. What decides which governs, and what if the assistant got both without the precedence rule?
  7. When is an explicit refusal appropriate? How should a blank output be scored?
  8. A 90-day refund answer appears after RF-v2:s01 was delivered. What would you investigate? How would the diagnosis change if the delivered context was only shipping?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. It matches the subject. The customer’s question requires specific conditions the page never states. The required evidence defines sufficiency.
  2. The approved account policy establishes the factual answer. The list and text of the authorized passages actually supplied establish whether the reply could be justified from its context. The shipping citation needs its own check.
  3. Two claims. One is the 30-day deadline measured from purchase and one is the two-hour processing promise. They can receive different verdicts.
  4. Verify the cited revision, authorization, whether it was supplied, and whether it supports the exact statement. An archived guide can open successfully and even contain the same words while failing the current-authority rule.
  5. Attach the deadline passage to the deadline claim and the receipt passage to the proof claim. If the same decision depends on both, record the two spans and the inference connecting them.
  6. Use the documented authority and effective period. A newer upload alone does not decide. If the writer received both with no resolution rule, treat the context conflict as a separate problem even if the reviewer has a policy key.
  7. It is appropriate when the authorized evidence cannot support an answer and the assistant says so without adding unsupported factual details. A blank output is a missing answer for review.
  8. With sufficient context, investigate answer generation or rule application and check the cited span. With only shipping, investigate the missing evidence in retrieval or prompt assembly and the failure to abstain. Both stages may need attention.

Guided Engineering Lab

Can We Trust Our RAG Assistant's Answers and Citations?

Northstar must decide whether a fictional replay is ready to pass its answer-quality gate. The cases cover refunds, shipping, warranty, and account access. The code contains the complete manifest, captured replies, claim annotations, and gold source mappings. In this policy snapshot, RF version 2, WA version 2, and version 1 of the other registered sources are current. The signed authority map independently selects the governing public passage for each approved fact. The shipping FAQ is indexed as current but contradicts the governing shipping passage. Northstar’s rubric flags conflicting active instructions delivered without a precedence rule. The staff-only fixture uses placeholder wording. Its reference is redacted in the report and its contents are excluded from public evidence.

Work a case by hand and match the evidence

Read R01’s question and open both supplied passages in the inline manifest. Underline the 30-day deadline and valid receipt condition in RF-v2:s01. The exact policy claims are supported and correct. The answer attached the shipping reference to its receipt claim. That passage resolves and happens to mention a receipt, but it gives shipping instructions and cannot establish what a refund requires. Mark one valid citation link out of two, and coverage of one out of two claims. Predict what changes when you repair the single receipt citation.

Then read R02. The same refund rule was present when the assistant answered 90 days. RF-v2:s01 is current and its citation exists, but no passage supports the 90-day deadline. Record a critical refund violation, an unsupported claim, and a citation error. Keep it visible even when R01 improves.

The lab distinguishes a passage the reviewer uses to establish the right answer from a passage the assistant was actually given. Read authority for the first and delivered for the second. The required tuple lists the facts this question needs. behavior records the reviewer’s label for the response. In claims, each entry stores the statement, its annotated value, and the cited spans. In a real evaluation compare annotations with the raw wording before trusting a tally.

Run the audit

The program uses Python’s dataclass to give each record named fields. frozen=True prevents assigning new values to those fields. The fields used in the historical records contain immutable values such as strings, integers, and tuples. replace(record, field=value) builds a new record for the replay. The original remains in the history and the new row replaces it only in the active set used for summaries. dict.fromkeys visits each link once in first-seen order. dict(source.facts) builds a lookup from the hand-labeled key and value pairs. Use summarize to see the denominators, including the number of answers and scorable claims.

The replay evaluates a finite worksheet. It uses pre-annotated facts rather than deciding whether a sentence entails another by itself. If an applied rule or several spans are needed for a single claim, write the inference and gold mappings manually. The lab’s simple pair matching does not perform arithmetic on dates, check arbitrary citation URLs, infer policy durations from free text, or simulate new model replies. An unknown supplied ID makes context unknown and excludes those claim support judgments. Duplicate references are counted once per claim and remain visible as a diagnostic. A known unauthorized citation is a critical failure even if the passage never reached the public context.

Select Copy Code, open the Python editor, replace any starter text with the full program, then click Run. Check the baseline transcript below. The program prints a public view of the audit record, with restricted references omitted or redacted. The fictional audit object retains the captured reply, question, policy snapshot, rubric, and detailed labels.

Open Python Editor

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

mode = "baseline"  # baseline, citation, stale-context, or answer-warranty
snapshot = "northstar-policy-2026-11-26"
rubric = "northstar-answer-v1"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Passage:
    document: str
    version: int
    audience: str
    text: str
    facts: tuple

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    key: str
    value: object
    text: str
    refs: tuple = ()

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Case:
    id: str
    question: str
    required: tuple
    delivered: tuple
    behavior: str
    reply: str
    claims: tuple = ()

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Audit:
    case: Case
    run: str
    policy_snapshot: str
    rubric: str
    visible: tuple
    context: str
    correctness: str
    claims: tuple
    abstention: str
    critical: tuple
    reasons: tuple
    decision: str

manifest = {
    "RF": 2, "WA": 2, "SH": 1, "AC": 1, "FAQ": 1, "RX": 1,
}
passages = {
    "RF-v2:s01": Passage("RF", 2, "public",
        "Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.",
        (("refund_days", 30), ("receipt", "valid receipt"))),
    "WA-v2:s01": Passage("WA", 2, "public", "Start a warranty claim from your order.",
        (("warranty_route", "order"),)),
    "WA-v1:s01": Passage("WA", 1, "public", "Start a warranty claim by emailing Support.",
        (("warranty_route", "email"),)),
    "SH-v1:s01": Passage("SH", 1, "public",
        "After 45 days without a receipt, contact us for shipping delays.",
        (("shipping_contact_days", 45),)),
    "FAQ-v1:s01": Passage("FAQ", 1, "public",
        "Contact us after 60 days about a shipping delay.",
        (("shipping_contact_days", 60),)),
    "AC-v1:s01": Passage("AC", 1, "public", "Reset your password from the sign-in page.",
        (("reset_route", "sign-in page"),)),
    "RX-v1:s01": Passage("RX", 1, "staff",
        "Fictional staff-note fixture. No real internal exception is reproduced.",
        (("warranty_route", "order"),)),
}
# The signed policy register names the governing passage for each known fact.
authority = {
    "refund_days": "RF-v2:s01", "receipt": "RF-v2:s01",
    "warranty_route": "WA-v2:s01", "shipping_contact_days": "SH-v1:s01",
    "reset_route": "AC-v1:s01",
}

def current(passage):
    return manifest.get(passage.document) == passage.version

def official_facts():
    facts = {}
    for field, ref in authority.items():
        source = passages[ref]
        if source.audience != "public" or not current(source):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid authority for {field}")
        facts[field] = dict(source.facts)[field]
    return facts

policy = official_facts()
deadline = Claim("refund_days", 30, "The deadline is 30 days from purchase.", ("RF-v2:s01",))
receipt = Claim("receipt", "valid receipt", "A valid receipt is required.", ("SH-v1:s01",))
warranty = Claim("warranty_route", "order", "Start the claim from your order.", ("WA-v2:s01",))
cases = (
    Case("R01", "What is the refund deadline, and what proof do I need?",
         ("refund_days", "receipt"), ("RF-v2:s01", "SH-v1:s01"), "ANSWER",
         "The deadline is 30 days from purchase [RF-v2:s01]. A valid receipt is required [SH-v1:s01].",
         (deadline, receipt)),
    Case("R02", "What is the deadline for a refund?", ("refund_days",),
         ("RF-v2:s01",), "ANSWER", "You have 90 days from purchase [RF-v2:s01].",
         (Claim("refund_days", 90, "You have 90 days from purchase.", ("RF-v2:s01",)),)),
    Case("R03", "Where do I start a warranty claim?", ("warranty_route",),
         ("WA-v1:s01",), "ANSWER", "Email Support to start a warranty claim [WA-v1:s01].",
         (Claim("warranty_route", "email", "Email Support to start a warranty claim.", ("WA-v1:s01",)),)),
    Case("R04", "Has my particular parcel arrived?", ("parcel_arrived",),
         ("SH-v1:s01",), "ABSTAIN", "I cannot verify your parcel's status from this information."),
    Case("R05", "Where can I reset my password?", ("reset_route",),
         ("SH-v1:s01",), "ANSWER", "Reset your password from the sign-in page [AC-v1:s01].",
         (Claim("reset_route", "sign-in page", "Reset from the sign-in page.", ("AC-v1:s01",)),)),
    Case("R06", "Where do I start a warranty claim?", ("warranty_route",),
         ("RX-v1:s01",), "ANSWER", "Start the claim from your order [RX-v1:s01].",
         (replace(warranty, refs=("RX-v1:s01",)),)),
    Case("R07", "After how many days should I contact support about shipping?",
         ("shipping_contact_days",), ("SH-v1:s01", "FAQ-v1:s01"), "ABSTAIN",
         "The supplied instructions disagree. I cannot confirm the deadline."),
    Case("R08", "Where do I start a warranty claim?", ("warranty_route",),
         ("WA-v2:s01",), "ABSTAIN", "I cannot tell you where to start."),
)

def validate(records):
    ids = set()
    for case in records:
        if not case.id or case.id in ids or not case.question or not case.required:
            raise ValueError("Expected a unique case ID, a question and required facts")
        if case.behavior not in {"ANSWER", "ABSTAIN"} or (case.behavior == "ABSTAIN" and case.claims):
            raise ValueError(f"{case.id}: invalid reply annotation")
        ids.add(case.id)

def can_read(ref):
    return ref in passages and passages[ref].audience == "public"

def evaluate(case, run):
    visible = tuple(ref for ref in case.delivered if can_read(ref))
    unknown_context = any(ref not in passages for ref in case.delivered)
    critical = set()
    reasons = set()
    if any(ref in passages and not can_read(ref) for ref in case.delivered):
        critical.add("authorization")
    available = {fact for ref in visible for fact in passages[ref].facts}
    approved = {fact for ref in visible if current(passages[ref]) for fact in passages[ref].facts}
    needed = set(case.required)
    present = {key for key, value in approved if key in policy and policy[key] == value}
    conflict = any(key in needed and value != policy.get(key) for key, value in approved)
    if unknown_context:
        context = "UNKNOWN"
        reasons.add("missing passage record")
    elif conflict:
        context = "CONTRADICTORY"
        reasons.add("context conflict")
    elif needed <= present:
        context = "SUFFICIENT"
    elif needed & present:
        context = "PARTIAL"
    else:
        context = "INSUFFICIENT"
    if context in {"PARTIAL", "INSUFFICIENT"} and needed <= policy.keys():
        reasons.add("required evidence missing")
    if any(not current(passages[ref]) for ref in visible):
        reasons.add("stale context")

    abstention = "N/A"
    correctness = "N/A"
    rows = []
    if not case.reply.strip():
        reasons.add("empty answer")
    elif case.behavior == "ABSTAIN":
        abstention = ("UNNECESSARY" if context == "SUFFICIENT" else
                      "UNKNOWN" if context == "UNKNOWN" else "APPROPRIATE")
        if abstention == "UNNECESSARY":
            reasons.add("unnecessary abstention")
    elif not case.claims:
        reasons.add("missing claim annotations")
    else:
        matched = set()
        mismatches = 0
        for claim in case.claims:
            key, value = claim.key, claim.value
            fact = (key, value)
            if key in policy and policy[key] == value:
                matched.add(key)
                truth = "MATCH"
            elif key in policy:
                mismatches += 1
                truth = "WRONG"
                reasons.add("wrong policy value")
                if key in {"refund_days", "receipt"}:
                    critical.add("refund policy")
            else:
                truth = "UNVERIFIABLE"
                reasons.add("claim outside policy key")
            support = ("UNKNOWN" if unknown_context else
                       "SUPPORTED" if fact in available else "UNSUPPORTED")
            if support == "UNSUPPORTED":
                reasons.add("unsupported claim")
            citations = []
            for ref in dict.fromkeys(claim.refs):
                if ref not in passages:
                    label = "UNKNOWN ID"
                elif not can_read(ref):
                    label = "RESTRICTED"
                    critical.add("authorization")
                elif ref not in visible:
                    label = "NOT SUPPLIED"
                elif not current(passages[ref]):
                    label = "STALE"
                elif fact not in passages[ref].facts:
                    label = "DOES NOT SUPPORT"
                else:
                    label = "VALID"
                citations.append(("[restricted]" if label == "RESTRICTED" else ref, label))
                if label != "VALID":
                    reasons.add("citation error")
            if not citations:
                reasons.add("missing citation")
            if len(claim.refs) != len(citations):
                reasons.add("duplicate citation")
            rows.append((key, truth, support, tuple(citations)))

        if all(truth == "MATCH" for _, truth, _, _ in rows) and needed <= matched:
            correctness = "CORRECT"
        elif matched & needed:
            correctness = "PARTIALLY CORRECT"
        elif mismatches:
            correctness = "INCORRECT"
        elif all(truth == "UNVERIFIABLE" for _, truth, _, _ in rows):
            correctness = "UNVERIFIABLE"
        else:
            correctness = "INCOMPLETE"
            reasons.add("required facts omitted")

    if critical or "unsupported claim" in reasons:
        decision = "FAIL"
    elif context == "SUFFICIENT" and correctness == "CORRECT" and not reasons:
        decision = "PASS"
    elif (abstention == "APPROPRIATE" and context == "INSUFFICIENT"
          and not needed <= policy.keys() and not reasons):
        decision = "PASS"
    else:
        decision = "REVIEW"
    return Audit(case, run, snapshot, rubric, visible, context, correctness, tuple(rows),
                 abstention, tuple(sorted(critical)), tuple(sorted(reasons)), decision)

def show(row):
    ids = ", ".join(row.visible) or "none"
    print(f"{row.case.id}: {row.context} | {row.correctness} | abstention={row.abstention} | {row.decision}")
    print(f"  supplied public: {ids}")
    for key, truth, support, refs in row.claims:
        links = ", ".join(f"{ref}={label}" for ref, label in refs) or "MISSING"
        print(f"  {key}: {truth}, {support}, {links}")
    reasons = ", ".join(row.reasons) or "none"
    critical = ", ".join(row.critical) or "none"
    print(f"  diagnostic: {reasons} | critical: {critical}")

def fraction(count, total):
    return f"{count}/{total}" if total else "N/A (0 eligible)"

def summarize(rows):
    known = [row for row in rows if row.context != "UNKNOWN"]
    answered = [row for row in rows if row.claims]
    claims = [claim for row in answered for claim in row.claims]
    scorable = [claim for claim in claims if claim[2] != "UNKNOWN"]
    links = [label for _, _, _, cites in claims for _, label in cites]
    abstained = [row for row in rows if row.abstention in {"APPROPRIATE", "UNNECESSARY"}]
    unsupported = sum(claim[2] == "UNSUPPORTED" for claim in scorable)
    rates = {
        "context": fraction(sum(row.context == "SUFFICIENT" for row in known), len(known)),
        "correct": fraction(sum(row.correctness == "CORRECT" for row in answered), len(answered)),
        "grounded": fraction(sum(all(c[2] == "SUPPORTED" for c in row.claims)
                                 for row in answered if row.context != "UNKNOWN"),
                             sum(row.context != "UNKNOWN" for row in answered)),
        "support": fraction(len(scorable) - unsupported, len(scorable)),
        "citations": fraction(links.count("VALID"), len(links)),
        "citation coverage": fraction(sum(any(label == "VALID" for _, label in c[3])
                                          for c in claims), len(claims)),
        "abstention": fraction(sum(row.abstention == "APPROPRIATE" for row in abstained), len(abstained)),
    }
    print("Rates:", " | ".join(f"{key}={value}" for key, value in rates.items()))
    print(f"Coverage: cases={len(rows)} context scored={len(known)} answers scored={len(answered)}"
          f" support claims scored={len(scorable)}")
    print(f"Counts: unsupported={unsupported} refund policy failures="
          f"{sum('refund policy' in row.critical for row in rows)}"
          f" authorization failures={sum('authorization' in row.critical for row in rows)}")
    decision = ("FAIL" if any(row.decision == "FAIL" for row in rows) else
                "PASS" if rows and all(row.decision == "PASS" for row in rows) else "REVIEW")
    print("Suite decision:", decision)

def replay(selected_mode):
    validate(cases)
    baseline = tuple(evaluate(case, "original") for case in cases)
    print(f"{snapshot} | {rubric} | public replay | {selected_mode}")
    if selected_mode == "baseline":
        for row in baseline:
            show(row)
        summarize(baseline)
        return baseline, baseline

    if selected_mode == "citation":
        index = 0
        revised = replace(
            cases[index], claims=(deadline, replace(receipt, refs=("RF-v2:s01",))),
            reply=cases[index].reply.replace("[SH-v1:s01]", "[RF-v2:s01]"))
    elif selected_mode == "stale-context":
        index = 2
        revised = replace(cases[index], delivered=("WA-v2:s01",))
    elif selected_mode == "answer-warranty":
        index = 7
        revised = replace(cases[index], behavior="ANSWER", claims=(warranty,),
                          reply="Start the claim from your order [WA-v2:s01].")
    else:
        raise ValueError("Use a documented replay mode")
    new = evaluate(revised, selected_mode)
    history = baseline + (new,)
    active = baseline[:index] + (new,) + baseline[index + 1:]
    for row in (history[index], history[-1]):
        print(f"Audit {row.run} | {row.case.reply}")
        show(row)
    print(f"Audit entries: {len(history)}; active cases: {len(active)}")
    summarize(active)
    return history, active

replay(mode)

Troubleshoot and hand off the decision

If the active case count grows to nine, check that you summarized the active rows instead of the entire history. If a citation resolves but fails, compare its passage text, version and role with the annotated claim. If R02 passes, reload the original program and confirm its saved value is 90, while the signed source still says 30. If R06’s restricted reference appears in the public result, inspect the display and authorization filters before continuing. Keep restricted raw traces in a protected reviewer store.

A sample report reads, “We changed R01’s receipt citation from shipping to the approved refund passage. The original REVIEW remains in the audit. One more supplied link supports its claim, so citation validity goes from 1/6 to 2/6. One more claim has a valid link, so coverage also goes from 1/6 to 2/6. The suite remains FAIL. R02 promises 90 days even though the writer received the 30-day rule. R06 exposed a staff-only reference. Replay R02 with the same current passage after correcting answer behavior. Verify on a public trace that the staff-only source never reaches the prompt or the reply.”

Finish when you can reproduce both transcripts, defend the denominators by counting cases and claims, and explain why the successful citation repair does not clear the policy or authorization gates. Run the assignment variants and compare their saved rows and totals with the answer key. Before considering an operational release, test unseen refund questions and independently verify the authorization controls.

For a real-model extension, keep one row per capture with model version, prompt version, query ID and text, evaluation timestamp, exact retrieved context in order with source IDs and versions, caller authorization, raw reply, atomic claim annotations, citation references, expected behavior, and rubric version. If saved as JSON, a text format for these named fields, compare the stored retrieved IDs with the passages actually placed in the prompt before grading. Have reviewers annotate supporting quotations and scope conditions on fresh cases. Measure replay and live behavior as separate experiments.

Common Mistakes

  • Scoring the top-ranked passage instead of checking what entered the prompt.
  • Giving a claim credit because its number occurs elsewhere in the document.
  • Counting a link that merely opens as evidence for the attached statement.
  • Treating a blank reply as successful abstention, or scoring unknown evidence as zero.
  • Replacing an old audit entry when a label or citation changes.

Historical evidence from the original repository.

Test 7: Groundedness Scoring

Recorded Results Available

What was tested
Check whether individual claims in healthcare bot replies are traceable to supplied source material.
How it was tested
Send source material, question, and response to a judge that returns a three-level groundedness verdict with reasoning. The source prompt and healthcare cases are documented. The walkthrough reproduces the judge prompt and the TC001 response. llama3.1:8b as the bot and gemma2:9b as the judge in the documented 22-case run.
Actual results
The summary table reports 5 Grounded, 17 Partial, 0 Ungrounded, and mean 2.23/3.
Original findings
The original manual review found that TC001 invented several specifics that the automated judge missed.
Evidence notes
The walkthrough assigns conflicting verdict descriptions to TC001 in different sections. Preserve both and use the case reasoning when reviewing the judge.

Test 9: RAG Evaluation

Recorded Results Available

What was tested
Evaluate retrieval, answer faithfulness, and keyword relevance on a document-backed banking assistant.
How it was tested
Retrieve three chunks and score the resulting answer along three axes. The report records retrieval candidates and case-level judgments. Local source documents and 25 cases in the saved walkthrough, including cross-document, unanswerable, and boundary questions. llama3.1:8b bot and mistral judge via Ollama. Keyword matching supplies the answer-relevance measure.
Actual results
The 25-case page reports 84% context relevance, 100% answer faithfulness, 66% answer relevance, and 83% overall.
Original findings
The walkthrough flags TC21 as an incorrect eligibility decision despite 100% context relevance and 100% faithfulness scores.
Evidence notes
The README mentions an earlier 21-case suite. The summary here uses the 25-case result page. The historical faithfulness verdict is not independently verified correctness.

Check the passages that reached the assistant, then check the policy claims and their cited spans. Keep the current-policy verdict, support verdict, and citation verdict visible. Use the review notes to choose a change at the right stage, rerun with controlled inputs, and preserve the original evidence.
