What You Will Learn

  • Reproduce a bad RAG answer and trace the evidence from the policy register through citations.
  • Test a suspected cause with an oracle context swap and a one-setting ranking change.
  • Compare a baseline and candidate on matched cases and spot regressions in important groups.
  • Apply quality, authorization, and latency gates to a reproducible RELEASE, HOLD, or REVIEW recommendation.

Why This Lesson Matters

Read this saved Northstar Support exchange. The customer asks, “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?” The assistant replies, “Yes. Refunds are available within 90 days. [DOC-REFUND-OLD]”

Open the approved policy. It gives customers 30 days from purchase and requires a valid receipt. Write down the expected answer and underline what would mislead this customer. Before changing anything, write down which record you would open next. The citation gives you a place to look, but you still need the saved ranking and the exact passage sent to the writer.

The policies, records, scores, timings, and captured replies in this chapter are fictional. Allow about 6.5 hours. Complete Context sufficiency, answer correctness and citations first. Variance, repetition and score aggregation and Comparing models, prompts and A/B variants are recommended. If you plan to report comparative confidence intervals, complete Confidence intervals, significance and sample size. The default lab replays annotated captures without any model calls.

Beginner Explanation

Follow the handoffs

Imagine a customer receives the wrong product. Check the order sheet, the packing slip, and the parcel. A correct item on the order sheet and the wrong item on the slip point you toward the handoff that copied the order. The parcel shows the outcome. The other records help explain where it started.

Open Northstar’s saved query and reply. From the reply alone, you know the customer got the wrong deadline. You do not yet know whether the assistant read the wrong policy or misread the right one. Start with three handoffs. What did search find? What did the writer actually receive? What did the writer say? The answer the customer sees is a symptom. Working back through these handoffs is failure attribution.

Ask which record would distinguish a missing policy from a bad decision using the right policy. A ranked list can show that the refund rule existed among the candidates. Only the selected context shows whether the assistant saw it. If the selected context contained the full current rule, compare its wording with the answer and citations. A candidate list is only one stage of the investigation.

Inspect the pipeline in order

A trace is the saved record of a case as it passes through the system. Start with the exact query, requested effective date, caller’s allowed role, expected answer facts, and authoritative policy version. Follow the same case ID through these stages.

  • Ingestion. Policy files enter the system and become source records with IDs, versions, status, and access labels. Compare the approved manifest, or version register, with the import log. Missing documents, duplicate IDs, bad metadata, broken links, or a missing access label can make later searches wrong or unsafe.
  • Cleaning. Raw text becomes searchable text. Compare the original with the cleaned text. Check whether a negation, decimal, or section boundary disappeared.
  • Chunking. Documents become small passages. Open neighboring chunks and check their source IDs. “A photo is required” and “except for a damaged sealed parcel” could get separated. Too little overlap can lose the exception. Excessive overlap or overly large chunks can duplicate material and consume input space. Too-small chunks can lose the subject of a rule.
  • Indexing. Chunks become searchable entries. Compare the chunk inventory with the indexed IDs. If a current chunk exists but the index missed it or kept an old revision, ranking never gets a fair chance.
  • Retrieval. A query gives a set of eligible candidates. Check expected evidence IDs and which chunks were eligible. A query saying “proof of purchase” can miss a passage that only says “receipt.” Filter by the caller’s permissions before ranking or displaying results.
  • Ranking. Matched candidates get scores and an order. Inspect scores, tie rules, and which passages fell below top-k. A high overlap on “45 days” can favor shipping over refunds.
  • Context selection. The ranked list becomes the passages inserted into the prompt. Inspect the actual selected IDs and text. A word or token budget, first-slot policy, duplication, competing versions, or truncation can drop the needed rule even when it ranked in the search results.
  • Answer generation. The query and delivered passages become the reply. Compare its atomic claims and decision against the approved policy and context. Look for unsupported claims, missing conditions, a wrong application of a rule, or an unnecessary refusal.
  • Citation generation. Claims get references to source spans. Inspect whether a citation is missing, unknown, unrelated, stale, or restricted. A working link can still fail to support its claim.
  • Evaluation. The saved trace and gold labels become a verdict. Check the case IDs, expected policy version, annotator notes, and denominators. A broken or outdated answer key can manufacture a “regression.”

If a record is missing, mark the gap. “No trace was saved” and “this passage was absent from a complete trace” are different observations. Inspect the first supported defect and keep downstream effects in the report. A contributing factor is one condition that helped produce the outcome, such as taking only the first passage. A root cause is an upstream condition you can change and test. Call a result confirmed only within the tested setting. A theory such as “the model prefers long passages” remains a hypothesis until a comparison isolates it. More than one cause can matter.

Use familiar labels in the case log. INGESTION for absent or malformed sources, CHUNKING for lost conditions at a boundary, RETRIEVAL for candidate or ranking failures (including a missing index entry if documented), CONTEXT_SELECTION for delivery failures, GENERATION for wrong use of sufficient evidence, CITATION for reference defects, AUTHORIZATION for a breached boundary, and EVALUATION_DATA for evidence that is too incomplete or inconsistent to score. Write the evidence beside every label. The lab can surface several at once and uses Step 2 to illustrate a chunking gap the main fixture does not simulate.

Make one controlled change

Place two copies of the saved prompt side by side. Keep the customer’s question identical. In the first copy, leave the old 90-day passage. In the second, replace just that passage with the approved 30-day rule and receipt condition. Keep the generator setup and scoring rules fixed. Before running the comparison, predict which error a change to the passage could fix and which error might persist. A reviewer-supplied context replacement is an oracle context swap. Compare baseline and oracle at both retrieval and answer stages. If the error persists with good evidence, inspect answer use. If it disappears, test the retrieval or selection hypothesis with a normal run. An oracle skips search selection, so it cannot establish that production search found the policy.

Try a realistic ranking change next. Freeze the case set, source versions, answer rubric, and all unrelated settings. Record the experiment ID and the baseline and candidate manifests. Include the dataset and corpus versions, chunk settings, retriever and ranking settings, selector budget, prompt version, model or capture version, rubric, and run timestamp if using live traces. If answer behavior is represented by prewritten captures, explain how each capture is keyed to the case and selected context. Changing which fixture is read lets you test reporting and comparison. It does not predict a new model reply.

Think about a current refund question and one about a historical shipping rule. A blanket penalty on old passages can help the current question and break the historical one. The correct historical version is determined by the approved effective date, independently of the search score. Test new thresholds and ranking weights on development cases. Reserve some cases in each important group for a later check. Once you use a held-out case to tune the change, it becomes a regression case. Keep it, and gather fresh held-out evidence.

Count changes on the same cases

A regression is a case that used to pass and now fails. A fix moves the other way. In a three-case example, refund fails and two other cases pass. The candidate fixes refund, breaks shipping, and keeps warranty passing. Both runs pass two of three. The paired counts expose one fix and one regression. Fix rate is 1/1 previously failing paired case. Regression rate is 1/2 previously passing paired cases. An unchanged failure also matters and stays visible. An unscored pair belongs in the coverage report, outside the fix and regression denominators.

A golden regression dataset stores approved expectations for each case. Keep query ID and wording, required passages and expected facts, expected citation versions, policy segment, as-of date, authorization role, and criticality. Treat it as versioned evidence. When policy changes, preserve old verdicts with the old labels and add reviewed expectations for the new version. Re-run on the same IDs before interpreting a difference.

Compute the following by hand for a case with two required chunks. Suppose the top two contain only one of them and the context has only one passage. Hit@2 is 1 because at least one gold chunk was retrieved. Recall@2 is 1/2. Context sufficiency is false because the complete answer needs both. If the reply makes two claims and only one is supported, claim support is 1/2. If it provides two claim–citation links and one is valid, citation validity is 1/2. By contrast, a case that refuses to guess provides zero links. Report the absent links and the failed answer separately. Zero links cannot certify good citations.

For the suite, average recall across judged cases and divide successful case outcomes by the number of scorable cases. Coverage uses all planned cases as its denominator. Divide supported claims by evaluated claims and valid links by supplied distinct claim–reference links. Show all numerator and denominator counts. When comparing runs, count fixes against previously failing matched cases and regressions against previously passing matched cases. No eligible cases yields N/A. When comparing groups such as refunds, missing receipts, shipping, warranties, account access, and restricted information, show the individual rows as well as any mean. A large group can hide a small critical group’s failure.

Write a decision that follows the evidence

A gate is a condition the candidate must satisfy, such as zero unauthorized disclosures. A guardrail limits an operational cost, such as latency. If a candidate adds two fixed cases while introducing an unauthorized citation, hold it even if the average goes up.

Tradeoffs deserve a controlled comparison. Larger top-k can improve recall at the cost of latency and context space. More overlap can preserve exceptions and increase duplicate text. Longer answers can cover more requirements and create more unsupported claims. Forcing higher answer coverage can encourage guessing. Finer citations can make verification easier and annotation slower. The lab uses illustrative latency computed from the candidate count and number of selected words. It does not measure a service.

On eight handpicked cases a one-case gain is 1/8 of the suite. That describes these cases and is too little evidence for a broad reliability claim. Keep case pairs intact for statistical comparisons. If a broader sample supports a gain, still check policy and authorization gates independently. RELEASE, HOLD, and REVIEW in this chapter are decisions under a documented fictional test policy.

Worked Demonstration

Example 1. Find where the 90-day error started

User question. “Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?”

Approved reference. The 2026 register selects RF version 2. “Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.” Version 1, saved as DOC-REFUND-OLD, allowed 90 days and is retained for archival use. The expected answer is no, with both requirements explained.

Follow the saved baseline trace in order. The import includes RF versions 1 and 2 with correctly labeled provenance. Both policy paragraphs became intact chunks with their original source versions. The ranked list is DOC-REFUND-OLD (6), RF-v2:c01 (4). The selector takes one passage, so only the old policy enters the prompt. Pause and predict which of the current requirements the writer can justify.

Actual LLM response. Fictional capture, “Yes. Refunds are available within 90 days. [DOC-REFUND-OLD]”

Assessment. Check the intake records first. Version 2 made it through import and chunking, and you can see it at rank 2. The first defect you can point to is that the archived version wins the ranking. Check the next record. The selector takes only the first result, so the writer never sees the approved rule. The 90-day claim and its stale citation follow that missing handoff.

Failure classification. Ranking, context selection, and a stale citation contribute. The reply’s wrong deadline fails the critical policy gate. The trace does not establish that the generator would ignore the approved rule if it saw it. In the oracle swap, hold these ranks and the rubric fixed, deliver RF-v2:c01, and score the prewritten answer associated with that context. Both required facts now match and cite the current passage. Hit@2 remains 1 in both. That supports a context-delivery explanation on these fixtures.

Example 2. A ranking fix harms a historical query

User question. Compare Q1’s current refund question, Q2’s missing-receipt question, and Q3’s “In 2025, when could I contact Support for a shipping delay?”

Approved reference. Q1 needs RF-v2:c01. Q2 needs MR-v1:c01, which says to download receipts in Orders. Q3 needs SH-v1:c01, the approved 2025 source with 45 days. SH-v2:c01 begins in 2026 and says 60 days.

Calculate a three-point penalty on older versions. Q1 starts with archive 6 and current 4. The archive drops to 3 and the current chunk wins 4 to 3. In Q2, receipt help stays 5 and the refund distractor stays 2, so nothing changes. Q3 starts with 2025 shipping 5 and 2026 shipping 4. The penalty makes the historical passage 2, so the future passage wins 4 to 2. Predict what the selector delivers on each case.

Actual LLM response. Three fictional captures in the penalized run give the current refund requirements, send the receipt user to Orders, and tell the 2025 shipping user the threshold was 60 days.

Assessment. Q1 is fixed, Q2 stays passing, and Q3 regresses. Hit@2 stays 3/3 on these three cases because their expected passages remain among the two ranked results. Supplying the correct passage first is the change that matters to this selector.

Failure classification. The global penalty causes a wrong-version selection for Q3. Apply the penalty only to current-policy requests, using the saved as-of date to recognize historical questions. Compare normal ranked runs on all cases and keep a separate check that an archive selected for a current request still fails.

Example 3. Decide whether an apparent improvement can ship

User question. The support team asks whether the global freshness change is safe on the eight matched lab queries.

Approved reference. The release policy requires eight scorable cases, complete evidence and supported citations, no new regressions, no critical policy, source-version, or authorization failures, at least one confirmed fix on a paired replay, and maximum illustrative latency at or below 55 ms. An oracle-only result is diagnostic evidence.

Actual LLM response. The baseline gives the 90-day reply on Q1 and Q7. With the first change, both refund replies use 30 days. Q3 changes from “The threshold was 45 days” to “The threshold was 60 days.” The other five captures stay the same.

Assessment. Baseline sufficiency and correctness are both 6/8, and citation validity is 6/8. The first candidate improves those counts to 7/8, 7/8, and 8/9 respectively. Coverage stays 8/8. The expected evidence remains in the top two for all eight. The second fix makes all eight correct, with 9/9 valid links. Maximum illustrative latency is 37 ms before any change and 41 ms after each change.

Failure classification. Candidate one is HOLD because of one new regression and one inappropriate source version, despite more passing answers. The scoped second repair clears the lab’s gates. Compare the final report with the original baseline as well as the immediately preceding run to see which cases changed and which historical failures remain in the audit. These results concern the eight fixtures.

Hands-On Python Exercise

Setup and run

For each step select Copy Code, open the linked editor, paste the full program, and click Run. Open the output disclosure after running. Predict the effect of the stated edit, apply it alone, and run again. Reload the original before you start another step. Each program uses inline fictional data and is independent.

Step 1 — Reproduce the incident

Compare a captured refund reply with the approved deadline and receipt rule. The dictionaries contain facts annotated by a reviewer. Square brackets read a named value, == compares two values, and an f-string inserts results where you use braces. Here None marks an omitted receipt claim.

Open Python Editor

question = "Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?"
policy = {"days": 30, "receipt": True}
retrieved = "DOC-REFUND-OLD"
answer = {"days": 90, "receipt": None}
print(question)
print("Supplied passage:", retrieved)
for key in policy:
    print(f"{key}: expected {policy[key]}, observed {answer[key]}")
print("Policy facts correct:", answer == policy)
Expected output
Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?
Supplied passage: DOC-REFUND-OLD
days: expected 30, observed 90
receipt: expected True, observed None
Policy facts correct: False

Experiment. Replace the answer dictionary with {"days": 30, "receipt": True}.

Expected output
Can I get a refund after 45 days without a receipt?
Supplied passage: DOC-REFUND-OLD
days: expected 30, observed 30
receipt: expected True, observed True
Policy facts correct: True

The policy facts alone now match. The supplied passage ID remains old, so you still need a context and support check. Editing a saved reply does not repair the pipeline.

Checkpoint. If the saved reply is corrected, which earlier artifact still needs investigation? The selected context still points to the archive.

Step 2 — Find where evidence disappears

Watch a required receipt span pass through four records. Each row has a stage name and the span IDs seen there. for stage, spans in rows unpacks each pair. break exits at the first complete record without the required span.

Open Python Editor

split_clause = True
rule = "RF:s01"
receipt = "RF:s02"
rows = [
    ("ingestion", (rule, receipt)),
    ("chunking: complete eligible units", (rule,) if split_clause else (rule, receipt)),
    ("retrieval", (rule,) if split_clause else (rule, receipt)),
    ("selected context", (rule,) if split_clause else (rule, receipt)),
]
for stage, spans in rows:
    print(stage, ", ".join(spans))
first_gap = "none"
for stage, spans in rows:
    if receipt not in spans:
        first_gap = stage
        break
print("First observed gap:", first_gap)
Expected output
ingestion RF:s01, RF:s02
chunking: complete eligible units RF:s01
retrieval RF:s01
selected context RF:s01
First observed gap: chunking: complete eligible units

Experiment. Set split_clause to False to represent a chunk boundary that keeps both required facts together.

Expected output
ingestion RF:s01, RF:s02
chunking: complete eligible units RF:s01, RF:s02
retrieval RF:s01, RF:s02
selected context RF:s01, RF:s02
First observed gap: none

The source imported successfully before either run. In the baseline the first recorded loss happens while forming eligible chunks. The toy records are linked to the setting. On a real trace inspect the exact outputs of each stage.

Checkpoint. If the whole source was absent at ingestion, would larger chunks help? No. Recover the approved source first.

Step 3 — Separate missing evidence from misusing it

Run a fixed wrong answer through a reviewer’s decision tree. A list stores findings so multiple diagnoses can coexist. append adds one label. elif would choose a single branch. Here the citation test uses its own if so it can flag a separate defect.

Open Python Editor

gold = "RF-v2:c01"
selected = ("DOC-REFUND-OLD",)
wrong_answer = True
citation = "DOC-REFUND-OLD"
findings = []
if gold not in selected:
    findings.append("MISSING EVIDENCE")
if gold in selected and wrong_answer:
    findings.append("GENERATION")
if citation != gold:
    findings.append("CITATION")
for finding in findings:
    print(finding)
Expected output
MISSING EVIDENCE
CITATION

Experiment. Keep the saved answer and citation fixed. Change selected to ("RF-v2:c01",).

Expected output
GENERATION
CITATION

The controlled context swap removes the evidence gap. A wrong answer against sufficient evidence now meets the answer-use finding, and the citation is still wrong. This rule grades a curated trace. It cannot tell how a real generator would respond to the swapped context.

Checkpoint. What stays wrong when the correct evidence arrives? The fixed 90-day claim and its citation still need attention.

Step 4 — Rerank a small lexical search

Award one point per distinct shared term, with an optional extra weight for matching refund. A set intersection & gives the overlap. The sort key (-row[1], row[0]) orders by decreasing score, then ID for ties. The same query and chunk strings are compared in both runs.

Open Python Editor

chunks = {
    "RF": "refund policy requires receipt",
    "SH": "shipping delay 45 days",
}
queries = {
    "Q1": "refund 45 days",
    "Q2": "shipping delay refund",
}
gold = {"Q1": "RF", "Q2": "SH"}
refund_weight = 1
for question, text in queries.items():
    results = []
    for key, passage in chunks.items():
        shared = set(text.split()) & set(passage.split())
        score = sum(refund_weight if word == "refund" else 1 for word in shared)
        results.append((key, score))
    ranked = sorted(results, key=lambda row: (-row[1], row[0]))
    print(question, ranked, "hit" if ranked[0][0] == gold[question] else "miss")
Expected output
Q1 [('SH', 2), ('RF', 1)] miss
Q2 [('SH', 2), ('RF', 1)] hit

Experiment. Set refund_weight to 3. Predict which question starts ranking the wrong first passage.

Expected output
Q1 [('RF', 3), ('SH', 2)] hit
Q2 [('RF', 3), ('SH', 2)] miss

Q1 gains the refund passage, because its single matched word is worth three points. Q2 also matches that word, but needs shipping evidence. Rerun both segments any time you change a ranking weight.

Checkpoint. Why inspect Q2 when the change targets Q1? A global scoring rule also changes other queries with the same term.

Step 5 — Count fixes and regressions on matched IDs

Compare the same three gold judgments. The pass flags represent completed evidence and answer checks. The pairs (False, True) and (True, False) mean a fix and a regression. A list comprehension walks every baseline ID to find its matching candidate result.

Open Python Editor

baseline = {"Q1": False, "Q2": True, "Q3": True}
shipping_regression = False
candidate = {"Q1": True, "Q2": not shipping_regression, "Q3": True}
pairs = [(baseline[key], candidate[key]) for key in baseline]
print("Baseline passes:", sum(baseline.values()))
print("Candidate passes:", sum(candidate.values()))
print("Fixed:", pairs.count((False, True)))
print("Regressions:", pairs.count((True, False)))
Expected output
Baseline passes: 2
Candidate passes: 3
Fixed: 1
Regressions: 0

Experiment. Set shipping_regression to True. Predict which case still improves and what the overall total hides.

Expected output
Baseline passes: 2
Candidate passes: 2
Fixed: 1
Regressions: 1

Read across the two runs by case ID. Q1 goes from fail to pass and Q2 goes from pass to fail. Q3 passes both times. The candidate and baseline each pass two of three, so the aggregate cannot show which customers gained or lost. Record both transitions and investigate Q2 before recommending the change.

Checkpoint. Should unknown replace false in a comparison? No. Keep that case in coverage and leave it outside paired change counts.

Step 6 — Inspect segments and policy gates

Group results by refund or shipping and count passes by segment. A tuple stores both outcomes for one proposed rollout scenario. any is true when at least one critical case fails.

Open Python Editor

scenario = "original"
changes = {
    "original": (True, False),
    "tradeoff": (False, True),
}
refund_ok, shipping_ok = changes[scenario]
rows = [
    ("refund", refund_ok, True),
    ("shipping", shipping_ok, False),
    ("shipping", True, False),
]
for group in ("refund", "shipping"):
    flags = [ok for segment, ok, _ in rows if segment == group]
    print(f"{group}: {sum(flags)}/{len(flags)}")
blocked = any(critical and not ok for _, ok, critical in rows)
print("Critical gate:", "HOLD" if blocked else "clear")
Expected output
refund: 1/1
shipping: 1/2
Critical gate: clear

Experiment. Change scenario to "tradeoff" to activate the second paired fixture.

Expected output
refund: 0/1
shipping: 2/2
Critical gate: HOLD

Shipping improves and refunds worsen. The total pass count stays at two. The refund failure blocks the change even though another segment improved.

Checkpoint. What would a report containing only overall accuracy hide? The critical failure newly introduced in refunds.

Step 7 — Preserve a failed trace while testing a repair

Build a small report that records the different layers. A frozen dataclass is a record whose fields cannot be reassigned. replace returns a new version of a record. Keep the baseline and append a candidate only when the repair is enabled.

Open Python Editor

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Run:
    id: str
    selected: str
    days: int
    citation: str

dataset = "northstar-v1"
case_id = "Q1"
gold = "RF-v2:c01"
ranked = ("DOC-REFUND-OLD", gold)
baseline = Run("baseline", ranked[0], 90, ranked[0])
repair = False
history = (baseline,)
if repair:
    history += (replace(baseline, id="oracle", selected=gold, days=30, citation=gold),)

print(f"NS-mini | {dataset} | {case_id} | pool={ranked}")
for row in history:
    sufficient = row.selected == gold
    correct = row.days == 30
    cited = sufficient and correct and row.citation == gold
    blocked = not correct
    findings = []
    if not sufficient:
        findings.append("CONTEXT_SELECTION")
    if not cited:
        findings.append("CITATION")
    print(f"{row.id}: {row.selected}, {row.days} days, cite={row.citation}")
    print(f"  Hit@2={int(gold in ranked)} context={int(sufficient)} correct={int(correct)} citations={int(cited)}")
    print(f"  stage={','.join(findings) or 'clear'} critical={int(blocked)}",
          "HOLD" if blocked else "REVIEW: diagnostic only")
print("Fixed:", int(len(history) == 2 and history[0].days != 30 and history[-1].days == 30))
print("New regressions:", int(history[0].days == 30 and history[-1].days != 30))
Expected output
NS-mini | northstar-v1 | Q1 | pool=('DOC-REFUND-OLD', 'RF-v2:c01')
baseline: DOC-REFUND-OLD, 90 days, cite=DOC-REFUND-OLD
  Hit@2=1 context=0 correct=0 citations=0
  stage=CONTEXT_SELECTION,CITATION critical=1 HOLD
Fixed: 0
New regressions: 0

Experiment. Set repair to True. This adds a prewritten capture using selected gold context. Predict the unchanged retrieval result and both decisions.

Expected output
NS-mini | northstar-v1 | Q1 | pool=('DOC-REFUND-OLD', 'RF-v2:c01')
baseline: DOC-REFUND-OLD, 90 days, cite=DOC-REFUND-OLD
  Hit@2=1 context=0 correct=0 citations=0
  stage=CONTEXT_SELECTION,CITATION critical=1 HOLD
oracle: RF-v2:c01, 30 days, cite=RF-v2:c01
  Hit@2=1 context=1 correct=1 citations=1
  stage=clear critical=0 REVIEW: diagnostic only
Fixed: 1
New regressions: 0

The context and captured answer now pass the narrow checks. Both audit rows remain intact and Hit@2 stays fixed. An oracle result tests the effect of supplied evidence in this fixture. A complete paired suite is needed for a release decision.

Checkpoint. Can the oracle result certify normal ranking? No. The experiment inserted evidence directly into the writer’s context.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1. Locate the missing evidence

A warranty query expects WA-v2:c01. The approved register names version 2. The import log has no WA row, and the ranked list has only account and shipping. Identify the earliest supported defect, the downstream symptom, and one test that would verify the repair.

Practice 2. Separate context selection from generation

For a refund question, RF-v2:c01 ranked second. In trace A the prompt contains only the first shipping passage. In trace B the prompt contains RF-v2:c01 with both requirements. Both replies say “Refunds are available for 90 days [RF-v2:c01].” Record the supported findings in each and design a context-only comparison.

Practice 3. Count matched outcomes

On Q1–Q5, baseline verdicts are FAIL, FAIL, PASS, PASS, FAIL. Candidate verdicts are PASS, FAIL, FAIL, PASS, UNKNOWN. Calculate matched coverage, fixes, regressions, fix rate, regression rate, and unchanged outcomes. Explain what to do about Q5.

Practice 4. Apply a release gate

A candidate fixes two of eight matched cases and breaks one. Valid citations rise from six of eight to eight of nine. Its worst illustrative latency is 41 ms under a 55 ms limit. The sole regression cites the 2026 shipping rule for a 2025 question. Apply the lab gate and give a targeted next test.

Independent Assignment

Use the complete guided lab program as the standalone answer key. Read Q1–Q8, their expected facts and sources, and the saved public role and effective date. Restore the original code between variants.

  1. Run baseline, freshness, and scoped. Compare the same IDs. For each changed case record the source version, relevant rank, selected ID, expected and observed claims, citations, and decision. Write the first verified defect and one unverified hypothesis separately.
  2. For Variant A set mode = "oracle". Only Q1 receives a direct gold-context override. Predict whether Hit@2 or the overall decision will change.
  3. For Variant B set mode = "budget". This compares the repaired configuration with an otherwise identical selector capped at eight words. Predict which policy drops out. Decide whether a lower latency justifies the result.
  4. Submit a report with explicit denominators, fixed and regressed IDs, critical failures, budget and authorization checks, and a RELEASE, HOLD, or REVIEW recommendation. Write a test that fails at the correct stage, even if a canned reply happens to be right.

Worked Solutions to Practice

Solution 1

The source failed to reach ingestion. Ranking the other passages is downstream of that gap. Compare the complete approved register with the import rows, correct the missing input, and assert that WA v2 is present in the chunk inventory and enters the candidate list for the same query.

Solution 2

A shows a context-selection defect because the correct passage ranked but was omitted. Its citation names a real passage that was absent from the prompt and that would not support 90 days anyway. B shows a generation or rule-use defect given sufficient context, alongside the separate citation support failure. For a real comparison use the same question, model, prompt template, and rubric with one swapped context. Re-run and save both replies. A fixed-answer replay can test the diagnosis without demonstrating how a live model reacts.

Solution 3

Four of five pairs are evaluable. Q1 is fixed, Q3 regresses, Q4 stays passing, and Q2 remains failing. Fix rate is 1/2, from the matched baseline failures Q1 and Q2. Regression rate is 1/2, from baseline passes Q3 and Q4. Q5 stays in planned coverage but is outside both change-rate denominators. Recover its missing assessment before making a release decision.

Solution 4

HOLD. The wrong effective version is a critical source-integrity failure and a new regression. Retain the original Q3 pass. Re-run an candidate that checks effective dates and assert that SH-v1:c01 is first and selected for 2025. Also assert that the archived refund version stays out of the selected context on current questions.

Both refund cases abstain because their first-ranked current policy exceeds eight words. Correctness, context, and passes drop from 8/8 to 6/8. Those cases provide zero links. Citation validity among the six supplied links remains 6/6. The two regressions block release despite lower illustrative latency. Test a larger budget or a compact approved chunk while keeping evidence and permission rules fixed.

Knowledge Check

  1. What can the 90-day reply alone establish, and which record would test whether the writer received the governing rule?
  2. The approved source register lists RF v2, but there is no RF v2 in the complete import log. Why is tuning rank scores a poor first test?
  3. Two neighboring chunks separate an exception from the rule it modifies. What comparisons would show whether overlap fixes the issue?
  4. Hit@2 is one, but the prompt contains only the first result and the gold chunk is second. Where is the observed gap?
  5. The complete current rule is selected and the reply still says 90 days. Which stage would you investigate?
  6. The answer is correct, but its citation opens a real shipping passage. Which metric should change when you repair just that reference?
  7. The pass count is unchanged after a rollout. How could one customer’s experience improve while another’s worsens?
  8. A candidate gets eight correct answers and cites a staff-only source in one public reply. Which decision follows the lab policy?

Knowledge Check Answers

  1. The reply establishes the wrong deadline as the symptom. Inspect the exact selected context and approved policy version to see whether the current rule reached the writer.
  2. The approved source was lost at import. Fix and verify ingestion, then check index and ranking. A score cannot move a missing record.
  3. Hold the query and policy fixed. Inspect the chunk boundaries before and after, then compare whether the rule and exception enter selected context together. Measure repeated text and latency separately.
  4. Required evidence was retrieved and ranked but omitted at context selection. Ranking may contribute if a one-slot selector follows that order.
  5. Inspect generation, especially the interpretation of the deadline, purchase date, and receipt rule. Check citations separately.
  6. Citation validity changes if the new link supports the claim. Answer correctness stays the same on the fixed reply. Citation coverage may also change.
  7. Matched results may include one fix and one regression that cancel in the total. Inspect the transition for each case ID.
  8. HOLD. Unauthorized citation is a blocking failure even when its associated claim happens to be correct.

Guided Engineering Lab

Why Did Our RAG Assistant Fail, and Is the Fix Safe to Release?

Northstar’s latest review found the 90-day error on Q1. The team has eight frozen cases across refund deadline, missing receipt, shipping, warranty, account access, escalation, outdated policy, and restricted information. The records below contain the full source manifest, approval years, whole-span chunks, per-case candidate score pools, caller roles, expected policy facts, and fictional captures with annotated claim–citation links. Each case is from a public request. The protected fixture is placeholder text. The public report can count an excluded candidate without printing its ID, contents, or score.

Work the incident by hand

Locate RF in the manifest and verify that 2026 names version 2. Compare its source row to the intact chunk RF-v2:c01. The fixture records cleaned text and one whole paragraph per chunk. Q1 scores the old chunk 6 and the current chunk 4, both in the recorded candidate pool. A two-point penalty produces a tie at 4, and the saved ID tie rule still puts the archived chunk first. Three points puts the current chunk first. Q3 already loses the historical passage at a penalty of two, so choosing a smaller global penalty cannot satisfy both cases. Taking the first passage delivers the old rule. The old citation resolves but names the wrong revision for this case. The saved 90-day reply contradicts approved policy, so log a critical policy error in addition to the ranking, context, and citation findings.

Before running the freshness change, subtract 3 from Q1’s old score and Q3’s historical score. Predict both rank orders. Then predict what will happen when the penalty is limited to current questions. Keep the question, permissions, corpus, capture lookup, and rubric fixed. The historical scope uses the request’s saved as_of year. It does not use a gold label as a routing input.

Decide the rubric before running

The selector takes the first ranked passage if it fits a 40-word budget. The replay looks up a captured reply by case ID and the first selected passage. Reply text, annotations, and claims are fixed teaching fixtures. The program joins the records and computes metrics. It does not call a model, rebuild a search index, infer entailment, or test actual permissions infrastructure. Read “No” in the current Q1 reply against the question yourself. The automatic checks compare the annotated deadline and receipt facts.

A scorable case passes when every gold span and expected fact is in approved selected context, the captured claims match the expected facts, and each claim’s cited reference resolves to an authorized, approved, selected passage containing the annotated fact. Any known policy contradiction on a critical case, wrong effective version in the selected context, or unauthorized passage in delivered or ranked results or references blocks release. A logged unauthorized candidate filtered before ranking is evidence that the boundary check worked in this fixture. Missing or invalid traces go to REVIEW unless a confirmed gate already blocks them.

For the suite, HOLD wins if any critical case is flagged, a matched regression occurs, or the maximum illustrative cost exceeds 55 ms. REVIEW applies when fewer than eight cases are scorable, any case lacks a matched scorable comparison, a fully passing result or supported citations, or there is no paired fix established by a normal ranking run. RELEASE requires every gate to pass on this fixture set. Case coverage uses all planned cases. Support and citation validity have separate claim and supplied-link denominators. The replay counts distinct failing cases, so two critical flags on Q1 count as one case. The cost formula starts at 20 ms, adds 3 ms per ranked candidate, and adds 1 ms per selected word. For Q3’s baseline result, that is 20 + 2×3 + 8 = 34 ms. These numbers illustrate a guardrail.

Run and inspect the audit

Python @dataclass(frozen=True) creates records whose fields cannot be reassigned. replace creates a new record with the named changes. tuple stores the ordered record history. None stands for a missing value, such as no historical year. sorted orders by negative score first, so high scores come first. dict.fromkeys groups duplicates for the link tally, and empty denominators print N/A. The traces preserve raw selected IDs and captures in memory, while the report prints a public view. Keep an append-only trace store and enforce access outside Python if deploying this pattern.

Select Copy Code, open the editor, paste the full program into an empty panel, and choose Run. The defaults validate the frozen source rows and report the baseline.

Open Python Editor

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

mode = "baseline"  # baseline, freshness, scoped, oracle, or budget
dataset = "northstar-regression-v1"
corpus = "northstar-corpus-v3"
rubric = "stage-rubric-v1"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    source: str
    version: int
    audience: str
    text: str
    facts: tuple

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Reply:
    text: str
    claims: tuple = ()

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Case:
    id: str
    segment: str
    question: str
    audience: str
    as_of: int | None
    gold: tuple
    expected: tuple
    pool: tuple
    critical: bool = False

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    id: str
    penalty: int = 0
    preserve_history: bool = False
    k: int = 2
    words: int = 40
    oracle: str = ""

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Trace:
    ranked: tuple
    selected: tuple
    reply: Reply | None
    latency: int
    blocked: int
    oracle: bool = False

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Result:
    case: Case
    config: Config
    trace: Trace
    hit: bool
    recall: float
    sufficient: bool
    correct: bool | None
    supported: int
    valid_refs: int
    links: int
    stages: tuple
    critical: tuple
    status: str

# The manifest records effective years; the source rows record passage versions and access.
source_rows = (
    ("RF-v2:c01", Chunk("RF", 2, "public",
        "Refund requests require a valid receipt and must be filed within 30 days of purchase.",
        (("refund_days", 30), ("receipt", "required")))),
    ("DOC-REFUND-OLD", Chunk("RF", 1, "public",
        "Requests for refunds may be filed within 90 days of purchase.",
        (("refund_days", 90),))),
    ("MR-v1:c01", Chunk("MR", 1, "public", "Download receipts in Orders.",
        (("receipt_route", "Orders"),))),
    ("SH-v1:c01", Chunk("SH", 1, "public", "For shipping delays contact Support after 45 days.",
        (("shipping_days", 45),))),
    ("SH-v2:c01", Chunk("SH", 2, "public", "For shipping delays contact Support after 60 days.",
        (("shipping_days", 60),))),
    ("WA-v2:c01", Chunk("WA", 2, "public", "Start warranty claims from your order.",
        (("warranty_route", "order"),))),
    ("AC-v1:c01", Chunk("AC", 1, "public", "Reset passwords from the sign-in page.",
        (("reset_route", "sign-in page"),))),
    ("ES-v1:c01", Chunk("ES", 1, "public", "Escalate unresolved cases from the case page.",
        (("escalation_route", "case page"),))),

)

def capture(text, ref, *facts):
    return Reply(text, tuple((key, value, ref) for key, value in facts))

def validate(records, source_rows):
    # Validate the original rows while duplicates are still observable.
    ids = [key for key, _ in source_rows]
    if len(set(ids)) != len(ids) or len({c.id for c in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("Duplicate passage or case ID")
    for key, chunk in source_rows:
        if (not chunk.text or chunk.audience not in {"public", "staff"}
                or chunk.version not in manifest.get(chunk.source, {}).values()):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid ingestion record: {key}")

def authorized(case, key):
    return key in chunks and chunks[key].audience in {"public", case.audience}

def approved(case, key):
    chunk = chunks[key]
    year = case.as_of if case.as_of is not None else 2026
    versions = manifest[chunk.source]
    published = [date for date in versions if date <= year]
    return bool(published) and chunk.version == versions[max(published)]

def replay(case, config):
    eligible = [(key, score) for key, score in case.pool if authorized(case, key)]
    blocked = sum(key in chunks and not authorized(case, key) for key, _ in case.pool)
    scored = []
    for key, score in eligible:
        versions = manifest[chunks[key].source]
        older = chunks[key].version != versions[max(versions)]
        if older and not (config.preserve_history and case.as_of is not None):
            score -= config.penalty
        scored.append((key, score))
    ranked = tuple(sorted(scored, key=lambda row: (-row[1], row[0]))[:config.k])
    oracle = config.oracle == case.id
    if oracle:
        selected = tuple(key for key in case.gold if authorized(case, key) and approved(case, key))
    else:
        # The fictional selector has one passage slot and a word budget.
        selected = tuple(key for key, _ in ranked[:1] if len(chunks[key].text.split()) <= config.words)
    reply = captures.get((case.id, selected[0])) if selected else abstention
    # Fixture cost in milliseconds, not a benchmark.
    latency = 20 + 3 * len(ranked) + sum(len(chunks[key].text.split()) for key in selected)
    return Trace(ranked, selected, reply, latency, blocked, oracle)

def assess(case, config, trace):
    findings = set()
    critical = set()
    ranked = {key for key, _ in trace.ranked if authorized(case, key)}
    visible = {key for key in trace.selected if authorized(case, key)}
    gold = set(case.gold)
    if any(key not in chunks for key in gold):
        findings.add("INGESTION")
    invalid_trace = (any(key not in chunks for key, _ in case.pool)
                     or any(key not in chunks for key, _ in trace.ranked)
                     or any(key not in chunks for key in trace.selected)
                     or (not trace.oracle and not visible <= ranked))
    if invalid_trace:
        findings.add("EVALUATION_DATA")
    if any(key in chunks and not authorized(case, key)
           for key in trace.selected + tuple(key for key, _ in trace.ranked)):
        findings.add("AUTHORIZATION")
        critical.add("authorization")
    if gold <= chunks.keys():
        if not gold <= ranked and not trace.oracle:
            findings.add("RETRIEVAL")
        elif not gold <= visible and not trace.oracle:
            findings.add("CONTEXT_SELECTION")
    stale = any(not approved(case, key) for key in visible)
    if stale:
        critical.add("source version")
        if not trace.oracle and not gold.intersection(key for key, _ in trace.ranked[:1]):
            findings.add("RETRIEVAL")
    available = {fact for key in visible if approved(case, key) for fact in chunks[key].facts}
    expected = set(case.expected)
    sufficient = gold <= visible and expected <= available
    if not gold or not expected:
        findings.add("EVALUATION_DATA")
    if trace.reply is None or not trace.reply.text.strip():
        findings.add("EVALUATION_DATA")
        return Result(case, config, trace, bool(gold & ranked),
                      len(gold & ranked) / len(gold) if gold else 0,
                      sufficient, None, 0, 0, 0, tuple(sorted(findings)),
                      tuple(sorted(critical)), "FAIL" if critical else "UNKNOWN")

    claims = {(key, value) for key, value, _ in trace.reply.claims}
    correct = claims == expected
    if sufficient and not correct:
        findings.add("GENERATION")
    if case.critical and any(
        key in dict(expected) and dict(expected)[key] != value for key, value in claims
    ):
        critical.add("critical policy")
    supported = sum(fact in available for fact in claims)
    valid = links = 0
    citation_failure = False
    for key, value, ref in dict.fromkeys(trace.reply.claims):
        links += bool(ref)
        if ref in chunks and not authorized(case, ref):
            findings.add("AUTHORIZATION")
            critical.add("authorization")
        passes = ref in visible and approved(case, ref) and (key, value) in chunks[ref].facts
        valid += passes
        citation_failure |= not passes
    if citation_failure:
        findings.add("CITATION")
    status = ("FAIL" if critical else "UNKNOWN" if "EVALUATION_DATA" in findings else
              "PASS" if sufficient and correct and not citation_failure else "FAIL")
    return Result(case, config, trace, bool(gold & ranked),
                  len(gold & ranked) / len(gold) if gold else 0,
                  sufficient, correct, supported, valid, links, tuple(sorted(findings)),
                  tuple(sorted(critical)), status)

def ratio(numerator, denominator):
    return f"{numerator}/{denominator}" if denominator else "N/A"

def summarize(rows, previous):
    a = {row.case.id: row for row in previous if row.status != "UNKNOWN" and row.correct is not None}
    scored = [row for row in rows if row.status != "UNKNOWN" and row.correct is not None]
    pairs = [(a[row.case.id].status, row.status) for row in scored if row.case.id in a]
    fixed = pairs.count(("FAIL", "PASS"))
    regressions = pairs.count(("PASS", "FAIL"))
    failures = sum(bool(row.critical) for row in rows)
    passes = sum(row.status == "PASS" for row in scored)
    guardrail = max((row.trace.latency for row in rows), default=None)
    valid = sum(row.valid_refs for row in scored)
    links = sum(row.links for row in scored)
    support = sum(row.supported for row in scored)
    claims = sum(len({(key, value) for key, value, _ in row.trace.reply.claims})
                 for row in scored if row.trace.reply)
    count = len(scored)
    mean_recall = (f"{sum(row.recall for row in scored) / count:.3f}" if count else "N/A")
    print(f"  Hit@2={ratio(sum(row.hit for row in scored), count)} Recall@2={mean_recall}"
          f" Context={ratio(sum(row.sufficient for row in scored), count)}"
          f" Correct={ratio(sum(row.correct is True for row in scored), count)}"
          f" Support={ratio(support, claims)} Citations={ratio(valid, links)}")
    print(f"  Pass={ratio(passes, count)} Coverage={ratio(count, len(rows))}"
          f" Fixed={ratio(fixed, sum(old == 'FAIL' for old, _ in pairs))}"
          f" Regressions={ratio(regressions, sum(old == 'PASS' for old, _ in pairs))}"
          f" Critical={failures} Max-ms={guardrail if guardrail is not None else 'N/A'}")
    if failures or regressions or (guardrail is not None and guardrail > 55):
        return "HOLD"
    if count < 8 or count != len(rows) or not links or valid != links or passes != count:
        return "REVIEW"
    if len(pairs) != len(rows) or not fixed or any(row.trace.oracle for row in rows):
        return "REVIEW"
    return "RELEASE"

def show(config, rows, previous):
    print(f"{config.id} | penalty={config.penalty} historical scope={config.preserve_history}"
          f" | k={config.k} words={config.words} oracle={config.oracle or 'none'}")
    prior = {row.case.id: row.status for row in previous}
    print("Case | Ranked candidates(scores) | Selected | Previous -> result | Findings | Critical")
    for row in rows:
        case, trace = row.case, row.trace
        ranked = ", ".join(f"{ref}({score})" for ref, score in trace.ranked if authorized(case, ref))
        chosen = ", ".join(ref for ref in trace.selected if authorized(case, ref))
        print(f"{case.id} | {ranked or '-'} | {chosen or '-'} | {prior.get(case.id, '-')} -> {row.status}"
              f" | {','.join(row.stages) or '-'} | {','.join(row.critical) or '-'}")
        if case.id in {"Q1", "Q3", "Q7"} and "authorization" not in row.critical:
            print(f"  reply: {trace.reply.text if trace.reply else '(missing)'}")
        if trace.blocked:
            print(f"  excluded before ranking: {trace.blocked} unauthorized candidate")
    decision = summarize(rows, previous)
    print("  Decision:", decision)

def run(choice):
    validate(cases, source_rows)
    plans = {
        "baseline": ("baseline",),
        "freshness": ("baseline", "freshness"),
        "scoped": ("baseline", "freshness", "scoped"),
        "oracle": ("baseline", "oracle"),
        "budget": ("baseline", "freshness", "scoped", "budget"),
    }
    history = ()
    print(f"NS-08-03 | {dataset} | {corpus} | whole-span-v1 | capture-v1 | prompt-v2 | {rubric}")
    for name in plans[choice]:
        config = configs[name]
        rows = tuple(assess(case, config, replay(case, config)) for case in cases)
        previous = history[-1][1] if history else ()
        show(config, rows, previous)
        history += ((config, rows),)
    print("Audit history:", " -> ".join(config.id for config, _ in history))
    return history

Audit history: baseline -> freshness

Now set mode = "scoped". This run preserves both earlier reports and adds a second repair that exempts explicitly historical requests from the freshness penalty. Restore the default context budget. Compare every output line with “Second repair” in the answer key. Check the three manifests in order. The paired fixes and regressions are measured against the preceding run each time. To compare the final configuration directly with the original, match the original and final rows by case ID.

Troubleshoot and hand off the decision

If Q3 still fails after the second repair, inspect its saved year and the printed historical scope. If Q1 fails, verify the approved RF row and selected context, then inspect the captured claim. If the oracle changes the candidate ranks, restore the original experiment. Check the access filter before troubleshooting scores if any restricted passage reaches the public ranked list or selected context. If coverage unexpectedly drops, inspect unknown IDs and missing captures before summarizing.

A sample report reads, “Hold the global penalty. Q1 and Q7 now receive RF version 2, but Q3 asks about 2025 and now receives SH version 2, which took effect in 2026. The gain from six to seven passes hides that regression. The second repair leaves explicit historical requests unpenalized and restores SH version 1 on Q3. The final run passes eight of eight with zero regressions against the preceding run, zero critical failures, and a maximum illustrative cost of 41 ms against a 55 ms limit. That earns RELEASE under the fixture policy. Keep the failed rows and repeat the comparison on unseen dated queries before making a production claim.”

Completion means you can reproduce all three lab reports, hand-score Q1 and Q3, explain why the oracle comparison leaves retrieval metrics untouched, and point to the original and intermediate failures in the final audit. Record a stage-specific test such as “for the 2025 shipping query, the selected passage must be SH-v1:c01.” Test both assignment variants and explain why the result applies to these fixtures. Fresh held-out cases and live evidence are needed for an operational release.

An optional live extension can capture query ID, corpus version, source and chunk versions, chunking configuration, retriever version and ranked candidates, exact selected context, caller authorization, prompt version, model version, captured reply and citations, evaluation labels, and timestamp. Preserve prompts and evidence across controlled comparisons, verify annotations with reviewers, and keep raw protected traces in an access-controlled store.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a correct search result as proof it reached the writer.
  • Changing scoring, chunking, and prompt instructions in the same experiment and attributing the outcome to one component.
  • Calling a historical source stale without checking which date the user asked about.
  • Counting missing traces as passes or discarding them from planned coverage.
  • Counting a repaired case while ignoring a regression or critical authorization gate.

What was tested
Evaluate retrieval, answer faithfulness, and keyword relevance on a document-backed banking assistant.
How it was tested
